options.rationale: MRI brain alone misses occult fractures; skeletal survey is mandatory even without external fracture evidence because clinically silent fractures are common. Would never alone be sufficient (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RANZCR Skeletal Survey for Suspected Non-Accidental Injury

options.text: Bedside eye examination by the paediatric registrar without pupil dilation today, with no skeletal imaging and no brain imaging arranged
options.rationale: Retinal haemorrhage detection requires dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy by an ophthalmologist; bedside undilated fundoscopy misses retinal haemorrhages. Would never be sufficient (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Coagulation screen alone and a routine outpatient paediatric follow-up arranged because the injury appears small and isolated today
options.rationale: Sentinel injuries in non-mobile infants predict escalating abuse; outpatient follow-up alone is unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

explanation.summary: Sentinel injuries (torn frenulum, bruise in non-mobile infant, intra-oral injury) trigger formal NAI workup: skeletal survey now and at 11-14 days, neuroimaging (CT or MRI), dilated indirect retinal exam by ophthalmology, coagulation and bone studies, plus parallel Child Protection and forensic paediatric service involvement.
key_points: Sentinel injuries precede serious abuse in 25-30% of fatal cases
Two skeletal surveys (now and 11-14 days) increases yield
Retinal exam requires dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy by ophthalmologist
Coagulation and bone screen rules out mimics, does not replace workup
Forensic paediatric service (VFPMS in Vic, NSW CASS equivalents) involved early
explanation.pearls: A torn frenulum in a non-mobile infant is the sentinel injury most commonly missed in primary care.

sources.label: RANZCR Skeletal Survey for Suspected Non-Accidental Injury

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is referred to a paediatric developmental clinic for behavioural and learning difficulties. He was placed in long-term foster care at 3 months. His birth mother is documented to have consumed alcohol at hazardous levels throughout pregnancy. School reports document impulsivity, poor adaptive functioning, and specific maths and language deficits despite intensive support. Cognitive testing (educational psychologist) shows FSIQ 78 with significant scatter and severe impairment in three neurodevelopmental domains (executive function, adaptive behaviour, language).

Physical growth tracks the 25th centile. On focused facial examination: smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion border, and short palpebral fissures (below 3rd centile for age) - all three sentinel features present. There is no head injury, no seizure disorder and no other syndromic features. The foster carer is engaged with an Aboriginal community-controlled health service.

data_table.Growth: Height and weight 25th centile, OFC 25th centile
data_table.Facial features: Smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion border, short palpebral fissures (<3rd centile)
data_table.Cognitive: FSIQ 78, severe impairment in executive function, adaptive behaviour, and language domains
data_table.Prenatal: Confirmed hazardous prenatal alcohol exposure throughout pregnancy
data_table.History: Foster care from 3 months, fully immunised, no other syndromic features

lead_in: Which Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD category best applies?

options.text: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder without confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure, attributing facial features and impairment to teratogenic effect
options.rationale: Exposure is confirmed; this category does not apply. Would be correct only when prenatal exposure history cannot be confirmed but features are otherwise consistent (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD).
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.text: ADHD combined presentation alone; the sentinel facial features are attributed to familial resemblance rather than prenatal alcohol teratogenicity
options.rationale: ADHD may coexist but does not capture facial dysmorphology or the breadth of FASD-specific neurodevelopmental impairment. Would be correct as a stand-alone diagnosis only without FASD features (Source: DSM-5; Australian Guide to FASD).
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.text: FASD with less than three sentinel facial features but with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure
options.rationale: He has all three sentinel features (smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion, short palpebral fissures), so the less-than-three category does not apply (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD).
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.text: Static encephalopathy of unknown cause because the measured IQ is above 70, with neurology follow-up for symptomatic management
options.rationale: FSIQ over 70 does not exclude FASD; diagnosis is made on neurodevelopmental domain impairment, not global IQ. Would be correct only for a non-FASD aetiology (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD).
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.text: FASD with three sentinel facial features (smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion, short palpebral fissures), severe impairment in at least three domains, plus confirmed exposure
options.rationale: The Australian Guide diagnoses FASD with three sentinel facial features when all three are present together with severe impairment in three or more of ten neurodevelopmental domains and confirmed or assumed prenatal alcohol exposure - the specific AU diagnostic threshold tested here.
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

explanation.summary: The Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD recognises two diagnostic categories: FASD with 3 sentinel facial features (smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion border, short palpebral fissures), and FASD with less than 3. Both require severe impairment in at least 3 of 10 neurodevelopmental domains and confirmed (or assumed) prenatal alcohol exposure.
key_points: Three sentinel facial features: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures
Severe impairment in >=3 of 10 neurodevelopmental domains required
Prenatal alcohol exposure confirmed OR assumed
IQ alone does not make or exclude the diagnosis
Domains include cognition, executive function, language, adaptive, motor, memory, attention, affect, social, sensory
explanation.pearls: Sentinel facial features only develop with first trimester exposure during a narrow window; their absence does not exclude FASD.

sources.label: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to a tertiary ED by her mother for review after losing 12 kg over five months. She has been progressively restricting her intake, exercising compulsively, and has missed three menstrual periods. She is medically naive and on no medications. On arrival she is alert and oriented, denies suicidal ideation, but is cold to touch and describes near-syncope on standing this morning.

Her current weight is 38 kg and her premorbid weight was 50 kg. Body mass index is 14.8 kg/m2 (well below the 3rd centile for age). Her supine heart rate is 38 beats per minute with a postural drop to systolic blood pressure of 78 mmHg standing. Core temperature is 35.4 deg C. Bedside ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 470 ms. Bloods reveal potassium 3.0 mmol/L, phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, magnesium 0.65 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, and liver enzymes mildly raised with ALT 78 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 bpm supine, BP 96/60 supine to 78/52 standing, T 35.4 deg C, RR 14 /min
data_table.Anthropometrics: Weight 38 kg, BMI 14.8 kg/m2 (<3rd centile), 24% weight loss over 5 months
data_table.ECG: Sinus bradycardia, QTc 470 ms, no arrhythmia
data_table.Investigations: K 3.0 mmol/L, PO4 0.7 mmol/L, Mg 0.65 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, ALT 78 U/L
data_table.Mental state: Cognitively intact, no SI, mildly depressed mood, motivated to recover

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home today with twice-weekly community eating disorder team review and oral potassium and phosphate replacement at home
options.rationale: Multiple MARSIPAN-AU high-risk criteria (HR under 40, postural BP drop, hypothermia, hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, QTc over 450 ms) mandate inpatient medical admission; outpatient is the under-triage anti-pattern. Would be appropriate only with low-risk physical parameters (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU Guide).

options.text: Admit to the paediatric ward under medical care with cardiac monitoring, cautious refeeding starting at 20 kcal/kg/day, electrolyte replacement, and ED team involvement
options.rationale: MARSIPAN-AU high risk criteria mandate medical admission with cardiac monitoring, cautious refeeding to prevent refeeding syndrome, electrolyte and glucose management, and dual physical and eating disorder team care, as per ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU.

options.text: Admit directly to a child and adolescent mental health inpatient unit today with full caloric refeeding at 50 kcal/kg/day starting from day one
options.rationale: Medical stabilisation precedes mental health admission in MARSIPAN-AU high-risk; aggressive 50 kcal/kg/day refeeding precipitates refeeding syndrome. Would be correct only after medical stabilisation and on a graded refeeding plan (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).

options.text: Transfer her today to a peripheral hospital for rapid IV crystalloid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg boluses and overnight monitoring
options.rationale: Aggressive crystalloid bolus risks cardiac failure in the malnourished heart; cautious volume correction with electrolyte replacement is needed, not resuscitation-style fluids. Would be correct only in haemorrhagic or septic shock unrelated to malnutrition (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).

options.text: Refer her today for outpatient review in an eating disorder day program with weekly bloods, ECG monitoring and a six week follow up plan
options.rationale: Day program does not address immediate medical risk; high-risk physical criteria mandate inpatient admission. Would be correct only for medically stable patients with adequate community supports (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).

explanation.summary: MARSIPAN-AU defines medical admission criteria for severe restrictive eating disorders. High risk features (bradycardia <40, postural BP drop >20 mmHg systolic, hypothermia <35.5, K <3.0, PO4 <0.5, glucose <3.0, QTc >450 ms, rapid weight loss >1 kg/week, BMI <14 in adolescents) mandate inpatient care with cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding.
key_points: Bradycardia <40 bpm = high risk
Postural drop >20 mmHg systolic = high risk
Hypothermia <35.5 deg C = high risk
Refeeding starts low (20 kcal/kg/day) and titrates
Dual medical + eating disorder team is the standard
explanation.pearls: The malnourished heart can fail on aggressive crystalloid bolus; treat the metabolic risk first.

stem:
A 17-year-old girl presents to her general practitioner for dental review following her dentist's discovery of bilateral enamel erosion on the lingual surfaces of her upper incisors. On gentle questioning she discloses six months of binge eating once or twice weekly followed by self-induced vomiting, with intermittent use of laxatives. She maintains a body mass index of 22 kg/m2 with stable weight.

She describes a marked sense of loss of control during binges, intense subsequent shame, and persistent overvaluation of body shape and weight. Her menstrual cycle remains regular and she is not currently using any contraception. She denies suicidal ideation but has felt low in mood and isolated from friends. Examination is unremarkable apart from mild parotid swelling and Russell's sign on the dorsum of one hand.

Bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc of 410 ms. Bloods show potassium 3.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, with normal phosphate, magnesium, and glucose. She lives at home with both parents and is in Year 12 studying for the HSC. She has not previously sought help.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, BMI 22 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Bilateral parotid swelling, Russell's sign, dental erosion, no postural hypotension
data_table.Investigations: K 3.4 mmol/L, HCO3 30 mmol/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, ECG QTc 410 ms
data_table.Mental state: Low mood, shame, no suicidal ideation, body image overvaluation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer her today for inpatient medical admission to a paediatric ward for refeeding under the MARSIPAN-AU protocol
options.rationale: MARSIPAN-AU medical admission criteria are not met (BMI normal, electrolytes near range, no bradycardia, normal QTc); inpatient admission is reserved for high physical risk. Would be correct only with high-risk vitals or electrolytes (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards Eating Disorders

options.text: Reassure her today and advise dietary balance with no specialist referral because weight is normal and physical risk is low
options.rationale: Bulimia carries significant medical and psychological morbidity even at normal weight; reassurance-only misses the disorder. Would be correct only in occasional subthreshold disordered eating without functional impairment (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards).
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards Eating Disorders

options.text: Prescribe high dose fluoxetine 60 mg daily today as first line monotherapy without any structured psychological therapy
options.rationale: Fluoxetine 60 mg may add benefit for bulimia in adults but CBT-ED is first-line; pharmacotherapy alone is not standard. Would be appropriate after CBT-ED failure or as add-on (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorder Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Commence outpatient enhanced cognitive behaviour therapy for eating disorders with GP medical monitoring and dental follow up
options.rationale: First line treatment for bulimia nervosa in adolescents is enhanced CBT-ED in the outpatient setting with regular medical monitoring of electrolytes, weight, and ECG, as per ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards and RANZCP Eating Disorder Guidelines.
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards Eating Disorders
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Prescribe oral potassium chloride supplementation today and review her in three months with no psychological intervention
options.rationale: Electrolyte replacement is supportive but does not treat the disorder; CBT-ED is the definitive first-line. Would be appropriate as a supportive adjunct alongside CBT-ED, not in isolation (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards).
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards Eating Disorders

explanation.summary: Bulimia nervosa in adolescents is treated first line with enhanced cognitive behaviour therapy for eating disorders (CBT-ED) on an outpatient basis, supported by general practitioner medical monitoring and dental care. Fluoxetine 60 mg may be added but is not first line monotherapy.
key_points: Russell's sign, parotid swelling, dental erosion: classic exam signs
Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting
First line: enhanced CBT-ED outpatient
Fluoxetine 60 mg is the SSRI of choice if pharmacotherapy added
Inpatient admission only if MARSIPAN-AU physical risk criteria met
explanation.pearls: Bulimic patients often present at normal weight; do not let normal BMI delay specialist referral.

sources.label: ANZAED Clinical Practice Standards Eating Disorders
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

stem:
A 16-year-old boy is seen in general practice with a 6-month history of being unable to fall asleep until 0200 to 0300 despite being in bed from 2200, severely impaired wake on school mornings at 0630, and missing first period most days. On weekends and during recent school holidays he sleeps from approximately 0300 to 1200 and wakes refreshed and functioning well.

He uses his phone in bed, denies caffeine after midday, denies illicit substance use, denies snoring or witnessed apnoeas, and a HEEADSSS screen is otherwise reassuring with no self-harm or pervasive low mood. His mother brought him today after two unsuccessful attempts at simply enforcing an earlier bedtime over the past month. He is otherwise well, on no medications, and his examination is unremarkable.

A sleep diary over the past 14 days confirms a stable late sleep onset with normal total sleep duration when free running. You diagnose delayed sleep-wake phase disorder and discuss management with him and his mother.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, BMI 22 kg/m2
data_table.Sleep diary: School nights: sleep onset 0200-0300, wake 0630; weekends: sleep onset 0300, wake 1200
data_table.Examination: Mallampati 1, no tonsillar hypertrophy, no obesity, alert in clinic
data_table.History: No medications, no substance use, occasional phone use in bed, no snoring

lead_in: Which initial management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Sleep hygiene counselling alone, with planned review in 6 weeks before considering any pharmacological or light-based measure
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene alone is insufficient once delayed sleep-wake phase disorder is established with impaired daytime function; behavioural plus chronotherapeutic measures are required from the outset, per Sleep Health Foundation Australia and RCH CPG: Sleep problems.

options.text: Low-dose melatonin 0.5 mg taken 5 to 7 hours before current sleep onset, with morning bright light and gradual schedule advance
options.rationale: Phase-advancing low-dose melatonin (0.3 to 0.5 mg) taken several hours before current sleep onset, combined with morning bright light and gradual schedule advance, is the evidence-based first-line regimen in Australian adolescent practice. The timing (well before bedtime, not at bedtime) and low dose are the levers that distinguish this from sleep-onset insomnia treatment, per Sleep Health Foundation Australia and RCH CPG: Sleep problems.

options.text: Melatonin 3 mg at the desired bedtime of 2200 with screen reduction advice and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Higher-dose melatonin at desired bedtime acts as a hypnotic rather than a phase-shifter; the chronobiotic effect requires a low dose taken hours before current sleep onset, per Sleep Health Foundation Australia.

options.text: Trial of temazepam at 2200 for 2 weeks to entrain an earlier sleep onset, then taper while consolidating sleep hygiene
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not indicated for circadian phase disorders in adolescents and risk dependence and rebound; they do not shift the circadian phase, per Sleep Health Foundation Australia.

options.text: Referral for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the sole initial intervention before any light or melatonin trial
options.rationale: CBT-I targets sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia, not a phase-delayed circadian rhythm; the primary lever is phase shifting (bright light AM, low-dose melatonin PM) with behavioural support, per Sleep Health Foundation Australia.

explanation.summary: Delayed sleep phase syndrome (DSPS) is the most common circadian rhythm disorder in adolescents. Sleep onset is consistently delayed; total sleep duration is normal when allowed to free run. Management combines sleep hygiene, scheduled morning bright light, evening blue light avoidance, and timed low dose melatonin.
key_points: Prevalence peaks at 7-16% in adolescents
Phase delay, not insomnia
Free-running weekend pattern is the diagnostic clue
Treatment: bright light AM, melatonin PM, screen reduction
Polysomnography normal architecture
explanation.pearls: If they sleep well from 3 am to midday on weekends, it is a clock problem, not an insomnia problem.

sources.label: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines

stem:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to a general practice by his parents with a six month history of nightly loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing followed by gasping arousals. He sleeps in unusual positions with neck extended and his parents describe loud restless sleep, occasional bed wetting, and morning headaches. His behaviour at preschool has changed with increased hyperactivity, poor concentration, and emerging difficulty with letter recognition.

He is not overweight, with growth tracking the 50th centile, and is fully immunised. He has had three episodes of acute otitis media in the past year and a current persistent mouth breathing pattern. On examination he has Brodsky grade 3 tonsillar hypertrophy that meets in the midline, an enlarged adenoid pad inferred from chronic mouth breathing, no Mallampati view assessable due to tonsillar size, and an otherwise normal cardiovascular examination with no parasternal heave.

There is no craniofacial syndrome, no neuromuscular disorder, and no family history of sudden cardiac death. He has no Indigenous status documented and lives in metropolitan Sydney with both parents and a younger sister.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 22 /min, BMI 16.0 kg/m2 (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Brodsky grade 3 tonsils, chronic mouth breathing, no parasternal heave, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Behaviour: Hyperactivity, poor concentration, declining letter recognition
data_table.History: Witnessed apnoeas, gasping arousals, morning headaches, secondary enuresis

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of intranasal corticosteroid spray for 12 weeks with a parental sleep diary and clinical review at end of trial
options.rationale: Intranasal steroids help mild OSA with adenoidal hypertrophy, but witnessed apnoeas, hyperactivity and tonsillar hypertrophy require ENT and sleep referral first. Would be correct in mild snoring without apnoea or daytime impairment (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

options.text: Commence stimulant methylphenidate based on the school report of hyperactivity and inattention noted in class
options.rationale: Untreated OSA fully mimics ADHD; starting stimulants before addressing sleep is the classic misdiagnosis anti-pattern. Would be correct only after OSA is treated and ADHD persists (Source: RACP Australian Guideline on ADHD).

options.text: Trial of CPAP at home overnight pending review without prior ENT review or sleep service involvement arranged
options.rationale: CPAP is reserved for residual OSA after adenotonsillectomy or where surgery is contraindicated; not first-line in a previously untreated child with surgical anatomy. Would be correct as second-line after failed surgery (Source: RCH CPG: OSA).

options.text: Reassure the family that loud snoring is developmentally normal in a 5-year-old and arrange routine review in 12 months
options.rationale: Snoring with witnessed apnoeas, behavioural change and morning headaches is clinical OSA, not a normal variant. Would never be correct in this presentation (Source: RCH CPG: OSA).

options.text: Refer to ENT for adenotonsillectomy assessment with paediatric sleep service involvement and consideration of polysomnography
options.rationale: Adenotonsillectomy is the first line treatment for paediatric OSA with adenotonsillar hypertrophy; ENT referral with sleep service involvement and PSG if available is the recommended pathway, as per RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea and ATS Statement on Paediatric OSA.
source_refs: ATS Clinical Practice Guideline Paediatric OSA

explanation.summary: Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea affects 1-4% of Australian children, peaks at 2-8 years (when tonsils are largest relative to the airway), and presents with witnessed apnoeas, gasping arousals, restless sleep with neck extension, mouth breathing, secondary enuresis, morning headaches and daytime behavioural changes - often mistaken for ADHD. Examination focuses on tonsil size (Brodsky grade), Mallampati score, mouth breathing, mid-face hypoplasia, growth failure or obesity. Polysomnography is the gold standard but not always required before referral. First-line therapy in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy is adenotonsillectomy via ENT, ideally with a paediatric sleep service involved for high-risk groups (under 3 years, severe OSA, obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial syndromes, neuromuscular disease). Intranasal corticosteroid plus oral montelukast is a reasonable medical option for mild OSA or while awaiting surgery.
key_points: Witnessed apnoeas + tonsillar hypertrophy = surgical pathway
OSA mimics ADHD; treat sleep before stimulants
Polysomnography is gold standard but ENT referral is not delayed waiting
CPAP reserved for residual OSA after surgery
Untreated OSA risks cor pulmonale and growth failure
explanation.pearls: Paediatric OSA from adenotonsillar hypertrophy can mimic ADHD because chronic sleep fragmentation produces inattention, irritability and hyperactivity; adenotonsillectomy resolves both sleep symptoms and behaviour in around 70% within 6 months (RCH CPG OSA).

sources.label: ATS Clinical Practice Guideline Paediatric OSA

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is referred by her general practitioner to a community paediatric service for assessment of probable attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. School and parent Conners 3 rating scales show clinically elevated inattention and hyperactive impulsive symptoms present since early primary school across home and school. Her mother reports persistent difficulty falling asleep, low mood since the start of the year with tearfulness on most school days, episodes of refusing to attend school, and a recent disclosure of being bullied for two years.

She avoids social activities, has lost two close friendships, and her academic performance has dropped sharply this year. She is otherwise well, growing along the 50th centile, takes no regular medications and has no medical comorbidity. Her hearing and vision screens at school have been normal in the past 12 months. There is no history of trauma, no head injury, and no Child Protection involvement.

The paediatrician is preparing to confirm a diagnosis using DSM-5 criteria and is considering whether and how to assess for comorbid conditions before any pharmacological treatment is considered.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 108/64 mmHg, growth 50th centile
data_table.Rating scales: Conners 3 inattention T-score 78, hyperactive-impulsive T-score 72 (both parent and teacher)
data_table.Social context: Two year bullying history, two friendship losses, school refusal episodes
data_table.Mental state: Tearful, low mood, sleep onset difficulty, no SI elicited but not formally screened

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step before starting medication?

options.text: Start immediate release methylphenidate today at low dose and titrate the dose while planning ongoing structured review
options.rationale: AADPA guidance requires systematic comorbidity assessment (anxiety, depression, learning disorder, sleep, substance use, trauma) before pharmacotherapy because comorbidities alter the plan. Would be appropriate after structured screen confirms uncomplicated ADHD (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Refer her today for full neuropsychological testing battery before any other clinical intervention or medication is considered
options.rationale: Routine neuropsychological battery is not required to confirm ADHD or guide pharmacotherapy. Would be appropriate only for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected specific learning disorder (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Perform structured assessment for common ADHD comorbidities with validated screens and address them in parallel with the ADHD treatment plan
options.rationale: The Australian guideline mandates structured assessment for common comorbidities at diagnosis because comorbidity rates exceed 60% and shape both the order and choice of intervention, as per the AADPA ADHD Guideline.

options.text: Refer her back to the school to manage bullying alone and review again in 6 months before any further clinical intervention
options.rationale: School bullying management is part of the plan but does not justify deferring diagnostic completion. Would never be correct as the sole next step (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Prescribe melatonin alone tonight for sleep without further ADHD-specific intervention or any structured comorbidity assessment
options.rationale: Sleep is one of multiple domains; isolated melatonin without comprehensive comorbidity assessment misses the broader picture. Would be correct only as adjunct after full screen (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).

explanation.summary: The Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD requires structured assessment for common comorbidities (anxiety, depression, learning disorder, ASD, sleep, tic, substance use, trauma) at diagnosis. Comorbidities are present in 60% or more and shape the order and choice of treatment.
key_points: Comorbidity rate >60% in paediatric ADHD
Screen at diagnosis, not after starting stimulants
Sleep disorders may mimic or worsen ADHD
Depression / anxiety often need treatment first
Bullying and trauma history are essential history elements
explanation.pearls: Untreated comorbid depression often blunts apparent stimulant response.

stem:
A 13-year-old girl in Year 7 has missed 18 of the last 30 school days. She presents on school mornings with abdominal pain, nausea, and tearfulness and is unable to leave the house once school is mentioned. She reports being terrified of going to school but cannot name a specific bully, teacher, or academic concern. She is happy to spend time with friends on weekends, attends netball training without difficulty, and goes to her grandmother's house overnight without distress.

She sleeps in her own room without separation distress. At a recent paediatric review the school counsellor noted that her academic performance was previously above average and a transition from primary to secondary school in February has been associated with the new symptoms. There is no history of trauma, no bullying disclosed. She is fully immunised, growing along the 50th centile, takes no medications, and has no medical disorder identified. On HEEADSSS the only significant finding is the school distress. Her parents are supportive and engaged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, BMI 21 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no peritonism, well outside school context
data_table.Mental state: Anxious on school mornings, euthymic at weekends, no SI, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.History: Year 7 transition February, no bullying disclosed, peer relationships intact

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Separation anxiety disorder with persistent excessive distress on separation from her primary attachment figures during the day
options.rationale: She separates without distress at netball, weekends and overnight at grandmother's; distress is school-specific not separation-driven. Would be correct only with distress on all separations from primary attachment figures (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: Conduct disorder with truancy and aggressive antisocial behaviour directed toward both peers and classroom teachers across multiple settings and contexts
options.rationale: She is distressed about not attending and not engaging in delinquent behaviour; this is the opposite of conduct disorder truancy. Would be correct only with rule violation and aggression (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: School refusal driven by anxiety in the context of a recent school transition with no co-occurring conduct disorder features
options.rationale: School refusal is the picture - clinically anxious, somatic on school mornings, intact functioning outside school, transition trigger - and is the recommended formulation for anxiety driven school avoidance without truancy or conduct features, as per Raising Children Network and RANZCP.

options.text: Functional abdominal pain alone with no underlying comorbid mental health driver and full resolution outside the school environment
options.rationale: Pain occurs only on school mornings, with anticipatory distress and avoidance, and resolves at weekends; somatic symptoms are part of the anxiety pattern, not isolated functional pain. Would be correct only if pain were context-independent (Source: Raising Children Network School Refusal).

options.text: Major depressive disorder with pervasive social withdrawal and anhedonia present across both school and non-school contexts
options.rationale: She engages happily on weekends and shows no anhedonia outside school; not depressive. Would be correct only with pervasive low mood and anhedonia across contexts (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: School refusal is anxiety driven school avoidance distinct from truancy: the child wants to be at school but is too distressed to attend. Treatment is a graded return to school with cognitive behaviour therapy, family support, and school engagement.
key_points: School-specific distress, NOT generalised separation difficulty
Distinguish from truancy (no academic concern, family knows)
Somatic symptoms (gut, headache) on school mornings only
Treatment: graded return + CBT + school collaboration
Transition periods (Year 7, after holidays) are common triggers
explanation.pearls: Watch for the weekend-functioning pattern; it is diagnostic for school refusal over separation anxiety.

sources.label: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines

stem:
A 13-year-old boy is seen at a community child and adolescent mental health service after 18 months of escalating behaviour: repeated school fights, theft from a local shop, deliberate fire-setting in a school rubbish bin, cruelty to the family cat on multiple occasions, breaking into a neighbour's shed and damaging tools, lying, breaking curfew, and overnight absconding. He shows little remorse.

He has had episodes of defiance and rule-refusal since age 6, but the present behaviours represent a clear escalation. There is no documented substance use disorder, no psychotic features, no manic features, and no significant trauma history disclosed. He has no intellectual disability and attends mainstream Year 8 inconsistently. He is up to date with immunisations and his physical examination is normal.

He meets DSM-5 criteria for adolescent-onset conduct disorder. His parents are exhausted, his school principal has indicated that one more incident will result in expulsion, and he and his parents have agreed to engage with treatment.

data_table.History: Fights, theft, fire-setting, animal cruelty, breaking and entering, lying, curfew breaking, low remorse
data_table.Duration: 18 months of escalating behaviour, defiant features from age 6
data_table.Mental state: No psychotic features, no manic features, no substance use disorder
data_table.Examination: Well, normal cardio-respiratory, no neurological deficit

lead_in: Which first-line evidence-based intervention is most appropriate to recommend?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily to target aggression and impulsivity, with monitoring of weight and metabolic parameters
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for conduct disorder and are reserved for severe persistent aggression unresponsive to psychosocial intervention, given significant metabolic and movement adverse effects, per RANZCP Practice Guidelines and RCH CPG: Behaviour.

options.text: Refer for structured family-based behavioural intervention (parent management training or multisystemic therapy); screen and treat comorbid ADHD, mood, substance use
options.rationale: Australian (RANZCP) and international evidence support structured family- and parent-based behavioural interventions (parent management training, multisystemic therapy, functional family therapy) as first-line for conduct disorder, alongside active screening and treatment of comorbid ADHD, mood, substance use and trauma, which co-occur in the majority of cases and worsen prognosis if missed, per RANZCP Practice Guidelines and headspace Clinical Toolkit.

options.text: Recommend a boot-camp style residential discipline program to interrupt the current escalating behavioural pattern in a structured environment
options.rationale: Boot-camp and Scared Straight programs have shown null or harmful effects on conduct disorder outcomes in randomised studies and are explicitly not recommended, per RANZCP Practice Guidelines. This is the anti-pattern tested here.

options.text: Individual psychodynamic psychotherapy weekly for 12 months as the sole intervention without parent or systemic involvement
options.rationale: Individual psychotherapy without family and systemic components is less effective than parent- and family-based interventions for conduct disorder in adolescents, per RANZCP Practice Guidelines.

options.text: Mandatory notification to police and child protection only, deferring any mental-health intervention until the legal pathway concludes fully
options.rationale: Engagement with justice and protective services where indicated does not replace evidence-based mental health treatment; delaying intervention worsens prognosis and is not consistent with stepped-care pathways, per RANZCP Practice Guidelines.

explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour violating the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms with three or more of fifteen criteria in the past 12 months across aggression, property destruction, deceit/theft, and serious rule violation. ODD lacks these severe features.
key_points: Conduct disorder = rights violation + 3 of 15 criteria in 12 months
ODD = argumentative / defiant / vindictive without rights violation
Antisocial personality disorder requires age 18+
Adolescent-onset conduct disorder has a better prognosis than childhood-onset
Screen for comorbid ADHD, substance use, mood, trauma
explanation.pearls: Fire-setting + animal cruelty + theft together is the conduct disorder triad.

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is reviewed by a child and adolescent psychiatrist after 8 weeks of structured cognitive behaviour therapy delivered weekly by a psychologist for a moderate to severe major depressive episode without psychotic features. She continues to have pervasive anhedonia, weight loss, early morning awakening, hopelessness, and passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. There is no substance use, no mania history, and she lives with both parents who are engaged in her care.

She has no medical comorbidity, no QT prolonging medicationsion intolerance, and her ECG is unremarkable with QTc 410 ms. Her clinician is now considering adding antidepressant pharmacotherapy. The family is concerned about the Therapeutic Goods Administration boxed warning regarding antidepressants and suicidal thinking in young people and wants to understand both the choice of medication and the monitoring required if treatment is started. The patient is open to medication trial with appropriate safety planning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, T 36.6 deg C
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, QTc 410 ms, no arrhythmia
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH all normal; urine pregnancy negative
data_table.Mental state: Pervasive anhedonia, early morning awakening, hopelessness, passive SI without plan
data_table.Medications: Nil regular, no QT prolonging agents

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate pharmacological choice with associated monitoring plan?

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 10 mg daily with weekly clinical review in the first 4 weeks for emergent suicidality, alongside ongoing CBT
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the first line antidepressant in paediatric MDD with the strongest evidence base; the TGA boxed warning mandates close clinical monitoring (weekly initially) for emergent suicidal thinking and behaviour, alongside continued psychological therapy, as per RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines and beyondblue Clinical Practice Guidelines.
source_refs: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines
beyondblue Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression Adolescents

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg extended release daily with monthly clinical review and no additional suicidal thinking monitoring planned
options.rationale: Venlafaxine is not first-line in adolescents (discontinuation symptoms, less favourable safety); fluoxetine is preferred. Weekly suicidality monitoring is required regardless of agent. Would be correct only after SSRI failure under specialist care (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Commence paroxetine 20 mg daily with monthly clinical review and no formal safety planning arranged for the next four weeks
options.rationale: Paroxetine is not recommended in adolescents due to short half-life, severe discontinuation and unfavourable risk-benefit. Would never be correct in this age group (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Commence amitriptyline 25 mg at night and titrate to therapeutic dose, with regular ECG monitoring planned over the coming months
options.rationale: TCAs are not effective in paediatric depression and carry overdose risk in an at-risk adolescent. Would never be correct for adolescent MDD (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Stop the current psychological therapy today and commence sertraline 50 mg daily as monotherapy without further structured psychological therapy
options.rationale: Combination psychological plus pharmacological therapy is recommended for moderate-severe adolescent depression; stopping therapy is the wrong direction. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Fluoxetine is first line antidepressant pharmacotherapy in adolescent major depressive disorder, used in combination with continued psychological therapy. The TGA boxed warning requires close clinical monitoring (typically weekly) for emergent suicidal thinking and behaviour during the first 4 weeks of treatment.
key_points: Fluoxetine = first line SSRI in adolescent MDD
Sertraline and escitalopram are second line
Boxed warning: emergent suicidal ideation in age <25
Weekly review in first 4 weeks then fortnightly
Continue CBT alongside antidepressant
explanation.pearls: Paroxetine and venlafaxine are not first line in adolescents due to discontinuation and tolerability concerns.

sources.label: RANZCP Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guidelines
beyondblue Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression Adolescents

stem:
A 14-year-old presents to a tertiary gender service for assessment having identified as a transgender boy for the past four years. He was assigned female at birth, has been consistently insistent and persistent regarding gender identity, has socially transitioned two years ago with family support including legal name change at school, and reports persistent and increasing distress related to ongoing pubertal development.

Menarche occurred at age 12 and he reports menstrual periods as a major and worsening source of dysphoria over the past 18 months. He is at Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair development with regular menstrual cycles every 28 days. He has been supported by an experienced child and adolescent psychiatrist for the past 18 months with no current major mental health condition; previous mild depressive symptoms have improved substantially with social transition and ongoing family acceptance.

data_table.Pubertal staging: Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair, menarche at 12, regular cycles
data_table.Mental health: 18 months psychiatric care, prior mild depression improved with social transition
data_table.Bone health: Bone age normal, no prior fractures, vitamin D 78 nmol/L, DEXA scheduled
data_table.Investigations: LH and FSH baseline normal, oestradiol mid follicular, normal pelvic ultrasound
data_table.Family + MDT: Both parents supportive, MDT includes endocrinology, psychiatry, gynaecology, fertility counselling

lead_in: According to current Australian standards of care, what is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence gender affirming testosterone immediately because the patient is past Tanner stage 2 and has already menstruated for some years
options.rationale: Gender-affirming hormones in under-16s are introduced through structured pathway with MDT consensus and informed consent including fertility; immediate testosterone without staged approach is not standard. Would be appropriate at a later stage after suppression and structured consent (Source: RCH Australian Standards of Care).
source_refs: RCH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines

options.text: Commence GnRH analogue puberty suppression following multidisciplinary review, with planned monitoring during therapy
options.rationale: GnRH analogue puberty suppression is the typical stage 1 intervention to halt further pubertal progression and dysphoria from menses in this Tanner 4 adolescent with consistent gender identity, MDT support, and family agreement; consent does not require court authorisation per Re Kelvin, as per the RCH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines.
source_refs: RCH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines
AusPATH Position Statement on Trans Youth

options.text: Refer to the Family Court for authorisation of stage 1 puberty suppression as the required pathway under current Australian law
options.rationale: Court authorisation is no longer required for stage 1 puberty suppression in Australia after Re Jamie (2013) and Re Kelvin (2017) where parents and clinicians agree. Would never be required in current Australian practice (Source: RCH Australian Standards of Care).
source_refs: RCH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines

options.text: Decline any medical intervention today until the patient reaches the age of 18 and continue with psychological support alone in the interim
options.rationale: Australian Standards explicitly do not require deferral to 18; staged medical intervention may begin earlier with MDT. Would be correct only with no MDT consensus or active contraindication (Source: RCH Australian Standards of Care).
source_refs: RCH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines

options.text: Perform irreversible chest reconstruction surgery now to relieve dysphoria before any further pubertal progression continues to develop
options.rationale: Surgical intervention is not stage 1 in Australian adolescent gender-affirming care; reversible medical intervention precedes adult surgery. Would never be correct as the next step (Source: RCH Australian Standards of Care).
source_refs: RCH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines

explanation.summary: Australian Standards of Care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents (RCH Melbourne) describe a staged pathway: stage 1 GnRH analogue puberty suppression, stage 2 gender affirming hormones, stage 3 surgery in adulthood. Court authorisation is not required where parents, clinicians and the Gillick competent young person agree (Re Kelvin 2017).
key_points: Stage 1: GnRH analogue puberty suppression (reversible)
Stage 2: gender affirming hormones (partially reversible)
Stage 3: surgery, generally in adulthood
Re Kelvin 2017: no court authorisation needed where consensus exists
MDT includes endocrinology, psychiatry, fertility counselling
explanation.pearls: Fertility counselling before stage 2 hormones is mandatory under the Australian Standards of Care.

sources.label: RCH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines
AusPATH Position Statement on Trans Youth

stem:
A previously well 5-year-old girl is brought to a Melbourne general practice with a 4-day history of crusted sores around the nose and right cheek that began after a minor scratch in the playground. She is systemically well and attending school. She has no drug allergies, no eczema and no household members with skin disease. She is afebrile with normal vital signs.

On examination there are three discrete lesions less than 3 cm in total area with classic honey-coloured crust, no surrounding cellulitis, no bullae, no lymphangitis and palpable but non-tender submandibular nodes under 1 cm. There is no mucosal involvement and no other skin lesions. She lives in a non-remote setting; the family does not identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. There has been no recent overseas travel and there is no local MRSA outbreak.

data_table.Examination: Three honey-crusted lesions <3 cm total area on face, no cellulitis, no bullae, no mucosal involvement
data_table.Social: Non-remote setting, attends school, no household skin disease

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Topical mupirocin 2% ointment to lesions three times daily for 5 days, with lesions kept covered or to remain home until lesions are dry; no oral antibiotics
options.rationale: Localised non-bullous impetigo in a low-prevalence non-remote setting (less than 3 small lesion areas) is treated topically with mupirocin or hydrogen peroxide cream per eTG. School exclusion until lesions are covered or have crusted; oral antibiotics are reserved for extensive disease, systemic illness, or high-prevalence/remote/Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander community settings where oral therapy is first-line, per eTG and RCH CPG.

options.text: Oral cefalexin up to 500 mg twice daily for 7 days plus daily chlorhexidine washes for the household
options.rationale: Cefalexin is broader than required and first-line oral when needed is flucloxacillin (or TMP-SMX in high-MRSA areas); oral therapy is not indicated for localised non-bullous impetigo. Would be correct only with widespread or systemic disease (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole twice daily for 5 days as empirical community-acquired MRSA cover
options.rationale: Empirical MRSA cover is reserved for confirmed/strongly suspected MRSA (Top End/central Australia high-prevalence settings). Would be correct only in remote-community or known high-MRSA-prevalence settings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: IV flucloxacillin up to 2 g six-hourly with admission for paediatric observation
options.rationale: IV is for severe cellulitis, abscess, systemic toxicity, or oral failure, none present. Would be correct only with systemic toxicity or facial cellulitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Reassurance and observation only with return at 7 days if not resolved
options.rationale: Topical treatment shortens duration and limits spread; observation alone leaves school/household contacts exposed. Would be correct only for a single resolving lesion already crusted (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Localised non-bullous impetigo in a well child in a non-remote Australian setting is treated topically with mupirocin (or hydrogen peroxide cream) and exclusion from school until lesions are crusted or covered, per eTG and RCH (eTG: Impetigo).
key_points: Topical first-line for limited disease in non-remote settings (eTG: Impetigo).
Oral flucloxacillin (or cefalexin if non-severe penicillin allergy) for extensive, systemic or high-prevalence settings (eTG: Impetigo).
School exclusion until lesions covered or crusted (NHMRC Staying Healthy).
explanation.pearls: Streptococcus pyogenes impetigo carries a small risk of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis - urinalysis any oedema/hypertension after impetigo (RCH CPG: Impetigo).

subtopic_detail: Non-bullous impetigo first-line therapy in primary care

stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents to a GP clinic with one day of low-grade fever (38.1 deg C), reduced oral intake and new tender oral and skin lesions. Her older brother attended childcare with a known outbreak of hand foot and mouth disease last week. She is fully immunised and previously well. On examination she has several shallow oral ulcers on the soft palate and buccal mucosa and small grey-roofed vesicles surrounded by an erythematous halo on the palms, soles and around the buttocks.

There is no rash on the trunk or scalp, no lymphadenopathy, no conjunctivitis and no genital or perianal blistering. Vitals are otherwise normal. Her mother is 30 weeks pregnant and asks specifically when the child can return to childcare.

data_table.Examination: Shallow oral ulcers; grey-roofed vesicles on palms, soles, buttocks; no truncal rash

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnosis-and-exclusion advice per current Australian guidance?

options.text: Hand foot and mouth disease; no formal exclusion is required under NHMRC Staying Healthy provided the child feels well enough to participate; advise good hand hygiene and cover any weeping lesions
options.rationale: Under NHMRC Staying Healthy (6th edition, current Australian guidance), formal exclusion is not required for HFMD provided the child is well enough to participate; advice focuses on hand hygiene and covering weeping lesions. Older 'until all blisters have dried' advice has been updated; this is the genuine AU-cut-off discrimination.

options.text: Hand foot and mouth disease; exclude until all blisters have completely dried, regardless of how well the child is
options.rationale: This is the legacy blanket rule, superseded by NHMRC Staying Healthy 5th edition which does not require exclusion. Would have been correct under the older guideline (Source: NHMRC Staying Healthy 5th edition).

options.text: Primary herpes simplex gingivostomatitis; exclude until afebrile and lesions crusted
options.rationale: Primary HSV gingivostomatitis gives clustered anterior oral vesicles, gum inflammation and bleeding without acral palm/sole lesions. Would be correct only with gingival involvement and no acral lesions (Source: RCH CPG: HSV).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cold sores and gingivostomatitis

options.text: Varicella; exclude for at least 5 days from rash onset and until all lesions have crusted
options.rationale: Varicella produces crops of vesicles on trunk/face/scalp evolving through stages, not acral vesicular sparing the trunk. Would be correct with classic centrifugal vesicular crops (Source: RCH CPG: Varicella).

options.text: Erythema multiforme minor; no exclusion required as the condition is non-infectious
options.rationale: EM has target lesions on limbs without palm-sole-buccal pattern; childcare exposure and classic distribution make HFMD overwhelmingly likely. Would be correct with target lesions and drug/infection trigger (Source: DermNet NZ).

explanation.summary: Hand foot and mouth disease is a common Australian childhood enteroviral illness, peaking in late summer and autumn, caused most often by Coxsackievirus A16 or A6 and enterovirus 71. Presentation is low-grade fever, anorexia, oral enanthem (tongue, buccal mucosa) and tender vesicles on palms, soles and buttocks, lasting 7-10 days. Severe forms with Coxsackie A6 produce widespread vesicular eruption (eczema coxsackium in atopic skin, mimicking eczema herpeticum), onychomadesis weeks later, and rarely myocarditis or aseptic meningitis with enterovirus 71. Management is supportive: paracetamol or ibuprofen, fluids, soft diet. No formal childcare exclusion is required under NHMRC Staying Healthy 5th edition because viral shedding continues for weeks; only severe cases or non-coping families need to stay home. Differentials are HSV gingivostomatitis (more localised, very tender, prolonged), varicella (centripetal rash, all stages, longer prodrome), and erythema multiforme.
key_points: Coxsackie A16 and enterovirus 71 most commonly responsible (RCH CPG).
Supportive care - oral analgesia, hydration; avoid mucosal lidocaine in young children (RCH CPG: Cold sores and gingivostomatitis).
Pregnancy contact: HFMD is not associated with congenital malformations; reassure (RANZCOG patient information).
explanation.pearls: Hand foot and mouth disease (typically Coxsackie A6 or A16, enterovirus 71) needs no formal childcare exclusion under NHMRC Staying Healthy 5th ed - the virus sheds for weeks regardless of skin healing. Eczema coxsackium in atopic infants can mimic eczema herpeticum but is enteroviral, not HSV.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cold sores and gingivostomatitis

subtopic_detail: Hand foot and mouth disease recognition and exclusion advice

stem:
A 6-year-old girl is seen with a 24-hour history of bilateral facial rash following a mild flu-like illness last week. She has had no fever, is eating normally and is attending school. On examination she has a confluent red rash on both cheeks with circumoral sparing and a faint lacy, reticular rash on the extensor surfaces of both forearms. She is afebrile with normal vital signs.

Her mother is 22 weeks pregnant and her younger brother has known sickle cell disease (HbSS) with a baseline haemoglobin of 78 g/L. The school has reported recent cases of slapped cheek disease. There is no recent overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 90, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Confluent erythematous rash both cheeks with circumoral sparing; lacy reticular rash on extensor forearms
data_table.Household: Mother 22/40 pregnant; brother has sickle cell disease (Hb baseline 78 g/L)

lead_in: Which household contact warrants the most urgent specific action, and what is the appropriate first investigation for that contact?

options.text: All family members: reassure that the index case is no longer infectious now that the rash has appeared; no further action required
options.rationale: Index case is no longer infectious after rash onset, but household contacts were exposed in the preceding viraemic week; brother with sickle cell disease and pregnant mother both need targeted action. Reassurance-only is the missed-aplastic-crisis trap (Source: RCH CPG: Parvovirus B19; RANZCOG).

options.text: Brother with sickle cell disease: clinical review and urgent FBC plus reticulocyte count; arrange admission for transfusion if Hb is markedly below baseline with reticulocytopenia (transient aplastic crisis)
options.rationale: Parvovirus B19 arrests erythroid precursors and precipitates transient red cell aplasia in patients with shortened red cell lifespan. The brother with HbSS is at highest immediate risk and requires urgent FBC plus reticulocyte count; transfusion is required if Hb has dropped substantially with reticulocytopenia. The pregnant mother needs serology and obstetric review but on a less immediate timeline (days, not hours), per RCH CPG and RANZCOG.

options.text: Mother: immediate empirical IVIG to prevent fetal hydrops irrespective of her immunity status
options.rationale: First-line for maternal exposure is parvovirus IgG/IgM serology; if seroconverting, serial fetal ultrasound with MCA-PSV detects fetal anaemia and guides intrauterine transfusion. IVIG is not standard maternal therapy (Source: RANZCOG).

options.text: Mother: termination counselling because of high fetal loss risk in the second trimester
options.rationale: Fetal loss risk is under 10 percent overall (highest under 20 weeks); management is serology and surveillance, not termination. Would never be the first action (Source: RANZCOG).

options.text: Index patient: exclude from school for a further 5 days because she is now most infectious
options.rationale: Viraemia has resolved by the time the slapped-cheek rash appears; the child is no longer infectious and school exclusion is not required. Would never be correct after rash onset (Source: CDNA Parvovirus SoNG).

explanation.summary: Erythema infectiosum is parvovirus B19 - by the time the slapped-cheek rash is visible, the index case is non-infectious. Highest-priority household action is to monitor the sibling with sickle cell disease for transient aplastic crisis (RCH CPG: Parvovirus B19).
key_points: Index no longer infectious once rash appears (NHMRC).
Aplastic crisis in chronic haemolytic anaemia (sickle cell, hereditary spherocytosis) - check FBC + reticulocyte (eTG).
Maternal exposure: serology first; if seroconversion, fetal MCA Doppler surveillance for hydrops (RANZCOG).
explanation.pearls: Adults often manifest as symmetrical polyarthritis rather than slapped cheek - consider parvovirus in PJM (post-viral arthritis) workup.

subtopic_detail: Erythema infectiosum and household risk stratification

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is reviewed in a community allergy clinic after two reactions to egg: hives and lip swelling, and a separate episode of vomiting plus audible wheeze within 20 minutes of ingestion. One reaction received adrenaline in the ED. There has been no hypotension or collapse. Skin prick test today shows an 8 mm wheal to egg white and specific IgE to egg white is 22 kU/L.

He has mild persistent asthma well controlled on a low-dose ICS. He weighs 17 kg. He has no other allergies. The family has not previously been prescribed an adrenaline autoinjector. Both parents have completed asthma first aid training and the childcare requires a written ASCIA plan.

data_table.Investigations: SPT egg white wheal 8 mm; sIgE egg white 22 kU/L
data_table.History: Two reactions to egg with wheeze and one ED adrenaline; mild persistent asthma on low-dose ICS

lead_in: Which combination of ASCIA action plan and autoinjector strength is correct?

options.text: ASCIA Action Plan for Allergic Reactions (non-anaphylaxis plan), no autoinjector, oral cetirizine PRN
options.rationale: Documented wheeze with food trigger meets criteria for anaphylaxis, requiring the Anaphylaxis plan plus autoinjector; asthma comorbidity strengthens this. Would be correct for confirmed allergy without anaphylaxis features (Source: ASCIA Action Plans).

options.text: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis with a 150 microgram adrenaline autoinjector (EpiPen Jr) given his current weight of 17 kg
options.rationale: ASCIA prescribes 150 microgram (EpiPen Jr) for weight 7.5 to 20 kg and 300 microgram (EpiPen) for over 20 kg (with 500 microgram for over 50 kg). He weighs 17 kg, so 150 microgram is correct. Documented anaphylaxis with respiratory involvement plus asthma is an indication for an autoinjector and Anaphylaxis Action Plan.

options.text: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis with a 300 microgram autoinjector (EpiPen)
options.rationale: 300 microgram is prescribed from 20 kg upwards under ASCIA; at 17 kg the 150 microgram device is correct. Would be correct from 20 kg (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Action Plan).

options.text: Refer for supervised oral food challenge to egg with no action plan until the challenge result is known
options.rationale: Recent objective anaphylaxis with large SPT wheal and elevated specific IgE makes confirmatory challenge unsafe and unnecessary. Would be correct only for low-risk equivocal results without recent anaphylaxis (Source: ASCIA Oral Food Challenges).

options.text: Discharge with an ASCIA Asthma First Aid Plan only, treating the wheeze as asthma-driven
options.rationale: Wheeze within 20 minutes of a known food trigger is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise; an asthma-only plan misses adrenaline prescription. Would never be correct in food-triggered wheeze (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Action Plan).

explanation.summary: Confirmed IgE-mediated egg allergy with respiratory involvement (anaphylaxis) plus asthma is a clear indication for an adrenaline autoinjector and an ASCIA Anaphylaxis Action Plan; device strength is weight-based and 150 microgram covers 7.5-20 kg (ASCIA Adrenaline Autoinjector Prescribing Guidelines).
key_points: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (red) for any patient prescribed an autoinjector (ASCIA).
EpiPen Jr 150 microgram for 7.5-20 kg; EpiPen 300 microgram for >20 kg (ASCIA).
Asthma comorbidity increases anaphylaxis severity and lowers threshold for autoinjector prescription (ASCIA).
explanation.pearls: Two devices are funded under the PBS for adrenaline autoinjector prescription in Australia.

subtopic_detail: ASCIA Action Plan selection in IgE-mediated food allergy

stem:
A 2-year-old boy with established atopic dermatitis returns to the GP for review after 6 weeks on hydrocortisone 1% applied sparingly once daily to active flares and intermittent moisturiser use. His mother reports nightly scratching, broken sleep for the whole family, and frequent flares despite avoiding soap and using cotton clothing. There is no honey-coloured crust, no clustered vesiclesitic spread.

He is otherwise well, fully immunised, has no food allergies and has a normal growth trajectory. Examination shows extensive erythema, lichenification and excoriation in the antecubital and popliteal fossae and on the cheeks, covering approximately 25 percent of the body surface area, with no overt secondary infection and no peri-orbital involvement. The mother is hesitant about stronger topical steroids because of online concerns about skin thinning, growth suppression and steroid-induced adrenal failure.

She has been using a single 50 g tube of bland moisturiser per week, applied only when the skin looks visibly dry. She has not been shown the fingertip-unit technique.

data_table.Examination: Erythema, lichenification, excoriation in flexures and cheeks; BSA ~25%; no honey crust, no vesicles
data_table.Current therapy: Hydrocortisone 1% sparingly once daily; moisturiser intermittently (50 g/week)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue hydrocortisone 1% ointment once daily to active eczema and add sedating oral cetirizine 5 mg nightly for pruritus with written instruction to limit moisturiser to dry areas
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines are not recommended for paediatric eczema itch (no evidence of benefit, daytime sedation), and continuing insufficient steroid potency perpetuates flares. Would be correct only for short-term sleep disturbance in eczema flares as adjunct (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema; ASCIA).

options.text: Step up to methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment daily to active eczema with at least 250 g per week of bland moisturiser and written fingertip-unit instructions
options.rationale: Moderate eczema unresponsive to a weak corticosteroid warrants stepping up to a moderately potent agent such as methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% applied daily to active areas, with generous emollient use (>=250 g/week for a young child) and structured fingertip-unit education to address steroid phobia (RCH CPG: Eczema; ASCIA: Eczema; eTG: Atopic dermatitis).

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone daily for 7 days to break the flare cycle followed by tapering wean over a further week, continuing hydrocortisone 1% once daily
options.rationale: Oral steroids cause rebound flares on withdrawal and are not recommended in paediatric atopic dermatitis except exceptional severe acute disease under specialist care. Would be correct only for severe acute flare under specialist oversight (Source: ASCIA; Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Start topical tacrolimus 0.03% ointment twice daily to all active areas and stop topical corticosteroids entirely while continuing intermittent emollient as the sole adjunct
options.rationale: Topical calcineurin inhibitors are useful steroid-sparing agents for flexures/face but are second-line in AU and not monotherapy in moderate disease. Would be correct as steroid-sparing addition on facial/flexural eczema (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric dermatology this week for systemic immunomodulation with methotrexate or ciclosporin without further trial of stepped-up topical corticosteroid therapy
options.rationale: Systemic immunomodulators are reserved for severe disease failing optimised topicals and phototherapy under paediatric dermatology; appropriate topical escalation has not been tried. Would be correct after failed maximised topical therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).

explanation.summary: Atopic dermatitis affects up to 30% of Australian children, with onset typically before age 5. First-line management is generous emollient use (200-300 g per week in a young child), gentle non-soap cleansing, lukewarm baths, and trigger avoidance. Topical corticosteroids are matched to severity and body site: mild (hydrocortisone 1%) for face, neck and flexures; moderate (methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%) for body and limbs; potent (betamethasone valerate 0.1%) for thickened plaques with specialist input. Steroid phobia drives undertreatment - explicit fingertip-unit instruction (one FTU treats two adult palms) is the single highest-yield intervention. After clearance, proactive twice-weekly application of topical steroid to relapse-prone sites halves flare rates. Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are steroid-sparing for face and intertriginous areas. Wet dressings, sedating antihistamines for nocturnal scratch, and dermatology referral for refractory disease.
key_points: Potency, not duration, is the primary lever when low-potency fails (RCH).
Emollient quantity is the single biggest predictor of flare frequency (RCH; ASCIA).
One fingertip unit covers approximately two adult palm areas (RCH CPG: Eczema).
explanation.pearls: Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment is a moderately potent steroid with low systemic absorption, making it the workhorse for moderate paediatric eczema flares; use proactively 2-3 times weekly to high-risk sites after acute control to halve relapse rates (RCH CPG Eczema).

subtopic_detail: Eczema severity step-up using fingertip units and topical potency

stem:
A first-time mother brings her 5-month-old breastfed infant to the GP for advice. The infant has moderate atopic dermatitis well-controlled on regular emollient and intermittent methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% under paediatric dermatology supervision. There is no history of immediate reactions to any food and no breast-milk-related symptoms. The mother and father both have hay fever and the mother has mild asthma.

The paternal grandfather has confirmed peanut allergy. The infant is starting to show developmental signs of readiness for solids - good head control, interest in food, loss of tongue thrust. She has read conflicting online advice about delaying highly allergenic foods, especially peanut, until age 1 to 'wait until the gut is more mature'. She asks specifically how and when peanut should be introduced.

She is not vegan and there is no cultural restriction. She specifically asks whether peanut should be deferred until 12 months because of the family history, and whether referral for skin prick testing should occur before any home introduction. The family wants a clear, written, ASCIA-aligned plan to give the childcare centre.

data_table.Background: 5-month-old, moderate eczema controlled on emollient + moderate TCS
data_table.Family history: Both parents atopic; paternal grandfather peanut allergic

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate advice regarding allergenic solid introduction?

options.text: Introduce smooth peanut butter or peanut paste from around 6 months while continuing breastfeeding and continue including it regularly in the diet
options.rationale: ASCIA recommends introducing common allergens including peanut, egg, dairy and tree nuts in the first year (around 6 months but not before 4 months) regardless of family history, and ongoing regular inclusion sustains tolerance (ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention).
source_refs: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention

options.text: Delay peanut introduction until 12 months of age given the strong family history of peanut allergy and continue exclusive breastfeeding with avoidance of all tree nuts
options.rationale: LEAP trial and ASCIA explicitly advise against delaying allergen introduction; delay increases not decreases food allergy risk. Would never be correct under current evidence (Source: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention).
source_refs: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention

options.text: Refer for skin prick testing to peanut and other common allergens before any home introduction is attempted, and defer introduction pending the result
options.rationale: Pre-screening with SPT in asymptomatic infants is not recommended because it identifies sensitisation, not clinical allergy, and leads to unnecessary avoidance. Would be correct only in infants with prior reaction (Source: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention).
source_refs: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention

options.text: Introduce peanut only in the supervised setting of the GP clinic given moderate eczema and parental atopy, with observation for 2 hours after the first dose
options.rationale: Routine in-clinic introduction is not recommended and is impractical; home introduction per ASCIA is the standard. Would be correct only for infants with prior reaction or severe eczema with documented sensitisation (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention

options.text: Replace breastfeeding with extensively hydrolysed formula from now to prevent food allergy and delay solid introduction until at least 9 months of age
options.rationale: Hydrolysed formulas are not recommended for allergy prevention and there is no reason to interrupt breastfeeding. Would never be correct for prevention (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines; ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention

explanation.summary: Introducing common allergenic foods including peanut in the first year of life (around 6 months, never before 4 months) and continuing regular exposure is the evidence-based primary prevention strategy endorsed by ASCIA and NHMRC (ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention).
key_points: Early introduction reduces peanut allergy risk (LEAP-aligned ASCIA position).
Continued regular intake is required to maintain tolerance (ASCIA).
Eczema severity increases risk of food allergy but is NOT a contraindication to early introduction (ASCIA).
explanation.pearls: Whole nuts are a choking hazard under age 5 - use smooth peanut butter or paste.

sources.label: ASCIA Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention

subtopic_detail: Atopic march counselling and early peanut introduction

stem:
A 3-year-old girl with previously confirmed IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy attends a paediatric allergy day-stay for a supervised oral food challenge. Her most recent reaction was 15 months ago with urticaria but no respiratory symptoms. She has well-controlled mild eczema and no asthma. Skin prick test today shows a wheal of 4 mm to cow's milk extract (negative control 0 mm, histamine 6 mm).

Specific IgE to cow's milk is 1.2 kU/L. She remains on a milk-free diet with calcium-fortified soy. After incremental doses up to a cumulative 200 mL of full-fat cow's milk over 3 hours she develops two small urticarial wheals on the trunk, no peri-oral swelling, no wheeze, and remains haemodynamically stable. Repeat observation at 90 minutes shows no progression and the wheals resolve with oral cetirizine.

The family asks whether milk can now be reintroduced freely at home or whether further specialist input is required before any dietary change. They request a written plan for childcare and for grandparents.

data_table.Pre-challenge: SPT cow's milk 4 mm; sIgE 1.2 kU/L; no asthma; last reaction 15 months ago (urticaria only)
data_table.Challenge response: Two urticarial wheals at 200 mL; no respiratory, GI, mucosal or cardiovascular features; resolved with cetirizine

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate interpretation and ongoing plan?

options.text: Failed challenge - continue strict milk avoidance and re-challenge in 12-18 months with an ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis and EpiPen Jr
options.rationale: Any objective allergic reaction during a supervised oral food challenge constitutes a failed challenge; the child remains allergic, milk avoidance continues, and an action plan with autoinjector is required pending repeat assessment in 12-18 months (ASCIA: Oral Food Challenges; ASCIA Action Plans).

options.text: Passed challenge - introduce cow's milk fully into the diet from tomorrow with no further action and discontinue calcium-fortified soy entirely without ongoing specialist follow-up
options.rationale: Reproducible urticaria during challenge meets failed-challenge criteria; this child is still allergic and unrestricted milk is unsafe. Would be correct only with no objective reaction across all dose steps and observation (Source: ASCIA Oral Food Challenges).

options.text: Equivocal challenge - commence the baked milk ladder at home over the next 6 weeks without further specialist input and reintroduce fresh milk if no symptoms arise
options.rationale: Baked milk ladder is specialist-directed; home titration after a failed open challenge is unsafe. Would be correct only after a specialist passes the baked milk ladder challenge (Source: ASCIA Milk allergy).

options.text: Passed challenge - replace soy with cow's milk over 7 days, reduce calcium supplementation and discharge from allergy follow-up with no autoinjector required
options.rationale: The challenge failed; substituting milk would expose to ongoing risk. Would never be correct after objective reaction (Source: ASCIA Oral Food Challenges).

options.text: Indeterminate challenge - administer same-day intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg and admit for 24 hours of cardiorespiratory observation before any further dietary advice
options.rationale: IM adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis; isolated cutaneous reactions without respiratory/CV/persistent-GI involvement are treated with antihistamine and observation. Would be correct only for anaphylactic reaction during challenge (Source: ASCIA; ANZCOR 9.2.7).

explanation.summary: An objective allergic reaction (even isolated urticaria) during a supervised challenge means the challenge has failed; ongoing avoidance with an Anaphylaxis Action Plan and adrenaline autoinjector is appropriate, with re-evaluation in 12-18 months (ASCIA: Oral Food Challenges).
key_points: Failed = ANY reproducible objective reaction (ASCIA).
Cutaneous-only reaction is not anaphylaxis but still constitutes failed challenge (ASCIA; ANZCOR).
Repeat challenge timing depends on age, severity and trajectory of sIgE/SPT (ASCIA).
explanation.pearls: Baked milk and baked egg ladders rely on conformational epitope denaturation by heat - around 70% of milk and egg-allergic children tolerate baked forms.

subtopic_detail: Oral food challenge interpretation for resolving cow's milk allergy

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a tertiary paediatric ED by his parents 2 hours after the sudden onset of widespread itchy wheals on the trunk, limbs and face, plus puffiness of the lips and right eyelid. He took ibuprofen 3 hours ago for a viral upper respiratory tract infection that started 4 days ago. He has no food triggers, no insect exposure and no recent new medications other than ibuprofen and a 2-day course of amoxicillin started yesterday for presumed otitis media.
