He has no asthma. On arrival his temperature is 37.4 deg C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 99% in room air and BP 105/68. He is settled, talking in sentences, with no stridor, no wheezeice. Lung auscultation is clear and he has brisk capillary refill. There is no abdominal pain, no vomiting and no hypotension.

data_table.Examination: Widespread wheals, lip and right eyelid swelling; no stridor, no wheeze, no tongue swelling, normal voice
data_table.Exposures: Ibuprofen 3 hours ago; amoxicillin day 2 for OM; viral URTI day 4

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 0.3 mg into the mid anterolateral thigh, IV fluid bolus normal saline and admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring overnight
options.rationale: Adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis (respiratory/CV/persistent severe GI); urticaria with angioedema but no airway or BP compromise does not meet criteria. Would be correct with stridor, wheeze, persistent vomiting or hypotension (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis).

options.text: Oral non-sedating antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine), withhold the ibuprofen and amoxicillin, observe for 4 hours and discharge with action plan if stable
options.rationale: Acute urticaria with angioedema but without anaphylaxis features is managed with a non-sedating H1 antihistamine, removal of suspected triggers (NSAID and likely amoxicillin in the setting of a viral URTI which can transiently amplify drug-rash risk), and observation; an ASCIA Action Plan for Allergic Reactions is appropriate at discharge (eTG: Urticaria; ASCIA: Urticaria; RCH CPG: Urticaria).

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus oral promethazine as a sedating antihistamine, with discharge if asymptomatic at 2 hours after a single dose
options.rationale: Promethazine is contraindicated under 2 years and not first-line in acute urticaria; corticosteroids have no acute benefit. Would never be correct (Source: ASCIA: Urticaria; TGA Promethazine warning).

options.text: Continue both amoxicillin and ibuprofen at current doses, add an oral non-sedating antihistamine for symptom control, and counsel that viral exanthem is the most likely cause
options.rationale: Continuing the NSAID and antibiotic that temporally preceded urticaria is unsafe pending allergy assessment; suspected triggers must be withheld. Would be correct only after specialist drug-allergy assessment clears them (Source: ASCIA: Drug allergy in children).

options.text: Refer for outpatient intramuscular omalizumab as first-line acute therapy for urticaria with angioedema and discharge after a single dose of oral antihistamine
options.rationale: Omalizumab is specialist treatment for chronic spontaneous urticaria failing high-dose antihistamines, not acute ED therapy. Would be correct only in chronic refractory urticaria under specialist care (Source: ASCIA: Urticaria).

explanation.summary: Acute urticaria with angioedema and no airway, respiratory or cardiovascular compromise is treated with a non-sedating antihistamine and trigger removal; adrenaline is reserved for true anaphylaxis (eTG: Urticaria).
key_points: Distinguish urticaria/angioedema from anaphylaxis by absence of respiratory/CV features (ASCIA).
Withhold suspected NSAID and antibiotic triggers; document for outpatient drug allergy assessment (ASCIA).
Steroids and sedating antihistamines are not first-line in acute paediatric urticaria (RCH; ASCIA).
explanation.pearls: Up to 80% of paediatric acute urticaria is viral, but co-exposure to NSAIDs or antibiotics complicates causality - delayed structured testing is needed.

subtopic_detail: Acute urticaria with angioedema in the ED

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is reviewed in general practice with a 6-week history of itchy, sharply demarcated dermatitis confined to a thin horizontal band across the upper abdomen and to both earlobes. The rash started 3 weeks after she received costume jewellery and a new metallic belt buckle for her birthday. There is no involvement of the rest of the trunk, no involvement of the hands or wrists, no joint pain, no oral lesionsrsonal or family history.

She is otherwise well, fully immunised, on no medications and has no history of eczema. Examination shows pink, scaly, lichenified plaques in the exact distribution of the buckle and earring posts with crisp angular borders and no spread to surrounding skin. Hand washing is performed with standard soap several times a day with no rash. Application of bland moisturiser has not helped.

data_table.Examination: Sharply demarcated, scaly, lichenified plaques confined to belt-buckle line on abdomen and to both earlobes; no spread, no mucosal involvement
data_table.History: New costume jewellery and metallic belt buckle 3 weeks before onset
data_table.Other: No atopy, no eczema, no systemic symptoms

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Allergic contact dermatitis to nickel with confirmatory referral for standard-series patch testing
options.rationale: Sharply demarcated dermatitis confined to sites of contact with costume jewellery and a belt buckle is highly suggestive of nickel allergic contact dermatitis, the most common contact allergen in Australian children; gold-standard confirmation is patch testing (Australasian Contact Dermatitis Society; DermNet NZ: Allergic contact dermatitis).

options.text: Irritant contact dermatitis from soap with skin scraping for fungal microscopy
options.rationale: Irritant dermatitis from soap affects hands/wrists, not belt line and earlobes; fungal scraping is for tinea (annular with central clearing). Distribution is the giveaway anti-pattern (Source: DermNet NZ).

options.text: Atopic dermatitis in flexural distribution with referral for serum total IgE
options.rationale: Atopic dermatitis involves antecubital and popliteal flexures, not contact-defined geometric patches; serum total IgE is not diagnostic. Would be correct with flexural pattern and atopic history (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema; ASCIA).

options.text: Tinea corporis with Wood's lamp examination at the bedside today
options.rationale: Tinea corporis is annular with raised scaly borders and central clearing; most dermatophytes do not fluoresce under Wood's lamp. Distribution and morphology are wrong here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Discoid nummular eczema with direct immunofluorescence biopsy for confirmation
options.rationale: Discoid eczema is multiple coin-shaped lesions in random distribution; direct immunofluorescence is for immunobullous disease. Distribution wrong; technique wrong (Source: DermNet NZ).

explanation.summary: Geometrically demarcated dermatitis matching contact-object footprint plus a temporal link to nickel-containing items strongly suggests nickel allergic contact dermatitis; patch testing is the gold-standard confirmatory test (Australasian Contact Dermatitis Society).
key_points: Allergic contact = delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity confined to contact site (DermNet NZ).
Nickel is the commonest contact allergen in children worldwide (ACDS).
Patch testing reads at 48 and 96 hours; SPT and serum IgE do not diagnose contact allergy (ACDS).
explanation.pearls: Australian standards mandate nickel release limits in jewellery similar to the EU directive - earring posts remain a common culprit.

subtopic_detail: Allergic versus irritant contact dermatitis discrimination in a child

stem:
A 4-year-old Aboriginal boy is referred from a remote community clinic to a regional paediatric service with a 6-week history of widespread itch, worse at night, and skin changes. He lives in a household with seven other people, three of whom also have itch. He has had two courses of topical hydrocortisone with no improvement. On examination he is well-grown, afebrile and systemically well.

There is hyperkeratotic, fissured scale on the palms, soles and elbows, multiple excoriated papules and a few burrows in finger web spaces and on the wrists. There is no facial or scalp involvement. He has no immune deficiency, no significant past medical history and is fully immunised. Skin scraping under microscopy shows mites and eggs. There is no secondary impetigo. The community has been advised by environmental health that there has been a recent cluster of scabies cases.

data_table.Examination: Hyperkeratotic palms/soles/elbows; burrows in finger webs and wrists; widespread excoriations; no facial or scalp involvement
data_table.Household: 8 people, 3 with itch; remote community with current scabies cluster
data_table.Microscopy: Mites and eggs visualised on scraping

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Permethrin 5% cream applied to the index patient only once now and repeated at 7 days, with continued hydrocortisone 1% for residual itch, no contact treatment and no environmental laundry measures
options.rationale: Failure to treat all household and close contacts simultaneously is the commonest cause of treatment failure; topical steroids do not address infestation. Would never be correct as the index-only approach (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual; RCH CPG: Scabies).

options.text: Permethrin 5% cream to the entire body of the patient and all household and close contacts simultaneously, repeat at 7-14 days, plus environmental measures (hot wash of bedding/clothing) and consider oral ivermectin given crusted features
options.rationale: Hyperkeratotic palms/soles in an endemic setting raises suspicion of crusted scabies; Australian guidance (eTG, RCH and CARPA) recommends whole-body permethrin to index plus all contacts simultaneously, repeat dose at 7-14 days, environmental decontamination, and consideration of oral ivermectin in crusted disease (eTG: Scabies; RCH CPG: Scabies; CARPA).

options.text: Oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg as monotherapy on day 0 and day 7 with no topical scabicide for the index patient or contacts, no environmental decontamination and no school exclusion
options.rationale: Ivermectin is an adjunct (crusted disease, outbreaks) and does not replace topical scabicide, contact treatment and environmental measures. Would be correct as add-on in crusted scabies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Benzyl benzoate 25% emulsion applied head to toe to the patient and all family members on 7 consecutive nights without repeat dosing, environmental laundry measures or specialist follow-up
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is alternative but irritant to paediatric skin and not first-line; 7 consecutive nights is not standard. Would be correct only as second-line when permethrin contraindicated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Defer all treatment pending dermatology incisional biopsy for definitive histological confirmation, with no interim scabicide therapy or household contact tracing today
options.rationale: Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopy; biopsy is unnecessary and delays definitive management of an outbreak. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies).

explanation.summary: Crusted scabies (especially in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities) requires simultaneous treatment of the patient and all household and close contacts with topical scabicide plus environmental measures, with oral ivermectin considered for crusted disease and outbreaks (eTG: Scabies; CARPA).
key_points: Treat all contacts simultaneously - lone treatment leads to recurrence (RCH).
Repeat permethrin at 7-14 days to cover newly hatched mites (eTG).
Crusted scabies is highly transmissible and a notifiable cluster trigger in some jurisdictions (CDNA).
explanation.pearls: Itch may persist 2-4 weeks after successful eradication - emollient and short-course low-potency steroid, NOT repeat scabicide.

subtopic_detail: Crusted scabies and household management in a paediatric setting

stem:
A 6-year-old boy presents to a general practice with a 4-week history of a progressively enlarging, tender, boggy scalp lesion with overlying pustules and patchy hair loss in the affected area. His older sister recently completed treatment for scalp ringworm at the same school. He has no fever, no headache and no neck stiffness. On examination he has a 4 cm boggy inflammatory plaque on the vertex with several superficial pustules, surrounding scale, broken hairs and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

There is no fluctuant abscess, no facial swelling and no cellulitic spread. Skin scraping and hair pluck for fungal microscopy and culture have been sent. He has no other dermatological disease and no allergies. His mother is worried about scarring alopecia and has read online about needing oral antibiotics for the pustules. The mother specifically asks whether incision and drainage of the boggy lesion is required and whether oral antibiotics for the pustules should be commenced today.

data_table.Examination: 4 cm boggy inflammatory scalp plaque with pustules and broken hairs; tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy; no fluctuant abscess
data_table.Investigations: Fungal microscopy and culture sent
data_table.Contacts: Sister recently treated for scalp ringworm

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment plan?

options.text: Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for at least 4-8 weeks plus a topical antifungal shampoo, with topical/oral antibiotics only if bacterial superinfection is proven
options.rationale: Tinea capitis with kerion always requires systemic antifungal therapy because topical agents do not penetrate the hair follicle; griseofulvin and terbinafine are first-line in Australian guidance and adjunctive antifungal shampoo reduces shedding (eTG: Dermatophyte infections; RCH CPG: Tinea).

options.text: Topical ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly and topical terbinafine 1% cream applied to the scalp lesion daily for 4 weeks with no systemic antifungal therapy
options.rationale: Topical therapy alone is inadequate for tinea capitis because dermatophytes invade hair shafts beyond topical penetration; systemic therapy is mandatory. Would be correct only for tinea corporis without scalp involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Incision and drainage of the boggy kerion under procedural sedation followed by oral flucloxacillin six-hourly for 7 days with no antifungal cover
options.rationale: Kerion is an inflammatory dermatophyte reaction, not a bacterial abscess; I&D worsens scarring and antibiotics do not treat the fungus. Would be correct only for confirmed bacterial scalp abscess (Source: DermNet NZ: Kerion).

options.text: Oral prednisolone once daily for 7 days as monotherapy to reduce scalp inflammation, with no antifungal therapy commenced until fungal culture returns
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy without antifungal cover risks worsening infection; some specialists use steroids as adjunct WITH antifungal for severe kerion. Would be correct only as adjunct to antifungal under specialist input (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Watchful waiting for 4 weeks pending the fungal culture result with no antifungal therapy in the interim and review only if the lesion enlarges
options.rationale: Delaying treatment risks permanent scarring alopecia and community transmission; empirical therapy based on clinical/microscopy is standard while awaiting culture. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Tinea).

explanation.summary: Tinea capitis with kerion requires SYSTEMIC antifungal therapy (griseofulvin or terbinafine) for several weeks plus adjunctive antifungal shampoo to reduce spore shedding; antibiotics are only added when bacterial superinfection is documented (eTG: Dermatophyte infections).
key_points: Topical therapy alone fails because of hair-shaft involvement (eTG).
Treat household and close contacts with antifungal shampoo to reduce transmission (RCH).
School exclusion is not required once treatment is commenced (NHMRC Staying Healthy).
explanation.pearls: Mistaking a kerion for a bacterial abscess and incising it is a classic exam trap - leave the scalp alone and treat the fungus.

subtopic_detail: Tinea capitis with kerion and systemic antifungal selection

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to general practice with a 6-week history of a slowly progressive linear band of small, slightly hypopigmented, mildly itchy papules along the side of her right leg. The band starts on the lateral thigh, follows a curving line down to the lateral ankle, does not cross the midline, and has no associated swelling, ulceration or pustules.

She is otherwise well, fully immunised, with no relevant past history. There has been no trauma, no insect bites at the siteo contact with anyone with similar rash. She has no eczema, no asthma and no recognised allergies. Examination shows a 30 cm linear band of pinhead-sized flat-topped papules in the line described, with no scaling, no indurationted lymphadenopathy. The mother is anxious about scarring and is keen to start any available treatment immediately.

data_table.Examination: 30 cm linear band of small flat papules along right leg following lines of Blaschko, no crossing of midline; no scaling, no induration, no nail change
data_table.Symptoms: Mild pruritus only; no systemic features
data_table.History: No trauma, no contact triggers, no atopic history

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Reassurance with bland emollient and a short course of mild topical corticosteroid (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) for pruritus, with expected spontaneous resolution over 1-2 years and warning that post-inflammatory pigment change may persist
options.rationale: Lichen striatus is a benign self-limiting eruption along lines of Blaschko that typically resolves spontaneously over 6-24 months; mild topical corticosteroid is used only for symptomatic pruritus and the family should be warned that pigmentary change may persist after resolution (DermNet NZ: Lichen striatus; Paediatric Dermatology Update RCH).

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric dermatology for incisional skin biopsy of the band to histologically exclude linear morphoea and other sclerosing dermatoses, with topical clobetasol commenced empirically pending result
options.rationale: Linear morphoea is sclerotic, indurated and causes atrophy or limb-length discrepancy; the soft, flat-topped papules here are classic lichen striatus. Would be appropriate only if the band were indurated or scleroatrophic (Source: DermNet NZ: Lichen striatus).

options.text: Commence methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment twice daily for 6 weeks along the entire band with monthly review for tapering, assessment of skin atrophy and consideration of switching to tacrolimus
options.rationale: Moderately potent steroids carry skin-atrophy risk on a young child's limbs and are unnecessary for a benign self-limiting condition. Would be correct only for severe pruritus refractory to mild steroid (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Refer for systemic immunosuppression with methotrexate given the linear distribution and 6-week chronicity, with weekly folic acid and monthly bloods for liver and renal function monitoring
options.rationale: Systemic immunosuppression has no role in self-limiting lichen striatus; this is the over-treatment anti-pattern. Would be correct only in linear morphoea with active inflammation (Source: DermNet NZ).

options.text: Treat with topical clotrimazole 1% antifungal cream applied to the band twice daily for 4 weeks as for cutaneous candidiasis with review at 2 weeks and oral fluconazole if no response
options.rationale: Candidiasis is intertriginous, moist and not arranged along Blaschko lines; morphology is wrong. Would be correct only with classic moist intertriginous beefy-red patches with satellite pustules (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Lichen striatus is a benign, self-limiting eruption of small flat papules arranged along the lines of Blaschko in pre-school and primary-school children; the management is reassurance plus mild symptomatic topical care (DermNet NZ: Lichen striatus).
key_points: Distribution along lines of Blaschko is the diagnostic feature (DermNet NZ).
Resolution usually within 6-24 months; pigmentary change can persist (DermNet NZ).
Differentiate from linear morphoea (sclerotic, indurated) and inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus (persistent, verrucous).
explanation.pearls: Lines of Blaschko reflect embryonic ectodermal migration patterns - they do NOT correspond to dermatomes.

stem:
A 14-year-old girl recently arrived from a country without routine MMR vaccination presents to a community health clinic with a 2-day history of fine pink maculopapular rash that began on the face and is spreading caudally. She has had a mild fever, a sore throat, and tender lumps behind both ears for 24 hours preceding the rash, along with mild joint discomfort in the hands.

She has not had any specific food trigger and there are no medications. She is otherwise well, eating, drinking and ambulant with stable vital signs (T 37.8, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 99%). On examination she has discrete tender post-auricular and sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild conjunctival injection, no Koplik spots, mild oropharyngeal redness, and a fading erythematous fine rash now on the trunk. There are no purpura, no oral ulcers and no joint swelling. The clinic has several pregnant women attending today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Fine maculopapular rash spreading from face to trunk; tender post-auricular and sub-occipital lymphadenopathy; mild conjunctival injection; no Koplik spots, no purpura
data_table.History: Unvaccinated; recent arrival from country without routine MMR; pregnant women in waiting room

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate public-health action?

options.text: Isolate the patient immediately, notify the local public health unit on clinical suspicion, and identify and counsel any pregnant contacts about rubella serology
options.rationale: Rubella is a notifiable disease in all Australian jurisdictions on clinical suspicion; immediate isolation prevents exposure of susceptible pregnant women (highest risk of congenital rubella syndrome at <20 weeks) and the public health unit coordinates contact tracing and serology (CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Rubella; NCIRS: Rubella).
source_refs: CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Rubella

options.text: Send rubella IgM and IgG serology and discharge home with no isolation pending the laboratory result before considering notification to the public health unit
options.rationale: Notification in Australia is on clinical suspicion and cannot await lab confirmation; failing to isolate exposes susceptible pregnant contacts. Would never be correct (Source: CDNA Rubella SoNG).
source_refs: CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Rubella

options.text: Administer MMR vaccination immediately to the patient and to any pregnant contacts in the clinic as urgent post-exposure prophylaxis for rubella
options.rationale: MMR is contraindicated in pregnancy and post-symptom-onset vaccination does not modify current illness. Catch-up MMR is planned for the patient at convalescence. Would never be correct as the immediate action (Source: NCIRS Rubella; Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone empirically pending blood cultures and PCR for meningococcal disease and admit for 24 hours of cardiovascular monitoring
options.rationale: Meningococcal disease has non-blanching purpuric rash with systemic toxicity, not blanching face-down maculopapular rash with post-auricular nodes. Distribution and rash type wrong (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Treat as measles with high-dose oral vitamin A and MMR post-exposure prophylaxis for unvaccinated household contacts within 72 hours of exposure
options.rationale: Measles requires Koplik spots, cough/coryza/conjunctivitis prodrome and a brick-red confluent face-down rash; absent here. Lymphadenopathy pattern fits rubella. Would be correct only with classic measles prodrome (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Rubella was eliminated as an endemic disease in Australia by 2018 through routine MMR vaccination (1st dose at 12 months, 2nd at 18 months, with the MMRV combination). Current cases are imported from countries with incomplete coverage, particularly in migrant and returning-traveller groups. Clinical presentation is mild: low-grade fever, lymphadenopathy (postauricular, suboccipital, posterior cervical), fine pink maculopapular rash starting on the face and spreading caudally, lasting 3 days, often with transient arthralgia in older children and adults. The serious consequence is congenital rubella syndrome in a non-immune pregnant contact (deafness, cataracts, congenital heart disease, microcephaly, intellectual disability); first-trimester transmission risk approaches 90%. Suspected rubella triggers immediate isolation, droplet precautions, and CDNA-mandated clinical notification to the public health unit on suspicion - do not await serology. Identify pregnant contacts, check immune status, and offer post-exposure assessment. MMR is contraindicated in pregnancy.
key_points: Face-to-caudal rash + post-auricular/sub-occipital nodes + mild arthralgia is the classical rubella triad (NCIRS).
Highest CRS risk if maternal infection at <16 weeks gestation (NCIRS).
MMR contraindicated in pregnancy - vaccinate post-partum (Australian Immunisation Handbook).
explanation.pearls: Rubella is notifiable to the local public health unit on clinical suspicion under each state's Public Health Act - serology takes 24-48 hours and the catastrophic risk is to non-immune pregnant contacts (congenital rubella syndrome). Isolate the patient and notify before swabbing (CDNA Rubella).

sources.label: CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Rubella

subtopic_detail: Rubella in an unvaccinated migrant teenager and public-health priorities

stem:
A 12-year-old boy with known peanut allergy and mild persistent asthma is brought to a metropolitan paediatric ED after a school excursion exposure. Witnesses describe sudden generalised urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting, audible wheeze and progression to a brief loss of postural tone within 15 minutes of eating a granola bar. The school nurse administered intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram via an EpiPen at 10 minutes and a second dose was given by paramedics 8 minutes later with sustained improvement.

On arrival to ED 45 minutes after the initial reaction he is alert, with HR 96, BP 108/64, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 2 L oxygen, with no audible wheeze, no stridor, mild residual peri-oral oedema and clearing urticaria. He has had no further drop in BP, no recurrence of wheeze, and no further vomiting. The family asks whether he can be discharged after a short observation. His usual asthma is well-controlled with no recent exacerbations.

data_table.Pre-hospital: 2 doses IM adrenaline (school then paramedics, 8 min apart) with sustained improvement
data_table.Vital signs on arrival: HR 96, BP 108/64, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 2 L O2
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild residual peri-oral oedema; no wheeze, no stridor; clearing urticaria
data_table.Background: Known peanut allergy; mild persistent asthma on ICS; well-controlled

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate disposition and observation plan?

options.text: Discharge home now with oral cetirizine 10 mg daily, a written ASCIA Action Plan for Allergic Reactions, a single in-date EpiPen and follow-up review in primary care within 48 hours of discharge
options.rationale: Early discharge after severe anaphylaxis (asthma comorbid, repeat adrenaline) underestimates biphasic risk; this is the under-observation anti-pattern. Would be correct only for mild single-episode anaphylaxis resolving with one adrenaline dose (Source: ASCIA).

options.text: Observe in the ED short-stay unit for 4 hours from the last adrenaline dose and discharge if asymptomatic with the standard discharge bundle, adrenaline autoinjector and 2-week allergy clinic follow-up
options.rationale: 4 hours is the minimum after uncomplicated anaphylaxis; severe features justify longer. Would be correct for uncomplicated mild reaction (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

options.text: Admit for at least 6-12 hours of monitored observation given severe features (two adrenaline doses, asthma, transient collapse) and discharge with updated Anaphylaxis Action Plan, two in-date adrenaline autoinjectors, ICS optimisation and immunology referral
options.rationale: ASCIA recommends extended observation (commonly at least 6-12 hours) after severe anaphylaxis or where any risk factor for biphasic or protracted reaction is present (need for repeat adrenaline, asthma comorbidity, hypotension/collapse, severe initial reaction); discharge should include an updated action plan, two adrenaline autoinjectors, asthma optimisation and specialist follow-up (ASCIA: Acute management of anaphylaxis; ASCIA Action Plans).

options.text: Admit to PICU for 24 hours of intubated airway monitoring with a continuous intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to MAP and prophylactic salbutamol nebuliser regardless of current clinical stability
options.rationale: He is currently stable without airway compromise; intubation/adrenaline infusion is for refractory anaphylaxis with airway or CV failure. Would be correct only with persistent hypotension or airway compromise (Source: ANZCOR 9.2.7; ASCIA).

options.text: Discharge after 1 hour of observation with a 3-day course of oral prednisolone as routine pharmacological prevention of a biphasic reaction without extended ED observation
options.rationale: Steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions and 1 hour is inadequate observation. ASCIA prioritises observation duration over routine steroids. Would never be correct (Source: ASCIA).

explanation.summary: Severe anaphylaxis (need for repeat adrenaline, asthma comorbidity, transient collapse) warrants extended monitored observation - commonly 6-12 hours - with discharge planning that includes an updated Anaphylaxis Action Plan, two adrenaline autoinjectors and immunology referral (ASCIA: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
key_points: Risk factors for protracted/biphasic reaction extend observation beyond 4 hours (ASCIA).
Steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions (ASCIA).
Discharge bundle: action plan, two devices, trigger education, asthma optimisation, specialist referral (ASCIA).
explanation.pearls: PBS allows two adrenaline autoinjectors per prescription - always prescribe two so one stays at school.

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis with biphasic risk - disposition decision

stem:
A 10-year-old girl presents to ED with a third episode in six months of recurrent, non-itchy, non-erythematous swelling of the face, hands and tongue lasting 36-72 hours each time, often preceded by colicky abdominal pain. There is never any urticaria, no hypotension, no respiratory distress and no clear food, medication or insect trigger. Two previous ED visits resulted in administration of intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous hydrocortisone and chlorphenamine with no apparent response and slow spontaneous resolution.

Her father has had similar episodes since childhood and her paternal uncle died from a 'throat swelling' aged 28. On examination today she is comfortable with non-pitting, non-erythematous swelling of the lips and left hand, no airway compromise, soft non-tender abdomen and normal vital signs. She has no known food, drug or environmental allergy and no asthma..

data_table.Examination: Non-pitting, non-erythematous lip and left hand swelling; no airway compromise; no urticaria; soft abdomen
data_table.Family history: Father with recurrent episodes since childhood; paternal uncle died from throat swelling age 28
data_table.Investigations: C4 low

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation and acute management?

options.text: Send serum tryptase during the current attack and commence intravenous adrenaline infusion with hydrocortisone as for refractory anaphylaxis unresponsive to intramuscular adrenaline
options.rationale: Tryptase rises in mast-cell-mediated reactions, not bradykinin-driven HAE; adrenaline/steroids/antihistamines are ineffective in HAE attacks. Would be correct only in suspected anaphylaxis or mastocytosis (Source: ASCIA: Angioedema; Australasian HAE consensus).

options.text: Send C1 inhibitor antigenic level and function (and consider SERPING1 testing); treat acute attack with C1 inhibitor concentrate (or icatibant) and arrange immunology follow-up for long-term prophylaxis planning
options.rationale: Low C4 between attacks plus dominantly inherited recurrent non-urticarial angioedema unresponsive to anti-allergic therapy is classical for HAE; diagnosis is confirmed by C1 inhibitor antigenic level and function, with SERPING1 testing in select cases, and acute attacks are treated with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant (a bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) (ASCIA: Hereditary angioedema; Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy HAE Position).

options.text: Send total IgE and a paediatric food-specific IgE panel and commence daily non-sedating antihistamine prophylaxis with up-titration as needed for symptom control
options.rationale: IgE testing is irrelevant in HAE (bradykinin-mediated); antihistamines do not prevent attacks. Would never be correct (Source: ASCIA: HAE).

options.text: Refer for contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and outpatient gastroenterology workup for the recurrent colicky abdominal pain in isolation without further immunology investigation
options.rationale: Bowel-wall oedema from HAE causes the colicky pain; isolated GI workup misses the unifying systemic diagnosis. Would be correct only with isolated GI symptoms and no angioedema (Source: ASCIA: HAE).

options.text: Commence daily oral tranexamic acid as immediate definitive long-term prophylaxis without C1 inhibitor testing or specialist immunology input at this presentation
options.rationale: Long-term HAE prophylaxis decisions require confirmed diagnosis and specialist input; tranexamic acid is sometimes used in children but is not empirical first-line and does not address the acute attack. Would be correct only after confirmed diagnosis and specialist review (Source: ASCIA: HAE).

explanation.summary: Recurrent non-urticarial angioedema lasting days, with abdominal pain, unresponsive to adrenaline/steroids/antihistamines, with a positive family history and low C4 is HAE; confirm with C1 inhibitor antigenic level and function and treat acute attacks with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant (ASCIA: Hereditary angioedema).
key_points: Low C4 between attacks is a useful screening clue (ASCIA).
Bradykinin-mediated - adrenaline/antihistamines/steroids ineffective (ASCIA).
Long-term prophylaxis options: C1-INH replacement, attenuated androgens (rarely in children), tranexamic acid, lanadelumab (specialist) (ASCIA).
explanation.pearls: Family history of fatal 'throat swelling' is a near-pathognomonic red flag for HAE - always ask about it in recurrent angioedema.

subtopic_detail: Hereditary angioedema versus allergic angioedema in a paediatric patient

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to a tertiary paediatric ED with a 4-day history of progressive fever, malaise, facial swelling and a widespread morbilliform rash that started on the trunk and spread to the limbs and face. He was started on carbamazepine 5 weeks ago for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. There is no preceding URTI, no new foodssect exposure. On arrival temperature is 38.9 deg C, HR 122, RR 24, SpO2 97% RA, BP 110/65.

Examination shows facial oedema, a confluent erythematous morbilliform eruption covering 70 percent of the body surface area without Nikolsky sign or epidermal sloughing, no mucositis, and palpable cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Investigations: WCC 18.0 x10^9/L with 12% eosinophils, ALT 320 U/L, ALP 250 U/L, creatinine 95 micromol/L (baseline 55), CRP 90 mg/L. Blood film shows atypical lymphocytes.

data_table.Examination: Facial oedema; confluent morbilliform rash 70% BSA; no Nikolsky, no mucositis; generalised lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.0 (12% eosinophils), ALT 320, ALP 250, creatinine 95 (baseline 55), CRP 90; atypical lymphocytes on film

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue carbamazepine at the current dose, treat as a self-limiting viral exanthem with supportive paracetamol and oral cetirizine, and review in clinic in 7 days
options.rationale: DRESS triad (drug exposure, eosinophilia, organ involvement) with facial oedema is diagnostic; continuing the trigger worsens organ injury. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions).

options.text: Stop carbamazepine immediately, admit for organ-function monitoring, commence systemic corticosteroid (e.g. prednisolone) and consult dermatology and immunology; document the reaction and avoid aromatic anticonvulsants
options.rationale: DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) typically presents 2-8 weeks after starting culprit drugs (aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, allopurinol, vancomycin); definitive management is immediate withdrawal of the culprit, admission for organ surveillance, systemic corticosteroid for moderate-severe disease and specialist input; cross-reactivity among aromatic anticonvulsants is well documented (eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions; ASCIA: Drug allergy in children; DermNet NZ: DRESS).

options.text: Diagnose Stevens-Johnson syndrome based on fever and rash and arrange transfer to a tertiary burns unit for crystalloid fluid resuscitation and burns-style dressing care
options.rationale: SJS/TEN is characterised by epidermal sloughing, Nikolsky sign and mucositis; none present here. Would be correct with mucositis and skin detachment (Source: DermNet NZ: SJS).

options.text: Diagnose incomplete Kawasaki disease, commence IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin and obtain urgent echocardiography to exclude coronary artery aneurysms
options.rationale: Kawasaki requires fever 5 days plus specific criteria and would not explain eosinophilia or a 5-week post-drug temporal link. Would be correct with fever 5 days plus 4-of-5 criteria (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki).

options.text: Switch carbamazepine to phenytoin at an equivalent maintenance dose and monitor liver function tests weekly without specific dermatology or immunology referral
options.rationale: Aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital) cross-react in DRESS and SJS/TEN; switching within class risks recurrence. Would never be correct; switch to a non-aromatic agent (Source: ASCIA Drug Allergy in Children).

explanation.summary: DRESS is a delayed (2-8 week) systemic drug hypersensitivity with fever, morbilliform rash, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ involvement (commonly hepatitis); management is immediate culprit withdrawal, organ surveillance, systemic corticosteroid for moderate-severe disease, and avoidance of aromatic-anticonvulsant cross-reactors (eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions).
key_points: Triggers: aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, allopurinol, vancomycin (ASCIA).
RegiSCAR criteria help score probability (DermNet NZ: DRESS).
Mortality up to 10% from hepatitis or reactivation of HHV-6 (DermNet NZ).
explanation.pearls: HLA-B*15:02 carriage (more common in some Asian ancestries) raises carbamazepine SJS/TEN risk - screen where indicated by ethnicity per Australian Medicines Handbook.

subtopic_detail: DRESS syndrome recognition after anticonvulsant exposure

stem:
A 15-year-old girl with a 14-week history of daily widespread itchy wheals appearing without identifiable trigger and lasting less than 24 hours per individual lesion, with occasional lip swelling, is reviewed in a paediatric allergy clinic. She has been taking cetirizine 10 mg daily for 8 weeks with partial benefit but daily lesions continue and sleep is broken. She has no anaphylaxis, no respiratory or cardiovascular features, no joint pain, no fever and no systemic upset.

Investigations show normal FBC, normal CRP, normal ESR, normal LFTs, normal TSH and negative coeliac serology. There is no preceding infection and no new medication. There is no clear physical trigger such as heat, cold, pressure or exercise. Symptoms are interfering with her schoolwork and mood.

data_table.History: 14 weeks daily wheals <24 hours each; occasional lip swelling; no anaphylaxis or systemic features
data_table.Trial: Cetirizine 10 mg daily for 8 weeks - partial response only
data_table.Investigations: FBC, CRP, ESR, LFTs, TSH, coeliac serology all normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue cetirizine 10 mg daily at the standard dose and add a 6-week course of oral prednisolone daily with no taper, then reassess for biologic therapy
options.rationale: Long-term oral steroids cause adverse effects without sustained benefit and high relapse on withdrawal in chronic urticaria. Would be correct only as a short bridging course in severe flares (Source: ASCIA: Chronic Urticaria).

options.text: Up-titrate the non-sedating H1 antihistamine to up to fourfold the standard dose (e.g. cetirizine 40 mg/day or equivalent) and review at 4 weeks before considering omalizumab
options.rationale: ASCIA and international urticaria guidance recommend stepwise up-dosing of a non-sedating H1 antihistamine to up to fourfold the standard dose for chronic spontaneous urticaria failing standard-dose therapy, with omalizumab as third-line for refractory disease (ASCIA: Chronic urticaria; EAACI/GA2LEN/WAO guideline endorsed by ASCIA).

options.text: Add a sedating antihistamine such as promethazine at bedtime as the primary add-on therapy for chronic urticaria refractory to standard-dose cetirizine
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines have cognitive and developmental concerns in children and are not preferred add-on; up-titration of non-sedating is preferred. Would be correct as adjunct at bedtime for severe sleep disturbance (Source: ASCIA: Chronic Urticaria).

options.text: Start intramuscular adrenaline 0.3 mg twice weekly as suppressive therapy until the wheals subside, with a written ASCIA Anaphylaxis Action Plan for school staff
options.rationale: Adrenaline has no role in chronic urticaria; it is reserved for acute anaphylaxis. Would never be correct (Source: ASCIA).

options.text: Commence ciclosporin in divided doses as the preferred next-line agent before any consideration of antihistamine up-titration or biologic omalizumab therapy
options.rationale: Ciclosporin is fourth-line after both up-titrated antihistamine and omalizumab fail. Would be correct only at that step (Source: ASCIA: Chronic Urticaria).

explanation.summary: Chronic spontaneous urticaria failing standard-dose non-sedating H1 antihistamine is managed by stepwise up-titration of the non-sedating antihistamine to up to fourfold the standard dose; omalizumab is reserved for those who do not respond (ASCIA: Chronic urticaria).
key_points: Avoid systemic corticosteroids for chronic urticaria - relapse on withdrawal (ASCIA).
Investigations beyond FBC/CRP/TFT only if specific clinical suspicion (ASCIA).
Omalizumab is PBS-listed in Australia for chronic spontaneous urticaria refractory to up-titrated H1 antihistamine.
explanation.pearls: Urticaria with INDIVIDUAL lesions lasting >24 hours, purpura or systemic features should prompt evaluation for urticarial vasculitis.

stem:
A previously well, immunocompetent 4-year-old boy is brought to ED on day 4 of varicella. The parents report new escalating severe pain in the left thigh disproportionate to skin appearance, a fresh fever spike to 39.6 deg C after defervescence yesterday, and reduced weight-bearing. He has not been on ibuprofen. On examination he is unwell-appearing, HR 160, RR 36, SpO2 97% RA, BP 88/50, capillary refill 3 seconds and cool peripheries.

Over the left antero-medial thigh there is a 6 cm area of dusky violaceous skin around two coalesced varicella lesions, exquisite tenderness extending beyond the visible edge, indurated subcutaneous tissue and no crepitus. There are typical varicella lesions at multiple stages elsewhere. WCC 22 x10^9/L with left shift, CRP 280 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L (baseline 45), Na 132 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6, HR 160, RR 36, SpO2 97% RA, BP 88/50, CRT 3 s
data_table.Examination: 6 cm dusky violaceous patch around varicella lesions on left thigh; tenderness beyond visible edge; indurated subcutaneous tissue; no crepitus
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 (left shift), CRP 280, lactate 4.2, creatinine 80 (baseline 45), Na 132

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Continue oral aciclovir six-hourly, observe in the short-stay unit for 4 hours and discharge home if the pain settles with simple analgesia and reassurance
options.rationale: Invasive bacterial soft-tissue infection complicating varicella with septic shock physiology - discharge risks death; this is the missed-nec-fasc anti-pattern. Would be correct only for simple post-varicella superinfection without shock (Source: RCH CPG: Necrotising Fasciitis).

options.text: Resuscitate with crystalloid, administer empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering Group A streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus (including clindamycin for toxin suppression) and arrange urgent surgical assessment for source control
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, induration beyond the visible margin, fresh fever after defervescence on day 4 of varicella and septic shock physiology indicate invasive Group A streptococcal soft-tissue infection (potentially necrotising fasciitis); resuscitation, empirical broad cover including clindamycin for toxin suppression and urgent surgical exploration are mandatory (RCH CPG: Cellulitis; eTG: Necrotising soft tissue infection; RCH CPG: Sepsis).

options.text: Apply topical mupirocin 2% ointment three times daily to the dusky area and commence oral cefalexin six-hourly for presumed impetiginised varicella lesions
options.rationale: Topical and oral therapy are inadequate for invasive soft-tissue infection with septic shock physiology. Would be correct only for localised cellulitis without systemic features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as definitive monotherapy for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome without empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics or surgical input
options.rationale: IVIG is an adjunct in streptococcal TSS and nec fasc but does not replace early empirical IV antibiotics and surgical source control. Would be correct as adjunct after antibiotics and source control commenced (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Obtain urgent MRI of the left thigh with contrast to characterise fascial involvement before commencing intravenous antibiotics, fluid resuscitation or surgical consultation
options.rationale: Nec fasc is a clinical diagnosis; imaging must not delay resuscitation, antibiotics or surgery. Would be correct only as a deferred adjunct if uncertain after surgical exploration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Worsening pain disproportionate to skin findings, fresh fever after defervescence, induration beyond visible margins and septic shock on day 4 of varicella signal invasive Group A streptococcal soft-tissue infection (possible necrotising fasciitis); management is resuscitation, empirical broad antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression, and urgent surgical exploration (eTG: Necrotising soft tissue infection).
key_points: Varicella is a strong risk factor for invasive GAS soft-tissue infection (RCH CPG).
Clindamycin added for exotoxin suppression (eTG).
Imaging must not delay source control (eTG).
explanation.pearls: NSAID exposure has been epidemiologically associated with increased severity of GAS soft-tissue infection in varicella - paracetamol is preferred for varicella fever in Australian paediatric practice.

subtopic_detail: Varicella complication in an immunocompetent child requiring escalation

stem:
An 8-year-old boy presents to a tertiary paediatric ED on day 3 of a febrile illness with progressive painful rash. He was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 9 days ago for recurrent UTI. Over the past 24 hours he has developed conjunctival redness with photophobia, painful oral erosions, dysphagia and dusky atypical targetoid macules on the trunk and face that are becoming confluent.

On examination temperature is 39.0 deg C, HR 140, RR 30, SpO2 96% RA, BP 95/55. There are haemorrhagic crusted lips, fibrinous oral mucosal erosions, conjunctival injection with serous discharge, urethral meatal erosion, and dusky atypical targetoid lesions over approximately 18 percent of body surface area with Nikolsky sign positive in two areas. Investigations show WCC 12 x10^9/L, CRP 70 mg/L, ALT 85 U/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L (baseline 50), Na 134 mmol/L, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. He has no immune deficiency and is otherwise well-grown. The retrieval team and burns unit are en route.

data_table.Examination: Haemorrhagic crusted lips, fibrinous oral erosions, conjunctivitis, urethral erosion; dusky atypical targetoid lesions ~18% BSA; Nikolsky positive
data_table.Investigations: WCC 12, CRP 70, ALT 85, creatinine 90 (baseline 50), Na 134, HCO3 18

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Cease trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole immediately, transfer to a centre with paediatric burns/intensive-care capability with ophthalmology and dermatology input, commence supportive care (fluid resuscitation, temperature control, analgesia, sterile non-adherent dressings, mucosal care), and document drug allergy and consider specialist-directed immunomodulation
options.rationale: SJS/TEN is a dermatological emergency - immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single highest-impact intervention and improves mortality; supportive care equivalent to burns management, multidisciplinary input (paediatric ICU, burns, ophthalmology to prevent symblepharon, dermatology) and consideration of specialist-directed immunomodulation (e.g. ciclosporin, IVIG, TNF-alpha inhibitor) are the standard approach (eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions; ANZBA paediatric SJS/TEN consensus; DermNet NZ: SJS).

options.text: Continue trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole at half dose, commence oral prednisolone daily with topical chlorhexidine 0.05% to mucosal surfaces twice daily, and admit for 24 hours of fluid balance and pain monitoring before reassessment
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug is unequivocally harmful in SJS/TEN; oral steroid monotherapy alone does not change mortality and chlorhexidine to denuded mucosa injures further. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: SCAR).

options.text: Treat as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome with intravenous flucloxacillin six-hourly plus encourage oral hydration with maintenance fluids, paracetamol for fever and observation in the ED short-stay unit for 24 hours before discharge
options.rationale: Staphylococcal scalded skin occurs predominantly in young infants, has minimal mucosal involvement and intact mucosae; this case has temporal drug link plus mucositis. Would be correct in an infant with intact mucosae and positive culture (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Diagnose incomplete Kawasaki disease, commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours and high-dose aspirin in four divided doses with echocardiography on day 3 of admission to exclude coronary aneurysms
options.rationale: Kawasaki has polymorphous rash and mucosal change but not skin sloughing, Nikolsky sign or atypical targets, and lacks a culprit drug link. Would be correct with fever 5 days plus Kawasaki criteria (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki).

options.text: Perform a 4 mm punch biopsy of involved skin in ED, send for routine histology and direct immunofluorescence, and defer all therapy including culprit drug withdrawal and transfer until the histology result is available
options.rationale: Biopsy confirms but must not delay culprit withdrawal, transfer or supportive care in a mucocutaneous emergency. Would be correct as adjunct after initial stabilisation (Source: DermNet NZ: SJS).

explanation.summary: SJS/TEN management priorities are: immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug, transfer to a specialist centre with burns and PICU expertise, multidisciplinary support including ophthalmology to prevent ocular sequelae, supportive care and specialist-directed immunomodulation; culprit withdrawal is the single highest-impact intervention (eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions).
key_points: Sulfa antibiotics, aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, NSAIDs are common triggers (eTG; ASCIA).
Ophthalmology input within 24 hours reduces chronic ocular morbidity (DermNet NZ).
SCORTEN at 24 hours and 72 hours stratifies mortality risk (DermNet NZ).
explanation.pearls: Always document SJS/TEN drug allergy in the eHealth record (My Health Record) and on a medical alert bracelet - re-challenge can be lethal.

subtopic_detail: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis early management in a child

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to his GP for a pre-kinder health check. He is otherwise well, growing along the 50th centile, fully immunised, with no exercise intolerance, syncope, cyanosis or breathlessness on play. There is no family history of sudden cardiac death or congenital heart disease, no recent sore throats, no joint pains, and no rashes. On examination he is pink and well perfused with normal femoral pulses, no thrill, a quiet S1 and S2 with no fixed splitting, and a soft musical murmur best heard at the lower left sternal edge while supine.

The murmur has a distinctly vibratory or twangy quality, occupies early to mid-systole, is grade 2/6 in intensity, softens considerably on sitting up, and almost disappears with the Valsalva manoeuvre. There is no diastolic component and no radiation to the neck or axilla.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 95/58 mmHg right arm
data_table.Examination: Pink, no clubbing or cyanosis, femoral pulses equal to brachials, apex non-displaced, no thrill, no diastolic component, no radiation to neck or axilla
data_table.Growth: Height and weight on 50th centile, head circumference appropriate

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that this is a Still's vibratory innocent murmur and document review at routine health checks; no investigations or paediatric cardiology referral are required
options.rationale: Vibratory grade 1-2 early systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge in a well 2-7-year-old that softens with Valsalva and on sitting is the classic Still's murmur. Per RCH CPG: Heart murmurs, an asymptomatic child with all innocent-murmur features (no diastolic component, no thrill, soft, varies with posture, normal pulses) does not require ECG, echo or referral.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Heart murmurs in children

options.text: Refer for paediatric cardiology assessment and echocardiogram because innocent murmurs cannot be distinguished from pathological murmurs on examination alone
options.rationale: AU primary-care guidance accepts clinical diagnosis of Still's murmur when all innocent features are present; routine echo is over-investigation. Would be correct only with any red-flag feature (diastolic component, harsh quality, abnormal pulses, failure to thrive) (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Arrange ECG and ASOT today and treat as possible acute rheumatic carditis pending results
options.rationale: No Jones features and no sore throat history; investigating ARF in an asymptomatic child with classic innocent murmur is inappropriate. Would be correct only in high-risk populations with sore throat history and Jones features (Source: RHDAustralia).

options.text: Arrange exercise stress testing to exclude hypertrophic cardiomyopathy before clearing for kindergarten sport
options.rationale: HCM has a harsh systolic murmur that INCREASES with Valsalva (opposite of this), often family history of sudden death. Would be correct only with that profile (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Document the murmur as a small ventricular septal defect and arrange echocardiogram within one month
options.rationale: Small VSD murmur is harsh, pansystolic, often with thrill, and does not soften with Valsalva; the described musical dynamic murmur is innocent. Would be correct only with the pansystolic VSD profile (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Innocent murmurs are common in well children. Still's is the prototypical vibratory early-systolic LLSE murmur of 2 to 7 year olds. Innocent murmurs are soft (grade 1 to 2), systolic only, position-dependent, and accompanied by normal pulses, S2, growth, and no symptoms.
key_points: Innocent murmurs: soft, systolic, sensitive to position, single S2, symptomless, small (grade 1 to 2)
Still's: vibratory LLSE, 2 to 7 years
Venous hum: continuous infraclavicular, abolished supine
Pulmonary flow: ULSE, blowing, often in adolescents
Carey-Coombs: mid-diastolic apical, ARF carditis
explanation.pearls: Red flags warranting echo: diastolic murmur, grade 3 or louder, harsh quality, abnormal S2, symptoms, abnormal pulses, syndromic features, or family history of sudden death.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Heart murmurs in children

stem:
An 8-month-old boy with known unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot presents to a regional ED with his mother. He is awaiting elective surgical repair scheduled in 6 weeks. This morning after a feed he became inconsolable, cried vigorously, and then turned a dusky blue colour with deep, rapid breathing. The episode has been going on for around 10 minutes by the time he reaches the resuscitation cubicle.

He has not vomited, has had no recent fever, and there is no diarrhoea or reduced wet nappies. Baseline SpO2 is usually 88 to 92% per cardiology letters. On arrival he is markedly cyanosed centrally with extremities mottled, breathing deeply at 70 per minute, and the previously loud harsh ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge is now barely audible. He has good IV access from the ambulance. His weight today is 7.8 kg and he has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 188 bpm, RR 70 /min, SpO2 62% on 15 L/min via non-rebreather, BP 78/46 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed, irritable but rousable, deep Kussmaul-like respirations, soft 1/6 ESM ULSE (previously 4/6), CRT 4 seconds peripherally
data_table.Background: Known TOF, awaiting repair, baseline SpO2 88 to 92%, no prior tet spells documented

lead_in: After applying high-flow oxygen, which single next intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous adenosine rapid push at the paediatric SVT dose followed by saline flush
options.rationale: Adenosine treats SVT, not a hypercyanotic spell; rhythm is sinus tachycardia from right-to-left shunting. Would be correct in narrow-complex SVT not responding to vagal manoeuvres (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot).

options.text: Knee-chest positioning with IV morphine slow push
options.rationale: First-line management of a tet spell is knee-chest positioning to raise systemic vascular resistance plus IV or IM morphine 0.1 mg/kg to abolish hyperpnoea and reduce infundibular spasm, as per RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot and AHA scientific statement.

options.text: IV furosemide to offload the right ventricle now
options.rationale: Furosemide reduces preload and worsens right-to-left shunting in a tet spell; volume expansion not depletion is needed. Would never be correct in a tet spell (Source: RCH CPG: ToF).

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion peripherally
options.rationale: PGE1 maintains ductal patency in duct-dependent neonatal lesions; at 8 months the duct is closed. Would be correct in a neonate with duct-dependent cyanotic lesion (Source: BMJ Best Practice: ToF).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Tetralogy of Fallot

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate bolus before any other intervention
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for documented severe acidosis after positioning, oxygen, fluids and morphine have failed. Would be correct only as final step in refractory tet spell with confirmed acidosis (Source: AHA scientific statement).

explanation.summary: A tet spell is a sudden increase in right-to-left shunt through the VSD due to infundibular spasm or a drop in SVR. The murmur softens because pulmonary flow falls. Stepwise management: calm the child, knee-chest position, 100% oxygen, IV fluid bolus 10 to 20 mL/kg, IV or IM morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then IV propranolol 0.1 mg/kg or phenylephrine if refractory.
key_points: Murmur softens during spell (less pulmonary flow)
Knee-chest raises SVR, reducing right-to-left shunt
Morphine reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm
Avoid agents that drop SVR or preload
Refractory: propranolol, phenylephrine, intubation, ECMO, urgent surgery
explanation.pearls: Beta-blockers are used both acutely and as a bridge to surgery to prevent spells; never give inotropes that increase contractility (worsens infundibular spasm).

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Tetralogy of Fallot

stem:
A 10-week-old term male infant is brought to a paediatric clinic by his parents because of poor feeding and slow weight gain. They report that he sweats profusely during breastfeeds, often pauses to catch his breath after a few sucks, and takes more than 40 minutes per feed. He has dropped from the 50th to the 9th weight centile over 6 weeks.

There has been no cyanosis, no syncope, and no fevers. At his newborn baby check a soft murmur had been noted and an echocardiogram at 4 weeks showed a moderately large perimembranous ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunt and mild left atrial and ventricular dilatation. He is now visibly tachypnoeic at rest, with intercostal recession, a hyperdynamic precordium, a 3/6 harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, and a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 170 bpm, RR 64 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 82/48 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Tachypnoeic with subcostal and intercostal recession, hyperdynamic precordium, 3/6 PSM LLSE with thrill, hepatomegaly 3 cm, mild bibasal crackles
data_table.Growth: Weight dropped from 50th to 9th centile since birth
data_table.Echo (4 weeks): Moderate perimembranous VSD, left-to-right shunt, mild LA and LV dilatation, normal LV function

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial medical management?

options.text: Reassure parents and review in 3 months expecting spontaneous closure
options.rationale: Spontaneous closure is common only for small muscular VSDs; failure to thrive and heart failure demand treatment. Would be correct only for a small muscular VSD without haemodynamic features (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Failure in Children).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children

options.text: Commence oral propranolol three times daily and high-energy formula
options.rationale: Beta-blockers are not first-line in infant left-to-right shunt failure; diuretic plus afterload reduction is standard. Would be correct in tet-spell prophylaxis or other specific indications (Source: BMJ Best Practice: VSD).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

options.text: Commence oral furosemide BD and an ACE inhibitor with high-energy feeds
options.rationale: Standard medical therapy of large VSD with heart failure in infancy is loop diuretic plus ACE inhibitor for afterload reduction plus calorie-dense feeds, with surgical closure typically before 6 to 12 months if failure to thrive or pulmonary hypertension persists, per RCH CPG and BMJ Best Practice.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children
BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
options.rationale: PGE1 is for duct-dependent lesions; a VSD with left-to-right shunt does not depend on the duct. Would be correct in duct-dependent cyanotic lesions (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

options.text: Commence oxygen therapy at 2 L/min via nasal prongs for resting tachypnoea
options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen lowers PVR and worsens pulmonary overcirculation in a VSD; this is the textbook iatrogenic error in left-to-right shunts. Would be correct only for documented hypoxaemia from another cause (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Failure).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children

explanation.summary: Symptomatic large VSD presents at 6 to 12 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance falls and left-to-right shunt increases. Features include tachypnoea, sweating with feeds, hepatomegaly and failure to thrive. Medical management is loop diuretic plus ACE inhibitor plus high-energy feeds, with surgical closure for ongoing failure to thrive, pulmonary hypertension, or large unrestricted shunt before fixed pulmonary vascular disease develops.
key_points: Murmur is harsh pansystolic LLSE, often with thrill
Furosemide 1 to 2 mg/kg BD plus ACE inhibitor (captopril or enalapril)
Avoid supplemental O2 (drops PVR, worsens shunt)
Surgery before fixed pulmonary vascular disease
Small muscular VSDs often close spontaneously
explanation.pearls: Symptoms typically appear at 4 to 8 weeks because pulmonary vascular resistance must fall before left-to-right shunting becomes haemodynamically significant.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children
BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

stem:
A preterm male infant born at 27 weeks gestation is now day 6 of life on the neonatal intensive care unit. Birthweight was 950 g. He was initially ventilated for surfactant-deficient lung disease and is currently on synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation with FiO2 0.35 and mean airway pressure 9 cm H2O. Over the past 24 hours he has required escalating ventilatory support, has developed widening pulse pressure, bounding femoral pulses, and a continuous murmur at the upper left sternal edge.

He has been passing only 0.8 mL/kg/h of urine despite normal fluid intake. A formal echocardiogram performed this morning confirms a haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus with a 2.4 mm internal diameter, left-to-right shunt, left atrium to aortic root ratio of 1.8, and reversed end-diastolic flow in the post-ductal descending aorta. Renal function and platelet count are within accepted neonatal limits and there is no evidence of necrotising enterocolitis or active intraventricular haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR per vent 50, SpO2 92% on FiO2 0.35, BP 48/22 mmHg (wide pulse pressure), MAP 31 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bounding peripheral pulses, hyperdynamic precordium, continuous machinery murmur ULSE, lungs with diffuse crackles
data_table.Echo: PDA 2.4 mm, LA:Ao 1.8, reversed end-diastolic flow descending aorta, no other structural disease
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 220 x10^9/L, creatinine 55 micromol/L, urine output 0.8 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
options.rationale: PGE1 keeps the duct open in duct-dependent lesions; here a haemodynamically significant PDA needs closure, not patency. Would be correct only for duct-dependent neonatal cyanotic lesions (Source: RCH NICU PDA Guideline).
source_refs: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus

options.text: Restrict fluids to a conservative ml/kg/day target and continue conservative management
options.rationale: Conservative is reasonable for non-haemodynamically significant PDA; this infant has clear significance (escalating ventilation, wide pulse pressure, reversed diastolic flow). Would be correct only for small non-significant PDAs (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

options.text: Refer for surgical PDA ligation now as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Surgical ligation is reserved for failure or contraindication of medical therapy; pharmacological closure is first-line. Would be correct after failed COX-inhibitor course or contraindication (Source: RCH NICU CPG: PDA).
source_refs: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus

options.text: Course of ibuprofen or indometacin for pharmacological PDA closure
options.rationale: In preterm infants with haemodynamically significant PDA and no contraindication (NEC, active IVH, renal failure, thrombocytopenia), a course of ibuprofen or indometacin is first-line pharmacological closure, per RCH NICU CPG: PDA.
source_refs: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus
BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

options.text: Commence oral paracetamol six-hourly indefinitely as definitive closure agent
options.rationale: Paracetamol is an emerging second-line as a 3-7 day course when COX inhibitors are contraindicated, not indefinite or first-line. Would be correct as a short course with contraindication to indometacin/ibuprofen (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

explanation.summary: Haemodynamically significant PDA in preterm neonates causes pulmonary overcirculation, prolonged ventilation, IVH, NEC and BPD. Echo criteria for significance include diameter > 1.5 mm, LA:Ao > 1.4, reversed diastolic flow in descending aorta. First-line closure is a COX-inhibitor course (ibuprofen or indometacin) or paracetamol if contraindicated, with surgical ligation if pharmacological therapy fails. Term PDA usually closes spontaneously within 72 hours; persistent term PDA is managed by elective device closure beyond infancy.
key_points: Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg then 5 mg/kg at 24 and 48 h is now preferred (less renal toxicity than indometacin)
Contraindications: NEC, IVH, oliguria, thrombocytopenia, sepsis
Surgical ligation if medical fails and PDA remains significant
Term infants: catheter device closure beyond infancy
Echo confirms significance before treatment
explanation.pearls: Indometacin reduces IVH rates but at the cost of more transient oliguria; ibuprofen has become the more widely used agent in Australian NICUs.

sources.label: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus
BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

stem:
A 6-day-old term male infant is brought to a regional ED by his mother. He was born by uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery at 39+2 weeks with birthweight 3.4 kg, passed all routine newborn checks, and was discharged at 36 hours of life. Over the past 24 hours he has fed poorly, has been increasingly lethargic, and his mother noticed his legs looking mottled and feeling cool while his upper body remained warm.

He has had no fevers and no vomiting. On arrival he is pale, lethargic, and grunting. Brachial pulses are easily palpable bilaterally, but the femoral pulses are absent. Pre-ductal SpO2 on the right hand is 96%, while post-ductal SpO2 on the right foot is 84%. Blood pressure in the right arm is 78/44 mmHg and in the right leg is 42/28 mmHg, giving a clear upper-to-lower limb gradient. The liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin and there is metabolic acidosis on the venous blood gas.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4 deg C, HR 180 bpm, RR 70 /min, BP arm 78/44 / leg 42/28 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Absent femoral pulses, brachial pulses present, mottled cool legs, warm upper body, hepatomegaly 3 cm, single loud S2
data_table.VBG: pH 7.18, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, HCO3 12 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management while awaiting transfer?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide and conservative fluid restriction
options.rationale: Diuresis is adjunctive for pulmonary congestion but does not address lethal ductal closure in duct-dependent systemic circulation. Would be correct only as adjunct once PGE1 has restored ductal flow (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cardiology).

options.text: Intramuscular vitamin K 1 mg and oral feeds withheld pending surgical review
options.rationale: Vitamin K does not treat duct closure; PGE1 is required to reopen the duct. Would be correct as routine post-birth, not as immediate management of duct-dependent shock (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation of the aorta

options.text: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen titrated to SpO2 above 95%
options.rationale: Supplemental O2 further constricts the ductus and accelerates collapse in duct-dependent systemic circulation; target SpO2 is 85-95 percent, not over 95. Would be correct only with confirmed non-cardiac hypoxaemia (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Intravenous adenosine rapid push to terminate suspected supraventricular tachycardia
options.rationale: No narrow-complex tachycardia described; differential pulses and saturation differential are diagnostic of coarctation. Would be correct in SVT (Source: RCH CPG: SVT).

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion via secure IV access
options.rationale: Duct-dependent systemic circulation from coarctation or interrupted aortic arch presents at day 5 to 10 with shock as the duct closes; PGE1 at 0.01 to 0.05 microg/kg/min reopens the duct and is the immediate life-saving therapy, per RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiology and BMJ Best Practice.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation of the aorta

explanation.summary: Critical coarctation presents at the end of the first week as the duct closes, producing shock, absent femoral pulses, upper-to-lower limb BP gradient, pre/post-ductal SpO2 differential, and metabolic acidosis. Immediate management is PGE1 infusion (commonly 0.01 to 0.05 microg/kg/min titrated), correction of acidosis, careful fluid resuscitation, and urgent transfer for surgical repair. Side effects of PGE1 include apnoea, fever, hypotension, and flushing; be prepared to intubate.
key_points: Duct-dependent systemic: coarctation, interrupted arch, critical AS, HLHS
PGE1 0.01 to 0.05 microg/kg/min IV
Apnoea is a common side effect; have airway ready
Avoid hyperoxia (constricts duct)
Definitive: surgical or catheter repair
explanation.pearls: If the duct closes before diagnosis, the infant can deteriorate from well to moribund within hours; any unwell neonate in the first 2 weeks needs femoral pulses and 4-limb BPs.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation of the aorta

stem:
A 5-month-old previously well girl is brought to a metropolitan ED by ambulance because of poor feeding and pallor for 3 hours. Her mother reports that she felt the baby's chest racing earlier this morning and noticed she was breathing fast and looking sweaty during a feed. There has been no fever, no diarrhoea, and no preceding viral illness over the past week.

On arrival to resus she is pale, mottled, and lethargic but responsive to voice. Femoral and brachial pulses are present but extremely rapid and impossible to count manually. A 12-lead ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 285 bpm with no clearly visible P waves and a constant RR interval. There are no delta waves on the resting trace once an experienced cardiologist reviews her baseline ECG from a previous well-child check. She has good peripheral IV access placed by paramedics en route. She is not yet hypotensive and remains alert.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 285 bpm (ECG), RR 60 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 76/48 mmHg
data_table.ECG: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia, rate 285, no visible P waves, constant RR, no QRS widening
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled, responsive, CRT 3 seconds, no hepatomegaly yet, lungs clear

lead_in: After applying continuous cardiac monitoring and defibrillation pads, what is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Crushed ice to the face for 30 seconds
options.rationale: In a haemodynamically stable infant with SVT, the diving reflex provoked by an ice bag to the face is the recommended vagal manoeuvre and can be attempted first while preparing adenosine, per RCH CPG: SVT and ANZCOR guideline 12.6.
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

options.text: Immediate unsynchronised defibrillation now
options.rationale: Unsynchronised defibrillation is for VF/pulseless VT; unstable SVT needs synchronised cardioversion at 0.5-1 J/kg. Would be correct in pulseless VT or VF (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

options.text: Intravenous verapamil by slow IV push
options.rationale: Verapamil is contraindicated under 12 months (risk of refractory hypotension and cardiac arrest). Would be correct only in older children with stable SVT and no Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion).

options.text: Oral propranolol as a stat dose
options.rationale: Oral beta-blockade is for chronic prevention, not acute termination in an unwell infant. Would be correct only as maintenance after acute conversion (Source: RCH CPG: SVT).

options.text: Right carotid sinus massage for 10 seconds
options.rationale: Carotid sinus massage is not used in infants; ice to the face is the recommended vagal manoeuvre at this age. Would be correct only in older children/adolescents and adults (Source: ANZCOR 12.6).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

explanation.summary: Infant SVT typically presents as poor feeding, pallor and tachypnoea with rates over 220 bpm and a narrow complex on ECG. In the stable infant: vagal manoeuvre (ice to face) then IV adenosine 0.1 mg/kg, repeat 0.2 mg/kg, then 0.3 mg/kg up to a single max of 12 mg, given rapidly into a large vein with saline flush. In the unstable infant proceed straight to synchronised DC cardioversion 0.5 to 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg.
key_points: Stable: ice to face, then adenosine 0.1 then 0.2 mg/kg
Unstable: synchronised cardioversion 0.5 to 1 J/kg
Avoid verapamil under 12 months
Maintenance with propranolol or flecainide guided by cardiology
Check for WPW on sinus ECG after termination
explanation.pearls: Adenosine causes a brief, alarming asystolic pause; counsel the team, have monitor/defib pads on, and use a 3-way tap so the saline flush immediately follows the bolus.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is referred to a paediatric cardiology outpatient clinic after two episodes of exertional syncope. The first occurred while sprinting at school athletics, with a brief loss of consciousness during which her friends say her limbs jerked for around 10 seconds before she came round confused for 30 seconds. The second was while jumping in a pool 6 weeks later.

There is no history of typical post-ictal phase, tongue biting, or incontinence. A maternal uncle died suddenly in his 20s while swimming; the family was told it was drowning.
