options.rationale: MCUG is invasive (catheter, ionising radiation) and is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound; it is not first-line in the RCH recurrent-UTI pathway. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection

options.text: Commence nightly trimethoprim as long-term prophylaxis without further imaging to delineate cortical scarring or reflux pattern
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is considered after risk stratification (proven high-grade VUR or significant scarring); empirical prophylaxis without imaging is not first-line in the RCH pathway. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection

options.text: DMSA scan in 4 to 6 months after the most recent UTI to detect cortical scarring, reserving MCUG for any abnormal DMSA result
options.rationale: Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; DMSA is not part of the RCH recurrent-UTI imaging cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection

options.text: Repeat renal ultrasound in 12 months and otherwise observe without any further imaging, with watchful waiting and return advice
options.rationale: Deferred imaging is inadequate after recurrent febrile UTI; the RCH pathway calls for a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound now and specialist referral, not a 12-month deferral. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: After recurrent febrile UTI in a young child, the RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric specialist referral. The NICE NG224 algorithm includes DMSA at 4 to 6 months; the RCH CPG has not adopted DMSA in its routine cascade. MCUG is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound. Constipation contributes substantially to recurrence and must be optimised.
key_points: RCH Melbourne recurrent UTI: non-urgent renal tract ultrasound plus paediatric referral
DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE construct, not part of the RCH cascade
MCUG reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound
Optimise constipation - reduces UTI recurrence
Prophylaxis individualised: high-grade VUR, severe scarring, breakthrough UTI
explanation.pearls: If you can fix the constipation you fix the UTI in many of these children.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Urinary tract infection

subtopic_detail: Imaging after a second febrile UTI in a young girl

stem:
A 17-month-old boy attends his GP for delayed 12-month immunisations because the family has been overseas. He is well, immunocompetent, with no chronic illness. His mother is on the bone marrow transplant register and has just commenced cyclophosphamide-based conditioning for an upcoming allogeneic transplant in 4 weeks; she lives in the same household. The boy's 4-year-old sister is also up to date.

His mother is concerned about the safety of his vaccines given her own state and asks the GP for advice. His outstanding 12-month vaccines include MMR, meningococcal ACWY and the third dose of 13vPCV. He has had no recent live vaccines, no immunosuppressive therapy of his own, and no contact with active tuberculosis. The mother's transplant team has been in contact with the family GP and a written summary of household infection-control measures is being prepared.

The mother has had her own pre-transplant influenza, pneumococcal and any catch-up inactivated vaccines administered as advised by haematology. The father is asymptomatic and fully vaccinated.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, HR 108, RR 26.
data_table.Examination: Well child, no rash, no respiratory or other illness.
data_table.Investigations: None indicated for the child.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate advice regarding his catch-up immunisations?

options.text: Defer all of the child's vaccines until after the mother's transplant and engraftment
options.rationale: Deferring all vaccines leaves the immunocompromised mother more vulnerable to vaccine-preventable disease in the home; child should be fully immunised, including most live vaccines. Would never be correct as blanket policy (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Give MMR and varicella as scheduled; routine isolation not required (manage rashes with aciclovir)
options.rationale: MMR and varicella vaccine viruses are not transmitted from immunocompetent vaccinees in routine contact (varicella vaccine virus transmission is rare and only from vesicular rash). Immunising household contacts of immunocompromised people is recommended. Rotavirus is the exception (faecal shedding) and would need hand hygiene precautions; he is too old for rotavirus anyway (NCIRS).

options.text: Replace MMR with an inactivated alternative because of household immunocompromise concerns
options.rationale: No inactivated MMR alternative exists on NIP; MMR vaccine viruses are not transmitted from vaccinees to contacts. Would never be correct (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Give the child oral typhoid (live) vaccine prophylactically because of expected hospital visits
options.rationale: Oral typhoid is not routinely indicated and not part of NIP catch-up; introduces a live oral vaccine inappropriately. Would never be correct (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Give only inactivated vaccines and avoid live vaccines until mother is post-transplant immune-reconstituted
options.rationale: MMR and varicella are NOT contraindicated in household contacts of immunocompromised people; he remains at risk if unprotected. Would never be correct (Source: NCIRS; eviQ).

explanation.summary: Live vaccines are contraindicated IN the immunocompromised person but in general are SAFE for their household contacts (MMR not transmitted; varicella vaccine virus transmission rare and only via vesicular rash). Rotavirus is the practical exception due to faecal shedding - hand hygiene needed for 4-6 weeks. Influenza inactivated is encouraged for household contacts annually.
key_points: Live vaccines contraindicated IN immunocompromised individuals
Household contacts SHOULD be immunised, including MMR and varicella
Manage post-varicella rash with covering/isolation
Rotavirus faecal shedding - hand hygiene precaution for 4-6 weeks
Influenza (inactivated) annually for all household contacts
explanation.pearls: Cocooning protects the immunocompromised; under-immunising the household is the opposite of safe.

subtopic_detail: Live vaccine considerations in a household with immunocompromise

stem:
A 5-month-old breastfed boy attends his GP with his father, who has read 'a lot online' and wants to delay the 6-month vaccines. The mother is supportive of vaccination and has asked the father to discuss it with the doctor. The father is hesitant rather than refusing; his main concerns are that 'too many vaccines at once overload the immune system' and that aluminium adjuvants 'cause autism'.

The infant is otherwise well, growing on the 50th centile, with no medical issues. He had his 2 and 4-month vaccines without adverse events. There is no household medical neglect and the parents otherwise engage with primary care.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile. HR 120, RR 30.
data_table.Examination: Well, growth on 50th centile.
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated.

lead_in: Which approach is most consistent with current Australian NCIRS SKAI and RACGP guidance for vaccine hesitancy?

options.text: Refuse to provide further GP care to the family until the father agrees to the standard immunisation schedule for both of his children
options.rationale: Withholding general care is unethical and not supported by RACGP/NCIRS; trusted continuity is a key driver of eventual acceptance. Would never be correct (Source: RACGP; NCIRS SKAI).

options.text: Motivational-interviewing-style consultation - presumptive language, explore concerns, share tailored evidence on immune-overload and aluminium myths, offer SKAI resources
options.rationale: NCIRS SKAI and RACGP recommend MI-style engagement: presumptive language, exploration of concerns, tailored factual rebuttal of specific myths, a clear clinician recommendation and signposting to reputable resources, with a planned follow-up. Adversarial debate and alternative schedules are less effective.

options.text: Notify child protection because vaccine refusal constitutes medical neglect under mandatory reporting obligations for treating clinicians in this family
options.rationale: Vaccine hesitancy in an otherwise well-cared-for child is not itself medical neglect. Would be correct only with broader documented neglect (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Offer a spaced-out alternative schedule giving only one vaccine per visit to accommodate parental concerns about immune overload from co-administration
options.rationale: Alternative schedules prolong susceptibility, increase visits/pain, and reinforce immune-overload misconception. Would never be correct (Source: NCIRS SKAI).

options.text: Refer to the Family Court to compel vaccination over parental objection
options.rationale: Court orders are a last resort after parental deadlock and other approaches have failed; initial step is shared GP-led discussion. Would be correct only after exhausted negotiation and ongoing risk to child (Source: NCIRS).

explanation.summary: Vaccine hesitancy is best addressed with a presumptive opening, motivational interviewing, exploration of specific concerns, tailored factual rebuttal, an explicit clinician recommendation, and signposting to evidence-based resources (NCIRS SKAI). Maintain the therapeutic relationship; many hesitant parents accept vaccines over time with continuity.
key_points: Presumptive opening: 'Today we'll do the 6-month vaccines.'
Motivational interviewing: explore, affirm, reflect, summarise
Address specific concerns with specific evidence
Make an explicit recommendation - 'I recommend...'
SKAI website is the Australian go-to resource
explanation.pearls: Don't try to win the argument in one visit; you are building a relationship that often takes 2-3 conversations to land.

subtopic_detail: Parental hesitancy about routine childhood vaccination

stem:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to his GP by his mother because of bow legs and reluctance to walk. He was born at term, exclusively breastfed until 12 months without vitamin D supplementation, and has had limited sun exposure as the family wear concealing clothing for cultural reasons and live in a southern Australian city. His diet is otherwise low in dairy.

There is no history of diarrhoea, fatty stools, recurrent infections, fractures or a family history of metabolic bone disease. He is on the 25th centile for length and 50th for weight. On examination he has frontal bossing, widening of the wrists, palpable rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, and genu varum. He has no carpopedal spasm and no seizure activity.

His mother is otherwise well but reports myalgia and fatigue. The infant takes solids three times a day, including iron-fortified cereal, but very little dairy or oily fish. There is no family history of consanguinity, fragility fractures, or genetic bone disease. He has met expected developmental milestones for fine motor and language but has been slower to walk; he took his first independent steps at 16 months and is now unsteady, with frequent falls noticed by his mother. The wrist X-ray was ordered after the GP examined him today and the radiologist phoned through the metaphyseal findings.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, HR 108, RR 26.
data_table.Examination: Frontal bossing, wrist widening, rachitic rosary, genu varum. No tetany. Length 25th centile, weight 50th.
data_table.Investigations: 25-OH vitamin D 18 nmol/L, calcium 2.10 mmol/L (corrected), phosphate 0.9 mmol/L, ALP 920 U/L (markedly elevated), PTH 14.2 pmol/L (high), creatinine 24 micromol/L. Wrist X-ray: cupping and fraying of the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Bisphosphonates orally to correct the bony lower limb deformity
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates have no role in nutritional rickets and may impair mineralisation; deformity usually corrects with vitamin D and calcium repletion. Would never be correct in nutritional rickets (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.text: A single high-dose 'stoss' of colecalciferol 600,000 IU orally with no follow-up
options.rationale: Stoss therapy carries hypercalcaemia risk in young children and limits follow-up biochemistry; daily replacement is safer and standard in Australia. Would be correct only in selected older children with adherence concerns under specialist input (Source: APEG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.text: IV calcium gluconate today and admit for cardiac telemetry monitoring
options.rationale: IV calcium is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, ECG changes); he is asymptomatic. Would be correct with tetany, seizures or ECG changes (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.text: Calcitriol (1,25-OH vitamin D) 0.25 microg daily orally as first-line
options.rationale: Calcitriol is reserved for vitamin D-dependent rickets, CKD and hypoparathyroidism; nutritional deficiency uses colecalciferol because 1-alpha-hydroxylation is intact. Would be correct in CKD or VDDR (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.text: Colecalciferol 1000-2000 IU daily for 3 months, optimise calcium, screen mother
options.rationale: Confirmed nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets (low 25-OH vitamin D <50 nmol/L, raised ALP and PTH, radiographic changes) is treated with colecalciferol 1000-2000 IU daily for 3 months in a toddler, plus 500 mg/day elemental calcium, with sun exposure counselling. Screen the breastfeeding mother because deficient mothers explain the infant's deficiency (RCH CPG Vitamin D; APEG/ASBMR consensus).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency
APEG/ASBMR Australian and New Zealand consensus on vitamin D

explanation.summary: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets is treated with colecalciferol (1000-2000 IU/day for toddlers; 600 IU/day prevention) for 3 months, with calcium intake optimisation and sun exposure counselling. Always screen the breastfeeding mother. The 25-OH vitamin D threshold for deficiency is <50 nmol/L (severe <30 nmol/L).
key_points: 25-OH vitamin D: <30 severe deficient, <50 deficient, 50-75 insufficient
Raised ALP and PTH are early biochemical markers
X-ray: cupping and fraying of metaphyses (wrist, knees, ankles)
Treat with colecalciferol (daily) - not calcitriol - for nutritional rickets
Screen the mother; vitamin D-deficient mothers explain vitamin D-deficient infants
explanation.pearls: If ALP is 'unbelievably high' in a toddler, think rickets before liver. ALP is the most sensitive biochemical sign.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency
APEG/ASBMR Australian and New Zealand consensus on vitamin D

subtopic_detail: Toddler with bow legs and biochemistry suggestive of metabolic bone disease

stem:
A 6-year-old boy (weight 22 kg) with known peanut allergy is brought to a tertiary ED by ambulance 25 minutes after biting a satay skewer at a family function. Within minutes he developed urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting, and audible stridor. He received IM adrenaline 300 microg into the lateral thigh by his parents at the scene and a second IM adrenaline 300 microg by paramedics 6 minutes later, with two boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg en route.

On arrival he is given high-flow oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather and a nebulised adrenaline 5 mg has just been started for persistent stridor. He has had no previous anaphylaxis admission and is not on beta-blockers. Despite these measures he remains hypotensive with ongoing wheeze, persistent stridor, and a flushed mottled appearance ten minutes after the second IM dose. The PICU registrar is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 91% on 15 L/min non-rebreather, BP 72/40 mmHg, T 36.8 deg C
data_table.Examination: Diffuse urticaria, marked lip and periorbital oedema, biphasic stridor, widespread expiratory wheeze, capillary refill 4 seconds, GCS 14 (drowsy but rousable)
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.29, lactate 4.4 mmol/L, K 3.6 mmol/L, glucose 6.1 mmol/L; tryptase taken; ECG sinus tachycardia
data_table.Medications received: IM adrenaline 300 microg x2, 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg x2, nebulised adrenaline 5 mg in progress, high-flow oxygen
data_table.History: Peanut allergy with prior urticaria only, no asthma, no beta-blocker use, fully immunised

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer IV hydrocortisone and IV chlorphenamine 2.5 mg, then reassess at 15 minutes
options.rationale: Steroids and antihistamines do not treat airway/CV collapse and have no role as the next escalation after adrenaline failure. Would be correct only as adjunct after definitive adrenaline (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Third IM adrenaline 300 microg into lateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes
options.rationale: After two or more IM doses without response, refractory anaphylaxis is declared; IV infusion is preferred for sustained titratable effect. Would be correct only if IV access were unavailable (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Commence an IV adrenaline infusion titrated to BP, with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Refractory anaphylaxis (persistent hypotension or airway compromise after at least two IM doses) is treated with a titrated IV adrenaline infusion starting at 0.1 microg/kg/min in a monitored area, with PICU involvement, as per ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines and RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis.
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Give IV glucagon as a bolus to overcome adrenaline-resistant shock from beta-blockade
options.rationale: Glucagon is for refractory anaphylaxis in beta-blocked patients; this child is not on beta-blockers. Would be correct only with documented beta-blocker use (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Give IV hydroxocobalamin for suspected concurrent cyanide-mediated vasodilation today
options.rationale: Hydroxocobalamin is the cyanide-toxicity antidote (smoke inhalation), no role in anaphylaxis. Would be correct only with smoke inhalation and suspected cyanide toxicity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis is failure to respond to two or more IM adrenaline doses. Management is an IV adrenaline infusion in a monitored area (PICU/ED resus) alongside ongoing fluid resuscitation, oxygen, and airway preparation. Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts, not next steps. Glucagon is reserved for beta-blocked patients.
key_points: Refractory anaphylaxis = persistent hypotension or airway compromise after >=2 IM adrenaline doses
Start IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microg/kg/min and titrate
Continuous cardiac monitoring is mandatory
Fluid resuscitation 20 mL/kg crystalloid boluses repeated as needed
Tryptase taken acutely and at 1-2 hours and at 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Stridor in anaphylaxis is laryngeal oedema, not bronchospasm; nebulised adrenaline buys time but does not replace IV adrenaline.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

stem:
An 18-month-old girl (weight 11 kg) with no prior seizure history is brought to a regional ED in active generalised tonic-clonic seizure that began 28 minutes ago at home. Paramedics gave buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg at 5 minutes and a second buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg at 15 minutes without termination. On arrival at 25 minutes she remains in generalised convulsion with eye deviation, frothing, and incontinence; IV access has just been secured on the second attempt and a bedside glucose is 4.8 mmol/L.

She had a brief febrile illness with rhinorrhoea over the preceding 48 hours and a temperature of 38.6 deg C recorded today, but there is no rash, no vomiting, and no known toxic ingestion accessible in the home. There has been no prior antiepileptic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 28 /min (intermittent), SpO2 94% on 8 L/min Hudson mask, BP 96/58 mmHg, T 38.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Generalised tonic-clonic activity, GCS 3 during seizure, pupils 4 mm equal reactive, no neck stiffness assessable, no rash, anterior fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8 mmol/L, VBG pH 7.20 pCO2 56 mmHg lactate 5.8 mmol/L, Na 137 mmol/L, Ca 2.30 mmol/L, FBC and CRP pending
data_table.Medications: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg at 5 min and 15 min, no other antiepileptics ever
data_table.History: First seizure, febrile URTI 48 h, fully immunised, no trauma, no toxin

lead_in: Following the APLS status epilepticus algorithm, what is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading over 20 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring
options.rationale: Phenytoin is acceptable but EcLiPSE and ConSEPT trials and updated APLS prefer levetiracetam, especially under 2 years where phenytoin extravasation risk is higher. Would be correct in older children with appropriate venous access (Source: APLS Australia Status Epilepticus).

options.text: IV phenobarbital 20 mg/kg loading over 20 minutes with airway support ready
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is the preferred second-line agent only in neonates; outside the neonatal period it is third-line. Would be correct in a neonate (Source: APLS Australia).

options.text: A third dose of buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg and continue to observe for spontaneous resolution
options.rationale: More than two benzodiazepine doses increases respiratory depression without improving termination; algorithm advances to second-line antiepileptic. Would never be correct (Source: APLS Australia).

options.text: IV levetiracetam 40 mg/kg (max 3 g) over 5 minutes with continuous monitoring
options.rationale: After two benzodiazepine doses, the current APLS Australia and RCH algorithm recommends IV levetiracetam 40-60 mg/kg as the preferred second-line agent in infants and children, supported by EcLiPSE/ConSEPT/ESETT data, as per APLS Australia Status Epilepticus Algorithm and RCH CPG: Status epilepticus.

options.text: Rapid sequence induction with thiopentone 4 mg/kg and intubation as primary seizure control
options.rationale: Thiopentone induction is for refractory status after second-line agents have failed; jumping straight to RSI skips the algorithm. Would be correct only in refractory status (Source: APLS Australia).

explanation.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus algorithm: oxygen, glucose check, two doses of benzodiazepine 5 minutes apart, then second-line antiepileptic at ~25 minutes. Following EcLiPSE/ConSEPT/ESETT, levetiracetam 40-60 mg/kg IV is the preferred second-line agent in children outside the neonatal period. If still seizing, proceed to RSI with thiopentone or midazolam infusion.
key_points: Two doses of benzodiazepine max before moving on
Levetiracetam preferred over phenytoin in young children
Phenobarbital is for neonates as second-line
Refractory status -> thiopentone RSI and PICU
Always check glucose, sodium, and consider non-convulsive causes
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine 100 mg IV should be considered in infants under 18 months with refractory seizures of unclear cause.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy with severe persistent asthma (one PICU admission 18 months ago for life-threatening wheeze, baseline fluticasone-salmeterol BD via spacer, salbutamol PRN) is brought to a tertiary ED after 12 hours of progressive wheeze triggered by a viral URTI in the family. In ED over the past 60 minutes he has received continuous back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 microg every 20 minutes for three doses, oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg with antiemetic cover, and high-flow oxygen at 10 L/min via nebuliser mask.

There has been no clinical improvement: he remains exhausted, leaning forward, speaking only in single words, and looks visibly tired between breaths. He has not yet received any IV bronchodilators, IV magnesium, or aminophylline. He is normotensive but markedly tachycardic with a fine tremor and palpitations from the salbutamol. There has been no fever, no foreign body history, and no preceding anaphylactic features. The PICU outreach team has reviewed at the bedside and recommends escalation but has not yet started any infusions while awaiting the ED decision.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 bpm, RR 42 /min, SpO2 88% on 10 L/min via nebuliser mask, BP 116/72 mmHg, T 37.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Tripoding, single-word speech, marked accessory muscle use, silent chest in upper zones, faint expiratory wheeze in lower zones, GCS 15 but visibly exhausted, fine tremor
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30 pCO2 50 mmHg HCO3 22 mmol/L lactate 3.8 mmol/L, K 3.0 mmol/L, glucose 9.4 mmol/L; CXR hyperinflation, no pneumothorax
data_table.Medications: Continuous nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium x3 doses, oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg given 35 min ago, no IV bronchodilator yet
data_table.History: Previous PICU admission age 7.5, fluticasone-salmeterol BD baseline, no LABA-only, no NSAID use

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg every 20 minutes and reassess in 1 hour
options.rationale: Already failed three back-to-back nebulised doses plus systemic steroid; persisting risks decompensation. Would be correct only at an earlier step before escalation (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma).

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate (max 2 g) over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe acute asthma failing oxygen, back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium and systemic steroid escalates to IV magnesium sulfate before IV salbutamol or aminophylline, as per RCH CPG: Asthma acute and Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory.

options.text: IV aminophylline loading over 60 minutes followed by maintenance infusion
options.rationale: Aminophylline is reserved for failure of IV magnesium and IV salbutamol due to narrow therapeutic index and arrhythmia risk. Would be correct as third-line in PICU (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: IV salbutamol bolus over 10 minutes followed by infusion
options.rationale: IV salbutamol typically follows IV magnesium; potassium 3.0 and lactate 3.8 will worsen with more beta-agonist. Would be correct after IV magnesium failure (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Immediate rapid sequence intubation with ketamine and rocuronium
options.rationale: Intubation in severe asthma risks bronchospasm, hypotension and barotrauma; reserved for impending arrest after maximal medical therapy. Would be correct only after maximal therapy and impending arrest (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Severe paediatric asthma is identified by tachypnoea, accessory muscle use, oxygen saturation under 92%, inability to complete sentences, agitation or drowsiness, and a silent chest (impending arrest). Stepwise Australian management is oxygen to maintain SpO2 over 94%, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 micrograms every 20 minutes for the first hour, systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg or IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg), then IV magnesium sulfate 25-50 mg/kg over 20 minutes if no improvement. Further escalation is IV salbutamol bolus then infusion, then IV aminophylline (rarely used now), with PICU transfer alongside. Intubation is the last resort: hypoxia and hypercapnia rise quickly post-intubation due to high airway pressures, so ketamine is the induction agent of choice for its bronchodilator effect. Permissive hypercapnia and lung-protective ventilation are the rule.
key_points: IV magnesium dose: 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 min
Silent chest indicates life-threatening asthma
Watch for hypokalaemia and lactic acidosis from salbutamol
Aminophylline is last-line because of arrhythmia risk
Involve PICU early when failing nebs + steroid
explanation.pearls: IV magnesium sulfate 25-50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes is the standard third-line agent in severe paediatric asthma not responding to back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium plus oral corticosteroid - works on bronchial smooth muscle Ca2+ channels (RCH CPG Asthma).

stem:
A 4-year-old boy (weight 16 kg) presents to a regional ED with 36 hours of fever and 6 hours of progressive lethargy following a varicella rash that began crusting 4 days ago. He has now had three 20 mL/kg boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride for hypotension and poor perfusion, with empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and IV clindamycin given for suspected invasive group A streptococcal septic shock.

Peripheral IV access only is available; the central line trolley has been requested but the local team is not credentialled to insert a femoral line, and the retrieval team is 45 minutes away. He remains shut down with cool mottled extremities to mid-thigh, prolonged capillary refill, narrow pulse pressure, and weak peripheral pulses. He has not yet received any inotrope or vasoactive infusion. Bedside echo by the retrieval consultant on tele-link shows a hyperdynamic underfilled left ventricle and no pericardial effusion. Lactate is rising despite ongoing resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 36 /min, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min Hudson mask, BP 74/40 mmHg, T 39.1 deg C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, cool mottled peripheries to mid-thigh, capillary refill 5 seconds, weak radial pulses, no rash beyond crusted varicella
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.21 lactate 5.6 mmol/L base excess -10, Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 248 mg/L, coagulation deranged
data_table.Fluid given: 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg x3 over 45 minutes; no albumin, no inotrope yet
data_table.Access: Two peripheral IV cannulae, no central line, intraosseous available

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in haemodynamic management?

options.text: Commence peripheral IV adrenaline infusion and titrate to perfusion
options.rationale: Cold septic shock in children (low cardiac output, high systemic vascular resistance) is treated with adrenaline as the first-line inotrope; when only peripheral access is available, dilute peripheral adrenaline is recommended over delay for central access, as per ANZICS Paediatric Septic Shock Guideline and Surviving Sepsis Campaign Paediatric Guidelines.
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12 Paediatric Advanced Life Support

options.text: Commence peripheral IV noradrenaline infusion as first-line vasopressor
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is first-line in warm shock (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure); this child has cold shock with vasoconstriction. Would be correct in warm shock (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric).

options.text: Give a fourth 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride before any inotrope
options.rationale: After 40-60 mL/kg in septic shock without response, further crystalloid risks pulmonary oedema; inotropes should be started. Would be correct only before reaching 40-60 mL/kg threshold (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric; FEAST trial).

options.text: Give IV hydrocortisone as the sole next haemodynamic intervention
options.rationale: Stress-dose hydrocortisone is for catecholamine-resistant shock or suspected adrenal insufficiency; not the next step before any inotrope. Would be correct after inotrope started and shock persists (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric).

options.text: Defer all inotrope infusion until a central venous line is inserted to avoid extravasation injury
options.rationale: Delaying inotrope for central access in fluid-refractory shock increases mortality; dilute peripheral or IO is recommended. Would never be correct (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric).

explanation.summary: Paediatric septic shock that is fluid-refractory after 40-60 mL/kg of crystalloid requires early inotrope. Cold shock (low cardiac output, narrow pulse pressure, prolonged capillary refill) is treated with adrenaline; warm shock (vasodilated, wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses) is treated with noradrenaline. Peripheral or intraosseous infusion is appropriate while central access is being arranged.
key_points: Cold shock -> adrenaline; warm shock -> noradrenaline
Do not delay inotrope for central line if peripherally feasible
Stop fluid boluses once signs of fluid overload appear
Stress-dose hydrocortisone for catecholamine-resistant shock
Source control and broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
explanation.pearls: Varicella plus septic shock equals invasive group A strep until proven otherwise; clindamycin is added to suppress toxin production.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 12 Paediatric Advanced Life Support

stem:
An 11-year-old girl (weight 38 kg) is admitted to PICU with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis (initial venous pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, corrected sodium 141 mmol/L at admission). She received an initial 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride for shock and was then commenced on a deficit-plus-maintenance regimen calculated for 7% dehydration over 48 hours, with an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/h started 1 hour after the fluids and added potassium 40 mmol/L once she had urinated.

Six hours into therapy the bedside nurse notes a 15-minute history of increasing headache, restlessness, and one episode of vomiting; over the past 20 minutes she has become more drowsy and confused, no longer engaging with her parents. Pre-decline GCS was 15; current GCS is 12 (E3 V3 M6). The most recent blood glucose is 14.2 mmol/L (was 32, falling at 3 mmol/L/h), sodium has fallen from 138 to 132 mmol/L despite the glucose correction (corrected sodium therefore falling), and she now has bradycardia and a rising blood pressure on the trend chart.

No focal neurology has yet been demonstrated; pupils are equal at 3 mm and reactive. The on-call PICU consultant has been called and the bed is being prepared for hyperosmolar therapy and possible intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62 bpm (was 110), RR 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 138/82 mmHg (was 102/64), T 36.8 deg C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6), drowsy and irritable, no focal weakness, pupils 3 mm equal reactive, no papilloedema, Kussmaul breathing resolving
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 14.2 mmol/L, ketones 3.8 mmol/L, Na 132 mmol/L (corrected was 141 at admission, now ~134), K 3.6 mmol/L, pH 7.22, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L; head CT not yet done
data_table.Fluids/insulin: 0.9% saline + KCl 40 mmol/L at deficit + maintenance for 7% over 48 h, insulin 0.05 units/kg/h, no dextrose yet added
data_table.Trajectory: Glucose falling 3 mmol/L/h, corrected Na falling, GCS dropping over 20 minutes

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reduce insulin infusion rate and add 5% dextrose to current fluid bag, continue current rate
options.rationale: Adding dextrose/reducing insulin is appropriate when glucose falls below ~14-17 mmol/L but does not address suspected cerebral oedema with bradycardia, hypertension and falling GCS. Would be correct at later glucose phase without cerebral oedema (Source: ISPAD DKA).

options.text: Increase IV fluid rate to replace deficit over 24 hours instead of 48 hours to improve cerebral perfusion
options.rationale: Increasing fluid worsens cerebral oedema; PECARN FLUID supports cautious rehydration with hyperosmolar therapy when oedema suspected. Would never be correct in suspected oedema (Source: ISPAD DKA).

options.text: IV hypertonic 3% sodium chloride 5 mL/kg over 10 minutes, reduce fluid rate, urgent CT
options.rationale: Bradycardia, hypertension, falling GCS, headache and vomiting are the Cushing-like triad of DKA-related cerebral oedema; immediate hyperosmolar therapy with 3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg (or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg) plus fluid rate reduction and head CT once stable are first-line, as per ISPAD DKA Guidelines and RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis.

options.text: IV dexamethasone for cerebral oedema and continue current fluid and insulin regimens
options.rationale: Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic oedema (tumour, meningitis) but has no role in DKA-related cytotoxic/osmotic oedema. Would never be correct in DKA cerebral oedema (Source: ISPAD DKA).

options.text: Intubate immediately and hyperventilate to pCO2 25-28 mmHg to lower intracranial pressure today
options.rationale: Prophylactic hyperventilation below pCO2 30 in DKA cerebral oedema worsens outcomes; intubation may follow but is not the first step before hyperosmolar therapy. Would be correct only after hyperosmolar therapy and clinical deterioration (Source: ISPAD DKA).

explanation.summary: DKA-related cerebral oedema presents 4-12 hours into treatment with headache, vomiting, falling GCS, bradycardia and hypertension. Immediate management is hyperosmolar therapy (3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), reduction of fluid rate by one-third, head-up positioning, and urgent imaging only once stabilised. Avoid aggressive hyperventilation.
key_points: Risk factors: new diagnosis, age <5, severe acidosis, high urea, low pCO2, bicarbonate use, rapid fluid
Treat clinically; do not wait for imaging
3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Reduce IV fluid rate; keep glucose falling no faster than ~5 mmol/L/h
Avoid pCO2 below 30 mmHg
explanation.pearls: Corrected sodium should rise as glucose falls; a falling corrected sodium is an early warning sign of cerebral oedema.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl (weight 14 kg) is brought into a regional ED resuscitation bay by ambulance after 6 hours of pallor, lethargy, and refusing fluids. Paramedics noted a narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 268 bpm on monitor with poor peripheral perfusion. She has had one previous documented episode of supraventricular tachycardia at age 18 months terminated by adenosine. On arrival she is pale, mottled, and increasingly drowsy.

She has poor peripheral pulses, no palpable femoral, and is barely rousable. IV access has just been obtained in the right antecubital fossa with a 22-gauge cannula on the second attempt. The rhythm strip from the ambulance shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves at a rate of 270 bpm; QRS duration 70 ms. Vagal manoeuvres (ice to face) were trialled at home by the mother and in the ambulance without effect. No drugs have yet been given in ED. The defibrillator is at the bedside with paediatric pads applied.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 270 bpm narrow complex, RR 36 /min, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min Hudson mask, BP unrecordable on cuff, T 37.0 deg C
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled to mid-thigh, capillary refill 5-6 seconds, GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5), no femoral pulse palpable, no murmurs audible
data_table.ECG: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia 270 bpm, QRS 70 ms, no visible P waves, no delta wave evident
data_table.Medications: Nil given in ED, vagal manoeuvres tried unsuccessfully
data_table.History: Prior SVT terminated by adenosine age 18 months, no structural heart disease known, no recent illness

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Rapid IV adenosine push then 10 mL saline flush via cannula
options.rationale: Adenosine is for stable SVT; this is haemodynamically unstable SVT requiring immediate synchronised cardioversion. Would be correct in stable SVT (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

options.text: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 1 J/kg with procedural sedation if no immediate delay
options.rationale: Unstable SVT in a child with shock requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion at 1 J/kg (then 2 J/kg if unsuccessful), with sedation only if it does not delay shock delivery, as per ANZCOR Guideline 12.7 and AHA PALS.

options.text: Unsynchronised defibrillation at 4 J/kg as for ventricular fibrillation now
options.rationale: Unsynchronised defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; delivering on a perfusing rhythm risks VF induction. Would be correct only in pulseless VT/VF (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

options.text: IV amiodarone loading over 20-60 minutes before any electrical therapy
options.rationale: Amiodarone is for refractory/recurrent SVT in stable patients or post-cardioversion; not before electrical therapy in unstable SVT. Would be correct as adjunct after cardioversion (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

options.text: IV verapamil as a slow push to break the re-entrant tachycardia
options.rationale: Verapamil is contraindicated under 1 year and unsafe with poor cardiac output (profound hypotension/arrest). Would never be correct in this patient (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

explanation.summary: Paediatric SVT with shock = immediate synchronised cardioversion at 1 J/kg, escalating to 2 J/kg. Stable SVT = vagal manoeuvres then adenosine 0.1 mg/kg, then 0.2 mg/kg. Avoid verapamil in young children and avoid unsynchronised shocks on perfusing rhythms.
key_points: Unstable = shock, altered mental state, hypotension; cardiovert immediately
1 J/kg synchronised, then 2 J/kg if unsuccessful
Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg then 0.2 mg/kg in stable SVT
Verapamil contraindicated under 1 year and in shock
Amiodarone is second-line for refractory cases
explanation.pearls: If rate is over 220 bpm in an infant or over 180 bpm in a child with abrupt onset and no P waves, think SVT, not sinus tachycardia.

stem:
A 14-month-old boy (weight 11 kg) presents to a regional ED with 12 hours of barking cough, hoarse cry and worsening stridor at rest. He received nebulised adrenaline 5 mg (1:1000) and oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg 45 minutes ago. He had transient improvement for 20 minutes but is now again stridulous at rest with worsening recessions, increasing work of breathing, intermittent quiet episodes followed by paradoxical chest movement.

He is restless and difficult to console, and SpO2 is dropping. There is no drooling, no fever above 38.0 deg C and no foreign body history. He is fully immunised. The anaesthetic and ENT registrars have been paged and are 5 minutes away. The team is preparing the difficult-airway trolley. Current observations: HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 88 percent on 8 L/min Hudson mask, BP 102/66, T 37.6 deg C, with marked biphasic stridor, severe recessions, intermittent paradoxical chest wall movement and circumoral cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 88% on 8 L/min Hudson mask, BP 102/66 mmHg, T 37.6 deg C
data_table.Examination: Marked biphasic stridor, severe sternal and subcostal recessions, intermittent paradoxical chest wall movement, restless and not consolable, cyanosis around the lips
data_table.Treatment given: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg x1 (45 min ago), oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (45 min ago)
data_table.History: Barking cough 12 h, no drooling, no high fever, fully immunised, no FB history

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait 30 minutes for dexamethasone to take full effect before any further intervention
options.rationale: Impending respiratory failure (hypoxia, exhaustion, paradoxical breathing); passive waiting is unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline 5 mg and continue ward observation; defer airway team involvement
options.rationale: Repeat adrenaline is reasonable as a bridge but does not substitute for definitive airway when impending failure is present. Would be correct only as bridge alongside airway team activation (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula oxygen 2 L/kg/min and reassess at 30 minutes without airway team involvement
options.rationale: HFNC does not bypass critical subglottic narrowing and must not delay airway team. Would be correct only in milder distress without impending failure (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline as a bridge while transferring with the airway team to theatre for gas inhalational induction by anaesthetics, with ENT present and a smaller-than-predicted ETT prepared
options.rationale: Severe croup unresponsive to initial adrenaline plus steroid with signs of impending respiratory failure requires definitive airway management in theatre under inhalational induction (preserving spontaneous ventilation), with ENT standby for surgical airway and a smaller-than-predicted ETT. Repeat adrenaline acts as a bridge during transfer.

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation in the ED with rocuronium and an age-appropriate cuffed ETT
options.rationale: RSI with paralysis risks losing the airway when bag-mask ventilation may be difficult; inhalational induction preserving spontaneous ventilation in theatre is standard. Would be correct only in catastrophic airway loss when inhalational induction impossible (Source: ANZCA airway guidance).

explanation.summary: Severe croup unresponsive to nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone with signs of impending respiratory failure (hypoxia, exhaustion, decreasing air entry, paradoxical breathing) requires definitive airway in theatre. Inhalational induction with preserved spontaneous ventilation is preferred over paralysis-based RSI. ENT must be on standby for a potential surgical airway, and a smaller-than-predicted ETT should be selected.
key_points: Repeat nebulised adrenaline every 20-30 minutes as needed as a bridge
Definitive airway in theatre when impending failure
Inhalational induction; avoid paralysis
Use ETT one size smaller than predicted
ENT for emergency surgical airway
explanation.pearls: Quiet stridor with exhaustion is more ominous than loud stridor with vigorous breathing.

stem:
A 13-year-old girl (weight 52 kg) is brought to ED by her parents after they found an empty 100-tablet bottle of paracetamol 500 mg in her room and a written note. She admits to taking tablets in two separate episodes over the past 18 hours: she states she took about 30 tablets approximately 14 hours ago after an argument with her sister, then a further 20 tablets about 4 hours ago when she decided she wanted to die.

She denies co-ingestion of other tablets, alcohol, or recreational drugs and there are no other empty packets in the home. She has no chronic medical illness, has a normal body mass index, is not on enzyme-inducing drugs (no carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, or isoniazid), and there is no chronic alcohol use, eating disorder, or malnutrition that would raise glutathione-depletion risk. She is fully alert with no nausea or right upper quadrant pain.

A paracetamol level taken on arrival (now 4 hours after the second ingestion and 18 hours after the first) is 320 micromol/L. ALT is 38 U/L and INR is 1.1; creatinine is 64 micromol/L; bicarbonate, lactate, and glucose are all normal. She has not vomited and has not yet received activated charcoal or N-acetylcysteine.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, RR 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 118/72 mmHg, T 36.8 deg C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, no jaundice, abdomen soft and non-tender, no asterixis, mood low but engaged
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol 320 micromol/L (4 h post second ingestion / 18 h post first), ALT 38 U/L, INR 1.1, creatinine 64 micromol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, VBG normal
data_table.Ingestion: Approx 30 x 500 mg paracetamol 14 h ago, then approx 20 x 500 mg paracetamol 4 h ago; total ~25 g ingested in staggered fashion
data_table.Other: No co-ingestants, no enzyme inducers, no chronic illness

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management decision regarding N-acetylcysteine?

options.text: Plot the 320 micromol/L level on the nomogram at 4 hours, withhold N-acetylcysteine
options.rationale: Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies only to single acute ingestions with known time; in staggered or unknown timing it cannot be used. Would be correct only for single acute ingestion with known time and level under treatment line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

options.text: Withhold N-acetylcysteine because ALT and INR are normal, and arrange repeat bloods in 8 hours to reassess
options.rationale: ALT and INR rise late (24-36 h); waiting in a staggered overdose over 200 mg/kg risks missing the treatment window. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence IV N-acetylcysteine 200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours immediately
options.rationale: Staggered paracetamol ingestion >200 mg/kg (or >10 g in adults) over <24 hours mandates immediate full-course IV N-acetylcysteine regardless of the nomogram level; the nomogram does not apply, as per Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness, RCH CPG: Paracetamol poisoning, and the Australian/New Zealand consensus statement on paracetamol overdose.
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus statement: paracetamol poisoning

options.text: Give activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally and reassess paracetamol level in 4 hours before deciding on N-acetylcysteine
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is useful within 1-2 h of ingestion; here ingestions are 18 h and 4 h old, minimal benefit, and NAC must not be delayed. Would be correct within 1-2 h of single ingestion (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence oral methionine 2.5 g every 4 hours for 4 doses as an alternative to IV N-acetylcysteine
options.rationale: Oral methionine is not used in current Australian practice; IV NAC is the standard. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Staggered paracetamol overdose (more than one ingestion within a 24-hour window) renders the Rumack-Matthew nomogram invalid. If the total dose exceeds 200 mg/kg or 10 g, give full-course IV N-acetylcysteine regardless of the level. Charcoal is only useful within 1-2 hours of ingestion. Normal ALT and INR at presentation do not exclude developing toxicity.
key_points: Nomogram applies only to single ingestions with known time
Staggered ingestion >200 mg/kg or >10 g -> immediate NAC
NAC regimen: 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h
Repeat paracetamol, ALT, INR at 8 h to decide on extension of NAC
Charcoal only if presentation within 1-2 h of ingestion
explanation.pearls: Massive ingestion (>30 g or paracetamol >1000 micromol/L at 4 h) may need double-dose NAC and dialysis consideration.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand consensus statement: paracetamol poisoning

stem:
A 7-year-old boy (estimated weight 24 kg) arrives in a tertiary trauma bay 65 minutes after being struck by a car as a pedestrian. Prehospital observations were HR 152, BP 76/40, GCS 14. He received 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride en route. FAST scan in the trauma bay is positive for free fluid in Morison's pouch and pelvis; he has an obvious right femur deformity in a traction splint, abrasions over the right chest wall, and bruising across the abdomen consistent with a seatbelt mechanism.

He is now drowsy with a GCS of 13, cool peripheries, and ongoing hypotension despite the prehospital crystalloid bolus. The on-call surgeon and interventional radiologist have been called. The blood bank has a paediatric massive transfusion pack available within 8 minutes. No tranexamic acid has yet been given. He has no known coagulopathy and no anticoagulants.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156 bpm, RR 32 /min, SpO2 96% on 10 L/min non-rebreather, BP 78/44 mmHg, T 35.6 deg C, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Bruised abdomen with seatbelt sign, positive FAST (Morison + pelvis), right femur deformity, capillary refill 4 s, cool peripheries to knees
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, base excess -8, INR 1.4, fibrinogen 1.6 g/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L, ionised Ca 1.05 mmol/L
data_table.Time: 65 minutes since injury, 10 mL/kg saline given prehospital, no blood products yet
data_table.History: No anticoagulants, no bleeding diathesis, fully immunised

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in haemodynamic resuscitation?

options.text: Activate paediatric massive transfusion protocol, IV tranexamic acid 15 mg/kg over 10 minutes, transfuse PRBC 10 mL/kg
options.rationale: Paediatric trauma with shock, positive FAST and lactic acidosis after 10 mL/kg crystalloid meets MTP activation criteria; TXA is indicated when given within 3 hours of injury at 15 mg/kg (max 1 g) followed by an infusion, and initial PRBC bolus is 10 mL/kg, as per CRASH-3/CRASH-2 paediatric data and RCH CPG: Trauma resuscitation.
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Give a further 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride and reassess before activating MTP
options.rationale: Large-volume crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy and acidosis in haemorrhagic shock; blood products are the next resuscitation fluid. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Trauma).

options.text: Transfuse PRBC 20 mL/kg alone and withhold tranexamic acid until thromboelastography results are available
options.rationale: TXA should be given empirically within 3 h of injury with significant bleeding; waiting for viscoelastic testing delays a time-critical intervention. Would be correct only outside the 3-h window (Source: ANZ Paediatric MTP).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Withhold tranexamic acid as it is contraindicated in paediatric trauma and give cryoprecipitate 10 mL/kg first to correct fibrinogen
options.rationale: TXA is not contraindicated in paediatric trauma; recommended within 3 h. Cryoprecipitate is used for fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L but is not the first product in MTP. Would never be correct (Source: ANZ Paediatric MTP).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Commence peripheral noradrenaline to maintain perfusion and defer blood products until SBP is restored
options.rationale: Vasopressors as primary treatment of haemorrhagic shock mask ongoing bleeding and worsen tissue perfusion; volume with blood products is the priority. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Trauma).

explanation.summary: Paediatric haemorrhagic shock not responding to a 10-20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, with positive FAST or known source of bleeding, requires MTP activation, balanced product resuscitation (PRBC:FFP:platelets ~1:1:1, initial PRBC 10 mL/kg), and empirical TXA within 3 hours of injury. Avoid further crystalloid where blood is available.
key_points: MTP activation: shock unresponsive to 10-20 mL/kg crystalloid or known major haemorrhage
TXA 15 mg/kg (max 1 g) over 10 min, then 2 mg/kg/h for 8 h
Aim ionised calcium >1.1 mmol/L; give calcium with each unit
Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy = lethal triad
Surgical or radiological source control as soon as possible
explanation.pearls: Children compensate longer then decompensate suddenly; do not be falsely reassured by a normal blood pressure early.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

stem:
A 5-month-old male infant (not yet sitting independently or rolling consistently) is brought to ED by his mother for a frenulum tear noted during a feed. Mother states he banged his face on the cot 2 days ago but the lip injury was only seen today. The father is a step-father who was alone with the infant on the day of the injury.

There is no past medical history of bleeding or bruising disorders. On examination there is a torn upper lip frenulum with surrounding bruising on the upper gum and a small yellow bruise over the left pinna. He is otherwise alert, well-perfused, feeding adequately on review, and has no acute distress. A previous ED record from 6 weeks ago notes a presentation for a left thigh bruise of unclear mechanism, dismissed as a possible cot-rail injury at the time. The Department of Communities and Justice has not previously been involved.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm, RR 36 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 90/56 mmHg, T 36.9 deg C
data_table.Examination: Torn upper lip frenulum with gum bruising, small yellow bruise over left pinna, no other external bruising on full skin exam, no torticollis, no head swelling, anterior fontanelle soft, retinal exam not performed
data_table.Development: Not yet rolling consistently, not sitting independently; pre-mobile per WHO milestones
data_table.Past presentation: ED visit 6 weeks ago for left thigh bruise, dismissed as cot-rail injury
data_table.Social: Mother and step-father carers, no prior child protection involvement

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure that frenulum tears are common in this age group, GP review in 1 week
options.rationale: Frenulum tear in a pre-mobile infant is a sentinel injury for NAI; never warrants outpatient reassurance. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).
source_refs: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

options.text: Send coagulation studies and FBC today, discharge home if all results are normal
options.rationale: Coagulation studies are part of workup but a normal screen does not exclude inflicted injury; discharge without protective action is unsafe. Would never be sufficient (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Refer to outpatient paediatrics in 2 weeks for assessment, with no statutory notification at this stage
options.rationale: Mandatory reporting is required at the time of clinical suspicion, not deferred. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG; state child protection legislation).
source_refs: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

options.text: Discharge with father supervised by mother only, after a verbal safety plan with mother
options.rationale: Discharging a pre-mobile infant with sentinel injury without statutory notification does not meet duty of care. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Admit, mandatory child protection notification, skeletal survey, ophthalmology fundoscopy, plain CT head
options.rationale: A frenulum tear or bruise in a pre-mobile infant (TEN-4 FACESp rule) is a high-risk sentinel injury for inflicted injury; the standard response is admission, mandatory notification, skeletal survey (NAI series), fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages, and CT head, with paediatric protection team involvement, as per RCH CPG: Child abuse and the RACGP child protection resource.
source_refs: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

explanation.summary: Sentinel injuries in pre-mobile infants (TEN-4 FACESp: Torso, Ear, Neck bruising; Frenulum, Angle of jaw, Cheek, Eyelid, Sclera, plus any patterned injury; under 4 months any bruising) require admission, mandatory child protection notification, skeletal survey, fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages, and CT head to assess for occult abusive head trauma.
key_points: Bruising/frenulum injury in a pre-mobile infant is NAI until proven otherwise
Mandatory reporting is statutory in all Australian states/territories
Skeletal survey + fundoscopy + CT head are minimum imaging
Coagulation screen to exclude bleeding diathesis is adjunctive
Involve paediatric child protection team and social work
explanation.pearls: Those who don't cruise don't bruise: any bruise in a non-mobile infant warrants child protection assessment.

sources.label: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

stem:
A 4-year-old unimmunised boy presents to a regional ED with 6 hours of high fever to 39.4 deg C, painful drooling, refusal to swallow and a muffled hot-potato voice. He sits forward on his mother's lap in a tripod posture with his neck extended. There has been no preceding barking cough and no hoarseness; the parents describe rapid onset over a single afternoon.

There is no history of choking on a small object, no recent dental work, and no preceding pharyngitis. He has not received nebulised adrenaline or steroid. The ED consultant has asked the team to avoid distressing the child and to call anaesthetics and ENT immediately. He is alert but anxious and looks toxic. HR 148, RR 32, SpO2 95 percent on room air, BP 102/64, T 39.4 deg C, with tripoding, drooling, mild inspiratory stridor and no barking cough.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 bpm, RR 32 /min, SpO2 95% on room air, BP 102/64 mmHg, T 39.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Tripoding, drooling, muffled voice, mild inspiratory stridor, no barking cough, no hoarseness, neck extended, anxious but alert
data_table.History: Unimmunised, no preceding URTI, rapid onset over hours, no FB choking event, no dental procedure
data_table.Treatments given: Nil so far; team avoiding distress and calling airway team

lead_in: Which combination of most likely diagnosis and immediate next step (without distressing examination) is most appropriate?

options.text: Acute epiglottitis (most likely Haemophilus influenzae type b given non-immunisation); keep the child calm on the parent's lap and proceed to theatre with anaesthetics and ENT for gas inhalational induction and definitive airway before any blood tests or imaging
options.rationale: Rapid onset of fever, drooling, muffled voice and tripoding without barking cough in an unimmunised child is classic for Hib epiglottitis. Definitive airway management in theatre by anaesthetics with ENT standby precedes investigations; cannulation, bloods and imaging are deferred until the airway is secured because distress can precipitate complete obstruction, per RCH CPG.

options.text: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup); give oral dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline in ED
options.rationale: Croup has coryzal prodrome with barking cough and hoarseness, not drooling, muffled voice or toxic appearance. Would be correct in barking cough without drooling (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Inhaled foreign body; arrange urgent rigid bronchoscopy in theatre
options.rationale: FB aspiration follows witnessed choking with focal asymmetry; no choking history plus high fever and toxic appearance make this unlikely. Would be correct with witnessed choking and focal signs (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Bacterial tracheitis complicating viral croup with Staphylococcus aureus; intubate in theatre with copious tracheal toilet
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis usually follows several days of croup-like illness; rapid single-afternoon onset and tripoding favour epiglottitis. Would be correct with preceding croup-like illness over days (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Retropharyngeal abscess; arrange contrast neck CT before airway management
options.rationale: Retropharyngeal abscess usually presents with neck stiffness/torticollis and preceding URTI or dental focus; CT-before-airway in a tripoding child with impending obstruction is unsafe. Would be correct with neck stiffness, no impending obstruction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Acute upper airway obstruction in a child requires rapid differentiation between croup, epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, foreign body, and retropharyngeal abscess. Epiglottitis features rapid onset, high fever, drooling, muffled voice, tripoding, no barking cough. In an unimmunised child Hib is the leading pathogen.
key_points: Epiglottitis: 4 Ds (drooling, dysphagia, distress, dysphonia), tripoding, no cough
Croup: preceding URTI, barking cough, hoarseness, stridor
Bacterial tracheitis: croup-like prodrome then toxic decline
Foreign body: sudden choking event, unilateral signs
Retropharyngeal abscess: neck stiffness, dysphagia, preceding URTI or dental
explanation.pearls: Keep the child calm on the parent's lap, do not examine the throat, call anaesthetics and ENT, and plan inhalational induction in theatre.

stem:
A 6-year-old boy (weight 22 kg) with newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is admitted to the paediatric oncology ward 12 hours after starting induction with high-dose steroid and his first dose of rasburicase. The bone marrow blast count at diagnosis was 92%, white cell count 142 x10^9/L, with bulky mediastinal disease on imaging. He has been on hyperhydration with 2.5 L/m2/day of isotonic fluid without potassium since admission.

Over the last 4 hours he has become increasingly nauseated and reports muscle cramps and tingling around the mouth, and is now passing only small volumes of dark urine. A repeat biochemistry panel ordered after the nursing staff noted reduced urine output shows the changes below. A 12-lead ECG performed because of the potassium result shows peaked T waves in the precordial leads and a PR interval of 220 ms. The renal registrar has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 124/78 mmHg, T 37.0 deg C
data_table.Examination: Mild Chvostek sign, no carpopedal spasm, no peripheral oedema, abdomen soft, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: K 6.9 mmol/L, urate 0.62 mmol/L, phosphate 3.4 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.78 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 48), urea 12.2 mmol/L, pH 7.31, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, urine output 0.3 mL/kg/h
data_table.ECG: Peaked T waves V2-V5, PR 220 ms, QRS 90 ms, no widening yet
data_table.Treatment so far: Hyperhydration without K, rasburicase 12 h ago, no calcium given, no insulin-glucose, no salbutamol

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next step in management?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg as the first agent to shift potassium intracellularly, then reassess ECG in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium but acts more slowly than calcium and does not protect the myocardium; calcium membrane stabilisation is the first step with ECG changes. Would be correct as second step after calcium (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia).

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate IV bolus as primary therapy to drive potassium intracellularly today
options.rationale: Bicarbonate has limited variable effect on potassium and worsens hypocalcaemia (already 1.78), risking tetany/arrhythmia. Would be correct only with severe metabolic acidosis and normocalcaemia (Source: APLS Australia).

options.text: IV 10% calcium gluconate over 5-10 minutes, then insulin-dextrose infusion, urgent dialysis
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves, prolonged PR) requires immediate myocardial protection with IV calcium gluconate, followed by potassium-shifting therapy (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol) and definitive removal via dialysis given the rising creatinine, oliguria and hyperphosphataemia of TLS, as per RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia, RCH CPG: Tumour lysis syndrome, and APLS Australia.

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate as the first intervention while ECG changes resolve spontaneously
options.rationale: Resin binders are slow-acting and unsuitable for immediate intervention with ECG changes; carry GI necrosis risk. Would be correct only as adjunct for chronic hyperkalaemia (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: IV furosemide as primary therapy to enhance renal potassium excretion in this oliguric child
options.rationale: Loop diuretics need functional kidneys and are ineffective in oliguric AKI from TLS; cardiac protection and dialysis are needed. Would be correct only in non-oliguric AKI with preserved function (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome (high urate, high phosphate, high potassium, low calcium, AKI) is a classic emergency in high-risk haematological malignancies. Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated in three steps: stabilise the myocardium (IV calcium gluconate), shift potassium (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate selectively), and remove potassium (dialysis when AKI is established, oliguric, or refractory).
key_points: Calcium gluconate 10% 0.5 mL/kg IV over 5-10 min for ECG changes
Insulin 0.1 unit/kg with dextrose 0.5 g/kg
Salbutamol nebulised 5 mg as adjunct
Dialysis criteria in TLS: oliguric AKI, K >7 refractory, severe hyperphosphataemia, fluid overload
Avoid potassium-containing fluids; rasburicase for high urate
explanation.pearls: Hypocalcaemia in TLS is precipitation as calcium phosphate; correct calcium cautiously only if symptomatic because raising it worsens calcium phosphate deposition.

stem:
A 6-day-old male term infant (birth weight 3.4 kg, now 3.2 kg) is brought to a regional ED with 12 hours of poor feeding, lethargy and grey colour. He was born at 39+4 weeks with Apgars 9 and 9 and discharged at 36 hours after a normal newborn examination. The newborn pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours was normal. There is no family history of congenital heart disease.

He is grey-mottled with cool peripheries and weak femoral pulses bilaterally. Four-limb BPs: right arm 78/50, right leg 52/30. Pre-ductal SpO2 (right hand) 92 percent, post-ductal SpO2 (foot) 78 percent. The precordium is hyperdynamic with a single loud S2 and no audible murmur. VBG: pH 7.18, lactate 6.2, BE -12, glucose 3.1, Na 136, K 4.6, Hb 168. Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary plethora. Echocardiography reveals critical coarctation with a closing PDA.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 64 /min, SpO2 pre-ductal 92% / post-ductal 78%, BP RA 78/50, RL 52/30, T 36.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Grey-mottled, cool to mid-thigh, weak femoral pulses, hyperdynamic precordium, single loud S2, no murmur, hepatomegaly 3 cm
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.18 lactate 6.2 mmol/L base excess -12, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, Na 136 mmol/L, K 4.6 mmol/L, Hb 168 g/L; CXR cardiomegaly + pulmonary plethora; echo: critical coarctation with closing PDA

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention and oxygen target?

options.text: IV indometacin to close the patent ductus arteriosus and reduce the right-to-left shunt across the ductal lesion immediately
options.rationale: Closing the duct in duct-dependent systemic circulation precipitates cardiovascular collapse; the goal is to keep the duct OPEN. Would never be correct in duct-dependent lesion (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

options.text: Adenosine rapid IV push for suspected supraventricular tachycardia, bypassing prostaglandin while awaiting paediatric cardiology review
options.rationale: No narrow-complex tachycardia over 220 bpm with absent P waves; picture is duct-dependent systemic shock not SVT. Would be correct only in SVT (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

options.text: Oral sildenafil to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance instead of maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandin in this duct-dependent infant
options.rationale: Sildenafil is used in persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn, not duct-dependent systemic lesions; does not maintain ductal patency. Would never be correct here (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

options.text: IV prostaglandin E1 infusion 10-50 ng/kg/min titrated to effect, airway support ready for apnoea; target pre-ductal SpO2 ~85-92% and avoid high FiO2
options.rationale: Duct-dependent systemic circulation with a closing PDA is reopened with prostaglandin E1 at 0.01-0.05 microgram/kg/min titrated to effect, with airway readiness for PGE-induced apnoea. High FiO2 is avoided because oxygen promotes ductal closure; target pre-ductal SpO2 about 85-92 percent.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

options.text: Commence head-box oxygen at FiO2 1.0 to maximise systemic saturations, with continuous pre- and post-ductal SpO2 and serial ABG monitoring
options.rationale: High FiO2 promotes ductal closure and worsens systemic perfusion in duct-dependent systemic lesions. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cardiology).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Neonatal collapse between days 3-14 with shock, pre/post-ductal saturation differential and weak femoral pulses should be assumed to be duct-dependent congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Treatment is IV prostaglandin E1 infusion to reopen the duct. Avoid high FiO2 and indometacin. Be ready for apnoea, fever, and hypotension as PGE1 side effects.
key_points: Duct-dependent systemic: coarctation, IAA, HLHS, critical AS
PGE1 0.01-0.05 microg/kg/min titrated to effect
Apnoea risk: anticipate intubation
Target SpO2 ~85-92%; avoid 100% oxygen
Retrieve early to cardiac centre
explanation.pearls: Differential SpO2 with lower foot than hand is highly suggestive of a duct-dependent systemic or mixing lesion; check four-limb BPs.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

stem:
A 14-year-old boy (weight 60 kg) with a mechanical mitral valve replacement on long-term anticoagulation is brought to ED 90 minutes after coming off his bicycle without a helmet. He had a brief loss of consciousness at the scene and one episode of vomiting. He is on dabigatran 110 mg twice daily (switched from warfarin 6 months ago due to INR variability); his last dose was 2 hours pre-injury.

On arrival his GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6) and dropping; he has a scalp haematoma over the right parietal area, equal but sluggish pupils, and a non-contrast CT head shows an acute right-sided subdural haematoma with 6 mm of midline shift. Neurosurgery plans urgent operative evacuation within the hour. INR is 1.2; aPTT 58 s; the thrombin time is markedly prolonged. He has no other major injuries on secondary survey.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, RR 18 /min, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min nasal prongs, BP 132/82 mmHg, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Right parietal scalp haematoma, equal sluggish pupils, no focal limb weakness, no other injuries
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast CT head: right subdural haematoma with 6 mm midline shift; neurosurgery for urgent evacuation
data_table.Anticoagulant: Dabigatran 110 mg BD, last dose 2 hours before injury (so ~3.5 h pre-decision)
data_table.Coags: INR 1.2, aPTT 58 s, thrombin time markedly prolonged

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate reversal strategy before craniotomy?

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg plus prothrombinex-VF as for warfarin reversal
options.rationale: Vitamin K and prothrombinex reverse warfarin; dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor not reversed by vitamin K. Would be correct in warfarin-treated patient (Source: ANZSBT Guidelines).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Andexanet alfa 400 mg IV bolus then 4 mg/min infusion as specific reversal
options.rationale: Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban), not dabigatran. Would be correct in apixaban/rivaroxaban-treated patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma infused over 1 hour as the primary reversal
options.rationale: FFP does not reliably reverse direct thrombin inhibitors and volume-loads the patient. Would be correct only as bridge when idarucizumab unavailable (Source: ANZSBT).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII IV as a universal haemostatic agent
options.rationale: Recombinant FVIIa is off-label, carries thrombotic risk especially with mechanical valve, and is not a specific reversal agent. Would never be correct as first-line (Source: ANZSBT).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g doses 15 minutes apart) as specific dabigatran reversal
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is a specific monoclonal antibody fragment that immediately neutralises dabigatran and is indicated for life-threatening bleeding (including intracranial haemorrhage) or urgent surgery in patients on dabigatran, as per Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular and ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines.
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

explanation.summary: Anticoagulant reversal in life-threatening bleeding is agent-specific: warfarin = vitamin K + prothrombinex (or FFP if PCC unavailable); dabigatran = idarucizumab 5 g IV; factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) = andexanet alfa where available, otherwise prothrombinex 50 IU/kg. A markedly prolonged thrombin time confirms dabigatran activity.
key_points: Warfarin -> vitamin K + prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg
Dabigatran -> idarucizumab 5 g IV (2 x 2.5 g)
Apixaban/rivaroxaban -> andexanet alfa; alternative prothrombinex
FFP is volume-heavy and slow; not first choice when PCC/antidote available
Thrombin time is sensitive to dabigatran effect
explanation.pearls: Always check the last dose time and renal function for DOACs; dabigatran is renally cleared and may persist longer in AKI.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

stem:
An 8-year-old boy presents to a regional ED with 3 weeks of polyuria, nocturia, polydipsia and 3 kg unintentional weight loss. He has been tired but is still attending school and eating normally. He has had no abdominal pain, no vomiting and no Kussmaul respiration. He has no past medical history, takes no medications, is fully immunised and has a maternal aunt with T1DM.

He is alert and well perfused with no signs of dehydration. Fingerprick glucose 22 mmol/L, capillary blood ketones 1.8 mmol/L. VBG: pH 7.35, HCO3 19. Na 138, K 4.2. He has no acetone breath and no abdominal tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 108/66 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, mucous membranes moist, capillary refill <2 seconds, no acetone breath, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 22 mmol/L, blood ketones 1.8 mmol/L, VBG pH 7.35, HCO3 19 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with urine dipstick and GP referral for fasting glucose and HbA1c tomorrow
options.rationale: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia with ketonaemia mandates same-day specialist paediatric review for insulin initiation and education. Would never be correct (Source: ISPAD; RCH CPG: T1DM).

options.text: Commence IV 0.9% saline at twice maintenance and a fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour as per the inpatient ketoacidosis protocol
options.rationale: DKA-protocol fluid plus insulin is reserved for pH under 7.30 or HCO3 under 15; this child's pH 7.35 and HCO3 are above threshold. Would be correct with pH under 7.30 or HCO3 under 15 (Source: ISPAD).

options.text: Admit under the paediatric diabetes team for diagnosis confirmation (HbA1c, type 1 antibodies), subcutaneous insulin initiation (basal-bolus), and structured family education with dietetics
options.rationale: New-onset T1DM without DKA (pH 7.30 or more, HCO3 15 or more, ketones present but child clinically well) is admitted for subcutaneous insulin initiation, education and family training, per RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus and the APEG handbook.

options.text: Single oral dose of metformin 500 mg and paediatric endocrinology outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Metformin is not first-line in suspected paediatric T1DM; insulin is required. Would be correct only in confirmed T2DM (Source: RCH CPG).
