options.text: Observe in short stay for 4 hours and discharge if glucose falls below 15 mmol/L
options.rationale: Glucose will not self-correct without exogenous insulin in T1DM. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: New-onset T1DM in a clinically well child without DKA (pH >=7.30, HCO3 >=15) is admitted for subcutaneous insulin commencement, glucose monitoring training and structured family education. DKA biochemical criteria are pH <7.30 or HCO3 <15 mmol/L with ketonaemia.
key_points: DKA criteria (ISPAD): hyperglycaemia >11 mmol/L + ketonaemia + pH <7.30 or HCO3 <15
Without DKA, use subcutaneous insulin and oral hydration
Outpatient initiation is not appropriate in Australian paediatric practice
Education covers carbohydrate counting, hypoglycaemia recognition, sick day rules
explanation.pearls: A pH of exactly 7.35 with bicarbonate 19 is not DKA. Do not start a DKA protocol on a child who does not need one.

stem:
A 12-year-old girl weighing 40 kg with a 2-week history of polyuria and polydipsia presents to a tertiary paediatric emergency department after a day of vomiting and abdominal pain. She is drowsy but rousable, with deep sighing respirations and acetone breath. Capillary glucose is 32 mmol/L and blood ketones are 5.8 mmol/L. A venous blood gas shows pH 7.08, HCO3 7 mmol/L, Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, urea 9.8 mmol/L and creatinine 88 micromol/L.

She has not previously been diagnosed with diabetes and is not on any chronic medication. There is no recent head injury, no seizure activity, and no concurrent gastrointestinal infection in the family. The senior registrar has commenced a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline over 30 minutes for clinically estimated 8 percent dehydration, an indwelling urinary catheter has been placed for hourly urine output measurement, and a second wide-bore IV cannula has been sited. The on-call paediatric endocrinologist and the PICU team have been informed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, RR 36 /min Kussmaul, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% on RA, T 37.0 deg C, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, abdomen soft mildly tender, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: BSL 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, VBG pH 7.08, HCO3 7, Na 132, K 4.4, Cl 102, urea 9.8, creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate insulin and fluid management plan immediately after the resuscitation bolus?

options.text: Insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h immediately with the bolus, maintenance fluids only after the second hour
options.rationale: Insulin should not start until at least 1 h after fluid resuscitation has begun, because early insulin increases cerebral oedema risk and rapid osmolar shifts. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: DKA).

options.text: IV insulin bolus 0.1 units/kg followed by infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h, deficit over 24 hours
options.rationale: IV insulin boluses are contraindicated in paediatric DKA (cerebral oedema risk); rapid deficit replacement under 48 h increases osmolar shifts. Would never be correct (Source: ISPAD 2022).

options.text: Use 5% dextrose with 0.45% saline from outset plus insulin infusion at 0.15 units/kg/h immediately
options.rationale: Dextrose addition before glucose falls below 14-17 mmol/L is inappropriate; 0.15 units/kg/h exceeds the 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h ceiling. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: DKA).

options.text: Start 0.9% saline maintenance plus deficit over 48 hours, insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h after 1-2 hours
options.rationale: ISPAD and the RCH DKA pathway use 0.9% saline (transitioned to 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose once glucose <14-17 mmol/L), with the calculated deficit replaced over 48 hours and insulin starting 1-2 hours after fluid resuscitation at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h to reduce cerebral oedema risk.

options.text: Replace deficit with 0.9% saline over 6 hours, insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h after bolus
options.rationale: Rapid 6-h deficit replacement and simultaneous insulin commencement substantially increase cerebral oedema risk; deficit is replaced over 48 h. Would never be correct (Source: ISPAD 2022).

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA: assume 5-8% dehydration; give one or two 10 mL/kg boluses of 0.9% saline only if shocked; replace remaining deficit over 48 hours; start insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h 1-2 hours after fluid resuscitation begins; switch fluid to 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose once glucose falls below 14-17 mmol/L; monitor neuro hourly.
key_points: Cerebral oedema risk factors: young age, new-onset DM, severe acidosis, low pCO2, high urea, bicarbonate therapy, rapid fluid, early insulin
Do not give insulin bolus
Replace K early once urine output established
Watch for headache, GCS drop, bradycardia, hypertension (Cushing response)
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema typically occurs 4-12 hours into therapy. The temptation to fix the numbers fast is the danger.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy weighing 30 kg is 6 hours into treatment of newly diagnosed diabetic ketoacidosis in a paediatric high dependency unit at a tertiary children's hospital. His initial pH was 7.02 with HCO3 5 mmol/L, glucose 38 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L (corrected sodium 142 mmol/L), potassium 4.6 mmol/L and chloride 100 mmol/L. He received a single 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline over 30 minutes, then maintenance fluid plus 48-hour deficit replacement using 0.9% saline with potassium chloride 40 mmol/L, and an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/h started 90 minutes after fluids commenced.

He has not received any sodium bicarbonate. Glucose is now 16 mmol/L, pH 7.18 and HCO3 11 mmol/L, and the nurses have just transitioned the fluid to 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose. Over the last 30 minutes the bedside nurse has noted progressively increasing irritability, a new complaint of headache, and now a single episode of non-bilious vomiting. On urgent reassessment his GCS has fallen from 15 to 11 (E3 V3 M5), with a heart rate that has slowed from 120 to 78 bpm and a rising blood pressure of 138/92 mmHg.

Pupils are 4 mm and sluggish bilaterally with no focal motor deficit and no posturing. The bedside glucose is 14 mmol/L and the most recent potassium was 3.9 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm (down from 120), BP 138/92 mmHg (up from 108/66), RR 14 /min, SpO2 98% on RA, T 36.9 deg C, GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5)
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, headache, one vomit, pupils 4 mm sluggish bilaterally, no focal neurology, fontanelle closed, no papilloedema visible
data_table.Investigations: BSL 14 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, last VBG pH 7.18 HCO3 11, urine output 1.5 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Increase IV fluid rate to twice maintenance and rebolus 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline to address suspected hypovolaemia
options.rationale: Bradycardia with hypertension and falling GCS is Cushing response indicating raised ICP from cerebral oedema; fluid expansion worsens oedema and rate must be REDUCED. Would never be correct (Source: ISPAD 2022).

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion and give an IV bolus of 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Glucose 14 is not the cause of declining GCS; stopping insulin worsens ketosis; picture points to cerebral oedema not hypoglycaemia. Would be correct only in confirmed hypoglycaemia (Source: ISPAD 2022).

options.text: 3% hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg IV over 15 minutes, reduce IV fluid rate by a third, urgent CT brain
options.rationale: Suspected DKA-associated cerebral oedema (declining GCS, headache, Cushing response, vomiting) is treated immediately with hypertonic saline 2.7-3% at 2.5-5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes (or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), reduction of IV fluid rate by one third, head-up 30 degrees, and neuroimaging only after stabilisation per RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis and ISPAD 2022.

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg infused over 30 minutes to correct the residual acidosis safely
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is an independent risk factor for DKA-associated cerebral oedema and is not indicated; pH already improving to 7.18. Would never be correct (Source: ISPAD 2022).

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial meningitis as cause of the altered consciousness today
options.rationale: LP in raised ICP risks coning and delays osmotherapy; the picture is cerebral oedema not meningitis. Would never be correct in suspected DKA cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: DKA).

explanation.summary: DKA-associated cerebral oedema occurs in approximately 0.5-1% of paediatric DKA episodes, typically 4-12 hours into therapy, and has a 20-25% mortality. Treatment is immediate hypertonic saline 3% (2.5-5 mL/kg over 10-15 min) or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 15-20 min, head up 30 degrees, reduction of fluid rate by one third, and urgent intensivist input. CT is only after stabilisation.
key_points: Clinical diagnostic criteria (Muir): abnormal motor/verbal response, decorticate or decerebrate posturing, cranial nerve palsy, abnormal respiratory pattern
Hypertonic saline 3% 2.5-5 mL/kg OR mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Reduce maintenance fluid rate by one third
Avoid hyperventilation below pCO2 35 mmHg unless herniating
explanation.pearls: A bradycardia in a child who was just tachycardic in DKA is cerebral oedema until proven otherwise. Treat first, image after.

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with T1DM diagnosed 8 months ago is found by her father unresponsive in bed at 06:30. She is on basal-bolus insulin glargine 8 units at dinner and aspart with meals; she had a heavier than usual swimming session yesterday afternoon. Her father estimates her current weight at 22 kg. Capillary glucose 1.6 mmol/L. She is breathing normally with a strong pulse but does not respond to her name, withdraws only to a sternal rub, and is having intermittent generalised tonic-clonic jerking.

There is no IV access at home. He has an in-date glucagon hypokit and an oral glucose gel in the fridge. Ambulance is 12 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 97% on RA, T 36.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive to voice, withdraws to pain, intermittent generalised tonic-clonic activity, airway patent
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate action by her father?

options.text: Place oral glucose gel between her cheek and gum and roll her onto her side
options.rationale: Oral glucose is contraindicated with reduced consciousness or active seizure (aspiration risk); parenteral glucagon is indicated. Would be correct only with alert child able to swallow (Source: APEG hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Administer IM glucagon 1 mg AND inject 2 units of insulin aspart to stabilise the response
options.rationale: 1 mg glucagon is the dose for 25 kg or more; she is 22 kg. Insulin is contraindicated in hypoglycaemia. Would be correct in over-25-kg child without insulin error (Source: APEG; Hypokit dosing).

options.text: Wait for the ambulance and let paramedics administer glucagon in 12 minutes
options.rationale: Severe hypoglycaemia with seizure needs immediate treatment; delay risks hypoxic injury and prolonged seizure. Would never be correct (Source: APEG).

options.text: Administer IM glucagon 0.5 mg from the hypokit (because she weighs under 25 kg) and place her in the recovery position; recheck glucose after 10-15 minutes and call paramedics to confirm next steps
options.rationale: Severe hypoglycaemia (unconscious or seizing) in a child UNDER 25 kg is treated with IM glucagon 0.5 mg; 1 mg is for at least 25 kg. The AU-specific weight threshold is the discriminator. Recovery position and ambulance attendance complete the response.

options.text: Give buccal midazolam to terminate the seizure before glucose correction
options.rationale: Hypoglycaemic seizure terminates with glucose, not benzodiazepine; midazolam first risks airway compromise without correcting cause. Would never be correct in hypoglycaemic seizure (Source: APLS Australia).

explanation.summary: Severe hypoglycaemia (BSL <4 mmol/L with reduced consciousness or seizure) in a child with T1DM is treated outside hospital with IM glucagon: 0.5 mg if <25 kg or <8 years, 1 mg if >=25 kg. In hospital, 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV is preferred. Mild hypoglycaemia (conscious, able to swallow) is treated with 10-15 g rapid-acting oral carbohydrate, then complex carbohydrate.
key_points: Treatment threshold BSL <4 mmol/L
Glucagon 0.5 mg <25 kg, 1 mg >=25 kg
Repeat BSL 15 minutes after treatment
Investigate cause: missed meal, exercise, insulin dose error, illness
explanation.pearls: Glucagon does not work well in glycogen-depleted states (alcohol, prolonged starvation, repeated hypoglycaemia). Give IV dextrose if available.

stem:
A 12-day-old male term infant presents to a regional ED with 3 days of poor feeding, vomiting and increasing lethargy. He was born at 39+2 NVD, birth weight 3.4 kg, exclusively breastfed, discharged at 48 hours with a normal newborn examination. The heel-prick screen has not yet returned. He has lost 14 percent of birth weight. There is no diarrhoea or fever.

He is pale, peripherally cool with CRT 4 seconds, sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. Genitalia are normal male with bilaterally descended testes and no hyperpigmentation. On arrival: HR 188, RR 56, SpO2 96 percent on room air, T 36.2, BP 62/38. Bloods: Na 124, K 7.2, glucose 2.4, urea 11, creatinine 62, pH 7.22, HCO3 14.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188 bpm, RR 56 /min, SpO2 96% on RA, T 36.2 deg C, BP 62/38 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds, normal male external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Na 124 mmol/L, K 7.2 mmol/L, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, urea 11 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L

lead_in: Which combination of most likely diagnosis and most discriminating biochemical signature is correct?

options.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causing hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and projectile non-bilious vomiting in the first 6 weeks of life
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis gives hypochloraemic hypokalaemic ALKALOSIS; this infant has HYPERkalaemia and ACIDOSIS (opposite). Would be correct with classic pyloric biochemistry (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Late-onset group B streptococcal sepsis with septic shock and acute kidney injury rather than any primary adrenal or mineralocorticoid dysfunction
options.rationale: GBS can present with shock but does not characteristically produce the specific Na-low, K-high, glucose-low pattern; electrolyte signature is the discriminator. Would be correct only with positive cultures and no electrolyte signature (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis).

options.text: Urea cycle defect with hyperammonaemic encephalopathy; the discriminating signature is raised ammonia with a respiratory alkalosis on blood gas
options.rationale: Urea cycle defects produce respiratory ALKALOSIS with hyperammonaemia, not hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis. Would be correct with high ammonia and respiratory alkalosis (Source: HMSANZ).

options.text: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 with systemic mineralocorticoid resistance; the discriminating signature is hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + metabolic acidosis with normal cortisol and elevated aldosterone
options.rationale: PHA1 shares the biochemistry but is much rarer; distinguished by elevated aldosterone with normal 17-OHP (opposite of CAH). Would be correct with normal 17-OHP and elevated aldosterone (Source: APEG).

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) with neonatal salt-wasting crisis; the signature is hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia + metabolic acidosis day 7-14
options.rationale: Day 7-14 presentation with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis and shock in either sex is salt-wasting CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency; males have normal external genitalia and so are missed clinically until biochemical crisis, per RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis and ESPE 2018.

explanation.summary: Classical salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents at day 7-14 with vomiting, lethargy, weight loss, dehydration and the characteristic electrolyte triad of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia with metabolic acidosis. Females are usually identified earlier from virilised genitalia; males present in crisis. Diagnosis is by markedly elevated 17-OH progesterone. Treatment is IV fluids, hydrocortisone, dextrose, and long-term hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone.
key_points: Newborn screen (when returned) shows raised 17-OH progesterone
Salt-wasting crisis day 7-14 is the classic timing
Initial bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline, then hydrocortisone 50-100 mg/m^2 IV
Long-term: hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone + salt supplementation in infancy
explanation.pearls: Any unwell second-week-of-life infant with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia is CAH until proven otherwise. The genitalia look normal in boys.

stem:
A 4-year-old girl with classical salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia is brought to the paediatric emergency department by her parents with 24 hours of fever, vomiting and reduced oral intake during a gastroenteritis outbreak at her childcare centre. Her regular medications are hydrocortisone 5 mg in the morning, 2.5 mg at midday and 5 mg at night, plus fludrocortisone 100 microg daily.

Her parents administered an extra oral hydrocortisone dose 6 hours ago but she vomited it back within 10 minutes and has not tolerated anything orally since. They did not have an in-date intramuscular hydrocortisone ampoule at home. On arrival she is drowsy and pale with markedly delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool peripheries and a thready pulse. Her body surface area is calculated at 0.7 m^2 and her weight today is 16 kg. Bedside glucose is 2.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 98% on RA, T 38.7 deg C, BP 78/44 mmHg, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, mottled peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, dry mucous membranes, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 2.8 mmol/L, point-of-care Na 130 mmol/L, K 5.4 mmol/L, weight 16 kg, BSA 0.7 m^2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 20 mg with oral rehydration solution and observe in short-stay for 4 hours
options.rationale: She is shocked, hypoglycaemic and vomiting; oral therapy is inappropriate, parenteral hydrocortisone with IV resuscitation is required. Would never be correct in adrenal crisis (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

options.text: IV dexamethasone, 10 mL/kg Hartmann's solution and IV ceftriaxone
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is unsuitable for adrenal crisis; high-dose hydrocortisone provides both effects. Would be correct only in cerebral oedema (which is not the issue) (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 50 mg bolus, 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis management is stress-dose IV hydrocortisone 50-100 mg/m^2 bolus (approximately 50 mg for a BSA of 0.7 m^2, or 2 mg/kg if BSA unknown), 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, and 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg for documented hypoglycaemia per RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology.

options.text: IM hydrocortisone 100 mg and oral fludrocortisone 100 microg as a double daily dose
options.rationale: IM is acceptable if no IV access, but IV is preferred when access available; oral fludrocortisone does not address acute crisis and is not stress-dosed. Would be correct only without IV access (Source: APEG).

options.text: IV methylprednisolone and a 20 mL/kg 3% saline bolus for presumed cerebral oedema
options.rationale: Methylprednisolone is not preferred; hypertonic saline is not indicated as she has only mild hyponatraemia not cerebral oedema. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Stress-dose hydrocortisone for paediatric adrenal crisis is 50-100 mg/m^2 IV (or 2 mg/kg if BSA unknown), followed by 50-100 mg/m^2/day in divided doses. Resuscitation is 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline, with 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid effect.
key_points: Bolus: 50 mg/m^2 IV or 2 mg/kg
Maintenance: 50-100 mg/m^2/day divided 4-6 hourly
Fluids: 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline; 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg if BSL <3.0
Dexamethasone is for diagnostic testing only, not crisis management
explanation.pearls: Every CAH family should carry an in-date IM hydrocortisone ampoule and have been trained in its use. Sick day rules: double or triple oral dose, switch to IM if vomiting.

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is referred by her GP for short stature. Her height has been below the 1st centile since age 5, and over the last 12 months her growth velocity has been 3 cm/year, having previously tracked along the 3rd centile. Her mid-parental height projects to the 25th centile. Her mother had menarche at age 13 and her father had a normal pubertal timing.

She has no chronic medications, no fatigue, and no family history of coeliac disease, IBD or thyroid disease. She has not yet had any breast development and there is no axillary or pubic hair. Her weight is on the 10th centile and BMI is normal. Examination shows a normal cardiovascular system with no radio-femoral delay or murmur, no goitrerological examination. Bone age performed last week is 9 years.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg, T 36.6 deg C, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Height below 1st centile, weight 10th centile, Tanner stage 1 breast and pubic hair, no dysmorphic features, no goitre, no cubitus valgus
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 9 years (chronological 11), MPH 25th centile, growth velocity 3 cm/year

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line investigation panel?

options.text: Growth hormone provocation testing with clonidine and arginine stimulation alone today
options.rationale: GH provocation testing is second-line after exclusion of systemic disease, hypothyroidism, coeliac and Turner; first-line is broad screening. Would be correct after first-line normal (Source: RCH CPG; APEG).

options.text: FBC, UEC, LFT, TSH/free T4, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), IGF-1, and karyotype
options.rationale: The standard first-line short-stature workup includes FBC, UEC, LFT, TSH/T4, coeliac serology, IGF-1, bone age and karyotype (in girls) to exclude systemic illness, hypothyroidism, coeliac, GH deficiency and Turner syndrome before specialist provocation testing per RCH CPG: Short Stature and ESPE consensus.

options.text: MRI brain with pituitary protocol plus dynamic GnRH stimulation testing now
options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is indicated after biochemical confirmation of GHD or with neurological features, not as first-line screen. Would be correct after confirmed GHD (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Random cortisol, ACTH and short Synacthen test to exclude Addison's as cause
options.rationale: Addison's is not a typical cause of isolated short stature with normal weight; targeted adrenal testing is not first-line. Would be correct only with hyperpigmentation or salt-craving (Source: APEG).

options.text: Faecal calprotectin and upper GI endoscopy to exclude inflammatory bowel disease cause
options.rationale: IBD workup is targeted to GI symptoms or abnormal first-line bloods; endoscopy is invasive not screening. Would be correct with GI symptoms or anaemia/raised CRP (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: First-line workup of short stature in a girl: FBC, UEC, LFT, TSH/free T4, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA), IGF-1 with IGFBP-3, vitamin D, bone age, and karyotype for any girl with unexplained short stature (Turner can present without classical features). Specialist GH testing and pituitary MRI are reserved for after this panel narrows the differential.
key_points: Growth velocity <5 cm/year between ages 4 and puberty is abnormal
Bone age delay >2 years suggests constitutional delay, hypothyroidism, GH deficiency or chronic illness
Karyotype mandatory in all unexplained short girls to exclude Turner
Mid-parental height = (mother + father)/2, minus 6.5 cm for girls
explanation.pearls: Turner syndrome can have a completely normal phenotype apart from short stature. Karyotype any girl who deserves a workup.

stem:
A 6-year-old girl is referred by her GP for breast development first noticed by her mother 8 months ago. Her mother also reports the recent appearance of fine axillary hair, mild adult-type body odour, and accelerated linear growth (she has crossed two centile lines on the height chart in the past year, from 50th to 90th centile). She has had no headaches, no visual symptomsleeding.

There is no neonatal history of seizures or hypothalamic insult. There is no exposure to topical oestrogen, no parental medications she could be accessing, no oestrogen-containing supplements in the household, and no soy-heavy diet. On examination she has Tanner stage 3 breast development with palpable glandular tissue, Tanner stage 2 pubic hair, fine axillary hair on inspection of the underarm, no acne, no cafe-au-lait maculesaly.

Bone age performed today is 9 years. Pelvic ultrasound shows a uterine length of 4.2 cm with an endometrial echo and bilateral ovaries with multiple small follicles and no ovarian cyst or mass.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84 bpm, BP 102/62 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, height 90th centile, weight 75th centile
data_table.Examination: Tanner B3 P2, fine axillary hair, mild body odour, no acne, no clitoromegaly, no abdominal mass, no cafe-au-lait macules
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 9 (chronological 6), pelvic US: uterus 4.2 cm with endometrial echo, ovaries bilateral follicles

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation to distinguish central from peripheral precocious puberty?

options.text: Pelvic MRI to look for an ovarian sex cord-stromal tumour producing oestradiol
options.rationale: Pelvic US already shows pubertal pattern without ovarian mass; pelvic MRI is reserved for US abnormality or suspected peripheral cause. Would be correct only with US abnormality (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: GnRH (or analogue) stimulation test measuring LH and FSH at 0, 30 and 60 minutes
options.rationale: GnRH (or GnRH analogue) stimulation testing with peak LH >=5 IU/L (or LH:FSH ratio >0.66) confirms central precocious puberty, while a suppressed LH response with elevated oestradiol points to a peripheral cause per RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty and ESPE consensus.

options.text: Serum 17-OH progesterone and DHEAS to exclude non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia
options.rationale: Non-classical CAH causes premature adrenarche (pubic/axillary hair, body odour) without breast development; this child has Tanner B3 breast indicating gonadarche. Would be correct with isolated adrenarche features (Source: ESPE).

options.text: Empirical commencement of a GnRH analogue (leuprolide) and monitor for breast regression
options.rationale: Treatment should not precede confirmation of diagnosis and underlying cause (including MRI in girls under 6-8 with central PP). Would never be correct without confirmation (Source: APEG).

options.text: MRI brain with pituitary protocol to look for a hypothalamic hamartoma before any biochemical testing
options.rationale: MRI is done after central PP is biochemically confirmed (or in girls under 6 with central features), not as the first discriminator. Would be correct after biochemical confirmation (Source: ESPE).

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty in girls is breast development before age 8 (or pubic hair/menarche before age 8/9). Central PP is gonadotropin-dependent (HPG axis activation); peripheral PP is gonadotropin-independent (ovarian, adrenal, exogenous). GnRH stimulation distinguishes the two: peak LH >=5 IU/L indicates central. Central PP in girls <6 years mandates MRI brain.
key_points: Random LH alone has poor sensitivity; stimulation is the test
Pubertal pelvic ultrasound: uterus >3.5-4 cm, endometrial echo, multifollicular ovaries
Bone age advancement >2 years suggests significant oestrogen exposure
Treatment for confirmed central PP is GnRH analogue to preserve adult height
explanation.pearls: Isolated premature thelarche (no growth spurt, no bone age advance, prepubertal LH response) does not need treatment, just surveillance.

stem:
A 9-day-old female infant has a positive newborn screening result from the Victorian newborn bloodspot screening program, with a TSH of 92 mIU/L on the day-2 sample (the laboratory cut-off used in Victoria is >=15 mIU/L on the dried bloodspot). She was born at 39+5 by uncomplicated NVD with a birth weight of 3.2 kg and Apgar scores of 9 and 9, has been exclusively breastfed every 3 hours, is feeding well, has had appropriate weight gain since the initial physiological loss and has passed meconium normally.

She has mild prolonged jaundice with a transcutaneous bilirubin of 180 micromol/L at day 9 but is otherwise well, with no lethargy, no constipationdistress reported by her parents. On examination she is alert, has an open posterior fontanelle of 1 cm, no umbilical hernia, no macroglossia and no palpable goitre or anterior neck mass. Confirmatory venous bloods drawn today show TSH 88 mIU/L, free T4 5 pmol/L and thyroglobulin 12 microg/L, with maternal thyroid antibodies still pending. A thyroid ultrasound and Tc-99m pertechnetate scan are being arranged through the nuclear medicine department.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 100% on RA, T 36.8 deg C, weight 3.25 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly jaundiced, posterior fontanelle 1 cm, no macroglossia, no umbilical hernia, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Bloodspot TSH 92 mIU/L, venous TSH 88 mIU/L, free T4 5 pmol/L, thyroglobulin 12 microg/L, bilirubin 180 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the bloodspot TSH at 4 weeks of age and only treat if it remains elevated
options.rationale: Confirmed venous TSH 88 with fT4 5 is unequivocal CH; delaying treatment 3 weeks significantly worsens neurodevelopmental outcome. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Commence oral levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day within 2 weeks of birth and review TFTs in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Confirmed congenital hypothyroidism requires levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day commenced as soon as possible and ideally within 2 weeks of birth to optimise neurodevelopmental outcome, with TFT review at 2 weeks aiming for free T4 in the upper half of the reference range per RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism and ESPE-ATA consensus.

options.text: Commence oral levothyroxine 2 microg/kg/day to avoid overtreatment and review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: 2 microg/kg/day is the adult-equivalent maintenance dose, markedly inadequate for neonatal CH (10-15 mcg/kg/day required). Would be correct only as adult maintenance, not neonatal initiation (Source: ESPE-ATA).

options.text: Defer treatment pending the result of the thyroid scan to determine the underlying aetiology
options.rationale: Treatment must not be delayed for imaging; scan can be done concurrently or after stabilisation. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Commence intravenous liothyronine (T3) 2 microg/kg/day in preference to oral levothyroxine for faster onset
options.rationale: Oral levothyroxine is the standard; T3 is reserved for myxoedema coma. Would never be correct in neonatal CH (Source: ESPE-ATA).

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism affects approximately 1 in 2000 newborns in Australia. Treatment with levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day started within 2 weeks of birth (ideally day 7-10) normalises IQ outcomes. Crushed tablets given with water or breast milk are preferred to liquid suspensions. Target free T4 in the upper half of reference range; aim TSH <5 mIU/L within 4 weeks.
key_points: Dose: levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day oral
Aetiology: thyroid dysgenesis (~80%) > dyshormonogenesis > transient
Imaging: Tc-99m or I-123 scan + ultrasound to characterise
Re-evaluation off treatment at age 3 if dyshormonogenesis suspected
explanation.pearls: Avoid giving levothyroxine with soy-based formula, iron or calcium, which markedly reduce absorption.

stem:
A 14-year-old girl is brought by her mother to the GP because of a 6-month history of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, gradual weight gain of 4 kg with no change in appetite, and a recent slowing of menstruation since menarche at age 12. She has had no neck pain or dysphagia. There is a family history of autoimmune disease, with her aunt having coeliac disease and her grandmother having vitiligo.

On examination she has a smooth, mildly enlarged, non-tender goitre approximately twice the normal size, dry skin, a delayed relaxation phase of the ankle reflex, and a heart rate of 56 bpm. Her height has tracked along the 25th centile but her growth velocity has fallen to 3 cm in the last year. Bloods today show TSH 78 mIU/L, free T4 6 pmol/L, anti-TPO antibodies 480 IU/mL (reference <35), anti-thyroglobulin antibodies 240 IU/mL, normal full blood count and normal electrolytes. Coeliac serology is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 56 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, T 36.1 deg C, BMI 70th centile
data_table.Examination: Smooth diffuse non-tender goitre, dry skin, delayed ankle reflex relaxation, no exophthalmos, Tanner B4 P4
data_table.Investigations: TSH 78 mIU/L, free T4 6 pmol/L, anti-TPO 480 IU/mL, anti-Tg 240 IU/mL, FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence oral levothyroxine 100 microg daily and recheck thyroid function tests in 6-8 weeks
options.rationale: Full adult replacement risks angina-like symptoms, tachyarrhythmia and behavioural symptoms in adolescents; titrate from lower dose. Would be correct only in severe hypothyroidism with myxoedema features (Source: RCH CPG: Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Commence carbimazole 15 mg daily plus propranolol 20 mg three times daily orally
options.rationale: Carbimazole/propranolol treat hyperthyroidism; this is hypothyroidism (high TSH, low fT4). Would be correct in hyperthyroidism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange thyroid ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration of the goitre before any treatment
options.rationale: Smooth diffuse goitre with anti-TPO is Hashimoto's; FNA is for discrete nodules or rapidly growing goitre. Would be correct with palpable discrete nodule (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Defer treatment for 3 months to allow for possible spontaneous resolution of subclinical disease
options.rationale: This is overt hypothyroidism (TSH 78, low fT4), not subclinical, requiring treatment. Would be correct only with subclinical (mildly raised TSH, normal fT4) (Source: ESPE).

options.text: Commence oral levothyroxine 50 microg daily and recheck TFTs in 6-8 weeks
options.rationale: Adolescent autoimmune (Hashimoto's) hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine 1.2-1.7 microg/kg/day (approximately 50 microg daily for a typical 14-year-old), titrating to TSH in the lower half of the reference range with TFTs at 6-8 week intervals per RCH CPG: Hypothyroidism and ESPE guidance.

explanation.summary: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the commonest cause of acquired hypothyroidism in Australian adolescents, with a female predominance and associations with type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease and Turner syndrome. Treatment is levothyroxine titrated to TSH in the lower half of reference range, with biochemical monitoring at 6-8 weeks then every 6-12 months when stable.
key_points: Dose: 1.2-1.7 microg/kg/day in adolescents
Anti-TPO positive in approximately 90% of Hashimoto's
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions (T1DM, coeliac)
Recheck after illness, weight change, pregnancy or new interacting medication
explanation.pearls: TSH may take 4-6 weeks to normalise even with adequate dosing; don't escalate too quickly on a 2-week recheck.

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is referred to the paediatric endocrinology outpatient clinic by her GP with a 3-month history of progressive unintentional weight loss of 6 kg despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, fine tremor, palpitations, mild anxiety, oligomenorrhoea and poor sleep, and a recent decline in academic performance noted by her teachers. Her mother has noticed that her eyes appear more prominent and that she has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and a tendency to fidget.

There is no recent viral illness, no anterior neck paindine-containing medication exposure, and no family history of thyroid disease, although a maternal cousin has type 1 diabetes mellitus and her grandmother has vitiligo. On examination she has a smooth diffuse non-tender goitre approximately twice normal size with an audible bruit on auscultation, mild bilateral proptosis with lid lag and lid retraction, fine resting tremor, warm sweaty palms, and a resting heart rate of 124 bpm in sinus rhythm.

Her bloods show TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 48 pmol/L (reference 9-19), free T3 18 pmol/L (reference 3.5-6.5), anti-TSH receptor antibody 12 IU/L (reference <1.75), and a normal full blood count including a neutrophil count of 4.2 x 10^9/L with normal LFTs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124 bpm sinus, BP 138/72 mmHg with wide pulse pressure, T 37.4 deg C, RR 18 /min
data_table.Examination: Smooth goitre with bruit, mild bilateral proptosis with lid lag, fine tremor, warm sweaty palms, no pretibial myxoedema
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 48 pmol/L, free T3 18 pmol/L, anti-TSHR Ab 12 IU/L, neutrophils 4.2 x 10^9/L, LFT normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line medical management?

options.text: Propylthiouracil 5-10 mg/kg/day orally as preferred thionamide due to peripheral T4-to-T3 block
options.rationale: PTU has a black-box warning for severe hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure; not first-line in paediatric Graves. Would be correct only with carbimazole intolerance, or first trimester pregnancy (Source: ESPE).

options.text: Definitive radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation as initial therapy without a trial of thionamide
options.rationale: Initial therapy is medical with thionamide for 18-24 months; radioiodine offered after relapse or in older adolescents with persistent disease. Would be correct after relapse (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperthyroidism).

options.text: Total thyroidectomy under general anaesthesia as first-line definitive therapy now
options.rationale: Surgery is for thionamide failure/intolerance, very large goitre, or Graves ophthalmopathy where radioiodine unsuitable. Would be correct in those specific situations (Source: ESPE).

options.text: Carbimazole 0.5-1 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses plus propranolol 1-2 mg/kg/day, monitor FBC/LFT
options.rationale: Australian and ESPE-recommended first-line therapy for paediatric Graves' disease is a thionamide (carbimazole preferred to propylthiouracil because of PTU hepatotoxicity in children) at 0.5-1 mg/kg/day with a beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms, baseline and serial neutrophil and LFT monitoring per RCH CPG: Hyperthyroidism and Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology.

options.text: Lugol's iodine 5-10 drops three times daily as monotherapy until normalisation of free T4
options.rationale: Inorganic iodine is used pre-operatively or in thyroid storm, not as chronic monotherapy. Would be correct only as pre-op or thyroid storm adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Paediatric Graves' disease accounts for approximately 95% of paediatric hyperthyroidism, with a strong female predominance. Initial therapy is carbimazole (preferred over PTU due to hepatotoxicity) for at least 18-24 months, with propranolol for adrenergic symptoms. Remission rate after a course is approximately 25-30%; relapse warrants discussion of definitive therapy (radioiodine or thyroidectomy).
key_points: Carbimazole 0.5-1 mg/kg/day, max 30 mg/day (titration regimen) or block-and-replace
PTU avoided in children except in thyroid storm or first trimester pregnancy
Monitor for agranulocytosis (FBC if sore throat or fever) and hepatotoxicity
Anti-TSHR Ab titre at end of treatment predicts relapse risk
explanation.pearls: Counsel families about agranulocytosis: any sore throat or fever on carbimazole = stop and check FBC.

stem:
A 5-year-old boy is referred from his GP for evaluation of polyuria and polydipsia of 4 months' duration. His parents estimate his fluid intake at approximately 4 litres per day, including overnight water bottles, and he is waking 3-4 times nightly to drink and urinate, with secondary nocturnal enuresis after being dry at night for the previous 18 months. He has had a 1 kg weight loss but is otherwise growing on the 25th centile and his pubertal stage is Tanner 1 as expected.

There is no history of head injury, no headachesetes mellitus such as polyphagia. His past history includes Langerhans cell histiocytosis diagnosed 18 months ago at age 3 with cutaneous and bony involvement, treated with vinblastine and prednisolone, that has been in apparent remission on surveillance imaging. On examination he is alert, well perfused, with normal vital signs and an unremarkable systemic examination, including normal fundoscopy and visual field examination by confrontation.

Bloods today show Na 148 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, urea 6.2 mmol/L, creatinine 38 micromol/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, calcium 2.4 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 305 mOsm/kg with a paired urine osmolality of 110 mOsm/kg measured on a morning sample.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, mucous membranes moist, no visual field defect, no papilloedema, no skin lesions visible
data_table.Investigations: Na 148 mmol/L, plasma osm 305 mOsm/kg, urine osm 110 mOsm/kg, SG 1.002, glucose 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Formal water deprivation test with paired plasma and urine osmolality, then desmopressin challenge
options.rationale: Water deprivation test risks dangerous dehydration when there is already biochemical evidence of inappropriate dilute urine in hypernatraemia; diagnosis is already established. Would never be correct (Source: BMJ Best Practice: DI).
source_refs: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

options.text: Desmopressin trial with measurement of urine osmolality response, followed by MRI brain with pituitary protocol
options.rationale: When plasma is already hyperosmolar (>295 mOsm/kg) with hypernatraemia and inappropriately dilute urine (<300 mOsm/kg), DI is biochemically confirmed and a desmopressin trial (urine concentrates >50% = central DI; no response = nephrogenic DI) with MRI brain (looking for loss of posterior pituitary bright spot, infiltrative disease) is appropriate, particularly with this child's LCH history per RCH CPG: Diabetes Insipidus.
source_refs: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

options.text: Renal ultrasound and urinary tract DMSA scan to assess for medullary cystic disease
options.rationale: Renal imaging is reasonable later if nephrogenic DI is confirmed by no desmopressin response; not first-line discriminator. Would be correct after confirmed nephrogenic DI (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test to exclude type 1 diabetes mellitus as the cause
options.rationale: Random glucose 4.8 and urine SG 1.002 exclude osmotic diuresis; this is hypotonic polyuria not DM. Would be correct only with hyperglycaemia and glycosuria (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: 24-hour urinary calcium and serum parathyroid hormone to exclude hypercalciuric nephrogenic DI
options.rationale: Calcium normal at 2.4; chronic hypercalcaemia is unlikely primary cause here; LCH-related central DI is most likely given history. Would be correct only with hypercalcaemia (Source: ESPE).
source_refs: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

explanation.summary: Diabetes insipidus is suggested by hypotonic polyuria with hypernatraemia and hyperosmolar plasma (>295) with inappropriately dilute urine (<300). Once biochemically confirmed without need for water deprivation, a desmopressin trial distinguishes central (urine concentrates) from nephrogenic (no response). MRI brain is mandatory in confirmed central DI to exclude tumour, infiltration (LCH, germ cell tumour) or malformation.
key_points: Hypernatraemia should be corrected slowly (<10-12 mmol/L per 24 hours) to avoid cerebral oedema
Causes of central DI: idiopathic, tumour (craniopharyngioma, germinoma), LCH, trauma, infection
Nephrogenic DI: X-linked AVPR2 mutation, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, lithium, sickle cell
Treatment of central DI: oral or intranasal desmopressin titrated to symptoms
explanation.pearls: LCH commonly involves the pituitary stalk and presents as central DI before any imaging-visible lesion. Repeat MRI 6-monthly if initial scan is normal.

sources.label: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

stem:
A 7-year-old girl is on day 3 of admission for culture-proven Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis. She is receiving IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily, has had dexamethasone for the first 4 doses, and is on maintenance IV fluids with 0.9% saline plus 5% dextrose at 70 mL/hour. Her GCS has improved from 12 on admission to 14 today. Overnight the nurse notes her urine output has fallen to 1.2 mL/kg/h and her morning bloods show Na 124 mmol/L (down from 137 yesterday), K 3.8, urea 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L, plasma osmolality 252 mOsm/kg.

A paired urine sample shows urine sodium 78 mmol/L and urine osmolality 510 mOsm/kg. On clinical examination she is alert, euvolaemic with capillary refill of 2 seconds, moist mucous membranes, no peripheral oedema, JVP not raised, and no postural drop. She has had a mild morning headache but no vomiting, no seizure activity and no focal neurological signs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, T 37.0 deg C, GCS 14, weight 25 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, euvolaemic clinically, no oedema, JVP not raised, no focal neurology, fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: Na 124 mmol/L, K 3.8, urea 3.2, plasma osm 252 mOsm/kg, urine Na 78 mmol/L, urine osm 510 mOsm/kg, urine output 1.2 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluid restriction to approximately two-thirds maintenance with daily electrolytes and strict fluid balance
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality > plasma osmolality and urine sodium >40 mmol/L in a non-seizing asymptomatic child meets criteria for SIADH, treated initially with fluid restriction (typically two-thirds maintenance) and serial monitoring per RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia and Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology.

options.text: 3% hypertonic saline 3-5 mL/kg IV bolus to correct sodium 5 mmol/L over 30 min
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is for symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, severe altered mental state) at Na under 125; she has mild headache only and is alert. Would be correct with seizures or altered mental state at Na under 125 (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia).

options.text: Increase maintenance fluid to 1.5 times maintenance with 0.9% saline to replace renal sodium losses
options.rationale: Increasing fluid worsens dilutional hyponatraemia in SIADH; this is not cerebral salt wasting (which is hypovolaemic). Would be correct in CSW with hypovolaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence oral tolvaptan 15 mg daily for selective V2 receptor antagonism today
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is rarely used in paediatrics, requires inpatient initiation, and is not first-line for transient post-meningitis SIADH. Would be correct only in chronic refractory SIADH (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Administer furosemide IV with potassium chloride supplementation and continue current fluids
options.rationale: Furosemide is sometimes adjunctive in chronic SIADH refractory to restriction; first-line is fluid restriction. Would be correct as adjunct after restriction fails (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: SIADH is a common complication of CNS infection in children. Diagnostic criteria require euvolaemia, hypoosmolar plasma (<275), inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg, usually >plasma), urine Na >40 mmol/L, normal renal/adrenal/thyroid function. First-line treatment is fluid restriction to two-thirds maintenance. Symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, severely altered mental state) is treated with 3% saline 3-5 mL/kg bolus aiming to raise sodium by 4-6 mmol/L. Correction rate should not exceed 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: Fluid restriction is first-line if asymptomatic
3% saline 3-5 mL/kg only if symptomatic (seizures, GCS drop)
Differentiate from cerebral salt wasting (CSW is hypovolaemic with high urine output)
Correction rate max 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Iso-osmolar hyponatraemia in a meningitis admission is more often hospital-acquired from hypotonic IV fluids than true SIADH; always check what's running.

stem:
A 14-year-old boy is referred to a paediatric weight management clinic with a BMI of 36 kg/m^2 (>99.9th centile), with weight gain accelerating since age 9. He was a normally grown infant with a healthy weight until age 8. He has no syndromic features, normal growth velocity, normal pubertal progression, and no developmental delay. He has obstructive sleep apnoea (AHI 18 events/h on polysomnography 6 months ago), insulin-resistant acanthosis nigricans at the neck, persistent right knee pain on impact, and self-reported low mood with school avoidance for the last 6 months.

His mother and uncle have type 2 diabetes; his father has had bariatric surgery. Investigations show fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.9%, fasting insulin elevated, ALT 78 U/L with hepatic steatosis on ultrasound, normal TSH and free T4, normal cortisol with no Cushingoid features, normal calcium and phosphate, and normal renal function. He attends a structured family-based lifestyle program weekly. His parents ask whether medication should be added.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80 bpm, BP 132/82 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, BMI 36 kg/m^2 (>99.9th centile)
data_table.Examination: Acanthosis nigricans neck and axillae, no striae, normal pubertal stage (Tanner G4 P4), no goitre, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.9%, fasting insulin raised, ALT 78 U/L, US: hepatic steatosis, TSH/free T4 normal, cortisol normal, AHI 18/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence oral metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1000 mg BD as adjunct to lifestyle
options.rationale: Metformin is the only oral agent approved for use in paediatric obesity-related insulin resistance with prediabetes/NAFLD as an adjunct to intensive lifestyle change in adolescents from age 10, particularly with HbA1c in the prediabetic range, hepatic steatosis and acanthosis nigricans per APEG position on adolescent metformin use and NHMRC obesity guidance.
source_refs: APEG Position Statement: Metformin in Adolescents
NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Overweight and Obesity

options.text: Commence orlistat 120 mg three times daily with meals as the preferred pharmacotherapy for adolescent obesity
options.rationale: Orlistat has limited efficacy and significant GI side effects in adolescents; not first-line in AU paediatric practice. Would be correct only after metformin failure with high-fat diet (Source: NHMRC Obesity Guidance).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Overweight and Obesity

options.text: Refer immediately for sleeve gastrectomy without any further trial of medical therapy
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is considered after intensive medical/lifestyle therapy failure at BMI over 40 (or over 35 with comorbidities) with MDT assessment. Would be correct only with established intensive treatment failure (Source: NHMRC).
source_refs: ANZMOSS Position Statement on Adolescent Bariatric Surgery

options.text: Commence liraglutide 3 mg subcutaneously daily as TGA-approved first-line adolescent obesity pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: GLP-1 agonists are emerging but TGA paediatric approval and PBS subsidy are limited; metformin remains first-line. Would be correct in selected cases with T2DM under specialist input (Source: NHMRC; TGA).
source_refs: APEG Position Statement: Metformin in Adolescents

options.text: Add a low-dose thyroid hormone supplement to increase basal metabolic rate today
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone in a euthyroid child is contraindicated and causes iatrogenic hyperthyroidism. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Australian management of adolescent obesity is structured family-based intensive lifestyle intervention (diet, activity, behaviour, sleep, screen time) with treatment of comorbidities (OSA, NAFLD, mental health). Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive: metformin is the most evidence-based oral agent for insulin resistance, prediabetes and NAFLD. Bariatric surgery (sleeve gastrectomy) is considered in selected adolescents with BMI >40 (or >35 with comorbidities) after multidisciplinary review. Always exclude secondary causes (hypothyroidism, Cushing, Prader-Willi, MC4R) before labelling primary obesity.
key_points: Metformin 500 mg BD, titrate to max 1000 mg BD if tolerated
Address OSA, NAFLD, mental health and joint pain in parallel
Bariatric criteria (AU): BMI >40 or >35 with comorbidity, age >=15-16, failed intensive therapy
Edmonton Obesity Staging System for Paediatrics (EOSS-P) for risk stratification
explanation.pearls: Acanthosis nigricans + prediabetic HbA1c in an adolescent is a strong indication for metformin; do not wait for overt T2DM to act.

sources.label: APEG Position Statement: Metformin in Adolescents
NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Overweight and Obesity
ANZMOSS Position Statement on Adolescent Bariatric Surgery

stem:
A 4-year-old girl with confirmed trisomy 21 attends her annual general paediatric review at a metropolitan outpatient clinic. She had a complete repair of a complete AVSD at age 7 months and has no residual significant intracardiac shunt on her most recent echocardiogram 6 months ago. She is in mainstream preschool with aide support, has gained 1.4 kg over the past year along her usual centile on the Down syndrome growth chart, and her parents have no specific concerns.

She is on no regular medications. Her most recent TSH 12 months ago was 4.2 mIU/L with a free T4 of 14 pmol/L, both within laboratory reference range. She has had no audiology concerns since her last test, no constipation, no cold intolerance, and her energy levels are normal for her. Her general examination today is unremarkable apart from typical syndromic facies, no goitre, and a flat well-healed midline sternotomy scar. Her mother asks specifically about routine bloods.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, T 36.7, BP 95/60, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Growth: Weight 14.8 kg (50th centile on T21 chart), Height 95 cm (25th centile on T21 chart)
data_table.Examination: Typical T21 features, no goitre, well-healed sternotomy, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Previous investigations: TSH 4.2 mIU/L, fT4 14 pmol/L (12 months ago)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate thyroid screening plan for this child?

options.text: Repeat TSH and free T4 only if symptoms of hypothyroidism develop
options.rationale: Symptom-based screening misses subclinical hypothyroidism (common and frequently asymptomatic in T21); biochemical surveillance is recommended. Would never be correct in T21 (Source: RCH CPG: Down Syndrome).

options.text: Repeat TSH and free T4 every 6 months until age 5, then annually
options.rationale: Six-monthly testing is recommended only in the first year (CH risk highest); from 12 months annual screening is sufficient. Would be correct only in the first year of life (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Annual TSH (with free T4 if TSH abnormal) lifelong
options.rationale: Australian and international Down syndrome guidance recommends annual thyroid screening from age 1 onwards, lifelong, because of the high cumulative incidence of acquired hypothyroidism and frequent subclinical disease in this population (RCH CPG: Down syndrome - health surveillance; AAP clinical report: Down syndrome).

options.text: TSH, free T4 and thyroid autoantibodies every 3 years
options.rationale: Three-yearly testing is too infrequent given high background incidence; routine autoantibodies are not standard. Would never be correct in T21 (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology for routine surveillance
options.rationale: Endocrinology referral is for abnormal results or clinical concerns; uncomplicated annual screening is primary/general paediatric care. Would be correct only with abnormal TSH/fT4 (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Children with trisomy 21 have a markedly increased lifetime risk of both congenital and acquired hypothyroidism, much of it subclinical. Routine annual TSH surveillance from age 1 onwards is recommended in Australian and international guidance (RCH CPG: Down syndrome; AAP Down syndrome health supervision).
key_points: Congenital hypothyroidism is screened on the newborn screen; thereafter, T21 children need ongoing periodic testing
Standard schedule: at birth (newborn screen), at 6 and 12 months, then annually for life
Annual surveillance even in asymptomatic, biochemically normal patients (RCH CPG: Down syndrome)
explanation.pearls: Symptoms of hypothyroidism are easily missed in T21 because hypotonia, constipation, and dry skin overlap with the syndromic baseline - biochemistry, not symptoms, drives detection.

subtopic_detail: Down syndrome - atlantoaxial instability and sport clearance
stem:
A 9-year-old boy with trisomy 21 attends his paediatrician for clearance to join a local junior trampolining club, having previously only participated in school swimming. His parents are keen because of his social benefit but want a clear answer on safety. He had a balanced AVSD repair at 5 months with no residual lesion and has been discharged from cardiology.

He has had no neck pain, no torticollisills, and no clumsiness compared with his usual baseline. His neurological examination today shows the expected mild generalised hypotonia of trisomy 21, symmetric reflexes with no clonus or upgoing plantars, normal tone in all four limbs, and a gait that is age-typical for him with no ataxia. He has never had a cervical spine X-ray. His mother asks whether he requires imaging or specialist review before starting trampolining, swimming and football at his new school.

data_table.Examination: Typical T21 features, mild generalised hypotonia, no torticollis, symmetric reflexes, plantars downgoing, no clonus, age-appropriate gait

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step before he begins trampolining?

options.text: Order routine flexion-extension and lateral cervical spine radiographs before clearing him for any sport participation
options.rationale: Routine flex-ext films in asymptomatic T21 children are no longer recommended (poor predictive value). Would be correct only with symptoms/signs of cord compression (Source: RCH CPG: Down Syndrome).

options.text: Clinical screen with focused history and neurological examination, and counsel that trampolining is high-risk and best avoided
options.rationale: Current guidance is symptom and examination based: ask about neck pain, torticollis, gait change, weakness, sphincter changes; examine for myelopathic signs. Sports involving forced cervical flexion or risk of head-first impact (trampolining, gymnastics, diving, rugby contact, boxing) are specifically discouraged in T21 because of the elevated background risk of atlantoaxial instability (RCH CPG: Down syndrome; AAP Down syndrome health supervision).

options.text: Refer urgently for MRI of the cervical spine before clearing him for any sport participation
options.rationale: MRI is reserved for symptoms/signs of cord compression (neck pain, torticollis, gait deterioration, incontinence, hyperreflexia); not routine pre-sport. Would be correct with neuro signs (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Clear him for trampolining and all contact sports given the entirely normal neurological examination today
options.rationale: Normal exam does not exclude AAI and does not negate elevated T21 risk; trampolining/gymnastics/diving/contact rugby remain discouraged. Would never be correct as blanket clearance (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Restrict him from all organised competitive sport until a paediatric orthopaedic spine specialist review
options.rationale: Blanket sport restriction is not recommended and deprives developmental/social benefit; many sports are encouraged with appropriate selection. Would never be correct as blanket restriction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Routine cervical spine radiography for asymptomatic children with Down syndrome has been abandoned in current Australian and AAP guidance because of poor predictive value. Sports clearance relies on a focused symptom-and-examination screen plus counselling about avoiding activities with forced cervical flexion or head-first impact, such as trampolining and gymnastics (RCH CPG: Down syndrome).
key_points: Screen by history (neck pain, torticollis, gait change, new incontinence, weakness) and examination (tone, reflexes, clonus, plantars, gait)
Trampolining, gymnastics, diving, boxing and certain contact codes are discouraged regardless of imaging
Image only when symptoms or signs raise concern, then with MRI for cord assessment
explanation.pearls: Atlantoaxial instability in T21 presents with subtle changes: torticollis, decline in handwriting or gait, new toe-walking, or new incontinence - all warrant urgent neurosurgical and imaging review.

stem:
A 3-year-old boy with trisomy 21 (AVSD repair at 6 months, normal TSH 5 months ago, fully immunised) is brought to the GP with 3 weeks of progressive lethargy, intermittent low-grade fevers without an obvious source, and new bruising over shins and trunk that he does not recall sustaining. He has been on no medications and has had no preceding viral illness.

On examination he is pale, has a smooth firm spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin, generalised non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy with the largest node 2 cm, multiple bruises in non-traumatic distribution and palatal petechiae. He is haemodynamically stable. Capillary FBC: Hb 68, WCC 22 with blasts on film, platelets 28. He is not febrile to a level requiring urgent neutropenic sepsis protocol but the GP wants the appropriate disposition.

data_table.Examination: Pale, splenomegaly 3 cm BLCM, generalised lymphadenopathy (largest 2 cm), bruising on shins and trunk, palatal petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Hb 68 g/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L (blasts on film), platelets 28 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure as likely viral illness and repeat FBC in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with circulating blasts plus hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy is leukaemia until proven otherwise; delay is unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG; ANZCHOG).

options.text: Empirical oral antibiotics for presumed occult bacterial infection and review at 48 hours without addressing the abnormal blast cells on the film today
options.rationale: Empirical oral antibiotics without focus and without addressing marrow failure delays diagnosis. Would be correct only with documented infective focus and normal bloods (Source: ANZCHOG).

options.text: Same-day transfer to a tertiary paediatric oncology service for marrow assessment, supportive care and isolation; confirm trisomy 21-specific TMD/ML-DS pathway awareness
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with circulating blasts, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy in a child with trisomy 21 is leukaemia until proven otherwise; T21 carries an approximately 10-20-fold increased risk of both ALL and AMKL (and a distinct ML-DS pathway). Same-day tertiary transfer for bone marrow biopsy, supportive care (transfusion as needed, neutropenic precautions) and oncology input is mandatory.

options.text: Order ferritin, B12 and folate to investigate the anaemia in primary care before any involvement of haematology-oncology services at this stage
options.rationale: Nutritional workup does not explain thrombocytopenia, blasts, splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Would be correct only in pure microcytic anaemia without these features (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Refer to outpatient general paediatrics for the next available clinic without same-day haematology-oncology involvement
options.rationale: Outpatient referral risks dangerous delay; needs same-day tertiary oncology assessment. Would never be correct (Source: ANZCHOG).

explanation.summary: Trisomy 21 confers a substantially increased risk of acute leukaemia: ALL across childhood and a unique predisposition to acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (AMKL) under age 4. Pancytopenia with circulating blasts demands urgent tertiary referral for marrow examination (RCH CPG: Suspected leukaemia).
key_points: Approximately 10-20-fold increased risk of leukaemia in trisomy 21 compared with the general paediatric population
AMKL predominates under age 4, ALL throughout childhood
Pancytopenia + blasts + organomegaly = same-day tertiary referral
explanation.pearls: Transient abnormal myelopoiesis in T21 neonates resolves spontaneously in most cases but predisposes to AMKL in the first 4 years - prior TAM is a flag for vigilance.

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with karyotypically confirmed 45,X Turner syndrome is reviewed in a tertiary endocrinology and general paediatric clinic. She was diagnosed in the newborn period after she presented with lymphoedema and a webbed neck; echocardiogram in the neonatal period showed a normally functioning bicuspid aortic valve with no coarctation. She is on subcutaneous growth hormone and her height has tracked along the Turner syndrome centile chart since starting therapy 18 months ago.

Her parents ask about the schedule of ongoing heart investigations because they have read about aortic complications in adult women with Turner syndrome. She is asymptomatic, has no exertional symptoms, plays normally with peers, and has no chest pain, syncope, or palpitations. On examination she has the expected Turner phenotype, a normal cardiac auscultation with no murmur today, and equal brachial and femoral pulses with no inter-limb blood pressure differential. Her last echocardiogram was 18 months ago and was unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 20, BP right arm 102/65, right leg 104/68, no inter-limb gradient
data_table.Examination: Turner phenotype, no murmur, S1 S2 normal, femoral pulses equal to brachial
data_table.Imaging: Bicuspid aortic valve known, last echo 18 months ago - no aortic dilatation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate ongoing cardiac surveillance plan?

options.text: Repeat the echocardiogram only if a new cardiac murmur or new symptom develops in future
options.rationale: Symptom-based surveillance misses progressive aortic dilatation (frequently silent in Turner and a major mortality cause). Would never be correct (Source: Australasian Turner Syndrome Clinical Guideline).

options.text: Echocardiogram every 5 years through childhood, then transition imaging to the adult cardiology service
options.rationale: 5-yearly imaging is insufficient given lifetime aortic root dilatation/dissection risk; more frequent imaging through childhood plus transition MRI is recommended. Would never be correct (Source: International Turner Syndrome Consensus).

options.text: Annual blood pressure measurement and ECG without further imaging unless symptoms arise
options.rationale: BP and ECG do not exclude aortic root dilatation or evolving coarctation; imaging surveillance is required. Would never be correct as sole surveillance (Source: International Turner Syndrome Consensus).

options.text: Serial childhood echocardiography (typically every 3 to 5 years) with a baseline cardiac MRI at adolescent transition
options.rationale: Current guidance recommends serial childhood echocardiography (typically every 3 to 5 years if the heart and aorta are normal, sooner if abnormal), with a transition cardiac MRI in adolescence to establish a baseline of the aortic dimensions for ongoing adult surveillance; this woman will need lifelong imaging because of the aortopathy risk associated with 45,X and bicuspid aortic valve (International Turner Syndrome Guideline 2017; Australian paediatric endocrine practice).

options.text: Cardiac MRI annually from age 6 onwards regardless of cardiac symptoms or echo findings
options.rationale: Annual MRI in a young child often requires sedation and is not warranted in asymptomatic patient with normal recent echo. Would be correct only with abnormal echo or symptoms (Source: International Turner Syndrome Consensus).

explanation.summary: Women with Turner syndrome have a substantially elevated lifetime risk of bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, aortic root dilatation, and dissection. Australian and international guidance recommends serial echocardiography through childhood, with a baseline cardiac MRI at adolescent transition and lifelong adult surveillance (International Turner Syndrome Guideline 2017).
key_points: Bicuspid aortic valve in 15-30%, coarctation in 7-12% of Turner syndrome cases
Aortic dissection risk is markedly elevated, particularly with bicuspid valve, coarctation, hypertension or pregnancy
Childhood echocardiography with transition MRI sets the baseline for adult surveillance
explanation.pearls: Indexed aortic size to body surface area (z-score) is used in children; in adults, ascending aortic size index >2.5 cm/m^2 flags very high dissection risk.

stem:
A 16-month-old girl with genetically confirmed Williams syndrome (7q11.23 microdeletion on chromosomal microarray) is reviewed in a tertiary metabolic clinic after a routine annual calcium check showed an elevated corrected calcium. She has known supravalvular aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 22 mmHg under cardiology follow-up, the characteristic elfin facies, and a sociable, indiscriminately friendly behavioural profile. Over the past 6 weeks her parents describe increased irritability, constipation despite adequate dietary fibre, polyuria with new night-time wetting after months of dry nappies, and reduced appetite.

She has been receiving a standard infant multivitamin including 400 IU/day vitamin D and her formula has been a regular age-appropriate cows-milk-based formula. She has had no recent vitamin D loading, no thiazide diuretic exposure, and no excessive sun exposure unusual for Brisbane.

data_table.Examination: Elfin facies, no goitre, no peripheral oedema, abdomen soft, no palpable mass, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.10 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.55 mmol/L, PTH suppressed 0.4 pmol/L, 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L, phosphate 1.2 mmol/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L, urinary calcium:creatinine ratio elevated
data_table.Imaging: Renal ultrasound: mild bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis
data_table.Medications: Multivitamin with 400 IU vitamin D daily

lead_in: Which single intervention is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase her oral fluid intake only and recheck the serum calcium in 6 weeks without other change
options.rationale: Hydration alone without removing vitamin D and limiting dietary calcium will not address the underlying problem and risks progressive nephrocalcinosis. Would never be correct in Williams hypercalcaemia (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome Health Supervision).

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone daily and continue her current diet and vitamin D supplements unchanged
options.rationale: Steroids are for refractory hypercalcaemia after dietary/supplement adjustment; first-line is removing vitamin D and calcium restriction. Would be correct only after first-line failure (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome).

options.text: Commence a single intravenous infusion of pamidronate in the day-stay unit and continue current diet
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates are for severe/symptomatic/refractory hypercalcaemia with long-lasting bone effects in young children; not first-line in mild-to-moderate disease. Would be correct only with severe refractory hypercalcaemia (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome).

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluid rehydration and intravenous furosemide infusion to promote urinary calcium excretion
options.rationale: Loop diuretics promote calciuria but are reserved for severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with adequate hydration; not first-line in mild outpatient disease. Would be correct in severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome).

options.text: Stop the vitamin D-containing multivitamin and start a low-calcium, vitamin D-free formula with endocrine input
options.rationale: Idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia is a recognised feature of Williams syndrome and the first-line intervention is to remove exogenous vitamin D, switch to a low-calcium specialty formula, and limit dietary calcium under specialist endocrine and dietetic guidance; this approach typically normalises calcium without bisphosphonate or steroid escalation (Williams Syndrome Association clinical care recommendations; AAP Health care supervision for children with Williams syndrome).

explanation.summary: Williams syndrome is a contiguous gene deletion at 7q11.23 - the deleted segment includes the elastin gene (ELN), which produces the syndrome-defining vasculopathy: deficient elastin in arterial walls drives supravalvular aortic stenosis and diffuse arteriopathy. The same deletion encompasses other genes regulating calcium homeostasis and vitamin D sensitivity, which is why children with Williams syndrome are predisposed to idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia (mechanism not fully characterised but reproducible across the cohort). The first-line approach for mild-to-moderate hypercalcaemia is dietary calcium restriction and vitamin D withdrawal with paediatric endocrine guidance; pharmacological escalation (steroids, bisphosphonates, loop diuretics) is reserved for refractory or severe cases (AAP Williams syndrome health supervision).
key_points: Annual calcium and urinary calcium:creatinine screening is recommended in Williams syndrome
Renal ultrasound assesses for nephrocalcinosis when hypercalcaemia is detected
Use low-calcium specialty formula and avoid vitamin D supplementation as first-line management
explanation.pearls: Suppressed PTH plus hypercalcaemia + nephrocalcinosis + elfin facies + supravalvular AS is a syndrome-defining cluster - send microarray for 7q11.23 deletion.

subtopic_detail: Noonan syndrome - feeding and cardiac surveillance
stem:
An 8-month-old boy referred from a regional paediatrician now has a confirmed PTPN11 pathogenic variant consistent with Noonan syndrome. His parents are seen in a metropolitan multidisciplinary Noonan clinic. He has known mild-to-moderate valvular pulmonary stenosis on his most recent echocardiogram with a peak gradient of 35 mmHg and no clinical decompensation. He has been a slow and reluctant feeder since birth, taking 60 to 90 minutes for a bottle, with frequent posseting, occasional choking on thin fluids, and a weight tracking along the 3rd centile despite caloric fortification advice.

He has had no aspiration pneumonias to date. He has the typical Noonan facies with hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, a webbed neck, and a pectus carinatum-excavatum combination. Developmentally he is mildly delayed in gross motor but has age-appropriate social engagement. Bleeding history is unremarkable with no easy bruising and no prolonged bleeding from heel pricks. His parents ask which specialist input is most important to add now to address the issue limiting his weight gain.

data_table.Growth: Weight 6.4 kg (3rd centile), Length 65 cm (10th centile)
data_table.Examination: Noonan facies, 3/6 ESM at upper LSE radiating to back, normal femoral pulses, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Echo: valvular PS, peak gradient 35 mmHg, normal RV function; FBC normal; coagulation screen pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next addition to his multidisciplinary management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric feeding service for multidisciplinary assessment with speech pathology and dietetics
options.rationale: Feeding difficulties are extremely common in Noonan syndrome and a leading cause of failure to thrive in infancy. A coordinated feeding assessment (speech pathology for swallow safety, dietetics for caloric optimisation, occupational therapy for sensory feeding behaviours) addresses the dominant clinical problem in this child (Noonan Syndrome Clinical Management Guidelines; RCH CPG: Failure to thrive).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.text: Refer urgently to cardiology for balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty to relieve the pulmonary stenosis gradient
options.rationale: Valvuloplasty in Noonan is for severe PS (peak gradient over 60 mmHg) or symptomatic disease, with reduced efficacy given dysplastic valve. Would be correct with severe PS gradient (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.text: Commence subcutaneous growth hormone therapy now to address his persistent short stature and weight
options.rationale: GH in Noonan is considered later in childhood after endocrinology assessment; not appropriate at 8 months with active feeding difficulties. Would be correct in older child after feeding stabilised (Source: APEG).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.text: Refer to paediatric haematology now for prophylactic platelet transfusions and ongoing infusion planning
options.rationale: Routine prophylactic platelet transfusions are not indicated in asymptomatic infants; baseline coagulation/platelet function assessment is appropriate. Would be correct only with active bleeding (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.text: Refer the parents to clinical genetics for counselling alone, without further specialist clinical input
options.rationale: Counselling alone does not address failure to thrive; immediate growth/feeding intervention is needed. Would be correct as part of broader plan, not alone (Source: Noonan Syndrome Consensus).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

explanation.summary: Noonan syndrome management is multidisciplinary, with feeding difficulties and growth failure dominating infancy in a substantial minority of children.
