Coordinated speech-pathology-led feeding assessment with dietetic input is the immediate priority once cardiac disease is stable below intervention thresholds (Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines).
key_points: Pulmonary stenosis is the most common cardiac lesion (around 50%) and is often dysplastic, frequently requiring surgical rather than balloon intervention if severe
Bleeding diathesis is common - check FBC, coagulation, and consider von Willebrand and platelet function before any surgery
Growth hormone consideration is later in childhood, after feeding and growth optimisation
explanation.pearls: Noonan syndrome is autosomal dominant - examine parents for subtle phenotype and consider parental molecular testing once the proband variant is known.

sources.label: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

stem:
A 12-year-old girl is referred by her GP to a paediatric cardiology and genetics service because her father was recently diagnosed with Marfan syndrome at age 41 after an acute type A aortic dissection that he survived following emergency surgery. A pathogenic FBN1 variant was identified on his diagnostic genetic panel. She is asymptomatic, plays netball at school, and has no chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or visual symptoms.

She has never had an ophthalmology slit-lamp examination or an echocardiogram. On clinical examination today she is tall for her age and family (height 168 cm, 95th centile; mid-parental centile 50th), with a moderate pectus excavatum, mild thoracolumbar scoliosis on standing radiograph (Cobb 18 degrees), a positive Steinberg sign on the right, and an arm span to height ratio of 1.04. She has no spontaneous pneumothorax history, no skin striae beyond unremarkable post-pubertal striae, and no dural ectasia symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Tall, pectus excavatum, mild scoliosis (Cobb 18), positive right Steinberg, arm span:height 1.04, no Walker-Murdoch, no high-arched palate, no skin hyperextensibility
data_table.Family history: Father - pathogenic FBN1 variant, type A dissection at 41 (survived)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order whole-exome sequencing now as the first-line genetic investigation for this asymptomatic teenager
options.rationale: Whole-exome sequencing is not appropriate as first-line when a specific familial variant is known; cascade testing is more efficient and definitive. Would be correct only without known familial variant (Source: Marfan Foundation).

options.text: Order a full multi-gene aortopathy panel (FBN1, TGFBR1/2, ACTA2, MYH11) as first-line genetic testing
options.rationale: Multi-gene panels are first-line when no familial variant is known; with a confirmed variant, cascade is faster, cheaper and definitive. Would be correct only without known familial variant (Source: Marfan Foundation).

options.text: Reassure that her habitus is familial and rescreen only if she later develops cardiovascular symptoms
options.rationale: Symptom-based screening in a first-degree relative of confirmed FBN1 variant carrier is unsafe; root dilatation is usually asymptomatic until dissection. Would never be correct (Source: Marfan Foundation).

options.text: Refer for empirical prophylactic beta-blocker therapy without genetic testing or baseline aortic imaging today
options.rationale: Medical therapy starts after diagnosis is made and aortic dimensions documented; empirical beta-blockade before confirming is premature. Would be correct after confirmed diagnosis (Source: Marfan Foundation).

options.text: Targeted cascade FBN1 testing for the familial variant, plus baseline echocardiogram and ophthalmology slit-lamp assessment
options.rationale: When a familial pathogenic FBN1 variant is known, targeted (cascade) genetic testing for that single variant is the most efficient confirmatory test in at-risk first-degree relatives, alongside baseline imaging of the aorta (echocardiogram +/- subsequent MRI/CT) and an ophthalmology assessment for ectopia lentis; the revised Ghent criteria include both genetic and clinical pathways to diagnosis (Revised Ghent criteria 2010; Marfan Foundation clinical care guidelines).

explanation.summary: When a familial pathogenic FBN1 variant is known, first-degree relatives undergo cascade targeted genetic testing combined with baseline aortic imaging and ophthalmology assessment. The revised Ghent criteria explicitly incorporate genetic findings to confirm or exclude Marfan syndrome in relatives (Revised Ghent criteria 2010).
key_points: Cascade testing of a known familial variant is the most efficient genetic strategy
Echocardiogram measures aortic root Z-score and screens for mitral valve prolapse
Ophthalmology slit-lamp examination is essential to detect ectopia lentis
explanation.pearls: A negative cascade test for a known familial pathogenic FBN1 variant effectively excludes Marfan syndrome in that relative and ends ongoing surveillance.

subtopic_detail: Marfan syndrome - aortic protection and activity
stem:
A 15-year-old boy with previously diagnosed Marfan syndrome on the basis of revised Ghent criteria and a confirmed FBN1 pathogenic variant attends his annual paediatric cardiology review at a tertiary centre. He plays competitive rowing five times per week, including ergometer sessions involving repetitive Valsalva. His most recent transthoracic echocardiogram shows an aortic root at the sinuses of Valsalva of 4.0 cm with a Z-score of 3.2 indexed to body surface area, increased from a Z-score of 2.5 one year ago.

There is mild aortic regurgitation. He has no history of dissection, no syncope, and no documented hypertension. He is currently not on any cardiovascular medications, having declined them previously because his aortic root was within range. His mother died of a presumed type A dissection in her late 30s.

data_table.Examination: Tall Marfanoid habitus, soft early diastolic murmur at LSE consistent with mild AR, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Imaging: Aortic root 4.0 cm, Z-score 3.2 (was 2.5 one year ago), mild aortic regurgitation, no dissection

lead_in: Which single management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue the current competitive rowing program, defer medication, and review again in 12 months' time
options.rationale: Z-score increase from 2.5 to 3.2 over 12 months warrants both pharmacological aortic protection and high-intensity isometric/burst-Valsalva sport modification. Would never be correct (Source: Marfan Foundation; Bethesda).

options.text: Commence beta-blocker (or losartan if intolerant), restrict competitive isometric and contact sport, repeat imaging every 6 months
options.rationale: An aortic root Z-score of 3.2 with rapid progression warrants commencement of beta-blockade (or angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan if intolerant), avoidance of competitive contact, isometric and burst-Valsalva sports, and intensified imaging surveillance every 6 months. Moderate aerobic exercise is encouraged (Marfan Foundation clinical care recommendations; AHA / Bethesda Conference guidance).

options.text: Refer immediately for prophylactic aortic root replacement surgery at the current aortic root diameter
options.rationale: Elective root replacement is at ~5.0 cm in adults (or smaller with rapid progression/family dissection); current diameter does not meet threshold. Would be correct at >=5.0 cm or rapid progression (Source: AHA).

options.text: Commence a beta-blocker but allow unrestricted rowing and rugby resistance work because medication is fully protective
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy does not substitute for activity modification; competitive contact/isometric/burst-Valsalva sport is restricted regardless of medication. Would never be correct (Source: AHA exercise guidance).

options.text: Stop all exercise indefinitely and avoid any organised or recreational physical activity going forward
options.rationale: Complete cessation is not recommended; moderate aerobic non-isometric exercise is encouraged for cardiovascular/psychosocial benefit. Would never be correct (Source: Bethesda/AHA).

explanation.summary: Aortic protection in Marfan syndrome combines pharmacotherapy (beta-blockade or angiotensin receptor blockade), activity modification (avoid competitive contact, isometric and burst-Valsalva sport, continue moderate aerobic activity), and serial imaging. Surgical thresholds are 5.0 cm aortic root, or smaller with rapid progression, family history of early dissection, planned pregnancy, or significant aortic regurgitation (Marfan Foundation clinical care recommendations).
key_points: Beta-blockade and angiotensin receptor blockade slow aortic root growth in Marfan syndrome
Family history of early dissection lowers the surgical threshold
Restrict competitive isometric/contact sports; encourage moderate aerobic exercise
explanation.pearls: Indexed aortic Z-score and rate of change matter more than a single absolute diameter when deciding to start or escalate therapy in a growing adolescent.

stem:
A 17-year-old woman is referred to a paediatric genetics service from a regional clinic for assessment of suspected Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Her sister, aged 21, was recently admitted to a metropolitan tertiary hospital after a spontaneous splenic artery rupture and underwent emergency embolisation; sister's subsequent connective tissue gene panel confirmed a pathogenic COL3A1 variant. The patient herself has generalised joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 7/9, soft velvety skin, easy bruising in unusual locations (forearms, thighs) that her mother has long attributed to clumsiness, and translucent skin over the chest wall with prominent visible veins.

She has had no major vascular events, but reports two episodes of mild epistaxis in the past year and a self-resolving spontaneous left-sided pneumothorax aged 14 (managed conservatively). She has thin lips, a thin nose, and prominent eyes. She has no marfanoid habitus, no aortic root dilatation on a recent echocardiogram (root 2.6 cm, Z-score 0.4), no ectopia lentis, no scoliosis, and a normal palate.

data_table.Examination: Beighton 7/9, soft velvety translucent skin, visible chest wall veins, easy bruising, thin lips, thin nose, prominent eyes; no marfanoid habitus, no aortic root dilatation
data_table.Family history: Sister with confirmed COL3A1 pathogenic variant, splenic artery rupture
data_table.History: Spontaneous pneumothorax age 14, recurrent epistaxis

lead_in: Which single statement most accurately reflects the most likely diagnosis and the best next step?

options.text: Hypermobile EDS - reassure and focus on physiotherapy and pain management, with no genetic testing arranged
options.rationale: Hypermobile EDS does not explain translucent skin, prominent venous pattern, spontaneous pneumothorax, easy bruising, or familial COL3A1 variant. Would be correct only in isolated hypermobility (Source: EDS Society Care Recommendations).

options.text: Vascular EDS - cascade COL3A1 testing, baseline non-invasive vascular imaging, celiprolol if confirmed, plus pregnancy counselling
options.rationale: The combination of translucent skin, characteristic facies, easy bruising in unusual locations, spontaneous pneumothorax, and a first-degree relative with a confirmed pathogenic COL3A1 variant strongly suggests vascular EDS. Cascade targeted testing for her sister's variant is the next step; if confirmed, baseline non-invasive vascular imaging, celiprolol (where available - the BBEST trial showed reduction in arterial events), avoidance of routine arteriography, and detailed pregnancy counselling are recommended (International EDS classification 2017; EDS Society care recommendations).

options.text: Marfan syndrome - arrange FBN1 testing and commence losartan empirically while awaiting confirmation of the diagnosis
options.rationale: No marfanoid habitus, no aortic root dilatation, no ectopia lentis, no high-arched palate; known familial COL3A1 not FBN1. Would never be correct (Source: Marfan Foundation).

options.text: Classical EDS - send COL5A1 and COL5A2 testing rather than the COL3A1 gene that her sister carries
options.rationale: Classical EDS features atrophic scarring and marked skin hyperextensibility; familial COL3A1 directs cascade not COL5A1/A2. Would be correct only with classical EDS features and family history (Source: EDS Society).

options.text: Confirmed vascular EDS - proceed directly to catheter arteriography to comprehensively map the entire arterial tree
options.rationale: Catheter arteriography in vascular EDS carries high arterial dissection risk; non-invasive MRA/CTA is preferred. Would never be correct (Source: EDS Society).

explanation.summary: Vascular EDS is a COL3A1 disease: pathogenic variants disrupt the type III collagen homotrimer, the dominant structural collagen of medium-sized arteries, alveolar septa, hollow viscus walls, and the dermal reticular layer. The phenotype follows directly from where type III collagen lives. Fragile arterial media drives spontaneous medium-vessel rupture and dissection (often without preceding aneurysm). Fragile alveolar walls produce spontaneous pneumothorax (a top-decile feature in adolescence). Capillary and venular fragility produces easy bruising in unusual locations. Depletion of dermal type III collagen thins the skin and exposes the subdermal venous network (translucent skin, prominent veins). Reduced subcutaneous fat over the face combined with thin nose, thin lips and prominent eyes gives the recognisable facies. The same defect underlies intestinal (sigmoid) and uterine (third-trimester) rupture and the substantially elevated pregnancy mortality. With a known familial pathogenic variant, management is cascade testing, non-invasive vascular imaging (MRA/CTA, NOT catheter arteriography because instrumentation tears the same vessels), celiprolol where available (BBEST trial reduced arterial events), avoidance of elective surgery and central venous access where possible, and pre-conception multidisciplinary counselling (International EDS classification 2017; EDS Society care recommendations).
key_points: Mechanism: COL3A1 variant -> defective type III collagen -> fragile medium arteries, alveolar walls, hollow viscera, dermis
Major diagnostic features of vEDS: arterial/intestinal/uterine rupture, family history of vEDS, characteristic facies, easy bruising
Celiprolol reduced arterial events in the BBEST trial; not yet routinely PBS-listed but used internationally
Pregnancy in vEDS carries substantially elevated mortality risk and warrants pre-conception multidisciplinary counselling
explanation.pearls: Avoid arteriography, central venous access where possible, and elective surgery in vEDS - tissue fragility makes surgical complications common and severe.

subtopic_detail: Fragile X - inheritance and carrier counselling
stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends a genetics outpatient clinic for counselling after her 5-year-old son was diagnosed with Fragile X syndrome on a clinically indicated FMR1 molecular test showing a full mutation expansion of approximately 380 CGG repeats. Her son has moderate intellectual disability, autistic features, and the classic phenotype. Targeted FMR1 testing of the patient herself reveals a premutation in the 80 CGG repeat range.

She is currently considering a second pregnancy and asks specifically about the risk to her future biological children, the implications for her own health, and the implications for her younger brother (aged 28) and her elderly father. Her brother and father are clinically asymptomatic. She has had no fertility issues to date and her menstrual cycles are regular.

data_table.Genetics: Index case (son): FMR1 full mutation (~380 CGG repeats); Mother (patient): FMR1 premutation (~80 CGG repeats)
data_table.Family history: Maternal grandfather alive aged 72, no known clinical issues; brother 28 - asymptomatic

lead_in: Which single statement is the most accurate counselling point?

options.text: Any future daughter who inherits her premutation will definitely develop full-syndrome Fragile X in childhood
options.rationale: Heterozygous females with full mutation often have variable milder phenotype from X-inactivation; premutation inheritance does not cause full Fragile X. Would never be correct (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).

options.text: Fragile X is autosomal recessive and her brother must be tested before he plans any pregnancy
options.rationale: Fragile X is X-linked, not autosomal recessive; this fundamentally changes carrier risk and reproductive counselling. Would never be correct (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).

options.text: Premutation alleles do not expand on transmission and never cause clinical disease in any carrier
options.rationale: Premutation alleles can expand on female-line transmission and cause clinical disease (FXPOI in ~20% of female carriers, FXTAS). Would never be correct (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).

options.text: Her father almost certainly carries the full mutation and has a 50% transmission risk to children
options.rationale: Male premutation carriers transmit only stable premutation to daughters, never the full mutation directly; her father almost certainly carries a premutation. Would never be correct (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).

options.text: Each future biological son has a 50% inheritance risk, and female-line premutations can expand to full mutation
options.rationale: Fragile X is X-linked. A female premutation carrier transmits the affected X with a 50% probability to each child; only female-line transmission carries the risk of CGG repeat expansion to the full mutation, with the expansion risk rising sharply once maternal premutation length exceeds approximately 90 to 100 repeats. A son who inherits the expanded full mutation will manifest the syndrome (RANZCOG carrier screening; National Fragile X Foundation clinical guidance).

explanation.summary: Fragile X is X-linked with CGG expansion of the FMR1 gene. Premutation (~55-200 repeats) carriers risk female-line expansion to full mutation (>200 repeats) and direct premutation-associated disease (FXPOI in females, FXTAS in older males). Counselling addresses transmission, expansion risk, reproductive options, and broader family cascade testing (National Fragile X Foundation; RANZCOG).
key_points: Premutation: ~55-200 CGG repeats; full mutation: >200 CGG repeats with FMR1 hypermethylation
Expansion to full mutation occurs only with female-line transmission; risk rises with premutation size
Reproductive options: prenatal diagnosis (CVS/amniocentesis), preimplantation genetic testing, gamete donation
explanation.pearls: Female premutation carriers are at risk of fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency - relevant when counselling about timing of family planning.

stem:
A 4-year-old previously well girl is brought to her GP because her mother has noticed an increasing number of pale brown skin patches over 2 years. There is no family history of neurofibromatosis or unexplained tumours. She is developmentally appropriate, fully immunised and otherwise well. On full examination today she has 7 well-demarcated cafe-au-lait macules across her trunk and limbs, all greater than 5 mm in longest diameter, and bilateral axillary freckling clearly visible.

She has no Lisch nodules visible on bedside ophthalmoscopy, no plexiform neurofibroma, no cutaneous neurofibroma, no symptoms of optic glioma, and no skeletal dysplasia. Growth is on the 50th centile (head circumference 75th). Vision and developmental screening today are normal.

data_table.Examination: 7 cafe-au-lait macules >5 mm, bilateral axillary freckling, no neurofibromas, no Lisch nodules on bedside exam, no skeletal abnormality

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate conclusion-and-next-step pair under the 2021 revised NIH/NF1 criteria?

options.text: She does not meet criteria because skin findings alone can never be diagnostic of NF1; do not refer to paediatric genetics or arrange surveillance
options.rationale: 2021 revised criteria allow diagnosis on two features and explicitly include 6+ CALMs plus skin-fold freckling without family history. Would never be correct (Source: 2021 Revised NIH/NF1 Criteria).

options.text: She meets criteria only if molecular NF1 gene testing returns a pathogenic variant; do not diagnose NF1 without sequencing confirmation first
options.rationale: Molecular confirmation is one criterion but not required when two clinical criteria are present. Would be correct only with one clinical feature plus molecular variant (Source: 2021 NIH).

options.text: She does not meet criteria because the cafe-au-lait macule threshold is at least 10 lesions over 15 mm in size in this prepubertal age group
options.rationale: Threshold is 6+ CALMs over 5 mm pre-pubertally (or over 15 mm post-pubertally), not 10. Would never be correct (Source: 2021 NIH).

options.text: She meets criteria (>=6 cafe-au-lait over 5 mm PLUS axillary freckling = two 2021 criteria); refer to paediatric genetics for NF1 surveillance pathway
options.rationale: Under the 2021 revised criteria she meets two features (macule count/size and skin-fold freckling). AU practice (RCH CPG: NF1) is then to refer for genetics, formal paediatric ophthalmology slit-lamp (Lisch nodules and optic pathway glioma screening), blood pressure monitoring annually (phaeochromocytoma/renovascular risk) and structured developmental and learning surveillance.

options.text: She meets criteria only if a first-degree relative also has clinically confirmed NF1 with documented genetic testing for a pathogenic variant
options.rationale: Affected first-degree relative is one of several alternative features, not required when two clinical features are present. Would be correct only with one clinical feature plus first-degree relative (Source: 2021 NIH).

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of NF1 is clinical, based on the 2021 revised NIH/NF1 criteria requiring two or more defined features. Cafe-au-lait macule threshold is 6 or more, >5 mm prepubertally or >15 mm postpubertally, and skin-fold freckling counts as a separate diagnostic feature (Revised NF1 diagnostic criteria 2021).
key_points: 6 or more cafe-au-lait macules with appropriate size threshold
Skin-fold freckling (axillary or inguinal) is a separate diagnostic feature
Other criteria: neurofibromas, optic glioma, Lisch nodules or choroidal abnormalities, distinctive bone lesion, pathogenic NF1 variant, affected first-degree relative
explanation.pearls: Even with diagnostic certainty by clinical criteria, NF1 children need structured surveillance for optic pathway glioma (under age 7), neurofibroma growth, scoliosis, and learning issues.

stem:
A 3-year-old boy with clinically diagnosed neurofibromatosis type 1 (multiple cafe-au-lait macules, bilateral axillary freckling, affected mother) is seen at his general paediatric clinic for a routine review. He is developmentally appropriate, has no headaches, no vomiting, and no obvious visual complaints. He has had no prior dedicated ophthalmology assessment. His mother has been told that NF1 children are at risk of optic pathway glioma but is unclear when surveillance should start and how often it should occur.

On examination today he has no obvious visual abnormality on bedside testing, no proptosis, normal pupils, and a fundus that is difficult to assess in clinic. There is no precocious puberty, no growth failure, and no new neurological deficit.

data_table.Examination: Multiple CALMs, bilateral axillary freckling, no proptosis, no precocious puberty, no focal neurology

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate surveillance plan for optic pathway glioma in this child?

options.text: MRI brain and orbits every 6 months as routine surveillance until age 8 regardless of symptoms
options.rationale: Routine screening MRI is not recommended in asymptomatic NF1 children (most OPGs are indolent); MRI is for clinical/ophthalmic abnormality. Would be correct only with visual change or ophthalmic abnormality (Source: AAP NF1 Health Supervision).

options.text: Refer only if visual symptoms develop, with no scheduled ophthalmology or imaging surveillance
options.rationale: Pre-verbal/young children cannot reliably report visual loss; scheduled ophthalmology detects OPG when intervention may preserve vision. Would never be correct (Source: AAP NF1).

options.text: Annual paediatric ophthalmology review (acuity, visual fields, fundus) until around age 7 to 8
options.rationale: Symptomatic optic pathway glioma in NF1 almost always presents under age 7. The standard surveillance approach is annual paediatric ophthalmology with formal visual acuity, colour vision, visual fields (when age-appropriate), and dilated fundus examination through early childhood; MRI is reserved for concerning ophthalmology findings (RCH CPG: NF1; AAP NF1 health supervision).

options.text: GP-led bedside visual acuity check at each routine immunisation visit only
options.rationale: Standard primary-care vision checks are not adequately sensitive for OPG in NF1; formal paediatric ophthalmology is required. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: RCH CPG: NF1).

options.text: Annual CT brain and orbits with intravenous contrast as routine optic pathway surveillance
options.rationale: CT delivers ionising radiation compounding NF1-associated second-tumour risk and is less sensitive than MRI for OPG. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Optic pathway glioma is the commonest CNS tumour in childhood NF1 and presents almost exclusively before age 7. Surveillance is by annual paediatric ophthalmology through early childhood, with MRI reserved for clinical or examination concern. Routine screening MRI is not recommended (RCH CPG: NF1).
key_points: Annual paediatric ophthalmology surveillance until approximately age 7 to 8, then less frequent
MRI when clinical concern arises (new strabismus, proptosis, precocious puberty, visual change)
Most NF1 OPGs are indolent and do not need treatment - surveillance triggers intervention only for clinical or imaging progression
explanation.pearls: Precocious puberty in NF1 should trigger MRI of the hypothalamic/optic chiasm region - it can be the first sign of an optic chiasm glioma.

stem:
A 7-month-old infant girl is brought to a regional paediatric ED with a 5-day history of new clusters of stereotyped flexion movements occurring on waking and after feeds. The clusters consist of brief symmetrical flexion of the neck, trunk, and arms occurring every 5 to 10 seconds for up to 2 minutes, after which she appears distressed and then drowsy.

Her mother has captured a video showing typical infantile spasms. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, but a fetal MRI at 30 weeks performed because of a cardiac rhabdomyoma seen on antenatal scan showed multiple cortical tubers. A postnatal genetic panel confirmed a pathogenic TSC2 variant. On general examination today she has 3 hypopigmented ash-leaf macules on her trunk and a developmental regression noted by her parents - she had been babbling and reaching for objects 6 weeks ago but is now less responsive and no longer reaches. EEG performed today shows hypsarrhythmia.

data_table.Examination: 3 ash-leaf macules, regression of social and motor milestones, no focal neurology
data_table.Imaging: Multiple cortical tubers on prior MRI; cardiac rhabdomyoma stable

lead_in: Which single first-line therapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Levetiracetam monotherapy
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is not first-line for infantile spasms; RCT evidence supports vigabatrin (in TSC) and hormonal therapy otherwise. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Spasms).

options.text: Oral prednisolone monotherapy
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy is first-line for infantile spasms without identified cause; in TSC-related spasms vigabatrin is preferred (RCT-superior). Would be correct in non-TSC infantile spasms (Source: International TSC Consensus 2021).

options.text: Sodium valproate monotherapy
options.rationale: Valproate is not first-line and is avoided in young female infants due to teratogenicity; lower efficacy than hormonal/vigabatrin. Would never be correct as first-line (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Vigabatrin monotherapy
options.rationale: In infantile spasms occurring in the context of tuberous sclerosis complex, vigabatrin is the first-line agent and is preferred over ACTH or prednisolone because of superior efficacy in this specific subgroup; visual field monitoring is required because of the recognised risk of peripheral visual field loss (RCH CPG: Infantile spasms; International TSC Consensus Recommendations 2021).

options.text: Ketogenic diet (first-line)
options.rationale: Ketogenic diet is recognised for refractory infantile spasms but not first-line; trial vigabatrin first in TSC. Would be correct after vigabatrin failure (Source: International TSC Consensus).

explanation.summary: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia in TSC are treated first with vigabatrin, which has superior efficacy in this subgroup compared with hormonal therapy. Visual field monitoring is essential because of the recognised risk of peripheral visual field constriction (International TSC Consensus 2021).
key_points: Vigabatrin first-line for TSC-related infantile spasms
Hormonal therapy (prednisolone or ACTH) first-line in non-TSC infantile spasms
Early recognition and treatment improves developmental outcome
explanation.pearls: An antenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma is a strong predictor of tuberous sclerosis - early genetic confirmation enables proactive surveillance for spasms, autism, and TAND.

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P1 woman is referred to tertiary fetal medicine after a 28-week scan showed a 14 mm well-circumscribed echogenic mass on the fetal interventricular septum and a second 8 mm mass on the LV free wall. Fetal cardiac function is preserved, there is no hydrops, no significant outflow obstruction and normal amniotic fluid volume. The woman has no personal history of seizures, facial angiofibromas or hypopigmented macules, and a normal renal ultrasound last year.

There is no family history of tuberous sclerosis. Dedicated reassessment of the fetal brain, kidneys and skeleton shows no other anomalies (acknowledging antenatal imaging limits).

data_table.Imaging: Fetal echo: 14 mm IVS rhabdomyoma + 8 mm LV free wall rhabdomyoma, preserved function
data_table.Family history: No known TSC; maternal clinical examination unremarkable

lead_in: Which combination of counselling, antenatal investigation and postnatal plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Multiple fetal cardiac rhabdomyomas are strongly linked to TSC (~75-80%); arrange fetal MRI for cortical tubers, plan TSC1/TSC2 sequencing postnatally
options.rationale: International TSC consensus: multiple fetal cardiac rhabdomyomas confer about 75-80 percent risk of TSC. Antenatal workup includes fetal MRI for CNS lesions; postnatal: clinical genetics, TSC1/TSC2 sequencing, dermatologic, ophthalmologic, neurology, renal and cardiac surveillance per RCH CPG.

options.text: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are almost always isolated benign tumours unrelated to any syndromic diagnosis; no further postnatal evaluation or genetic testing required
options.rationale: Although lesions regress, multiple rhabdomyomas are strongly associated with TSC and require workup. Would never be correct (Source: International TSC Consensus).

options.text: Antenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma is essentially diagnostic of Williams syndrome; arrange 7q11.23 microarray and avoid further multisystem surveillance investigations
options.rationale: Williams causes supravalvular AS and elfin facies, not cardiac rhabdomyomas. Would never be correct (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Antenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma is most commonly associated with Noonan syndrome (RASopathy); arrange a RASopathy gene panel and skip the fetal MRI now
options.rationale: Noonan cardiac involvement is pulmonary valve stenosis and HCM, not rhabdomyomas. Would never be correct (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Lesions typically grow rapidly after birth and require surgical excision in the neonatal period without any further syndromic evaluation or follow-up
options.rationale: Rhabdomyomas typically peak in the third trimester and regress after birth; surgery is reserved for haemodynamic obstruction or refractory arrhythmia. Would be correct only with obstruction or arrhythmia (Source: International TSC Consensus).

explanation.summary: Multiple antenatal cardiac rhabdomyomas should trigger evaluation for tuberous sclerosis complex with fetal brain MRI and postnatal molecular testing of TSC1/TSC2. The cardiac lesions themselves usually regress, but the syndromic implications drive longitudinal surveillance for spasms, TAND, renal and pulmonary disease (International TSC Consensus 2021).
key_points: Multiple fetal rhabdomyomas: about 75-80% are associated with TSC
Single rhabdomyoma: TSC association lower but still warrants assessment
Cardiac lesions typically regress; surveillance is for syndromic, not cardiac, indications
explanation.pearls: Postnatal mTOR inhibitor therapy (sirolimus or everolimus) can shrink TSC-related tumours including SEGAs, renal angiomyolipomas, and rhabdomyomas in selected cases.

subtopic_detail: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome - hypocalcaemia and immune workup
stem:
A 5-day-old term male neonate is reviewed on the postnatal ward after a 90-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure that terminated spontaneously. He was born at 38+5 weeks by uncomplicated NVD. Antenatal scans identified interrupted aortic arch type B for which he is scheduled for repair next week. Examination shows hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears with deficient ear lobes, and a small mouth with high-arched palate.

The postnatal CXR shows no clear thymic shadow. Investigations: ionised calcium 0.78 mmol/L (low), magnesium 0.85 (normal), glucose 3.4, PTH inappropriately low for the calcium. There has been no maternal calcium-altering medication exposure.

data_table.Examination: Hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears, high-arched palate; cardiac murmur of IAA-B
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 1.62 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.78 mmol/L, magnesium 0.85 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, PTH inappropriately low
data_table.Imaging: No clear thymic shadow on CXR; IAA-B confirmed on echo

lead_in: Which combination of first-line genetic investigation and live-vaccine planning is most appropriate?

options.text: Chromosomal microarray as first-line genetic test for 22q11.2 microdeletion; withhold live vaccines pending T-cell subset confirmation
options.rationale: The combination of conotruncal cardiac anomaly (IAA-B), hypocalcaemia with inappropriately low PTH, suspected thymic hypoplasia and characteristic facies is the classic 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) phenotype. CMA is first-line and detects atypical deletion sizes that FISH may miss. Live vaccines must be withheld until cellular immunity is confirmed by T-cell subsets, per Australian Immunisation Handbook and RCH CPG.

options.text: Standard G-banded karyotype looking for trisomy 22 or other numerical aneuploidies as the first-line genetic test
options.rationale: 22q11.2 deletion is sub-microscopic and is not detected by standard karyotype; CMA or targeted FISH is required. Would never be correct (Source: HGSA).

options.text: Repeat newborn bloodspot screening card focused on congenital hypothyroidism as the first-line diagnostic workup
options.rationale: CH screening does not address the syndromic combination of cardiac anomaly, hypocalcaemia and thymic hypoplasia. Would be correct only with isolated CH (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Maternal serum vitamin D level only as the first-line investigation before any other targeted genetic or immune testing
options.rationale: Maternal vitamin D deficiency can cause neonatal hypocalcaemia but does not explain cardiac/thymic/facies. Would be correct only with isolated hypocalcaemia (Source: APEG).

options.text: Trans-fontanelle cranial ultrasound at the cotside as the next investigation before any further genetic or immune workup
options.rationale: Cranial US does not investigate the unifying syndromic diagnosis. Would be correct only with intracranial concern (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is a microdeletion disrupting development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and related neural crest derivatives. The features cluster because they share embryological origin: conotruncal cardiac anomalies (interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot) arise from failed neural crest migration into the cardiac outflow tract; hypoparathyroid hypocalcaemia from failed parathyroid development (third/fourth pouch); thymic hypoplasia with T-cell lymphopenia from failed thymic development (third pouch); palatal anomalies and velopharyngeal insufficiency from disrupted pharyngeal arch derivatives; characteristic facies from neural crest contributions to facial mesenchyme. Chromosomal microarray is the first-line genetic test; immunology (T-cell subsets) should run in parallel, and live vaccines are deferred until immune competence is confirmed (RCH CPG: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome).
key_points: Cardiac anomalies: interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot are typical
Defer live attenuated vaccines (e.g. rotavirus, BCG, MMR, varicella) until immune competence confirmed
Calcium, T-cell subset and immunoglobulin assessment guide ongoing care
explanation.pearls: Velopharyngeal insufficiency, hypernasal speech, and learning difficulties often dominate the phenotype in older children with 22q11.2 deletion.

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born male is brought to the ED with a 10-day history of vomiting after every feed, now forceful and arching over the shoulder. The vomit is milky, never green or blood-stained. He is hungry immediately after vomiting and feeds vigorously. Birth was 39+4 NVD, weight 3.6 kg. Today his weight is 3.5 kg (50th to 3rd centile cross), capillary refill 3 seconds, anterior fontanelle slightly sunken.

A 1 cm mobile firm mass is palpable in the right epigastrium after a test feed, with visible peristalsis crossing the upper abdomen left to right. Venous blood gas: pH 7.51, pCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3 38 mmol/L, Na 134, K 3.1, Cl 89, glucose 4.2 mmol/L. The paediatric surgical registrar wants to know the next step.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 44, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 98%, weight 3.5 kg.
data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, CRT 3 s, mucous membranes dry. Soft abdomen, palpable olive RUQ, visible peristalsis.
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.51, pCO2 50, HCO3 38, Na 134, K 3.1, Cl 89, glucose 4.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for Ramstedt pyloromyotomy after a single saline bolus, with electrolyte correction deferred to the postoperative period
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is never a surgical emergency; operating on an alkalotic, hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic infant risks post-anaesthetic apnoea (compensatory CSF alkalosis). Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis).

options.text: Resuscitate with 0.9% saline, then maintenance and replacement with 0.45% saline plus 5% dextrose plus potassium until Cl over 100, HCO3 under 30, K over 3.5 mmol/L; confirmatory ultrasound; then pyloromyotomy
options.rationale: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis must be corrected before pyloromyotomy. AU-recommended targets are Cl over 100, HCO3 under 30, K over 3.5 mmol/L. Ultrasound (muscle thickness over 3 mm, channel length over 14 mm) confirms diagnosis, per RCH CPG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Paediatric Fluid and Electrolyte.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Paediatric Fluid and Electrolyte

options.text: Commence omeprazole orally and review in clinic in one week as outpatient reflux management
options.rationale: Projectile non-bilious vomiting with palpable olive and hypochloraemic alkalosis is pyloric stenosis, not GORD. Would be correct in mild reflux without electrolyte disturbance (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Request urgent upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation before any fluid resuscitation or surgical referral
options.rationale: Vomiting is non-bilious; upper GI contrast is for suspected malrotation with bilious vomiting. Would be correct with bilious vomiting (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Trial extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 weeks as cow's milk protein allergy is the most likely diagnosis
options.rationale: CMPA does not produce hypochloraemic alkalosis or palpable olive. Would be correct with blood-streaked stools and dermatitis (Source: ASCIA).

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis (3-6 weeks, male predominant 4:1, first-born) produces hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, gastric outlet obstruction, and loss of HCl in vomit. The resulting hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis must be corrected before pyloromyotomy.
key_points: Classic age 3-6 weeks, M:F 4:1, first-born predominance
Non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry vomiter, weight loss
VBG: low Cl, low K, high HCO3, alkalotic pH
USS criteria: muscle thickness greater than 3 mm AND channel length greater than 14 mm
Correct fluids and electrolytes BEFORE theatre to avoid post-op apnoea
explanation.pearls: If the infant is alkalotic, do not let them go to theatre. The anaesthetist will hand them back.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Pyloric Stenosis
Therapeutic Guidelines: Paediatric Fluid and Electrolyte

subtopic_detail: Infant with non-bilious projectile vomiting and electrolyte disturbance

stem:
A 14-month-old previously well boy presents with an 8-hour history of episodic screaming in 15-20 minute cycles, drawing his knees up to his chest, with pallor and limpness between episodes. His mother describes one stool 90 minutes ago that was dark red and mucousy, like jam. There has been one episode of non-bilious vomiting. He had a viral URTI 5 days ago.

There has been no foreign travel and no unwell contacts. On examination he is now quiet and pale, HR 152, CRT 3 seconds, T 37.1 degC. The abdomen is soft with a vague sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant and an empty right iliac fossa. There is no peritonism, no guarding. Bedside ultrasound performed by the paediatric registrar shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant with concentric rings of bowel wall. A surgical registrar and an interventional radiologist are both immediately available.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152 bpm, RR 32, BP 92/58, T 37.1 degC, SpO2 99%, CRT 3 s.
data_table.Examination: Pale, lethargic between episodes. Sausage mass RUQ, empty RIF (Dance sign). No peritonism, no guarding.
data_table.Investigations: POCUS: target sign RUQ, concentric rings of bowel-within-bowel.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and arrange outpatient paediatric review the following day given the absence of frank peritonism on examination
options.rationale: Confirmed intussusception with red-currant stool requires immediate reduction; delay risks ischaemia and perforation. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Resuscitate with IV fluid and antibiotics, NG decompression, air-contrast enema with surgery on standby
options.rationale: Pneumatic (air) enema is the first-line treatment in haemodynamically stable children without peritonism, with success rates of 75-90% in Australian centres. Resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, NG decompression and surgical standby for the 1% risk of perforation during reduction are mandatory (RCH CPG; RANZCR Paediatric Imaging).

options.text: Proceed directly to laparotomy for open manual reduction without attempting radiological reduction first
options.rationale: Surgery is for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or pathological lead point; no peritonism here and air enema has higher success/lower morbidity. Would be correct with peritonism or failed enema (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Perform contrast CT abdomen to confirm the diagnosis before any therapeutic intervention is undertaken
options.rationale: US is gold-standard; CT adds radiation and delay without changing management. Would be correct only with diagnostic uncertainty on US (Source: RANZCR; RCH CPG).

options.text: Admit for observation overnight on clear fluids and re-image with ultrasound the following morning
options.rationale: Conservative observation of confirmed ileocolic intussusception causes progressive ischaemia; reduction within 24 h has best success. Would never be correct in confirmed cases (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception (6 months to 2 years, peak 5-9 months) typically follows a viral illness with Peyer patch hypertrophy as the lead point. Triad of colicky pain, vomiting and red-currant stool is the late presentation. Diagnosis is by USS (target/donut sign on cross-section, pseudokidney sign longitudinally) and reduction is by pneumatic (air) enema.
key_points: Peak age 5-9 months; consider pathological lead point if outside 3 months to 5 years (e.g. Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, HSP)
Triad (pain, vomiting, blood per rectum) present in less than 50%
USS first-line; air enema first-line treatment
Air enema success 75-90% in Australia; perforation rate less than 1%
Surgery if peritonism, perforation, failed enema or pathological lead point
explanation.pearls: Recurrence after successful enema reduction occurs in approximately 10% and is usually within 24-48 hours. Discharge planning includes return-precaution counselling.

subtopic_detail: Toddler with intermittent colicky pain and bloody stool

stem:
A 38-hour-old term male born at 39+5 by NVD to a G2P1 mother with an uneventful pregnancy is brought to the special care nursery by the midwife. He has had three episodes of vomiting in the last 90 minutes, the most recent two clearly bilious (bright green) and photographed on the midwife's phone for the registrar to review. He passed meconium at 18 hours of age and has been breastfeeding poorly since the second feed, latching but suckling weakly and falling asleep.

Birth weight 3.4 kg, current weight 3.25 kg, representing a 4% drop. On examination he is irritable with HR 178, RR 62, CRT 3 seconds, T 36.4 degC, SpO2 96% in room air. The abdomen is mildly distended in the upper abdomen without obvious mass, soft, with sluggish bowel sounds. There is no inguinal hernia, no anal stenosis, and no perianal abnormality.

Antenatal scans had not commented on intra-abdominal anatomy beyond reporting a normal anatomy scan at 20 weeks, with no polyhydramnios noted. An NG tube is placed and immediately drains 25 mL of bilious fluid with relief of distension. The neonatal registrar has IV access through a peripheral cannula and is preparing maintenance fluids and a 10 mL/kg saline bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 62, T 36.4 degC, SpO2 96% RA, CRT 3 s, weight 3.25 kg.
data_table.Examination: Irritable, mildly distended abdomen, soft, no mass, sluggish bowel sounds. No hernia, normal anus.
data_table.Investigations: NG aspirate 25 mL bilious. IV access x 1, fluids being prepared.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Upper GI contrast study within the next hour, paediatric surgical team aware and theatre standby
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Upper GI contrast is the gold-standard investigation, showing an abnormal duodeno-jejunal junction position and a corkscrew or beak appearance if volvulus is present. This must occur with surgical standby because volvulus requires laparotomy within minutes to hours to prevent loss of the midgut (RCH CPG; ANZNN).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Conservative management with NG decompression and IV fluids overnight, with reassessment in the morning
options.rationale: Watch-and-wait for bilious neonatal vomiting can result in complete midgut loss within 4-6 h of established volvulus. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Malrotation).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound looking for the whirlpool sign before considering further imaging today
options.rationale: USS whirlpool sign is supportive but absence does not exclude malrotation; upper GI contrast is definitive. Would be correct only as adjunct, not gold-standard (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Plain supine abdominal radiograph alone to exclude duodenal atresia as the diagnosis
options.rationale: Plain AXR may show double-bubble or paucity of distal gas but is insufficient to confirm/exclude malrotation. Would be correct only as initial screen with upper GI to follow (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Contrast enema looking for microcolon to exclude meconium ileus as diagnosis
options.rationale: Meconium ileus is a differential but in a term infant with meconium passed at 18 h, malrotation is more likely. Would be correct only with strong meconium ileus features (CF family history, microcolon suspicion) (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. The midgut twists around a narrow mesenteric pedicle and can necrose within hours. Upper GI contrast is the gold-standard investigation. The corrective operation is a Ladd procedure: counter-clockwise detorsion, division of Ladd bands, broadening of the mesentery, appendicectomy, and placement of small bowel on the right.
key_points: Any green vomit in the first month is malrotation/volvulus until excluded
Upper GI contrast = gold standard (DJ flexure should be left of midline at the level of pylorus)
USS whirlpool sign is supportive but not definitive
Operation = Ladd procedure
Time from established volvulus to midgut loss may be as short as 4-6 hours
explanation.pearls: If you are ever the most senior person at the bedside of a green-vomiting neonate, your job is to phone the paediatric surgical centre before you have all the answers.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

subtopic_detail: Bilious vomiting in the first 48 hours of life

stem:
An 8-year-old boy presents with a 22-hour history of central abdominal pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa 8 hours ago. He has vomited twice, has not eaten since lunch yesterday, and has a temperature of 38.1 deg C. He is reluctant to walk and held his right hip flexed on arrival. There is no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms, no foreign travel and no sick contacts.

He is not on medication and is fully immunised. On examination HR 112, RR 22, BP 108/68, abdomen with localised tenderness at McBurney point, voluntary guarding without rebound, positive cough sign. There is no generalised peritonism. Bloods: WCC 14.8 x10^9/L (neutrophils 11.2), CRP 38 mg/L. Urinalysis is negative. Paediatric Appendicitis Score is 7/10. Radiology offers an ultrasound within the hour.

data_table.Examination: Reluctant to walk, McBurney tenderness, voluntary guarding, positive cough sign, no rebound.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.8 (neutrophils 11.2), CRP 38, urinalysis negative. PAS 7/10.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step, and what is the appropriate plan if ultrasound is non-visualising?

options.text: Discharge home with simple analgesia and safety-net advice given the absence of rebound peritonism
options.rationale: PAS 7, WCC 14.8, CRP 38 and migratory pain is high-probability appendicitis; discharge is unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Appendicitis).

options.text: Order contrast CT abdomen and pelvis as the first-line imaging investigation
options.rationale: CT is for diagnostic uncertainty after US or when US is non-visualising in larger children; US is first-line to minimise paediatric radiation. Would be correct only after non-visualising US (Source: RANZCR).

options.text: Ultrasound RIF first; if positive (non-compressible blind-ending tubular structure over 6 mm with hyperaemia) proceed to laparoscopic appendicectomy with IV pre-operative antibiotics; if non-visualising, admit for serial clinical reassessment with repeat ultrasound or CT escalation as needed
options.rationale: Ultrasound is first-line paediatric imaging in Australia. A visualised appendix over 6 mm non-compressible with hyperaemia triggers laparoscopic appendicectomy with preoperative ceftriaxone plus metronidazole. Non-visualisation occurs in 20-40 percent and does not exclude appendicitis; serial examination (with or without CT escalation) is the correct next step rather than discharge, per RCH CPG and RANZCR.

options.text: Treat with IV cefotaxime and metronidazole as antibiotic-only therapy without surgical intervention
options.rationale: Antibiotic-only management is a research approach in selected uncomplicated cases, not standard AU practice; confirmation must precede non-operative trial. Would be correct only in research protocols (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Order MRI abdomen and pelvis as the first-line investigation to avoid ionising radiation
options.rationale: MRI is not routinely available out-of-hours and is not first-line; US gives best speed-to-diagnosis. Would be correct only with CT contraindication and US non-visualising (Source: RANZCR).

explanation.summary: Paediatric appendicitis diagnosis is clinical plus imaging. The Paediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS) stratifies: 1-3 low (discharge with safety net), 4-6 intermediate (USS, observe), 7-10 high (surgical review, USS if needed, appendicectomy). USS is first-line imaging; CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty after non-diagnostic USS.
key_points: PAS components: anorexia, nausea/vomiting, migration, RIF tenderness, cough/percussion/heel-tap tenderness, fever greater than or equal to 38, WCC greater than 10, neutrophils greater than 7.5
USS first-line: appendix diameter greater than 6 mm, non-compressible, hyperaemic, periappendiceal fluid
Laparoscopic appendicectomy with preoperative IV antibiotics (e.g. cefazolin + metronidazole per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Non-visualising USS does not exclude appendicitis; serial exam by paediatric surgical team
CT reserved for diagnostic uncertainty after USS
explanation.pearls: A child who refuses to climb onto the bed or who walks bent over is telling you the diagnosis.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Appendicitis

subtopic_detail: School-age child with right iliac fossa pain

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to a regional emergency department at 03:00 with sudden severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep 4 hours ago, associated with one episode of vomiting. There is no dysuria, no urethral discharge. He is not sexually active. On examination he is in significant pain, the left hemiscrotum is swollen, erythematous and tender, the left testis is high-riding with a transverse lie, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left.

Prehn sign is negative (lifting the testis does not relieve pain). The right testis is normal. Urinalysis is negative for leucocytes and nitrites. The nearest paediatric surgical service is 90 minutes away by road. The local on-call general surgeon is in-house. Bedside Doppler ultrasound is not immediately available; the sonographer is on call from home and estimates a 45-minute arrival time.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum swollen, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn sign.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative. Doppler USS not available for 45 minutes.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait for the on-call sonographer to arrive and perform Doppler ultrasound before any surgical decision
options.rationale: Torsion is clinical; US must not delay exploration. Salvage falls from over 90 percent within 6 h to under 10 percent beyond 24 h. Would never be correct in classic torsion presentation (Source: RCH CPG; USANZ).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

options.text: Commence IV ceftriaxone and doxycycline for presumed bacterial epididymo-orchitis without surgical exploration
options.rationale: Picture (high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn, sudden onset, no urinary symptoms) is torsion not epididymo-orchitis. Antibiotics waste ischaemic time. Would be correct only with epididymo-orchitis features (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum

options.text: Proceed immediately to scrotal exploration with consent for bilateral orchidopexy or orchidectomy if non-viable
options.rationale: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis warranting immediate surgical exploration. The salvage window is 4-6 hours from onset of pain (currently 4 hours in this scenario). In regional Australia the on-call general surgeon performs exploration rather than transferring; bilateral orchidopexy is standard because the bell-clapper anatomy is bilateral in approximately 80% (RCH CPG; USANZ Position Statement).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

options.text: Attempt manual detorsion in the open-book direction (lateral rotation) then discharge home with urology outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Manual detorsion may be attempted while preparing theatre but does not replace surgical exploration and fixation. Discharge without fixation risks re-torsion. Would never be correct as definitive (Source: USANZ).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

options.text: Transfer the patient by road to the paediatric surgical service 90 minutes away for definitive management
options.rationale: Adding 90 min of transfer when local capability exists pushes total ischaemic time over 6 h. Would be correct only when local paediatric surgical capability is unavailable (Source: USANZ).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis treated by immediate scrotal exploration. Salvage rates depend on duration of ischaemia: greater than 90% within 6 hours, approximately 50% at 12 hours, less than 10% beyond 24 hours. Bilateral orchidopexy is performed because the bell-clapper deformity is bilateral in approximately 80%.
key_points: Hallmarks: sudden onset pain (often wakes from sleep), high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn
Differentials: epididymo-orchitis (usually febrile, dysuria, gradual onset), torsion of appendix testis (blue dot sign, less severe), incarcerated hernia
Imaging should not delay exploration when the clinical picture is clear
Bilateral orchidopexy at exploration
Salvage rate greater than 90% within 6 hours
explanation.pearls: When the question gives you a 6-hour window and an obvious clinical diagnosis, the wrong answers are usually 'order an imaging test' or 'transfer'.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with acute unilateral scrotal pain

stem:
A 12-hour-old term female born by elective lower-segment caesarean for breech presentation at 39+2 weeks has had two episodes of bright-green vomiting after attempted breastfeeding. Antenatal scans at 12 and 20 weeks were reported as normal; nuchal translucency was low risk. Birth weight 3.1 kg, Apgars 9 and 9. She has not yet passed meconium. On examination HR 162, RR 56, T 36.8 deg C, SpO2 97% on room air.

The abdomen is mildly distended in the upper abdomen with a flat lower abdomen and visible epigastric fullness. There is no obvious mass, no inguinal hernia, and the anus is patent on inspection. A nasogastric tube is placed and aspirates 30 mL of bilious fluid. The on-call paediatric registrar is reviewing the supine abdominal radiograph and considering whether the appearance is consistent with duodenal atresia rather than malrotation with midgut volvulus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 56, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: Upper abdominal distension, flat lower abdomen, patent anus, no hernia. NG bilious aspirate 30 mL.
data_table.Investigations: Supine AXR pending interpretation.

lead_in: Which radiographic finding most reliably differentiates duodenal atresia from malrotation with midgut volvulus, and what is the implication for next investigation?

options.text: Multiple dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and soap-bubble appearance, suggesting meconium ileus and prompting contrast enema
options.rationale: Soap-bubble (Neuhauser) is meconium ileus, not duodenal atresia or volvulus. Would be correct in meconium ileus (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Pneumatosis intestinalis with portal venous gas, suggesting necrotising enterocolitis
options.rationale: Pneumatosis and portal venous gas are NEC findings, clinically and radiographically distinct. Would be correct in NEC (Source: RCH CPG: NEC).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Double bubble sign with absent distal bowel gas, supporting duodenal atresia; proceed to fluid resuscitation and surgical referral without urgent upper GI contrast
options.rationale: Duodenal atresia produces a classic double bubble (dilated stomach and proximal duodenum) with NO distal bowel gas. In contrast, malrotation with volvulus typically shows some distal gas with a paucity, and the diagnostic test is an URGENT upper GI contrast study showing corkscrew or duodenojejunal junction to the right of midline. Recognising the no-distal-gas double bubble as duodenal atresia therefore obviates upper GI contrast and allows direct fluid resuscitation and surgical referral, whereas any uncertainty mandates urgent contrast study, per RCH CPG.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Free intraperitoneal gas under the diaphragm with a football sign, suggesting perforation
options.rationale: Free gas indicates perforation, not uncomplicated atresia or volvulus. Would be correct in perforation (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Corkscrew appearance of the duodenum visible on the supine plain film
options.rationale: Corkscrew is a fluoroscopic finding on upper GI contrast in malrotation with volvulus, not a plain-film sign. Would be correct on upper GI contrast, not on plain film (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in the neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. The framework of differentials includes malrotation/volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunal/ileal atresia, meconium ileus (CF), Hirschsprung disease, NEC, sepsis-related ileus, and incarcerated inguinal hernia. Plain radiograph plus upper GI contrast distinguish these.
key_points: Double bubble + no distal gas = duodenal atresia (30% trisomy 21)
Double bubble + distal gas = malrotation with partial obstruction
Multiple dilated loops + soap-bubble = meconium ileus (suspect CF)
Pneumatosis = NEC
Free gas / football sign = perforation
explanation.pearls: If the lower abdomen is scaphoid in a vomiting neonate, suspect a high obstruction; if it is distended, suspect a low obstruction.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

subtopic_detail: Neonate with green vomiting on day 1 - differential framework

stem:
A 16-month-old boy of Anglo-Australian background presents with severe constipation since the second week of life. His mother reports he passed meconium at 52 hours of age, required digital stimulation to pass stool for the first 6 months, and was breastfed exclusively until 6 months when solids were introduced uneventfully. He now stools once every 5-7 days, with explosive decompression when finally passing.

His growth has crossed centiles downwards from the 50th at birth to the 9th today. He is now febrile at 38.6 degC, lethargic, with foul-smelling green-tinged diarrhoea overnight, mild abdominal distension, and tachycardia at 148. His abdomen is distended and tympanic, with no obvious mass and no organomegaly. PR examination is performed gently by the paediatric registrar and produces an explosive release of gas and liquid stool with relief of distension.

He has had multiple aperient trials including macrogol and lactulose without sustained improvement, and dietary fibre optimisation through the maternal and child health nurse. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis or thyroid disease. Newborn screening for cystic fibrosis was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, RR 32, T 38.6 degC, weight on 9th centile (was 50th at birth).
data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen, explosive PR release. Lethargic.
data_table.Investigations: Pending.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate definitive investigation?

options.text: Sweat chloride test to exclude cystic fibrosis as the cause of meconium delay
options.rationale: CF can cause meconium ileus but does not explain chronic explosive PR decompression or current enterocolitis. Would be correct as adjunct workup in suspected CF (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.text: Anorectal manometry alone as the single definitive diagnostic test for this
options.rationale: Anorectal manometry shows absent RAIR but is technically difficult in young children and supportive only; biopsy is gold-standard. Would be correct as supportive test in older children (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.text: Contrast enema with assessment for transition zone, followed by trial of laxatives
options.rationale: Contrast enema may show transition zone and reversed recto-sigmoid ratio but is supportive only; biopsy is required. Empirical laxatives miss the disease. Would be correct as initial radiological assessment, not definitive (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.text: Full-thickness rectal suction biopsy with assessment for ganglion cells and acetylcholinesterase staining
options.rationale: Rectal biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung disease, demonstrating absent ganglion cells in the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses with hypertrophied nerve trunks staining positive for acetylcholinesterase. The current presentation is Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, which carries up to 30% mortality if untreated (RCH CPG; ANZ Paediatric Surgery).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.text: Faecal calprotectin and stool MCS as the initial diagnostic test
options.rationale: Calprotectin is for suspected IBD, not Hirschsprung; stool MCS may identify enterocolitis pathogens but does not diagnose aganglionosis. Would be correct in suspected IBD (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease is congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel due to failed migration of neural crest cells. Suspect in any infant with delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, chronic constipation from birth, or failure-to-thrive. Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is the life-threatening complication.
key_points: Meconium passed greater than 48 hours after birth in approximately 90%
Rectal biopsy is gold standard: absent ganglion cells, hypertrophied nerves, positive acetylcholinesterase
Contrast enema: transition zone, reversed recto-sigmoid ratio
Definitive treatment: pull-through procedure (Soave, Swenson, Duhamel)
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis: fever, distension, foul diarrhoea; mortality up to 30% if missed
explanation.pearls: An infant who needs digital stimulation to pass meconium is telling you the diagnosis; do not wait for failure-to-thrive.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

subtopic_detail: Toddler with delayed meconium and chronic constipation

stem:
A 28+5 week preterm female born at birth weight 1.05 kg is now on day 11 of life in the neonatal intensive care unit. She was extubated to CPAP on day 4 and trophic feeds of expressed breast milk were introduced on day 5 and advanced to 60 mL/kg/day by day 10. Over the last 12 hours she has had two large bilious gastric aspirates, abdominal distension increasing from 25 cm to 28.5 cm girth, and one episode of bright red blood in the stool.

She has become apnoeic with three desaturations to less than 80% in the last hour requiring stimulation. HR has risen from 145 to 178. T is 36.0 degC, BP 48/22 mmHg with mean arterial pressure 30. CRT is 4 seconds. The abdominal wall is shiny with bluish discolouration over the right flank. WCC has fallen from 9.2 to 4.1 x10^9/L, platelets from 224 to 86, CRP risen from less than 5 to 92 mg/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L.

The supine abdominal radiograph shows multiple dilated loops of bowel with intramural gas (pneumatosis intestinalis) and a curvilinear lucency over the liver consistent with portal venous gas. There is no free intraperitoneal gas on a left lateral decubitus film. The paediatric surgical service has been consulted by phone.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 70, T 36.0 degC, BP 48/22 (MAP 30), SpO2 88% on CPAP, CRT 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Distended shiny abdomen with bluish flank discolouration. PR bright red blood.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.1, platelets 86, CRP 92, lactate 4.8. AXR: pneumatosis + portal venous gas, no free gas.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until blood culture results are available to avoid promoting antibiotic resistance and unnecessary coverage
options.rationale: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes must commence immediately on NEC suspicion. Waiting for cultures delays critical therapy. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.text: Continue enteral feeds at current volume and add oral probiotics to reduce bacterial gut translocation
options.rationale: Established NEC mandates immediate NBM; continuing feeds worsens ischaemic injury. Probiotics are prophylactic in some units but no role in established NEC. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.text: Proceed immediately to laparotomy regardless of radiographic findings of pneumatosis or perforation
options.rationale: Surgery is for perforation (free gas, fixed loop, deterioration despite medical management). Bell IIB without perforation is medical with surgical standby. Would be correct only with perforation or clinical deterioration (Source: RCH CPG NEC).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.text: Nil by mouth, OG free drainage, IV benzylpenicillin/gentamicin/metronidazole, TPN, serial films, paediatric surgical involvement
options.rationale: This is Bell stage IIB NEC (pneumatosis with portal venous gas, no perforation). Management is medical: NBM, OG decompression, triple antibiotics (penicillin/gentamicin/metronidazole per Therapeutic Guidelines), TPN, serial AXR every 6 hours for 48-72 hours to detect perforation. Surgery is indicated for perforation (Bell IIIB) or clinical deterioration (RCH CPG NEC; ANZNN).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.text: Place a peritoneal drain at the bedside as definitive treatment without commencing antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Peritoneal drainage is a salvage technique for unstable ELBW with perforation; not a substitute for antibiotics or definitive laparotomy. Would be correct only as salvage in unstable ELBW (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Necrotising enterocolitis is a multifactorial inflammatory/ischaemic injury to immature gut, peaking at 28-32 weeks corrected age in the second to third postnatal week. Bell staging: I suspected (non-specific), II definite (IIA pneumatosis, IIB pneumatosis + portal gas), III advanced (IIIA critically ill no perforation, IIIB perforation).
key_points: Peak: 28-32 weeks corrected, day 7-14 of life
Risk factors: prematurity, formula feeding, rapid feed advance, hypoxia, sepsis
Pneumatosis intestinalis is pathognomonic
Management: NBM, OG decompression, triple antibiotics, TPN, serial AXR
Surgery for perforation, fixed dilated loop, abdominal wall erythema/discolouration, or deterioration
explanation.pearls: A shiny abdomen with bluish discolouration is a late sign of full-thickness bowel wall ischaemia and is a call to the operating room.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

stem:
A 22-month-old girl is brought to a rural emergency department 70 minutes after her older brother saw her swallow a small shiny disc that he had taken from a household remote control. He believes she put it directly in her mouth and swallowed it. She is now drooling slightly, refuses to drink, has had one episode of non-bloody vomiting but is not in respiratory distress.

There is no stridor, no wheeze, no blood in the saliva. HR 134, RR 28, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99% in room air. Examination of the oropharynx is unremarkable; the abdomen is soft and non-tender. The mother brings the empty battery compartment of the remote and the parents identify the missing battery as a CR2032 lithium coin cell (20 mm diameter).

The emergency department has plain radiography but no on-site paediatric endoscopy. The nearest paediatric centre with interventional endoscopy is 2 hours by road or 45 minutes by retrieval helicopter (currently available). A chest and abdominal radiograph shows a round radio-opaque disc with a double-rim (halo) appearance at the level of T2-T3 in the oesophagus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 134, RR 28, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Drooling, refuses fluids, no stridor, no respiratory distress.
data_table.Investigations: CXR/AXR: 20 mm disc with double-rim sign at T2-T3 oesophagus.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer by road over 2 hours; no oral honey as child is under 24 months
options.rationale: Honey contraindication is for under-12 months (botulism risk); this child is 22 months. Helicopter is faster than 2-h road transfer for an oesophageal battery. Would be correct only under 12 months (Source: RCH CPG; NHMRC Infant Feeding).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

options.text: Discharge home with safety-net advice to return if symptoms worsen, given the child appears clinically stable on arrival
options.rationale: Any oesophageal button battery is a surgical emergency regardless of current symptoms; delay risks perforation, TOF and aorto-oesophageal fistula. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG; ACCC).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

options.text: Induce vomiting with oral ipecac syrup at the bedside now to expel the swallowed battery
options.rationale: Induced emesis is contraindicated (aspiration, further oesophageal injury); ipecac is no longer recommended by PIC for any ingestion. Would never be correct (Source: PIC).

options.text: Wait 4 hours and repeat radiograph to see whether the battery has spontaneously passed the lower oesophageal sphincter
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is unsafe for oesophageal battery; 4-h delay pushes beyond 2-h necrosis threshold. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

options.text: Activate retrieval for endoscopic battery removal within 2 hours; oral honey en route if age >12 months and airway intact
options.rationale: Button battery in the oesophagus is a time-critical emergency: tissue injury begins within 15-30 minutes and full-thickness necrosis can occur within 2 hours. The Australian Resuscitation Council and RCH CPG recommend honey (or sucralfate) every 10 minutes in children over 12 months with no airway compromise to coat the battery and reduce alkaline injury, while urgent endoscopic removal is arranged. Helicopter retrieval is faster than road (RCH CPG; Poisons Information Centre).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

explanation.summary: Button battery in the oesophagus causes alkaline electrolysis injury within 15-30 minutes and can perforate within 2 hours. Australian guidelines (RCH, Poisons Information Centre, ACCC) recommend immediate endoscopic removal, honey every 10 minutes in children over 12 months while awaiting endoscopy, and notification of PIC on 13 11 26.
key_points: Double-rim (halo) sign on AP radiograph distinguishes battery from coin
Step-off sign on lateral
Oesophageal lodgement = endoscopic removal within 2 hours
Honey 10 mL every 10 minutes (children over 12 months) reduces injury severity
Avoid in infants under 12 months (botulism); avoid if airway compromised
explanation.pearls: Coins are smooth and round and easy to ignore. The double rim on the AP film and step-off on the lateral are how you do not miss the diagnosis.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion
ACCC Product Safety Australia - Button Batteries
