A 5-week-old term male infant is brought to a regional ED by his parents after a single rectal temperature of 38.4 deg C taken because he was unsettled and feeding poorly for the last 8 hours. He was born by normal vaginal delivery at 39+2 weeks with no risk factors for early-onset sepsis: maternal GBS swab negative at 36 weeks, no prolonged rupture of membranes, no intrapartum fever.

He had an unremarkable nursery course and went home on day 2. He is exclusively breastfed and has been gaining weight along the 50th centile. He has had no cough, no diarrhoea, and there are no sick contacts. He has not yet received any immunisations as his 6-week appointment is next week. On examination he is mottled peripherally, with a soft anterior fontanelle, no focus of infection, and a capillary refill of 3 seconds. He has been crying weakly but is consolable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 deg C rectal, HR 184 bpm, RR 56 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 76/42 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mottled peripheries, CRT 3 s, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no focal infection, no rash, weak cry
data_table.History: Term NVD, GBS negative, no maternal fever, exclusively breastfed, not yet immunised

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen after blood, urine and CSF are obtained?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg eight-hourly as initial empirical monotherapy with no other antibiotic added at this stage
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates and very young infants because of bilirubin displacement and calcium incompatibility; cefotaxime is preferred in this age group, and combination therapy is required for Listeria and Gram-negative cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin as the Australian regimen, adding cefotaxime at meningitic doses if meningitis is suspected
options.rationale: Australian practice for the febrile infant under 3 months is intravenous benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin/ampicillin) for Listeria and group B Streptococcus, plus gentamicin for Gram-negative cover; cefotaxime at meningitic doses is added when meningitis is suspected on cerebrospinal fluid, or empirically if lumbar puncture is deferred and meningitis cannot be excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Intravenous ampicillin 50 mg/kg plus intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg without gentamicin, as per the US AAP febrile-infant pathway
options.rationale: This is the US AAP / Boston-criteria regimen; Australian practice adds gentamicin in this age group for broader Gram-negative cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg plus intravenous gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg eight-hourly to cover Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negative pathogens
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin does not cover Listeria, group B Streptococcus, or many Gram-negative urinary pathogens, and lacks meningeal penetration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg as a single dose with planned review in 4 hours pending blood and urine results before further escalation
options.rationale: Any febrile infant under 3 months requires a full septic workup and parenteral antibiotics until cultures are negative at 36-48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

explanation.summary: Fever in an infant under 3 months mandates a full septic workup (blood, urine via suprapubic aspiration or catheter, cerebrospinal fluid) and empirical intravenous antibiotics. Australian guidance (RCH Febrile child, Therapeutic Guidelines, AMH Children's Dosing Companion) gives benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin/ampicillin) plus gentamicin in this age group; cefotaxime at meningitic doses is added when meningitis is suspected. Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because of bilirubin displacement and calcium incompatibility.
key_points: Under 3 months: benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin per Australian guidance
Add cefotaxime at meningitic doses when meningitis is suspected
Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates due to bilirubin displacement and calcium incompatibility
Cerebrospinal fluid should be obtained before antibiotics unless contraindicated
Continue antibiotics until cultures are negative at 36-48 hours
explanation.pearls: The US AAP / Boston-criteria cefotaxime plus ampicillin regimen omits gentamicin; Australian practice includes gentamicin in this age band for broader Gram-negative cover.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis evaluation in the febrile young infant

stem:
A 7-year-old previously well boy is brought to the ED at 0200 hours with a 14-hour history of fever, lethargy, leg pain and a rash that started 3 hours ago. His mother says he received his 4vMenACWY vaccine at 12 months and a MenB vaccine privately at age 3, but no booster since. He attends a metropolitan primary school and a 9-year-old classmate was hospitalised yesterday with a similar illness.

On arrival he is mottled with cold peripheries and a capillary refill of 4 seconds. There is a non-blanching purpuric rash on both shins and the buttocks with several lesions over 4 mm and one early ecchymotic lesion of about 1 cm. He is rousable but irritable, with a GCS of 14, and complains of severe calf pain. The ED registrar gives IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg and a 20 mL/kg fluid bolus.

A lumbar puncture is deferred because of his haemodynamic instability and an emerging coagulopathy on the venous gas (lactate 4.2 mmol/L). Blood culture and a meningococcal PCR (EDTA) are obtained. The infectious diseases registrar asks about public health management of close contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 deg C, HR 168 bpm, RR 36 /min, BP 86/48 mmHg, SpO2 95% on room air, CRT 4 s
data_table.Examination: Mottled cold peripheries, purpuric rash shins/buttocks, one 1 cm ecchymotic lesion, irritable, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.2 (neutrophils 1.1) x 10^9/L, platelets 84 x 10^9/L, INR 1.6, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, CRP 96 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate public-health and contact-management action?

options.text: Notify the local public health unit only after the meningococcal PCR returns positive, and prescribe ciprofloxacin only to household contacts
options.rationale: Suspected IMD is notifiable immediately on clinical suspicion in all AU jurisdictions; waiting for PCR delays prophylaxis. Would never be correct (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease SoNG).

options.text: Notify public health immediately, give ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally as a single dose to all the boy's school classmates and teachers
options.rationale: Chemoprophylaxis is targeted to close contacts within 7 days before symptom onset (household, intimate kissing, childcare under 6, healthcare with significant exposure), not 'all' contacts. Would never be correct as a blanket measure (Source: CDNA).

options.text: Notify public health within 5 working days, no chemoprophylaxis needed because he received MenACWY and MenB vaccines
options.rationale: Vaccination of the index case does not negate prophylaxis for close contacts; IMD is urgently notifiable (hours, not days). Would never be correct (Source: CDNA).

options.text: Notify public health immediately on clinical suspicion; ciprofloxacin 250 mg orally as single dose for household and close contacts
options.rationale: Invasive meningococcal disease is notifiable immediately on clinical suspicion. Chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin 500 mg in adults, 250 mg in children 5 to 12 years, 30 mg/kg up to 125 mg under 5 years; or ceftriaxone IM if pregnant) is given to close contacts within the 7-day exposure window, ideally within 24 hours, as per CDNA Invasive meningococcal disease SoNG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

options.text: Notify public health immediately and give rifampicin 600 mg twice daily for 4 days to household contacts
options.rationale: Rifampicin is second-line (compliance, drug interactions, resistance); ciprofloxacin single-dose is first-line in non-pregnant contacts. Would be correct only with quinolone contraindication (Source: CDNA).

explanation.summary: Invasive meningococcal disease is an urgent notifiable condition in every Australian state and territory. Close contacts within the 7 days before symptom onset receive single-dose ciprofloxacin (ceftriaxone IM in pregnancy) ideally within 24 hours. Index-case vaccination does not exempt contacts.
key_points: Notify on clinical suspicion (do not wait for PCR or culture)
Close contacts: household, household-like, intimate kissing, childcare under 6 yr, unprotected airway HCW exposure
Ciprofloxacin doses: 500 mg adult, 250 mg child 5 to 12 yr, 30 mg/kg (max 125 mg) under 5 yr
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose if pregnant or ciprofloxacin contraindicated
Offer MenB and MenACWY vaccination to close contacts if not up to date
explanation.pearls: Gram-negative diplococci on CSF Gram stain plus purpura equals meningococcus; Gram-positive diplococci plus older child equals pneumococcus; Gram-negative coccobacilli in unimmunised child equals Hib.

subtopic_detail: Identification and public-health response to invasive meningococcal disease

stem:
A 9-year-old previously well girl presents to the tertiary paediatric ED with 3 days of fever, headache and confusion, and one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes at home that resolved spontaneously without intervention. Her mother describes intermittent inappropriate laughter and word-finding difficulty for the last 24 hours and a sense that the child has been smelling something burnt that nobody else in the household can smell.

There is no rash and no neck stiffness, and she has had no foreign travel, no mosquito-exposed regional travel to northern Australia or to Murray-Darling river settings, and no animal bites or scratches. Her immunisations are up to date for the standard NIP schedule (no Japanese encephalitis vaccine because of no risk exposure recorded). On examination she has a low-grade fever, her GCS fluctuates between 13 and 15, she has subtle right-sided pronator drift and expressive dysphasia, and the rest of the cranial nerve and peripheral neurological examinations are normal.

There are no purpuric lesions on full skin survey. CT brain is unremarkable. MRI is scheduled for the morning. LP is performed: opening pressure 22 cm H2O, CSF clear, WCC 96 x 10^6/L (90% lymphocytes), protein 0.92 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L (paired serum 5.1), Gram stain negative; CSF HSV, VZV, enterovirus and meningococcal PCR are pending, and an autoimmune encephalitis panel including anti-NMDAR antibodies has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 deg C, HR 108 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 110/70 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating GCS 13 to 15, expressive dysphasia, right pronator drift, no neck stiffness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (WCC 96, 90% lymphs), protein 0.92 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, CT brain normal, MRI pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management decision?

options.text: Commence IV aciclovir at the paediatric encephalitis dose q8h empirically while awaiting CSF HSV PCR
options.rationale: Olfactory hallucinations, dysphasia, temporal-lobe-localising features and a lymphocytic CSF in a child are HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise. Empirical IV aciclovir 500 mg/m^2 (about 20 mg/kg under 12 years) q8h must be started immediately because delay increases mortality and morbidity, per RCH CPG: Meningitis encephalitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

options.text: Commence high-dose IV methylprednisolone for presumed anti-NMDAR encephalitis pending antibody results today
options.rationale: Anti-NMDAR is a differential, but immunotherapy without first excluding/treating HSV is dangerous (steroids worsen untreated HSV). Would be correct only after HSV PCR negative and clinical features pathognomonic for NMDAR (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence IV ceftriaxone and dexamethasone, withhold antivirals until PCR results
options.rationale: CSF is lymphocytic with normal glucose - bacterial meningitis is unlikely; HSV must be empirically covered without waiting for PCR. Would be correct only with neutrophilic CSF and low glucose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange urgent EEG and defer all therapy until non-convulsive status epilepticus is fully excluded
options.rationale: EEG aids diagnosis but is not a reason to delay empirical aciclovir in suspected encephalitis. Would be correct only as adjunct to confirmed treatment (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Commence IV ribavirin for suspected Japanese encephalitis given the recent Murray Valley exposure risk
options.rationale: No specific antiviral for JEV and no Murray Valley exposure described; JEV is supportive care with vaccination for prevention. Would never be correct (Source: NCIRS).

explanation.summary: Suspected viral encephalitis with focal features (especially temporal-lobe localisation, olfactory hallucinations, dysphasia) mandates empirical IV aciclovir while CSF HSV PCR and MRI are pursued. Autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDAR) is a key differential, especially in children and young women with prominent psychiatric features, dyskinesias and autonomic instability.
key_points: Aciclovir dose: 500 mg/m^2 (or 20 mg/kg) q8h IV under 12 years; 10 mg/kg q8h adolescents and adults
Maintain hydration and monitor renal function (crystal nephropathy)
MRI: HSV shows temporal lobe T2/FLAIR hyperintensity; anti-NMDAR often normal MRI
EEG: HSV periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs); anti-NMDAR extreme delta brush
Anti-NMDAR triggers include ovarian teratoma; treat with IVIG/plasmapheresis plus steroids
explanation.pearls: Olfactory hallucinations and dysphasia point to the temporal lobe; assume HSV and start aciclovir while you investigate.

subtopic_detail: Encephalitis with focal neurology in a school-aged child

stem:
A previously well 5-year-old boy presents to his GP with 4 days of fever, productive cough and reduced activity. He is fully immunised on the Australian NIP including 13vPCV, and has had no foreign travel or sick contacts. He is alert, well perfused, taking oral fluids and about 75 percent of usual food, with no recessions or grunting. SpO2 is 96 percent on room air.

Auscultation reveals bronchial breathing and crackles in the right lower zone. A chest X-ray performed because of the persistent fever shows right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. His weight is 18 kg. He has no known drug allergies and has not received antibiotics in the previous 3 months.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 deg C, HR 112 bpm, RR 28 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 100/64 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breath sounds and crackles right lower zone, no recessions, no grunting, alert and active
data_table.Investigations: CXR right lower lobe consolidation, no effusion

lead_in: Which oral antibiotic regimen is most appropriate as outpatient first-line therapy?

options.text: Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Dose too low; Therapeutic Guidelines and AMH Children's specify 25-30 mg/kg eight-hourly for paediatric CAP to cover pneumococci with reduced penicillin susceptibility. Would be correct at higher dose, not lower (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) eight-hourly for 5 days
options.rationale: First-line for uncomplicated CAP in a well child tolerating oral therapy with SpO2 over 92 percent: oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) eight-hourly for 5 days, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and RCH CPG: Pneumonia. Five days is the current AU-recommended duration for uncomplicated CAP.

options.text: Azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Macrolides are added for atypical infection (school-age, persistent fever, first-line failure), not monotherapy first-line for typical lobar CAP. Would be correct in atypical pneumonia presentation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5/3.2 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Augmentin is reserved for aspiration pneumonia or amoxicillin failure; clavulanate is unnecessary and adds side effects. Would be correct for aspiration pneumonia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Cefalexin 25 mg/kg six-hourly for 7 days
options.rationale: Cefalexin has poorer activity than amoxicillin against penicillin-non-susceptible pneumococcus; not first-line for CAP. Would be correct only with confirmed penicillin allergy and non-severe disease (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in a previously well child over 1 month is treated with oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) q8h for 5 days. Admission and IV antibiotics are reserved for SpO2 under 92%, severe respiratory distress, inability to tolerate oral therapy, dehydration, or complications such as empyema.
key_points: Amoxicillin first-line; covers pneumococcus including penicillin-non-susceptible strains at high dose
Add or substitute macrolide if atypical features (older child, gradual onset, dry cough, headache, extrapulmonary signs)
5-day course non-inferior to longer in mild-moderate CAP
Reassess at 48 to 72 hours if no improvement
CXR not routinely required to diagnose CAP
explanation.pearls: If a well-looking older child gets worse on amoxicillin, think Mycoplasma and add roxithromycin or azithromycin.

subtopic_detail: First-line antibiotic for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with right lower lobe pneumonia diagnosed 5 days ago by her GP has been on oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg q8h but is brought to the tertiary paediatric ED after 48 hours of persistent high fevers, increasing respiratory effort, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and a new reluctance to lie on her left side. She is fully immunised including 13vPCV.

On arrival she is febrile to 39.6 deg C, has a respiratory rate of 38 /min with mild subcostal recessions, SpO2 91% on room air, and dullness to percussion with reduced breath sounds over the right lower and mid zones with bronchial breathing above. She is tolerating sips of fluid only and is reluctant to take deep breaths. A chest X-ray shows a right-sided opacification of the lower two-thirds of the hemithorax with blunting of the costophrenic angle and a meniscus sign suggestive of a moderate effusion.

Bloods show WCC 24 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 21), CRP 268 mg/L, and a normal lactate. Blood cultures are taken and IV flucloxacillin and cefotaxime are commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 deg C, HR 138 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 91% on room air, BP 104/64 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recessions, dull right base, reduced breath sounds, bronchial breathing above, splinting on right
data_table.Investigations: CXR right effusion two-thirds hemithorax with meniscus, WCC 24 (N 21) x 10^9/L, CRP 268 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide drainage decisions?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT chest to assess for necrotising pneumonia or lung abscess
options.rationale: CT is for suspected necrotising pneumonia, abscess, or non-diagnostic US or for operative planning; not first-line due to paediatric radiation. Would be correct after non-diagnostic US (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.text: Repeat plain chest X-ray in lateral decubitus position for layering effusion
options.rationale: Lateral decubitus films are largely obsolete; chest US is more accurate at distinguishing simple from complicated effusion. Would never be correct in modern practice (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia).

options.text: Diagnostic thoracocentesis only, with pleural fluid pH, LDH, glucose and Gram stain
options.rationale: Diagnostic tap may be performed but in paediatric empyema imaging-guided assessment is first; pleural pH/biochem is not first investigation. Would be correct as adjunct, not first investigation (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Bedside chest ultrasound to characterise effusion (size, septation, loculation) and guide drainage
options.rationale: Chest ultrasound is the first-line imaging in paediatric parapneumonic effusion. It is radiation-free, more sensitive than X-ray for septations, and directly guides whether intercostal drain plus intrapleural fibrinolytics or primary VATS is required, as per RCH CPG: Pneumonia and BMJ Best Practice.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.text: Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage for microbiology and cytology of fluid
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is for suspected foreign body, atypical organisms in immunocompromised, or persistent atelectasis. Would be correct only in those situations (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Complicated pneumonia in children spans simple parapneumonic effusion, empyema, necrotising pneumonia and lung abscess. Chest ultrasound is the first-line imaging to size and characterise pleural fluid. Effusions with septations or pus on ultrasound, or a thickness over 2 cm with clinical deterioration, are drained, typically with an intercostal catheter plus intrapleural fibrinolytics (alteplase plus dornase) or with primary VATS in selected centres.
key_points: Ultrasound first-line: anechoic equals simple, complex septated equals empyema
Drain if pus, septations, or large effusion with respiratory compromise
Intrapleural fibrinolytics (tPA plus DNase) reduce need for VATS
Necrotising pneumonia and lung abscess seen better on contrast CT
Continue IV antibiotics targeting Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus (including community-acquired MRSA if local prevalence)
explanation.pearls: If a previously responding pneumonia stops responding by day 5, scan with ultrasound before reaching for a new antibiotic.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

stem:
A 9-week-old infant is brought to the ED by her parents after three brief cyanotic episodes at home, the last preceded by a paroxysm of coughing that ended in a deep gasping noise. She has been coryzal for 10 days and her cough has worsened in the last 4 days with occasional post-tussive vomiting. She has not received any immunisations because her parents have been delaying the 6-week schedule.

Her mother completed a course of antibiotics 2 weeks ago for a chest infection diagnosed at the GP as pertussis. The infant was born at 38 weeks and her mother did not receive a pertussis vaccine in pregnancy. On examination she is afebrile, has minimal increased work of breathing between paroxysms, and her chest is clear. SpO2 between coughing episodes is 97% on room air but dropped to 78% during the cough observed in ED.

There is a single sub-conjunctival haemorrhage. Bloods show WCC 38 x 10^9/L with an absolute lymphocytosis of 28 x 10^9/L. Nasopharyngeal aspirate for Bordetella pertussis PCR has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 152 bpm, RR 44 /min between paroxysms, SpO2 97% baseline (78% with cough)
data_table.Examination: Sub-conjunctival haemorrhage, paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop, otherwise well between episodes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 38 (lymphocytes 28) x 10^9/L, CXR clear, NPA pertussis PCR pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate antibiotic regimen for this infant?

options.text: Oral roxithromycin 4 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days, admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Admission for cardiorespiratory monitoring is appropriate in any infant under 6 months with confirmed or strongly suspected pertussis (apnoea risk), but roxithromycin is not the preferred macrolide in this age group: azithromycin has the stronger paediatric evidence base, a shorter 5-day course and is recommended first-line. Roxithromycin is acceptable only in older children needing a macrolide alternative (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral azithromycin once daily for 5 days, admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with pertussis are admitted for monitoring because of apnoea and pneumonia risk. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days is the antibiotic of choice in this age group; it does not alter the established disease course but reduces transmission. Notify public health and offer post-exposure prophylaxis to close contacts, as per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and CDNA Pertussis SoNG.

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole twice daily for 14 days, admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Admission is appropriate, but TMP-SMX is second-line only when macrolides are contraindicated and is avoided under 2 months (kernicterus risk). It is not first-line for a 9-week-old with macrolide-sensitive pertussis. Would be correct only over 2 months with macrolide contraindication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: IV ceftriaxone once daily for 7 days continuously
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone has no role in pertussis (macrolide-sensitive organism) and avoided under 1 month. Would never be correct in pertussis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Withhold antibiotics; they do not change clinical course once paroxysms have begun
options.rationale: Antibiotics beyond 21 days of cough don't alter clinical course but are still given within 3 weeks to reduce transmission, especially in infants. Would never be correct in this presentation (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG).

explanation.summary: Pertussis in an unimmunised young infant is treated with azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days and admission for apnoea and cyanosis monitoring. Public health notification is required. Close-contact post-exposure prophylaxis (azithromycin) is offered to household and high-risk contacts within 21 days of exposure.
key_points: Azithromycin first-line under 1 month and onwards: 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days
Notify public health on clinical suspicion
Marked lymphocytosis (greater than 20 x 10^9/L) is a classic finding
Maternal pertussis vaccination at 20 to 32 weeks protects young infants
Hospitalised infants need negative-pressure or single-room droplet isolation until 5 days of antibiotics complete
explanation.pearls: An afebrile infant with paroxysmal cough, post-tussive emesis and lymphocytosis is pertussis until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Pertussis in the unimmunised young infant

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the GP after his father, a recently arrived migrant from a high-tuberculosis-incidence country in South-East Asia, was diagnosed last week with smear-positive cavitating pulmonary tuberculosis sensitive to all first-line drugs on rapid molecular testing. The boy has been well, has no cough, no feversht along the 50th centile on his growth chart. He has not received BCG vaccination as it is not on the routine Australian schedule.

He shares a bedroom with his father and has slept in the same bed during the 8 weeks prior to his father's diagnosis. On examination he is well, alert and interactive, with no peripheral or cervical lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, and a clear chest on auscultation. The local public health unit asks the GP to coordinate his contact assessment. A chest X-ray is performed and is reported as normal.

A Mantoux tuberculin skin test using 0.1 mL of 10 TU/mL purified protein derivative is placed in the left forearm and read by the public health nurse at 72 hours, showing an induration of 12 mm with surrounding erythema. HIV serology is non-reactive. The mother asks whether an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) such as QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus would be more accurate in her son and whether he needs treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, clear chest, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CXR clear, Mantoux 12 mm induration at 72 h, HIV non-reactive, no BCG history

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the Mantoux in 8 weeks because 12 mm without BCG may be non-specific
options.rationale: Induration 12 mm in a non-BCG child with smear-positive household contact exceeds the 10 mm threshold; treat as LTBI without repeat. Would never be correct (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).

options.text: Reassure that the Mantoux is negative because it is under 15 mm and discharge with no further investigation
options.rationale: In AU, Mantoux 10 mm+ in non-BCG (or 5 mm+ in HIV/immunosuppression) is positive. Would never be correct (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).

options.text: Order IGRA (QuantiFERON or T-SPOT) instead because it is more specific and avoid further skin testing
options.rationale: IGRA has reduced sensitivity in under-5s and is not preferred sole test; Mantoux remains test of choice for young children. Would be correct in older children (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).

options.text: Start a 6-month course of rifampicin monotherapy without isoniazid today
options.rationale: Rifampicin 4 months monotherapy is alternative but AU default is isoniazid 6-9 months with pyridoxine for paediatric LTBI. Would be correct only with INH intolerance or resistance (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).

options.text: Diagnose latent TB and commence isoniazid daily for 9 months with pyridoxine
options.rationale: A non-BCG child with a household smear-positive contact and Mantoux 10 mm or more, normal CXR and no clinical features of active disease has latent TB infection. The standard Australian paediatric regimen is isoniazid 10 mg/kg (max 300 mg) daily for 9 months with pyridoxine to prevent peripheral neuropathy; isoniazid plus rifampicin for 3 months is an alternative, as per CDNA Tuberculosis SoNG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

explanation.summary: Paediatric TB contact assessment uses Mantoux as the primary test in children under 5 years (IGRA has reduced sensitivity), with cut-offs of 10 mm or more in non-BCG, 5 mm or more in HIV/immunosuppressed, and 15 mm or more in low-risk BCG-vaccinated. Active disease is excluded clinically and with CXR before starting latent TB treatment.
key_points: Mantoux cut-offs: 5 mm (HIV/immunosuppressed/recent contact in some settings), 10 mm (non-BCG migrant/contact), 15 mm (low risk)
IGRA unreliable under 5 years; not first-line in this age group in Australia
Isoniazid 10 mg/kg (max 300 mg) daily for 9 months with pyridoxine for paediatric LTBI
Alternatives: rifampicin 4 months; isoniazid + rifampicin 3 months; weekly isoniazid + rifapentine 3 months (children 2 yr and over)
Notify the state TB control unit; arrange contact tracing of the entire household
explanation.pearls: In any child under 5 with a household TB contact, treat as if infected even with a negative Mantoux until a follow-up test at 8 to 12 weeks confirms otherwise; the window period matters.

subtopic_detail: Latent and contact tuberculosis investigation in a young child

stem:
A 16-year-old male attends the GP alone requesting a confidential review after an episode of condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new partner 18 hours ago. He says the partner has subsequently disclosed by message that he is HIV positive but has been on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load for 2 years. The patient is otherwise well, has no symptoms, has had no other recent sexual exposures, is up to date with hepatitis B vaccination, and has not used injecting drugs.

He has heard about post-exposure prophylaxis online and asks whether he needs it. He is afraid of his parents finding out. He is articulate, demonstrates clear understanding of confidentiality, his health, and the implications of testing and treatment. He says he is willing to attend the local sexual health clinic but only if his Medicare claim history will not appear on his parents' Medicare statement.

There are no concerns about coercion or capacity. He has no penicillin or other drug allergies, and his renal function is normal on a recent school medical.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 76 bpm, BP 124/72 mmHg, RR 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, no rash, no mucosal lesions, normal external genitalia
data_table.History: Condomless receptive anal intercourse 18 h ago; partner HIV positive on ART with undetectable VL for 2 yr

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Document Gillick competence and refer to sexual health clinic same day; PEP not indicated as source confirmed undetectable (U=U); baseline HIV/HBV/syphilis serology
options.rationale: The Australian PEP guidelines (ASHM) explicitly state that a known source with a documented sustained undetectable viral load (U=U) is not a recognised indication for PEP because the risk of HIV transmission is effectively zero. Confidential adolescent care under Gillick competence applies, and baseline plus follow-up testing remains appropriate. Confidentiality concerns are addressable via bulk-billed sexual health services that do not generate Medicare statements visible to parents, as per ASHM PEP Guidelines and RACGP Red Book.

options.text: Prescribe a 28-day course of tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir empirically and arrange baseline HIV testing at the GP
options.rationale: Empirical PEP not appropriate when source has sustained undetectable VL (U=U); GP prescribing of PEP is discouraged in favour of specialist. Would be correct only with detectable source VL (Source: ASHM PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Defer all testing and management until the parents are informed because the patient is still a minor under 16
options.rationale: Gillick-competent adolescent consents to confidential HIV testing/treatment without parental involvement; mandatory disclosure is incorrect. Would never be correct (Source: RACGP).

options.text: Perform an HIV antibody-only test today and reassure that, if it returns negative, he does not need PEP
options.rationale: Antibody-only tests miss the window period; 4th-gen Ag/Ab assay detects p24 earlier. Would never be correct as sole test (Source: ASHM).

options.text: Inform the patient that PEP is no longer available in Australia and that PrEP is the only option for future exposures
options.rationale: PEP remains available across Australia (tenofovir-emtricitabine plus third agent, 28 days, within 72 h), just not indicated in U=U scenarios. Would never be correct (Source: ASHM PEP).

explanation.summary: Confidential adolescent sexual health care relies on Gillick competence assessment. PEP (tenofovir-emtricitabine plus a third agent, 28 days) is indicated for significant HIV exposures within 72 hours when the source is HIV positive with detectable or unknown viral load, or unknown HIV status with significant risk. Sustained undetectable viral load on ART (U=U) effectively eliminates transmission risk and PEP is not indicated. Fourth-generation HIV assays are first-line for diagnostic testing.
key_points: Gillick/Fraser competence allows confidential adolescent sexual health care
Fourth-gen HIV assay detects p24 antigen plus antibodies
PEP within 72 h (ideally under 4 h); standard tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir or raltegravir for 28 days
U=U (undetectable equals untransmittable) source equals no PEP indication
Baseline testing: HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, STI screen; follow-up HIV at 6 and 12 weeks (or earlier with fourth-gen)
explanation.pearls: Confidentiality in adolescent care is preserved by bulk-billed sexual health clinics that don't itemise Medicare statements; tell every teenager who is scared of being seen.

subtopic_detail: HIV testing and post-exposure prophylaxis in the adolescent

stem:
A 13-month-old infant has been brought to the GP 60 hours after she shared a paediatric outpatient waiting room for 90 minutes with a child later confirmed by PCR to have measles. She was due to receive her first MMR vaccine at the 12-month visit but it was deferred 2 weeks ago because of an intercurrent febrile illness. Her older sister, aged 4, is in the same household and is fully immunised.

Her mother is 22 weeks pregnant and her serological status for measles is unknown. The household also includes her grandmother, aged 68, who was born in 1958 in Australia and has no recorded MMR doses, and an uncle with cystic fibrosis (post-lung-transplant 4 years ago, on tacrolimus and prednisolone). The GP confirms the public health unit has already issued a contact-tracing alert. The infant is currently well, afebrile, and has no rash, no coryza and no conjunctivitis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 124 bpm, RR 28 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no rash, no Koplik spots, no conjunctivitis, no coryza
data_table.History: Exposure 60 h ago, due first MMR but deferred 2 weeks ago, household includes pregnant mother, unvaccinated grandmother, immunosuppressed transplant uncle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate post-exposure measure for the index 13-month-old infant?

options.text: Give intramuscular normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG) because she is under 9 months
options.rationale: She is over 9 months and MMR within 72 h is preferred PEP; NHIG/IVIG is for under 9 months, pregnant susceptibles, and significantly immunocompromised. Would be correct only under 9 months (Source: CDNA Measles SoNG; NCIRS).

options.text: Administer MMR now (within 72 hours of exposure), notify public health, repeat MMR at 18 months
options.rationale: For susceptible contacts aged 9 months and over without contraindications, MMR vaccine within 72 hours of first exposure is the preferred post-exposure prophylaxis. If given to an infant aged 9 to 11 months it counts as a dose but the routine 12-month and 18-month doses are still given. Measles is urgently notifiable, as per CDNA Measles SoNG and NCIRS Measles vaccine.

options.text: Withhold post-exposure prophylaxis because she is currently asymptomatic; arrange measles serology day 14
options.rationale: Susceptible exposed contacts should be offered PEP (MMR within 72 h or NHIG/IVIG within 6 days); waiting for serology delays effective prophylaxis. Would never be correct (Source: CDNA).

options.text: Administer MMR vaccine plus oral ribavirin for 7 days starting today
options.rationale: No specific antiviral for measles; supportive care plus vitamin A in selected cases. Would never be correct (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Reassure that maternal antibody will protect her until she is 12 months old
options.rationale: She is already 13 months, maternal antibody waned, and she is unvaccinated; she needs PEP. Would be correct only in younger infant with maternal immunity (Source: NCIRS).

explanation.summary: Measles post-exposure prophylaxis depends on age, gestation and immune status. Susceptible contacts 9 months and older receive MMR within 72 hours; under 9 months, pregnant non-immune women, and immunocompromised contacts receive NHIG (or IVIG) within 6 days of exposure. Notify the public health unit immediately on suspicion or confirmed exposure. Long-term complications include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) 7 to 10 years after infection.
key_points: Infectious from 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset
MMR within 72 h of exposure if 9 months or older and no contraindication
NHIG/IVIG within 6 days for: under 9 months, pregnant non-immune, immunocompromised
Notify on clinical suspicion (urgent notification)
Vitamin A reduces complications in severely affected children and in low-vitamin-A settings
explanation.pearls: An MMR dose at 9 to 11 months for outbreak or post-exposure use does not replace the routine 12-month and 18-month doses; document but still give both.

stem:
An 8-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, currently in the consolidation phase of a Berlin-Frankfurt-Munster protocol and on dexamethasone, vincristine and intrathecal methotrexate, is brought to the day oncology unit after a confirmed face-to-face household exposure to his 5-year-old sister, who developed a vesicular varicella rash on her trunk and face this morning. He has not had clinical varicella infection at any time in the past, did not complete the varicella vaccination schedule because of his oncology diagnosis at the time of his routine 18-month appointment, and was last on the day oncology ward yesterday for his scheduled intrathecal chemotherapy.

The patient is currently afebrile and entirely asymptomatic, with no rash, no oral lesions and no respiratory or constitutional symptoms; his most recent full blood count 2 days ago showed a WCC of 1.8 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 0.7 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.9 x 10^9/L, and platelets 84 x 10^9/L. His baseline varicella IgG taken at diagnosis was negative. The exposure occurred 36 hours ago, and the local paediatric oncology consultant is available by phone.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 92 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no rash, no oral lesions, no respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: WCC 1.8 (neutrophils 0.7) x 10^9/L, platelets 84 x 10^9/L, varicella IgG negative on baseline

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate intervention for this patient?

options.text: Live attenuated varicella vaccine 0.5 mL subcutaneously within 5 days of exposure
options.rationale: Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in significantly immunocompromised patients on chemo. Would be correct only in immunocompetent contacts within 5 days (Source: NCIRS Varicella Vaccine).

options.text: Oral valaciclovir q8h for 7 days starting from day 7 after exposure
options.rationale: Prophylactic oral aciclovir from day 7 post-exposure is an alternative when VZIG unavailable; VZIG preferred in significantly immunocompromised. Would be correct as alternative when VZIG unavailable (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Oral aciclovir six-hourly for 5 days starting immediately today
options.rationale: Immediate aciclovir treats established varicella, not pre-symptomatic prophylaxis; VZIG is preferred PEP in significantly immunocompromised contacts. Would be correct only with established lesions (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Observation only and IV aciclovir q8h if a rash develops
options.rationale: Observation alone misses the window for passive immunisation; VZIG within 96 h (up to 10 days) attenuates disease. Would never be correct in significantly immunocompromised contact (Source: NCIRS).

options.text: Zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) intramuscularly within 96 hours of exposure (up to 10 days)
options.rationale: Significantly immunocompromised varicella-susceptible contacts (including children on chemotherapy, transplant recipients, and those on high-dose corticosteroids) should receive VZIG as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within 96 hours but up to 10 days. Other indicated groups include non-immune pregnant women and neonates of mothers with peripartum varicella (5 days before to 2 days after delivery), as per NCIRS Varicella vaccine and the Australian Immunisation Handbook.

explanation.summary: VZIG (or IVIG when VZIG unavailable) is given to susceptible high-risk contacts after significant varicella exposure: significantly immunocompromised patients, non-immune pregnant women, and neonates exposed to peripartum maternal varicella. Live varicella vaccine is contraindicated in this group. Maternal varicella before 20 weeks risks congenital varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia, cicatricial scarring, microcephaly, eye defects); peripartum maternal varicella threatens neonatal varicella with high mortality.
key_points: VZIG ideally within 96 h, up to 10 days from exposure
Varicella vaccine contraindicated in significant immunosuppression
Congenital varicella syndrome risk highest with maternal infection 8 to 20 weeks gestation
Neonatal varicella: maternal rash 5 days before to 2 days after birth equals VZIG to neonate plus aciclovir if symptomatic
Treat established varicella in immunocompromised with IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg q8h
explanation.pearls: If you have to think about whether someone is significantly immunocompromised, they probably are; phone for VZIG and don't wait for the rash.

subtopic_detail: Varicella post-exposure prophylaxis in the immunocompromised host

stem:
A 3-year-old previously well, fully immunised girl is brought to her GP with 12 hours of right ear pain and a mild fever. She has been clingy but is eating and drinking normally with no vomiting and no neck stiffness. This is her first episode and she has no high-risk background (no cleft palate, no immunodeficiency, not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander).

On examination her left tympanic membrane is normal and her right tympanic membrane is erythematous and bulging with the membrane intact and no otorrhoea. She is afebrile in clinic at 37.8 deg C. Her mother reports she settles with paracetamol.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 deg C, HR 110 bpm, RR 24 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 100/62 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right TM erythematous and bulging, intact, no otorrhoea, left TM normal, no mastoid tenderness, no neck stiffness
data_table.History: First episode, fully immunised, no high-risk background, eating/drinking normally

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Regular analgesia (paracetamol with or without ibuprofen) and safety-net advice to return or recommence antibiotics if not improving at 48 to 72 hours
options.rationale: Australian guidance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, RCH CPG: AOM) reserves antibiotics for children under 6 months always, under 2 years with bilateral disease, otorrhoea, systemically unwell, or high-risk groups (Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background, immunocompromised, cochlear implants). A low-risk, well, over-2 child with unilateral AOM and an intact TM is managed with analgesia and watchful waiting.

options.text: Immediate oral amoxicillin at half the standard AOM dose three times daily for 5 days
options.rationale: AU dose for AOM when antibiotics indicated is amoxicillin 30 mg/kg eight-hourly for 5 days, not 15 mg/kg; and antibiotics are not first-line in low-risk children. Would be correct only at correct dose for high-risk indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Immediate oral amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Augmentin is for amoxicillin failure, recent amoxicillin use, or recurrent AOM, not first uncomplicated episode. Would be correct only with prior amoxicillin failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Immediate oral cefaclor three times daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Cefaclor has poor activity against penicillin-non-susceptible pneumococcus and risks serum-sickness-like reactions; not first-line. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Topical ciprofloxacin 0.3% ear drops twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Topical quinolone drops are for AOM with perforation, otorrhoea through grommet, or chronic suppurative OM; TM intact here. Would be correct only with perforation/grommet/CSOM (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Most AOM in well low-risk Australian children resolves without antibiotics. Indications for immediate antibiotics: under 6 months, under 2 years with bilateral disease, otorrhoea (perforated or grommet), severe systemic symptoms, immunocompromised, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background, cochlear implants, or failure to improve at 48 to 72 hours. First-line amoxicillin 30 mg/kg (max 1 g) q8h for 5 days; amoxicillin-clavulanate for failure or recurrence.
key_points: Analgesia is the priority regardless of antibiotic decision
Antibiotic indications: under 6 mo always; under 2 yr bilateral; otorrhoea; severe; high risk
First-line: amoxicillin 30 mg/kg q8h x 5 days
Topical antibiotics for perforation or grommet discharge
Review at 48 to 72 h; reconsider antibiotics if no improvement
explanation.pearls: In remote and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, AOM is treated more aggressively because of the high burden of chronic suppurative otitis media; the threshold for antibiotics is much lower.

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the ED with 24 hours of progressive right eyelid swelling and redness on a background of 4 days of purulent nasal discharge and intermittent facial pain. He is fully immunised including 13vPCV and Hib. He has had a temperature of up to 39.2 deg C at home. On examination the right upper and lower eyelids are warm, erythematous and tense; the eye itself is closed by swelling but can be opened with gentle effort.

The conjunctiva is mildly injected. He reports pain when asked to move the eye and has restricted upgaze and lateral gaze on the right with a sense of pressure. Visual acuity in the affected eye is reduced to 6/18 from a documented 6/6 at school screening 4 months ago, and there is a relative afferent pupillary defect on swinging-flashlight testing. He has no proptosis measured by Hertel exophthalmometry. The left eye is normal. He has no neck stiffness and no focal neurology.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 deg C, HR 128 bpm, RR 24 /min, BP 108/66 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Right eyelid swelling, painful EOM with restricted upgaze and lateral gaze, RAPD, VA 6/18 right vs 6/6 left, no proptosis on Hertel
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 15), CRP 142 mg/L, blood culture taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral cefalexin q6h for 7 days and review by GP in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral and outpatient are for uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis without orbital involvement; painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, proptosis or vision change mark orbital cellulitis. Would be correct only in preseptal cellulitis without orbital signs (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: IV flucloxacillin q6h monotherapy and ophthalmology review in the morning
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy does not cover sinus pathogens (pneumococcus, Strep anginosus, anaerobes) and Haemophilus driving orbital cellulitis. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: MRI orbits in the morning before any antibiotics, to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Imaging required but antibiotics must not be delayed; CT sinuses/orbits with contrast is the standard urgent imaging, not MRI (more rapidly available, identifies subperiosteal collection). Would be correct as adjunct, not delaying antibiotics (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Urgent contrast CT sinuses/orbits, admit, IV ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin + metronidazole, urgent ophthalmology and ENT
options.rationale: This child has features of orbital (postseptal) cellulitis: painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, reduced visual acuity and RAPD. Urgent CT sinuses and orbits with contrast identifies subperiosteal abscess and sinus disease. Empirical IV therapy must cover sinus pathogens (ceftriaxone), Staphylococcus aureus (flucloxacillin) and anaerobes (metronidazole), with urgent ophthalmology and ENT input for possible surgical drainage, as per RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Single dose of oral prednisolone and observation, on the assumption of allergic angioedema
options.rationale: Allergic eyelid swelling is bilateral, itchy, non-tender, with no vision/movement effect; this is bacterial orbital cellulitis. Would be correct only in allergic angioedema with bilateral involvement (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum and presents with eyelid swelling and erythema but normal eye movements, vision and pupil response. Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis includes proptosis, painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, reduced visual acuity, or RAPD and demands urgent CT sinuses and orbits, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering sinus organisms, anaerobes and Staphylococcus aureus, and joint ophthalmology and ENT input for possible drainage of subperiosteal abscess.
key_points: Preseptal: lid swelling, no proptosis, normal EOM, normal vision
Postseptal: any of proptosis, painful EOM, ophthalmoplegia, reduced VA, RAPD
Imaging: CT sinuses and orbits with contrast (not MRI first-line for speed)
Empirical IV: ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin + metronidazole
Drain subperiosteal abscess if large, vision-threatening or non-responsive to 48 h IV
explanation.pearls: Always test eye movements, visual acuity and the pupil in any swollen eyelid; a missed orbital cellulitis can blind a child in 24 hours.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is brought to a tertiary paediatric ED by her parents on day 10 of consolidation chemotherapy with high-dose methotrexate and cytarabine. She has a tunnelled Hickman line in situ for 4 months, has been febrile for 4 hours with a single reading of 38.6 deg C documented at home by her parents, has had new rigors over the last 30 minutes, and her parents report increasingly rapid breathing and that she has been progressively more lethargic over the last hour with reduced eye contact.

On arrival to the resuscitation bay she is mottled with cold peripheries and a capillary refill of 5 seconds, BP 78/40 mmHg, HR 162 bpm, RR 40 /min, SpO2 94% on 4 L/min nasal prongs, T 39.4 deg C. There is no obvious focus of infection on rapid head-to-toe examination, the Hickman exit site is clean and not erythematous, her chest is clear, and there is no abdominal tenderness or perianal lesion.

Her full blood count two days ago showed neutrophils 0.2 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.4 x 10^9/L, haemoglobin 92 g/L, and platelets 28 x 10^9/L. A repeat FBC, blood cultures drawn from both Hickman lumens and a peripheral site simultaneously, venous lactate, VBG, EUC, LFTs, coagulation, group and screen, urinalysis and a portable CXR are being arranged in parallel with resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 162 bpm, RR 40 /min, BP 78/40 mmHg, SpO2 94% on 4 L/min, CRT 5 s
data_table.Examination: Mottled cold peripheries, lethargic, no rash, no mucositis bleeding, Hickman line site clean, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Recent neutrophils 0.2 x 10^9/L, platelets 28 x 10^9/L, lactate pending, no known resistant organisms

lead_in: After 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus is initiated, what is the single most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: IV cefepime 50 mg/kg q8h monotherapy
options.rationale: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy with cefepime is a reasonable empirical regimen in stable high-risk febrile neutropenia, but this child is in septic shock with profound prolonged neutropenia and an indwelling central line, where Australian paediatric guidance recommends adding an aminoglycoside for synergistic Gram-negative cover and considering early vancomycin. Monotherapy here under-treats the shock physiology and the line-infection risk (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: IV ceftriaxone daily plus IV vancomycin six-hourly
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone does not cover Pseudomonas; antipseudomonal cover is mandatory in febrile neutropenia. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus IV gentamicin, add vancomycin if line infection suspected or shock persists
options.rationale: High-risk febrile neutropenia with septic shock and an indwelling Hickman line in a profoundly neutropenic patient requires antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside for synergy and Gram-negative cover. Piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg (piperacillin component) q6h plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily is standard, with vancomycin added if suspected central line infection, mucositis, MRSA risk, or ongoing instability, as per RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

options.text: IV meropenem 20 mg/kg eight-hourly as broad-spectrum monotherapy
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for second-line use in febrile neutropenia: known or suspected ESBL colonisation, severe sepsis not responding to first-line antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside, or significant beta-lactam allergy precluding piperacillin-tazobactam. First-line empirical therapy here is piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Delay antibiotics until blood cultures return positive to ensure organism-directed therapy today
options.rationale: Antibiotics must be given within 60 min (ideally 30 min in septic shock); each hour of delay increases mortality. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia).

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is fever 38.0 deg C or more (single reading 38.5 deg C or sustained 38.0 deg C) with ANC under 0.5 x 10^9/L (or expected to fall). Empirical antibiotics within 60 minutes (within 30 minutes if septic shock). High-risk or haemodynamically unstable patients: piperacillin-tazobactam plus aminoglycoside; add vancomycin if line infection, MRSA risk, mucositis, or shock. Source control includes line removal if persistent positive cultures.
key_points: ANC under 0.5 x 10^9/L defines neutropenia
Antibiotics within 60 min (30 min if shocked)
First-line high-risk: piperacillin-tazobactam + gentamicin (+/- vancomycin)
Add antifungal cover if persistent fever beyond 96 h
G-CSF for prolonged neutropenia; cannot replace antibiotics in acute phase
explanation.pearls: Time to antibiotics is the single most modifiable predictor of mortality in paediatric febrile neutropenia; the line must be in and antibiotics running before the imaging trolley arrives.

subtopic_detail: Febrile neutropenia with septic shock in the immunocompromised child

stem:
A 5-year-old previously well boy is brought to a metropolitan paediatric emergency department because of right hip pain and refusal to weight-bear for the past 18 hours. His mother reports a coryzal illness that resolved 10 days ago and no history of trauma. Immunisations are up to date and he is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. On arrival he is alert, holds his right hip in slight flexion, abduction and external rotation, and cries with passive internal rotation.

He has no rash, no other joint involvement and no overlying erythema or warmth at the hip. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and peripheral pulses are normal. He was given paracetamol 2 hours ago at triage. The ED registrar performs an ultrasound which demonstrates a moderate right hip effusion. Bloods and a plain pelvic radiograph have been arranged. The orthopaedic registrar asks for risk stratification using the Kocher criteria before deciding on theatre versus observation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7 deg C, HR 128 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 102/64 mmHg, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Holds right hip in flexion / abduction / external rotation, painful log-roll, no overlying erythema, refuses to bear weight even with paracetamol on board
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.8 x10^9/L (neutrophils 9.6), CRP 38 mg/L, ESR 52 mm/h, blood culture pending, pelvic XR no fracture or SUFE, hip US moderate effusion

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and ibuprofen for simple analgesia and arrange GP review in 48 hours for a likely post-viral self-limiting hip presentation with planned reassessment
options.rationale: All four Kocher criteria met giving ~99 percent probability of septic arthritis; discharge with analgesia risks irreversible cartilage damage. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

options.text: Admit for observation and serial examinations with maintenance IV fluids, withholding empirical antibiotics until a repeat CRP and full blood count at 12 hours have been reviewed
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics and aspiration in 4-of-4 Kocher risks irreversible cartilage and femoral head damage; time-to-washout correlates with outcome. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.text: Commence empirical oral flucloxacillin six-hourly and arrange outpatient orthopaedic clinic review the following week with safety-net advice for parents
options.rationale: Oral therapy and outpatient are inappropriate for high-probability septic arthritis of the hip; IV after aspiration is mandated and oral switch is only after cultures known. Would be correct only as step-down after IV course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.text: Arrange urgent ultrasound-guided hip aspiration in theatre, send synovial fluid for cell count and culture, then commence empirical IV flucloxacillin after sampling
options.rationale: With four Kocher criteria positive and a sonographic effusion, the predicted probability of septic arthritis is approximately 99 percent; urgent aspiration (often combined with arthrotomy and washout) confirms the diagnosis and decompresses the joint, with empirical IV flucloxacillin started immediately after sampling to cover Staphylococcus aureus, per RCH CPG: Acute limp and Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.text: Order an urgent contrast MRI of the hip and pelvis and defer joint aspiration and antibiotics until imaging has formally excluded coexisting osteomyelitis or pelvic abscess
options.rationale: MRI has role with suspected osteomyelitis after equivocal initial assessment but should not delay aspiration and antibiotics in 4-of-4 Kocher patient with confirmed effusion. Would be correct only with equivocal Kocher and effusion uncertainty (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria (fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WCC >12) stratify septic arthritis risk in a child with an acutely irritable hip; 4 of 4 predicts approximately 99 percent probability. Definitive management is urgent aspiration / washout plus empirical IV antistaphylococcal therapy, per RCH CPG: Acute limp.
key_points: Kocher 0/4 ~ 2 percent, 1/4 ~ 3 percent, 2/4 ~ 40 percent, 3/4 ~ 93 percent, 4/4 ~ 99 percent
Empirical flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus, the commonest pathogen
Kingella kingae cover (e.g. cefazolin) considered in under 4 year olds in some centres
Antibiotics after sampling unless the child is septic and aspiration is delayed
explanation.pearls: Transient synovitis classically follows a viral URTI by 1-2 weeks but the child is afebrile and will mobilise with analgesia; fever plus refusal to weight-bear despite analgesia is a major red flag (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

subtopic_detail: Paediatric orthopaedics - septic arthritis vs transient synovitis

stem:
A 12-year-old boy with a BMI of 30 kg/m^2 presents to his GP with a 6-week history of intermittent left knee and anterior thigh pain that has progressed over the past week to an antalgic limp. He denies any specific injury and has been otherwise well. He is in the early stages of puberty (Tanner 2 pubic hair). On examination the left lower limb is held in slight external rotation with the patient supine.

When the GP attempts to flex the left hip, the leg obligately externally rotates. Hip internal rotation and abduction are reduced compared with the right side, but there is no joint warmth, no effusion clinically and no overlying erythema. He is afebrile with normal observations. He weighs 78 kg. Plain anteroposterior pelvic radiographs are obtained and reported by the radiologist as showing a widened, irregular left proximal femoral physis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 86 bpm, RR 16 /min, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait, externally rotated left lower limb at rest, obligate external rotation on hip flexion, reduced internal rotation and abduction, no warmth or effusion
data_table.Investigations: AP pelvis - widened irregular left proximal femoral physis; frog-lateral pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the family, advise simple oral analgesia with paracetamol and review the child in clinic in 6 weeks if symptoms persist or worsen with ongoing activity
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion and widened physis are pathognomonic of SUFE; delay risks stable-to-unstable slip with much higher AVN risk. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE).

options.text: Refer for routine paediatric orthopaedic outpatient assessment within the next 2 weeks and allow continued partial weight-bearing on the affected limb in the interim period
options.rationale: Continued weight-bearing risks progression to unstable slip; child must be made non-weight-bearing and referred urgently. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Order an outpatient MRI of the left hip within the next 7 days to exclude an idiopathic femoral head osteonecrosis before any orthopaedic referral or non-weight-bearing measures
options.rationale: Perthes is 4-8 years with femoral head fragmentation, not physeal widening; this 12-year-old with raised BMI and physeal widening has SUFE. Would be correct in 4-8-year-old with classic Perthes XR (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Make the child strictly non-weight-bearing (wheelchair or crutches), arrange immediate transfer to the nearest paediatric orthopaedic unit and request a frog-lateral pelvic radiograph
options.rationale: This is a stable SUFE with classic obligate external rotation and a widened physis on AP view; frog-lateral views improve sensitivity. The child must be made non-weight-bearing immediately and admitted for in-situ percutaneous pinning to prevent progression and avascular necrosis, per RCH CPG: SUFE.

options.text: Arrange an outpatient MRI of the left knee given the predominant knee pain to exclude meniscal injury or osteochondritis dissecans before any hip-focused intervention
options.rationale: Referred knee pain is classic for hip pathology in adolescents; hip exam and pelvic XR have localised the lesion. Would never be correct as next step (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: SUFE typically affects overweight adolescents around puberty and presents with vague hip, thigh or knee pain and an externally rotated, antalgic gait. The key examination sign is obligate external rotation on hip flexion. Management is urgent non-weight-bearing transfer for in-situ pinning, per RCH CPG: SUFE.
key_points: Perthes age 4-8 years, SUFE adolescent (typically 10-15)
Bilateral SUFE in up to 25 percent over time - many centres pin both prophylactically
Stable = able to bear weight (with crutches); unstable = cannot bear weight even with aids
Unstable slips carry up to 50 percent risk of avascular necrosis
explanation.pearls: Any adolescent with knee or thigh pain needs a hip examination; missed SUFE is a leading cause of preventable adolescent hip morbidity (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE).

stem:
A 13-year-old male competitive basketballer presents to his GP with a 6-week history of bilateral anterior knee pain that is worse during and after training, jumping and stair climbing, and that settles with rest. He denies any acute injury and has had no swelling, locking or giving way. He has had a recent growth spurt of 8 cm over the past 12 months.

On examination both knees show localised tenderness and a palpable bony prominence at the tibial tuberosity, with reproduction of pain on resisted knee extension and on direct pressure over the tuberosity. There is no joint effusion, no warmth, no ligamentous laxity and no patellar grind. He has full painless range, no nocturnal pain, no constitutional symptoms and no inguinal lymphadenopathy. He is afebrile with normal observations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 78 bpm, RR 14 /min, BP 112/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bilateral tibial tuberosity tenderness with prominent bony enlargement, pain on resisted knee extension, no effusion, full ROM, stable ligaments
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure with the clinical diagnosis of Osgood-Schlatter, advise relative activity modification, ice and simple analgesia, and continue sport within pain tolerance
options.rationale: Bilateral tibial tuberosity tenderness in an adolescent during a growth spurt with reproducible pain on resisted knee extension and no red flags is diagnostic of Osgood-Schlatter (traction apophysitis); imaging is not required and management is conservative, per RCH CPG: Knee pain.

options.text: Order bilateral knee MRI to exclude osteochondritis dissecans and refer to paediatric orthopaedics
options.rationale: MRI/orthopaedics are for atypical (unilateral, nocturnal pain, locking, persistent past skeletal maturity); typical bilateral apophysitis does not need them. Would be correct with atypical features (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Apply long-leg plaster casts bilaterally for 6 weeks then reassess for ongoing apophyseal fragmentation
options.rationale: Casting is not recommended for Osgood-Schlatter and causes deconditioning; relative rest preserves strength and growth. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Inject intralesional corticosteroid into the tibial tuberosity bilaterally to reduce inflammation
options.rationale: Intralesional steroid near an open apophysis risks soft tissue atrophy, depigmentation, growth disturbance. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Arrange plain knee radiographs in both AP and skyline views to confirm the diagnosis and exclude tibial tuberosity avulsion fracture
options.rationale: Plain films not routine for typical Osgood-Schlatter; tuberosity fragmentation is a normal variant. Would be correct only with atypical features (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Osgood-Schlatter is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity at the patellar tendon insertion, typical in adolescents during a growth spurt who do jumping or running sports. Diagnosis is clinical and management is conservative with activity modification, ice and analgesia, with reassurance that symptoms resolve at skeletal maturity, per RCH CPG: Knee pain.
key_points: Bilateral involvement in 25-50 percent
Continue sport within pain tolerance
Imaging only if atypical (unilateral, nocturnal, locking) to exclude tumour or OCD
Symptoms usually self-limit by closure of tibial tuberosity apophysis (~16 years)
explanation.pearls: Persistent unfused ossicle in the patellar tendon after skeletal maturity may need excision but is rare (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain).

stem:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to her GP after a school nurse noticed asymmetry of her back during a routine screening assessment. She has no back pain, no neurological symptoms and no functional limitation, and dances three times a week without difficulty. She had menarche 6 months ago. On examination, when she bends forward (Adams forward bend test) there is a clearly visible right thoracic rib prominence.

Standing posture shows a right shoulder higher than the left and asymmetric flank crease. There is no leg-length discrepancy on examination. Neurological examination is normal, including abdominal reflexes and lower limb tone, power, reflexes and sensation. There are no skin stigmata of spinal dysraphism (no hairy patch, lipoma or sacral dimple). A standing posteroanterior spinal radiograph is ordered and reports a right thoracic curve with a Cobb angle of 28 degrees and Risser stage 2.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 deg C, HR 72 bpm, RR 14 /min, BP 108/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right thoracic rib prominence on Adams forward bend, right shoulder elevation, no leg length inequality, normal neurology, no cutaneous spinal stigmata, Tanner 4
data_table.Investigations: Standing PA spine - right thoracic curve, Cobb 28 degrees, Risser 2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the patient and family, discharge with no follow-up arrangements as she is currently asymptomatic and reports no functional or postural concerns
options.rationale: Cobb 28 degrees in skeletally immature girl (Risser 2, recent menarche) has significant progression risk and needs specialist follow-up. Would be correct only in skeletally mature patient with stable Cobb under 25 (Source: AAOS Scoliosis Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange routine GP review in 6 months with a repeat standing posteroanterior spinal radiograph at that time to reassess Cobb angle and Risser stage progression
options.rationale: 20-40 degree curves in skeletally immature meet threshold for orthopaedic referral and possible bracing; surveillance alone risks missing progression. Would be correct only in skeletally mature with stable Cobb under 25 (Source: AAOS).

options.text: Refer to a paediatric orthopaedic / spinal surgeon for consideration of bracing given a Cobb angle of 28 degrees in a skeletally immature patient
options.rationale: Australian guidelines refer skeletally immature adolescents with Cobb angles of 20 degrees or more to a spinal service; bracing is typically considered between 25 and 40 degrees in skeletally immature patients to prevent progression, per RCH CPG: Scoliosis.

options.text: Refer urgently to spinal surgery for posterior spinal instrumentation and fusion given the visible deformity, asymmetric shoulders and a 28-degree thoracic Cobb angle
options.rationale: Surgery is for Cobb over 45-50 degrees that continues to progress, not 28; bracing is first-line at this Cobb. Would be correct at Cobb over 45-50 with progression (Source: AAOS).

options.text: Order an urgent whole-spine MRI under sedation to exclude syringomyelia given the visible right thoracic curve and shoulder-height asymmetry on standing examination
options.rationale: MRI is for atypical features (left thoracic, rapid progression, neuro signs, painful, juvenile under 10, cutaneous stigmata); right thoracic curve in adolescent is typical adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Would be correct with atypical features (Source: AAOS).

explanation.summary: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is screened with the Adams forward bend test (positive rib prominence) and quantified with the standing Cobb angle. Australian referral cut-offs are: <20 degrees - observe with skeletal maturity assessment; 20-40 degrees in a skeletally immature patient - refer for bracing consideration; >40-50 degrees with progression - surgical referral. Atypical features mandate MRI, per RCH CPG: Scoliosis.
key_points: Right thoracic, painless, neurologically normal AIS is typical
Risser stage 0-2 = high risk of progression
Bracing aims to halt progression, not correct the curve
Red flags for MRI: left thoracic curve, neurology, pain, age <10, cutaneous stigmata
explanation.pearls: A scoliometer reading of 7 degrees or more on the Adams forward bend roughly corresponds to a 20 degree Cobb angle and triggers radiographic assessment (Source: Spine Society of Australia).

stem:
A term female infant is being examined on day 2 of life on the postnatal ward. She was born by elective caesarean at 39+1 weeks for breech presentation that did not respond to external cephalic version. Birthweight was 3520 g. There is a family history of developmental dysplasia of the hip in her older sister who required a Pavlik harness.

She is breastfeeding well and has passed urine and meconium. On hip examination today, the Ortolani manoeuvre on the left hip elicits a palpable clunk as the femoral head reduces into the acetabulum with abduction. The right hip is stable. There is no leg-length discrepancy or asymmetric thigh skin creases. Neurological examination including primitive reflexes is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 142 bpm, RR 46 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Positive Ortolani sign on left hip (clunk on abduction reduction), Barlow negative on right, no leg length discrepancy, normal Moro and tone
data_table.Risk factors: Female, breech to term, first-degree family history of DDH

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that hip clunks at this age are usually benign and arrange a routine 6-week paediatric review without specialist input or imaging today
options.rationale: Positive Ortolani is a clinically dislocated reducible hip, not a benign click; same-admission orthopaedic referral is mandatory. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

options.text: Order an immediate plain anteroposterior pelvic radiograph to assess acetabular index and the Shenton line before referral
options.rationale: Plain XR is unreliable before 4-6 months (femoral heads not ossified); US is the neonatal imaging modality. Would be correct in older infant over 4-6 months (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedic surgery now for assessment and Pavlik harness application, and arrange a static and dynamic hip ultrasound
options.rationale: A frankly positive Ortolani with risk factors (female, breech, family history) mandates urgent paediatric orthopaedic referral, supervised Pavlik harness fitting, and ultrasound (Graf classification, static and dynamic) for morphology, per RCH CPG: DDH and the Australian national hip surveillance guidance.

options.text: Apply double nappies between the legs to maintain abduction and review the infant in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Double-nappying is not evidence-based and delays definitive Pavlik harness in a frankly dislocated hip. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Arrange an outpatient hip ultrasound at 6 weeks as standard risk-factor screening
options.rationale: 6-week screening is for at-risk infants with normal clinical exam; positive Ortolani requires immediate referral. Would be correct only with risk factors and normal exam (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Newborn DDH screening combines clinical examination (Barlow provocative test for dislocatability, Ortolani manoeuvre for reduction of a dislocated hip) with selective ultrasound at 6 weeks for risk factors (female, breech, first-degree family history, oligohydramnios). A positive Ortolani is dislocated hip and warrants immediate paediatric orthopaedic referral and Pavlik harness, per RCH CPG: DDH.
key_points: Ultrasound preferred over XR until femoral head ossifies (~4-6 months)
Pavlik harness from diagnosis, weaned around 6-12 weeks of treatment
Six-week ultrasound for risk factors with normal clinical exam
After ~6 months of age, closed reduction in theatre +/- spica is required
explanation.pearls: Asymmetric skin creases alone are NOT specific for DDH, but limited or asymmetric abduction beyond the neonatal period is the most reliable sign (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

subtopic_detail: Developmental dysplasia of the hip - neonatal exam

stem:
