An 8-month-old girl is brought to her GP because her parents have noticed her left leg appears shorter than the right when they change her nappy. She was born at term, was not breech, and the newborn check was documented as normal. There is no family history of hip problems and she had no hip ultrasound. She is meeting developmental milestones, including sitting independently, and has not yet started cruising.

On examination, with the infant supine and hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees, the left knee sits lower than the right (positive Galeazzi sign). Hip abduction is reduced on the left (60 degrees versus 80 degrees on the right). There is asymmetry of the thigh and gluteal skin creases. There is no warmth or tenderness and the infant is afebrile with normal neurology. The mother asks whether ultrasound is still useful at 8 months and is anxious about radiation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 126 bpm, RR 32 /min
data_table.Examination: Positive Galeazzi (apparent shortening of left thigh), reduced left hip abduction (60 vs 80 deg), asymmetric skin creases, no warmth, normal neurology
data_table.Past: Normal newborn examination, no neonatal hip ultrasound, no risk factors documented

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Static and dynamic Graf-classified hip ultrasound
options.rationale: US is best up to 4-6 months while femoral heads are unossified; by 8 months the ossific nucleus obscures landmarks. Would be correct only under 4-6 months (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

options.text: MRI pelvis under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: MRI is for postoperative assessment or atypical/complex cases; not first-line for suspected late-presenting DDH. Would be correct in postop assessment (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Plain anteroposterior pelvic radiograph
options.rationale: After approximately 4-6 months of age the proximal femoral epiphysis ossifies and plain AP pelvic radiography (assessing acetabular index, Shenton line, Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines) becomes the imaging of choice for DDH, per RCH CPG: DDH.

options.text: CT pelvis with three-dimensional reconstruction
options.rationale: CT carries unnecessary radiation and is for surgical planning in older children with complex deformity. Would be correct in operative planning (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Bone scintigraphy with Tc-99m MDP
options.rationale: Bone scintigraphy has no routine role in DDH; it is for osteomyelitis or occult bone pathology. Would never be correct in suspected DDH (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: DDH that escapes newborn screening may present later with leg-length asymmetry (positive Galeazzi sign), limited hip abduction, asymmetric thigh creases, or an abnormal gait once walking. Imaging choice is age dependent: ultrasound under 4-6 months, plain AP pelvic XR thereafter, per RCH CPG: DDH.
key_points: Late DDH may need closed reduction in theatre +/- spica from approximately 6 months
Older late presentations may require open reduction and femoral or pelvic osteotomy
Galeazzi sign is unreliable in bilateral DDH
Shenton line on AP pelvis is the key radiographic clue
explanation.pearls: All infants who fail to walk by 18 months or who walk with a Trendelenburg gait need a pelvic XR to exclude missed DDH (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

stem:
A 3-year-old previously well boy is brought to ED with a 4-day history of a painless intermittent limp affecting the right leg. He had a coryzal illness 2 weeks ago that has now resolved. He has had no fevers, no rashes and no recent trauma. He is fully immunised and not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. On examination he ambulates with a Trendelenburg gait favouring the right side.

Hip abduction and internal rotation are mildly reduced on the right compared with the left. He is afebrile and there is no warmth, swelling or tenderness at the right hip, knee, ankle or foot. He will bear weight, although with a limp, and engages happily with the toys in the cubicle. Bloods show WCC 8.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 4.2), CRP 6 mg/L. Bedside hip ultrasound shows a small right hip effusion. The mother asks whether ALL or Perthes need to be excluded today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 104 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 96/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Trendelenburg gait, mild reduction in right hip abduction and internal rotation, no warmth or swelling, weight-bearing, afebrile, alert and playful
data_table.Investigations: WCC 8.4 (N 4.2), CRP 6, ESR 18, hip US small right effusion, AP pelvis pending

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Septic arthritis of the right hip joint with bacterial synovitis
options.rationale: Kocher 0/4 gives ~2 percent probability of septic arthritis; clinically very unlikely. Would be correct with elevated Kocher score (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

options.text: Transient (irritable hip) synovitis following recent viral upper respiratory tract illness
options.rationale: Mild post-viral limp in a 3-15 year old with low-grade or no fever, normal inflammatory markers, weight-bearing and a small effusion is classic for transient synovitis, the most common cause of atraumatic limp in this age group, per RCH CPG: Acute limp.

options.text: Perthes disease of the right femoral head with early epiphyseal involvement
options.rationale: Perthes is 4-8 years with insidious painless limp and characteristic XR (subchondral fracture, fragmentation); at age 3 with acute post-URTI onset, it's unlikely. Would be correct in 4-8-year-old with XR changes (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis of the right hip in an obese child
options.rationale: SUFE is adolescent (10-15 years, often overweight, peripubertal); rare in 3-year-old without endocrine predisposition. Would be correct in adolescent (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presenting with limp and disproportionate bone pain
options.rationale: ALL presents with night pain, systemic symptoms, cytopenias and disproportionately raised inflammatory markers; this child has benign profile. Would be correct with red flags (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Limp in the 3-10 year age group is most commonly transient (irritable hip) synovitis following a viral illness, classically Kocher 0-1 of 4. The clinician must actively exclude septic arthritis (Kocher), Perthes (age 4-8, insidious, XR fragmentation), and malignancy (night pain, systemic features), per RCH CPG: Acute limp.
key_points: Under 3: think DDH, septic arthritis, NAI, fracture (toddlers fracture)
3-10: transient synovitis, Perthes, septic arthritis, JIA, ALL
Adolescent: SUFE, sports injury (apophysitis, OCD), JIA
Always include NAI in pre-mobile children with limp
explanation.pearls: Transient synovitis settles within 7-10 days with rest and analgesia; persistent limp beyond 2 weeks should re-prompt imaging and bloods to exclude Perthes or chronic infection (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

stem:
A 4-year-old Aboriginal girl living in a remote Northern Territory community presents to the clinic with 36 hours of right ear pain and fever. Her mother reports that she has had three episodes of ear discharge in the past year and frequent colds. She is up to date with immunisations including PCV. On examination she is alert, well-perfused and tolerating oral fluids.

Otoscopy of the right ear shows a bulging, opaque, erythematous tympanic membrane with no perforation and no visible discharge. The left tympanic membrane is dull but intact with a visible air-fluid level. There is no mastoid tenderness, no facial nerve palsy and no postauricular swelling. She has no penicillin allergy. The clinic nurse has commenced paracetamol and the doctor is choosing antibiotic therapy in line with the current eTG and CARPA Standard Treatment Manual. The clinic nurse asks whether watchful waiting is appropriate.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 deg C, HR 118 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Right TM bulging, opaque, erythematous, intact; left TM dull with air-fluid level; no mastoid tenderness; oropharynx clear
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Watchful waiting with regular paracetamol for analgesia and structured otoscopic review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is for well low-risk non-Indigenous children over 2 years; Aboriginal children have markedly elevated risk of chronic suppurative OM and require antibiotic treatment. Would be correct only in non-Indigenous low-risk child (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin three times daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend amoxicillin first-line for AOM in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, with a longer duration (typically 7 days) than the 5 day course used for low-risk non-Indigenous children, to reduce risk of progression to chronic suppurative otitis media, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and CARPA Standard Treatment Manual.

options.text: Oral cefuroxime axetil twice daily for a 3-day short course
options.rationale: Oral cephalosporins are not preferred first-line for AOM in AU; amoxicillin has adequate pneumococcal cover and 3-day course is insufficient for high-risk children. Would be correct as second-line with adequate duration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Topical ciprofloxacin 0.3% ear drops two drops twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Topical quinolone drops are for AOM with discharge through perforation/grommet or CSOM, not intact-TM AOM. Would be correct only with perforation/grommet/CSOM (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin single weight-based dose at the clinic today
options.rationale: IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is for ARF secondary prophylaxis and GAS syndromes, not first-line AOM. Would be correct only in ARF prophylaxis indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children warrants antibiotics rather than watchful waiting because of the very high baseline rates of recurrent AOM, perforation and chronic suppurative otitis media. First-line is amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily, typically for 7 days in high-risk children, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and the CARPA Standard Treatment Manual.
key_points: Watchful waiting only for well, non-Indigenous, age >2, unilateral AOM
Always treat: <6 months; <2 years with bilateral disease; severe symptoms; otorrhoea; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander; immunocompromised; cochlear implant
Amoxicillin/clavulanate if no response by 48-72 hours
Topical ciprofloxacin if perforation or grommet discharge
explanation.pearls: Document tympanic membrane appearance carefully; CSOM (discharge >2 weeks through perforation) carries lifelong hearing and language consequences and is a public health priority (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual).

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media - Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander child duration

stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents to a tertiary paediatric ED with a 5-day history of left ear pain initially diagnosed as AOM by the GP and treated with oral amoxicillin. Over the past 24 hours her mother reports new posterior auricular swelling, displacement of the pinna and worsening fever despite the antibiotics. There is no history of recent travel and immunisations are up to date.

On examination the left auricle is protruding outwards and downwards. There is a fluctuant, erythematous, tender swelling behind the left ear that obliterates the post-auricular sulcus. Otoscopy shows a bulging, erythematous left tympanic membrane with pus visible behind it; the right ear is normal. There is no facial nerve palsy, no neck stiffness deficit. She is alert and interactive but in pain.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 152 bpm, RR 28 /min, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Left auricle protruding outwards and downwards, fluctuant tender postauricular erythematous swelling obliterating sulcus, bulging erythematous left TM with pus, GCS 15, no neck stiffness, no facial nerve palsy
data_table.Investigations: WCC 21.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 16.4), CRP 162 mg/L, blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Change current oral amoxicillin to oral amoxicillin/clavulanate twice daily for 10 days and arrange GP review in 48 hours to assess for improvement
options.rationale: Acute mastoiditis with fluctuant subperiosteal abscess; oral therapy is inadequate, urgent IV antibiotics, imaging and ENT input are mandatory. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Mastoiditis).

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous flucloxacillin six-hourly as monotherapy and arrange routine outpatient ENT clinic review within 1 week of discharge home
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin does not adequately cover pneumococcus and other AOM pathogens driving mastoiditis; broader cover and urgent ENT input are required. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Admit, commence IV ceftriaxone, request urgent CT temporal bones with contrast and urgent ENT review for consideration of cortical mastoidectomy and myringotomy
options.rationale: Acute mastoiditis with subperiosteal abscess requires admission, IV broad-spectrum cover (e.g. ceftriaxone, with metronidazole added if intracranial extension), contrast CT temporal bones to define abscess and exclude intracranial complications, and urgent ENT for cortical mastoidectomy +/- myringotomy +/- grommet, per RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

options.text: Perform urgent lumbar puncture in ED for cell count, protein, glucose and culture and commence empirical IV ceftriaxone for suspected intracranial extension from the ear
options.rationale: No signs of meningitis (no neck stiffness/photophobia/altered GCS); LP not required. Intracranial complications excluded by CT. Would be correct only with meningitis signs (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI brain with MR venography to exclude lateral sinus thrombosis and intracranial abscess before commencing any intravenous antibiotic therapy or surgical input
options.rationale: Imaging required but must not delay IV antibiotics and ENT; CT temporal bones with contrast is first-line (rapidly available, characterises bone). Would be correct only as adjunct, not delaying treatment (Source: RANZCR).

explanation.summary: Acute mastoiditis is the commonest suppurative complication of AOM and presents with postauricular swelling, protruding pinna and obliteration of the postauricular sulcus, often after failed oral therapy. Management is admission, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone), urgent contrast CT temporal bones and urgent ENT for surgical drainage, per RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis.
key_points: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest pathogen; consider PCV failure
CT temporal bones with contrast identifies subperiosteal abscess and bony erosion
Add metronidazole if intracranial extension; obtain MR venography for sinus thrombosis
ENT may perform cortical mastoidectomy plus myringotomy with grommet insertion
explanation.pearls: Always palpate and inspect behind the ear in any child with persistent fever despite AOM treatment - missing mastoiditis risks intracranial spread, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and facial nerve palsy (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis).

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media complications - acute mastoiditis

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to his GP by his mother because his preschool teacher reports he frequently says "what?" and is increasingly inattentive in group sessions. He has had four episodes of GP-diagnosed acute otitis media in the last 12 months, all treated and resolved. He has had no ear pain or discharge for the past 3 months. His speech and language are mildly behind peers but he is using full sentences.

He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and lives in a household with no smokers. On otoscopy both tympanic membranes appear retracted and dull with visible air-fluid levels and reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Tympanometry performed in the rooms shows bilateral type B (flat) tracings. The mother brings audiology results performed last week showing a bilateral conductive hearing loss of 35 dB. His mother asks whether antibiotics or a steroid spray could resolve the effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 deg C, HR 92 bpm, RR 18 /min
data_table.Examination: Bilateral retracted dull TMs with air-fluid levels, reduced TM mobility, no perforation, no discharge, mildly delayed expressive language
data_table.Investigations: Tympanometry bilateral type B (flat); audiology bilateral conductive hearing loss 35 dB

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin three times daily for 10 days as empirical treatment for chronic middle ear effusion and review at the end of the course
options.rationale: OME is not acute infection and routine antibiotics are not recommended; do not change long-term outcomes. Would never be correct in OME (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Prescribe intranasal fluticasone 50 microgram daily plus oral cetirizine 5 mg daily for 3 months to address presumed allergic contribution to chronic middle-ear effusion
options.rationale: Intranasal steroids and antihistamines not recommended for OME (no meaningful improvement in hearing/effusion). Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Watchful waiting for a further 6 months without repeat audiology, tympanometry or specialist review given the absence of acute ear pain or discharge
options.rationale: Bilateral OME over 3 months with hearing loss over 25 dB and language/behaviour impact crosses threshold for ENT referral. Would be correct only without hearing loss or language impact (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Refer to ENT for consideration of bilateral grommet insertion given persistent bilateral OME >3 months with bilateral conductive hearing loss >25 dB and emerging language and behavioural impact
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance refers children with bilateral OME persisting >=3 months with hearing loss >=25 dB or with developmental, language or behavioural concerns to ENT for tympanostomy tube consideration, per RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion and NICE NG98.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Refer to a paediatric audiologist for hearing aid fitting as definitive long-term management of the bilateral conductive hearing loss without ENT or grommet consideration
options.rationale: Hearing aids are alternative when surgery contraindicated or declined; grommets remain first-line surgical management. Would be correct only with surgical contraindication (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

explanation.summary: OME (glue ear) is the most common cause of acquired hearing loss in children and is diagnosed by retracted dull TMs with effusion, reduced TM mobility, and type B tympanograms. Referral criteria are bilateral OME for 3 months with hearing loss >=25 dB or language / developmental impact, per RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion.
key_points: Most cases resolve spontaneously within 3 months
No role for routine antibiotics, antihistamines or steroids
Lower threshold for grommets in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children given CSOM risk
Pneumatic otoscopy and tympanometry are key diagnostic tools
explanation.pearls: Always check the language and developmental trajectory in recurrent AOM - the indication for grommets is functional impact, not the eardrum appearance alone (Source: NICE NG98).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

subtopic_detail: Otitis media with effusion - referral threshold

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the GP after the third episode of right-sided epistaxis this month. Each episode has been brief (5 to 10 minutes), stopped with pressure, and has occurred when he was picking his nose. He is otherwise well, with no bruising, no bleeding from other sites and no family history of bleeding disorders. He is on no medication.

Anterior rhinoscopy reveals a small visible vessel and a crust over the right Little area, with no active bleeding; the left nasal cavity is clear. There is no septal haematoma, no mass and no facial deformity. He has full eye movements, no proptosis, no neck masses and no lymphadenopathy. Full blood count and coagulation screen are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 86 bpm, RR 18 /min, BP 102/64 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Visible vessel and crust at right Little area, no septal haematoma, no mass, no proptosis, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, coagulation screen normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to ENT for examination under general anaesthetic to exclude juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
options.rationale: JNA affects adolescent males with unilateral nasal obstruction and severe recurrent epistaxis with mass; digit-trauma anterior bleeding in 6-year-old is not the JNA picture. Would be correct in adolescent male with mass (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Apply topical antiseptic ointment (Naseptin or paraffin) twice daily for 2 weeks plus reinforce first aid technique (pinch the soft part of the nose, lean forward, 10 to 15 minutes)
options.rationale: Recurrent anterior epistaxis at Little area in a child is most often due to digit trauma and mucosal dryness. First-line management is topical antiseptic ointment plus reinforced first aid, which reduces recurrence in randomised trials. Silver nitrate cautery is reserved for failure of conservative care, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis.

options.text: Perform bedside silver nitrate cautery bilaterally to Little area today with topical antibiotic ointment for 1 week
options.rationale: Bilateral simultaneous septal cautery risks septal perforation; cautery is unilateral and second-line after failed conservative therapy. Would be correct as unilateral second-line (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Insert an anterior Merocel nasal pack into the right nostril and remove at 48 hours in the GP rooms
options.rationale: Packing is uncomfortable in children and is for ongoing bleeding not controlled by first aid; not appropriate as outpatient management. Would be correct only with active uncontrolled bleeding in ED (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Commence oral tranexamic acid three times daily for 6 weeks as antifibrinolytic prophylaxis
options.rationale: Oral TXA has no role as first-line for mucosal-trauma epistaxis with normal coagulation. Would be correct only as second-line adjunct (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Most paediatric epistaxis is anterior from Little area (Kiesselbach plexus) and is provoked by digit trauma and mucosal dryness. Management is reinforced first aid, topical antiseptic ointment and treatment of underlying contributors. Cautery, packing or ENT referral are reserved for ongoing bleeding, atypical features or red flag presentations, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis.
key_points: First aid: pinch soft part of nose, lean forward, 10-15 minutes continuous
Naseptin twice daily for 10-14 days has trial evidence for recurrence reduction
Avoid in peanut/soya allergy - use paraffin alternative
Red flags: unilateral severe bleeds in adolescent boy (JNA), nasal mass, bleeding from other sites
explanation.pearls: Consider non-accidental injury or a coagulation disorder if multiple bruising sites or family history of bleeding are present (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis).

subtopic_detail: Paediatric epistaxis - first aid and management

stem:
A 4-year-old girl presents to her GP with a 3-day history of a tender red swelling in front of the right ear. Her mother reports a small pit in front of the right ear since birth that has occasionally discharged a small amount of fluid but has never been red or swollen before. On examination there is a 1.5 cm tender, erythematous, fluctuant swelling immediately anterior to the right ear at the level of the helical root, centred over a visible pit.

The pinna, ear canal and tympanic membrane are normal. There is no facial nerve weakness, no cervical lymphadenopathy and no parotid swelling. She is afebrile and otherwise well. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 22 /min
data_table.Examination: 1.5 cm tender erythematous fluctuant swelling over visible right preauricular pit; normal pinna, EAC and TM; no facial nerve weakness; no parotid swelling

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan now, and what is the appropriate timing of definitive surgery?

options.text: Oral di/flucloxacillin six-hourly for 7 days now, with incision and drainage if not settling at 48 to 72 hours; refer to ENT for elective complete sinus excision once the acute infection has fully resolved (typically 6 weeks)
options.rationale: An acutely infected pre-auricular sinus is treated with anti-staphylococcal oral antibiotic and I&D if abscess fails to settle. Definitive excision is delayed until after the acute inflammation resolves because operating on inflamed tissue increases recurrence; the planes are clearer at 4-6 weeks, per RCH CPG: Pre-auricular sinus and Therapeutic Guidelines.

options.text: Urgent total parotidectomy on suspicion of an infected first branchial cleft anomaly with facial nerve involvement
options.rationale: First branchial cleft anomalies are rare with peri-auricular sinus tracts related to facial nerve; typical pre-auricular pit at the helical root is not this. Would be correct only with first branchial cleft anomaly anatomy (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Reassurance and review only if the lesion enlarges or discharges further
options.rationale: An infected pre-auricular sinus requires antibiotic treatment and ENT referral for definitive excision; observation alone risks abscess progression. Would be correct only for asymptomatic non-discharging pit (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Express the sinus contents by firm squeezing today plus topical mupirocin 2% three times daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Squeezing spreads infection and damages adjacent tissues; systemic antibiotics with surgical drainage if needed is appropriate. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Same-day complete excision of the sinus tract under general anaesthesia with antibiotic cover
options.rationale: Operating on acutely inflamed sinus increases recurrence (obscured planes); excision is deferred until acute infection settled. Would be correct after acute infection resolved (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: A pre-auricular sinus is a common congenital tract anterior to the helical root. Asymptomatic pits do not need treatment, but recurrent infection or abscess formation is an indication for elective complete surgical excision after antibiotic treatment of the acute episode, per RCH CPG: Pre-auricular sinus.
key_points: Most common organism in infection is Staphylococcus aureus
Incomplete excision leads to high recurrence; refer to ENT for full tract excision
Differential: branchial cleft anomaly, sebaceous cyst, infected lymph node
May be associated with syndromal hearing loss in some series - check newborn hearing
explanation.pearls: Bilateral pre-auricular pits warrant renal ultrasound only if there are associated syndromal features or family history; the routine ultrasound for all isolated pits is not supported (Source: RCH CPG: Pre-auricular sinus).

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the GP with his fourth episode of severe sore throat in 8 months. Each episode has lasted 5-7 days with fever above 38.5 deg C, white tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. In total over the past 12 months he has had four documented episodes of tonsillitis. Each episode has been seen by a clinician with positive examination findings consistent with bacterial tonsillitis and treated with a course of oral antibiotics (phenoxymethylpenicillin).

The family reports significant school absence and parental work disruption. There is no history of obstructive sleep apnoea, no failure to thrive and no immunodeficiency. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Examination today shows large, partially scarred tonsils with no acute exudate. He is afebrile. The family asks specifically about tonsillectomy referral now, long-term penicillin prophylaxis, a throat swab for asymptomatic strep, and immunology workup for recurrent infections.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 88 bpm, RR 18 /min
data_table.Examination: Large scarred tonsils, no acute exudate, no cervical lymphadenopathy, well grown along 50th centile
data_table.Past history: Four documented episodes of tonsillitis in last 12 months, each clinician-confirmed and antibiotic-treated

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric ENT for elective tonsillectomy given that he meets Paradise criteria for surgical management of recurrent severe bacterial tonsillitis in childhood
options.rationale: Paradise criteria require 7 episodes in 12 months, 5/year for 2 years, or 3/year for 3 years; 4 episodes in 12 months does not meet criteria. Would be correct only when Paradise criteria met (Source: ENT Society Australia).

options.text: Continue watchful waiting with documented sore throat diary, treat acute episodes with phenoxymethylpenicillin and reassess against Paradise criteria over the next 12-24 months
options.rationale: He has 4 episodes in 12 months and is approaching but does not yet meet Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy; documented surveillance with episode characterisation over the next 1-2 years guides decision-making while avoiding surgery that may not change long-term course, per RCH CPG: Sore throat.

options.text: Commence long-term oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily prophylaxis for 12 months to suppress recurrent group A streptococcal pharyngitis episodes
options.rationale: Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is for ARF secondary prevention, not recurrent bacterial tonsillitis without ARF. Would be correct only with ARF indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Take a throat swab today for group A streptococcus PCR and treat with phenoxymethylpenicillin if positive
options.rationale: Asymptomatic GAS carriage is common in children and does not warrant treatment; swabs not indicated in asymptomatic children outside ARF-prevention. Would be correct only in symptomatic episode or ARF prevention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Refer to paediatric immunology for assessment of suspected primary immunodeficiency given the four episodes of bacterial tonsillitis in the past 12 months
options.rationale: 4 tonsillitis episodes in a well-grown child does not meet criteria for immunodeficiency workup; referral threshold is recurrent serious infections at multiple sites. Would be correct with multi-site recurrent serious infections (Source: ASCIA).

explanation.summary: The Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy require well-documented severe, recurrent bacterial tonsillitis episodes meeting frequency thresholds: 7 in 1 year, OR 5 per year over 2 years, OR 3 per year over 3 years. Each episode must include fever >38.3, exudate or lymphadenopathy or positive throat swab, and have been treated with antibiotics or seen by a clinician, per RCH CPG: Sore throat.
key_points: Episodes must be documented, severe and clinician-confirmed
Other indications: OSA, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), suspected malignancy
Surgical risks: post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage (primary and secondary)
Adenotonsillectomy preferred for OSA
explanation.pearls: Most children with recurrent tonsillitis improve over 1-2 years even without surgery; the Paradise trial showed only a modest absolute reduction in episodes at 2 years and the effect attenuates over time (Source: Paradise et al. NEJM 1984).

stem:
A 9-month-old girl is brought to the GP after her grandmother noticed that the left pupil appeared white in a recent flash photograph. The mother reports the eye otherwise looks normal, the baby fixes and follows in good light and reaches for toys with both hands. She was born at term by normal vaginal birth with an unremarkable antenatal course.

The parents do not recall whether the red reflex was specifically examined on the newborn check. There is no family history of retinoblastoma or other eye disease. On examination with an ophthalmoscope held at arm's length the right pupil shows a normal red reflex but the left pupil shows a clearly visible white reflex (leukocoria). There is no strabismus, no nystagmus and no proptosis. The cornea is clear and the anterior chamber appears normal. Visual behaviour is reduced when the right eye is occluded.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 122 bpm, RR 30 /min
data_table.Examination: Left leukocoria with absent red reflex on direct ophthalmoscopy; right red reflex normal; no strabismus; clear cornea; normal anterior chamber

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that white reflex on flash photographs is usually benign and review at the routine 12-month immunisation visit
options.rationale: Leukocoria is never normal and mandates same-day to next-day paediatric ophthalmology to exclude retinoblastoma. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Leukocoria).

options.text: Refer to a community optometrist for paediatric vision testing in 4 to 6 weeks
options.rationale: Optometry deferral risks unacceptable delay; retinoblastoma is curable when caught early but devastating when missed. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Refer urgently (within 24 to 48 hours) to a paediatric ophthalmologist for examination under anaesthetic to assess for retinoblastoma and other causes of leukocoria
options.rationale: Persistent unilateral leukocoria in an infant requires urgent paediatric ophthalmology referral. EUA is the diagnostic step; differential includes retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, persistent fetal vasculature, Coats disease and toxocariasis. Imaging is staging not screening, per RANZCO and RCH CPG.

options.text: Order outpatient MRI brain and orbits under GA as the initial investigation to characterise any intraocular mass before specialist ophthalmology referral
options.rationale: MRI is for staging once retinoblastoma is diagnosed; first step is paediatric ophthalmology EUA, not pre-emptive imaging. Would be correct only after EUA-confirmed diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Patch the right (unaffected) eye for 2 hours daily for amblyopia management of the left eye and review in 3 months
options.rationale: Patching is for confirmed amblyopia AFTER the underlying lesion has been identified and treated; occluding now could delay diagnosis. Would never be correct as first step (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is the cardinal sign of retinoblastoma and other sight-threatening pathology in infants. Red reflex examination should be performed at every newborn, 6 week and 6 month check. Any persistent abnormality requires urgent paediatric ophthalmology referral, per RANZCO Position Statement and RCH CPG.
key_points: Retinoblastoma is the commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood (most cases under 5)
Bilateral disease suggests germline RB1 mutation and trilateral risk (pineal)
Other causes of leukocoria: congenital cataract, PFV, Coats disease, ROP, toxocariasis
Treatment includes focal therapy, systemic / intra-arterial chemotherapy and enucleation
explanation.pearls: Parents often notice leukocoria first in flash photographs; never dismiss the parent who brings a photograph of a white pupil (Source: RANZCO).

subtopic_detail: Red reflex abnormality - leukocoria and retinoblastoma

stem:
A 3-day-old term male infant is brought to ED by his parents because of bilateral profuse purulent eye discharge that began 24 hours ago and is rapidly increasing. He was born by normal vaginal birth at 39+2 weeks weighing 3220 g. The pregnancy was unbooked because the mother (a 19-year-old who recently migrated and was lost to antenatal care) presented in labour at the nearest hospital.

Antenatal STI screening was not performed. The baby has otherwise been feeding and behaving normally. On examination there is profuse yellow-green purulent discharge from both eyes with marked eyelid oedema (chemosis) so pronounced that the lids cannot be readily opened. The cornea on the small visible portion looks slightly hazy on the right. He is afebrile with normal observations. There is no other rash, no hepatosplenomegaly and no other focus of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 148 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral profuse purulent eye discharge, marked chemosis preventing easy lid opening, possible right corneal haze, no rash, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Maternal history: Unbooked pregnancy, no antenatal STI screening, age 19, recently migrated

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Send eye swab for Gram stain, bacterial culture and Chlamydia / Neisseria gonorrhoeae PCR, admit, commence IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, perform saline eye irrigation and request urgent paediatric ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis with marked chemosis in the first week of life with maternal risk factors must be treated as Neisseria gonorrhoeae until proven otherwise; gonococcal ophthalmia can perforate the cornea within 24 hours. Management is admission, IV third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime preferred in jaundiced neonates over ceftriaxone), copious saline irrigation and urgent ophthalmology, per RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

options.text: Prescribe topical chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops one drop to each eye six-hourly for 7 days and review at the GP clinic the following day to assess improvement
options.rationale: Topical chloramphenicol alone is inadequate for gonococcal ophthalmia (corneal penetration, disseminated infection risk); systemic therapy required. Would never be correct in gonococcal ophthalmia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence oral azithromycin once daily for 3 days as empirical therapy for likely Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis without admission or specialist input
options.rationale: Chlamydial conjunctivitis presents at 5-14 days with mucopurulent discharge and less severe chemosis; this hyperacute first-week purulent presentation is gonococcal. Would be correct in chlamydial pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is most likely chemical (silver nitrate) conjunctivitis from birth, irrigate with normal saline, and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Chemical conjunctivitis is in first 24-48 h, mild and self-limiting; silver nitrate is not used in Australia. Would never be correct in this presentation (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Apply topical aciclovir 3% eye ointment five times daily for suspected neonatal herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis and arrange paediatric review the following day
options.rationale: Neonatal HSV presents with vesicular skin/keratitis with dendritic ulcer/systemic illness, treated with IV high-dose aciclovir not topical. Would be correct only with HSV-specific findings (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis in the first 28 days of life. Timing helps differentiate aetiology: chemical 24-48 hours, gonococcal day 2-5 (hyperacute, severe chemosis, corneal risk), chlamydial day 5-14 (mucopurulent, milder), HSV day 6-14 (vesicles, dendritic keratitis, systemic). Suspected gonococcal disease mandates IV third-generation cephalosporin, irrigation and urgent ophthalmology, per RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis.
key_points: Notify chlamydial and gonococcal infection to public health
Treat both mother and partners; arrange contact tracing
Cefotaxime preferred over ceftriaxone in jaundiced neonates (bilirubin displacement)
Chlamydia adds risk of pneumonia (interstitial pattern at 4-12 weeks)
explanation.pearls: Gonococcal ophthalmia can perforate the cornea within 24 hours; treat empirically while awaiting microbiology (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to her GP with 24 hours of progressive left eyelid swelling and redness that started after an insect bite on the eyelid the previous afternoon. She has been afebrile, well, eating and drinking normally. There is no preceding sinusitis and no recent dental infection. On examination she has erythema and swelling of the left upper and lower eyelid with localised tenderness at the bite site, but she can open the eye spontaneously.

Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes, pupillary responses are equal and brisk with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and full eye movements are present with no pain on movement. There is no proptosis, no chemosis and the conjunctiva is white. Otoscopy and oropharyngeal examination are normal. There is no facial nerve weakness and the contralateral eye is normal. The mother specifically asks whether admission for IV antibiotics is needed today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 20 /min
data_table.Examination: Left upper and lower eyelid erythema and swelling, eye opens spontaneously, VA 6/6 bilateral, equal pupils no RAPD, full eye movements painless, no proptosis, no chemosis, white conjunctiva
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone daily, flucloxacillin six-hourly and metronidazole eight-hourly with urgent contrast CT of sinuses and orbits
options.rationale: Admission, IV broad-spectrum and contrast CT are for orbital (postseptal) cellulitis: pain on eye movement, restricted motility, proptosis, reduced acuity or RAPD; absent here. Would be correct only with orbital signs (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin or amoxicillin/clavulanate and review at 24 hours with explicit safety-netting for pain on eye movement, restricted movement, proptosis, reduced visual acuity, fever or unwell appearance
options.rationale: This is preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis (Chandler stage I): normal acuity, full painless eye movements, no proptosis, no RAPD, no chemosis, child well. Outpatient oral antibiotics with strict safety-netting and 24 hour review is appropriate, per RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Apply warm compresses to the eyelid four-hourly and prescribe topical chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment three-hourly to the affected lid for 7 days without systemic antibiotics
options.rationale: Topical and warm compresses do not penetrate the lid soft tissues adequately for cellulitis; systemic antibiotics required. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric ophthalmology for surgical incision and drainage of a suspected lid abscess
options.rationale: No fluctuant collection described; preseptal cellulitis without abscess is managed medically. Would be correct only with palpable fluctuant abscess (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone daily for 5 days alongside oral antibiotics to reduce eyelid swelling more rapidly and accelerate symptom resolution
options.rationale: Systemic steroids not indicated for periorbital cellulitis and may obscure progression to orbital cellulitis. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum and presents with eyelid swelling and erythema without ocular dysfunction. Postseptal (orbital) cellulitis additionally features painful or restricted eye movements, proptosis, reduced visual acuity, RAPD or chemosis and requires admission, IV antibiotics, contrast CT and urgent ENT / ophthalmology involvement, per RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis.
key_points: Always test acuity, pupil and eye movements in any swollen eye
Postseptal causes - paranasal sinusitis (ethmoid), trauma, dental
Chandler stages: I preseptal, II orbital cellulitis, III subperiosteal abscess, IV orbital abscess, V cavernous sinus thrombosis
Threshold to admit is low in young (<1 yr), immunocompromised, unable to attend review
explanation.pearls: Insect bite, hordeolum (stye) or contiguous skin infection are common preseptal triggers; sinusitis is the commonest postseptal trigger (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

subtopic_detail: Periorbital cellulitis - Chandler I outpatient management

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to her GP because her grandmother thinks she has a squint. The mother is unsure. She was born at term, met milestones and has otherwise been well. There is no family history of strabismus, amblyopia or significant refractive error. On examination she has a broad nasal bridge and prominent epicanthic folds. Hirschberg corneal light reflex test is centred symmetrically in both pupils.

The cover-uncover test reveals no movement of either eye when the other is occluded. Eye movements are full in all directions of gaze. Red reflex is normal bilaterally and visual behaviour is age-appropriate with good fixation and following.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 108 bpm, RR 24 /min
data_table.Examination: Broad nasal bridge with prominent epicanthic folds; symmetric Hirschberg corneal light reflex; cover-uncover test no movement; full eye movements; bilateral normal red reflex

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric ophthalmology for examination under anaesthesia and consideration of strabismus surgery
options.rationale: No true strabismus on Hirschberg or cover-uncover; this is pseudoesotropia and surgery is not indicated. Would never be correct in pseudoesotropia (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Reassure that this is pseudoesotropia from epicanthic folds, document normal Hirschberg and cover-uncover testing, and book the routine 4-year preschool vision screen; advise return if any new objective squint is noted
options.rationale: Symmetric corneal light reflex and a negative cover-uncover test with epicanthic folds is pseudoesotropia; the apparent squint resolves as facial features mature. Reassurance with routine preschool screen is appropriate, per RANZCO and RCH CPG: Vision screening.

options.text: Patch the left eye for 2 hours daily for 3 months to prevent amblyopia
options.rationale: Patching is for confirmed amblyopia after specialist diagnosis; occluding a child without amblyopia is harmful. Would never be correct without confirmed amblyopia (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Commence topical atropine 1% to the right eye to penalise the dominant eye for presumed left amblyopia
options.rationale: Atropine penalisation is for confirmed amblyopia; no role with normal vision and no strabismus. Would be correct only with diagnosed amblyopia (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Order outpatient MRI brain and orbits under sedation to exclude a sixth nerve palsy
options.rationale: 6th nerve palsy gives limited abduction and incomitant esotropia; full eye movements and negative cover-uncover exclude this. Would be correct only with limited abduction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Pseudoesotropia is the appearance of crossed eyes caused by epicanthic folds, broad nasal bridge or close-set eyes, with normal alignment on Hirschberg and cover-uncover testing. True strabismus is asymmetric Hirschberg or shows movement on cover-uncover. Any true strabismus persisting beyond 4 months of age requires paediatric ophthalmology referral to prevent amblyopia, per RANZCO and RCH CPG: Vision screening.
key_points: Esotropia inwards, exotropia outwards, hypertropia upwards, hypotropia downwards
Persistent strabismus beyond 4 months requires referral
Sudden onset incomitant strabismus needs urgent imaging (cranial nerve palsy, raised ICP)
Routine preschool vision screen catches missed amblyopia
explanation.pearls: Always document the test you used (Hirschberg, cover-uncover, cover-cross-cover) - parental and grandparental concern alone is enough to warrant active testing in any child (Source: RANZCO).

subtopic_detail: Childhood strabismus - true esotropia versus pseudoesotropia

stem: A 22-month-old boy refuses to crawl after 24 hours of fever and irritability. He is fully immunised. He lies still with the left hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and screams on any movement of it.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 degrees C, HR 178 /min, BP 78/40 mmHg, capillary refill 4 s
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 198 mg/L, hip ultrasound large effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Sepsis pathway, cultures, antibiotics, urgent hip washout
options.rationale: This child is in compensated septic shock with septic arthritis of the left hip (4 of 4 Kocher, large effusion). Australian paediatric sepsis pathway recommends 10 mL/kg crystalloid boluses with reassessment between, blood culture before antibiotics where possible, and empirical IV anti-staphylococcal cover (flucloxacillin); in under-4s a second-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin is added to cover Kingella kingae. Definitive management requires urgent surgical washout, per RCH CPG: Sepsis, RCH CPG: Acute limp and Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.text: Fluids, vancomycin and meropenem, admit to intensive care
options.rationale: 20 mL/kg boluses now discouraged in favour of 10 mL/kg with reassessment (fluid overload risk); vancomycin alone misses Gram-negatives in septic arthritis. Would be correct in some adult/older child protocols at 20 mL/kg (Source: APLS Australia).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.text: Red cells and urgent contrast MRI before any antibiotic
options.rationale: No evidence of anaemia or blood loss; crystalloid is first-line. MRI may complement but must not delay antibiotics and source control. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Paracetamol and reassessment in 4 hours in the resus bay
options.rationale: Shock and confirmed septic arthritis - observation delays time to antibiotics and source control. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Ceftriaxone alone, with an arterial line before surgery
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation must not be deferred; ceftriaxone alone has gaps for severe staphylococcal infection and is not preferred monotherapy. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

explanation.summary: An unwell toddler with hip septic arthritis and shock requires simultaneous resuscitation (10 mL/kg crystalloid boluses with reassessment), early empirical IV antibiotics after blood culture (flucloxacillin plus an agent active against Kingella kingae in under-4s such as cefazolin), and urgent orthopaedic source control. Vancomycin is added when MRSA risk is high or central line associated, per RCH CPG: Sepsis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections.
key_points: Recent oropharyngeal lesion is a hook for Kingella kingae - it enters through breached oral mucosa
Australian paediatric sepsis pathway: 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, reassess, repeat as needed
Source control (washout) is as important as antibiotics in septic arthritis
Add vancomycin for MRSA risk (e.g. remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, line-associated, severe systemic illness)
explanation.pearls: Bacteraemia precedes joint seeding; always draw blood cultures with the first peripheral cannula before antibiotics where it does not delay therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis in unwell child - resuscitation and source control

stem:
A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community presents to the local clinic with a 10 day history of migratory arthritis affecting his right knee, then left ankle and now both wrists. The pain is severe enough to limit weight-bearing. He recalls a sore throat 3 weeks ago that resolved without medical review. He has not had any rash, no nodules and no chorea.

On examination he has warm, tender, swollen wrists bilaterally with limited range of movement; the knee and ankle are no longer involved. There is no rash, no subcutaneous nodules and no abnormal involuntary movements. Cardiovascular examination reveals a soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla that has not previously been documented. Investigations are back. The clinic team asks whether this could be post-streptococcal reactive arthritis, JIA, HSP or Lyme arthritis given the migratory pattern and remote setting.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 deg C, HR 124 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 102/62 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bilateral warm tender swollen wrists; cardiac apical pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla; no rash; no nodules; no chorea
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.6, CRP 78 mg/L, ESR 64 mm/h, ASOT 850 IU/mL (elevated), anti-DNase B elevated, echocardiogram shows mild mitral regurgitation with no chamber dilatation
data_table.Past: No previous documented ARF, fully immunised, no penicillin allergy

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis affecting multiple joints in additive pattern without convincing evidence of carditis on echocardiogram in this Aboriginal child from a remote community
options.rationale: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis lacks evidence of carditis and has additive (not migratory) pattern; child has objective carditis on echo. Would be correct only without carditis and additive arthritis (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Jones).

options.text: Acute rheumatic fever fulfilling Australian modified Jones criteria for a high-risk population with carditis and migratory polyarthritis as a definite first episode in this Aboriginal child
options.rationale: In an Aboriginal child from a remote community (high-risk population) the modified Australian Jones criteria require 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor with evidence of preceding GAS infection. This child has 2 majors (carditis on echo and polyarthritis) plus elevated inflammatory markers and ASOT, fulfilling definite ARF, per RHDAustralia 2020 guideline.

options.text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis polyarticular subtype with incidental cardiac murmur and elevated streptococcal serology unrelated to the migratory arthritis presentation in this school-aged child
options.rationale: JIA requires 6 weeks of persistent arthritis and is not associated with new pansystolic mitral murmur and elevated strep serology. Would be correct only with 6+ weeks chronic arthritis (Source: ACR).

options.text: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) presenting with arthritis as the dominant initial feature ahead of any palpable purpuric rash, abdominal pain or renal involvement
options.rationale: HSP requires palpable purpura on dependent areas plus arthritis/abdominal pain/renal involvement; absent here. Would be correct with palpable purpura and IgA features (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Lyme arthritis from Borrelia burgdorferi infection acquired locally in the remote Australian setting
options.rationale: Indigenous Lyme disease is not established in Australia; no relevant travel history, migratory polyarthritis plus carditis plus positive strep fits ARF. Would never be correct in Australia (Source: NHMRC Lyme statement).

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed by the Australian modified Jones criteria, with a lower threshold for diagnosis in high-risk populations (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori and Pacific peoples). Major manifestations are carditis (subclinical detectable on echo), arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules; minors include fever, raised ESR / CRP, monoarthralgia, prolonged PR. Evidence of preceding GAS (ASOT, anti-DNase B, throat swab) is required, per RHDAustralia 2020 guideline.
key_points: High-risk: 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor + GAS evidence
Standard-risk: same plus more stringent arthritis definitions
Treat acute episode with bed rest, NSAIDs (after diagnosis), eradicate GAS
Secondary prophylaxis with IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21-28 days until at least age 21 and 10 years from last episode
explanation.pearls: Even subclinical mitral regurgitation on echocardiogram now counts as carditis under the 2015 / 2020 Australian modified Jones criteria; always obtain echo when ARF is suspected (Source: RHDAustralia 2020).

subtopic_detail: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis versus acute rheumatic fever

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to his GP with recurrent severe right-sided epistaxis over 4 months. Each episode lasts over 20 minutes and on two occasions has required ED attendance for anterior packing. He also reports 3 months of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and intermittent right cheek fullness. There is no history of trauma, no significant nose picking and no family history of bleeding disorders.

He is on no medication. He is otherwise well and growing along the 50th centile. Anterior rhinoscopy reveals a pink-grey mass filling the posterior right nasal cavity that bled briskly on attempted swab. Full blood count and coagulation screen are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 84 bpm, RR 16 /min, BP 116/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right posterior nasal pink-grey mass, brisk bleeding on touch, right-sided nasal obstruction, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no facial nerve weakness
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, coagulation screen normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure as benign anterior Little area epistaxis and prescribe topical Naseptin twice daily for 2 weeks with first-aid advice
options.rationale: Severe recurrent unilateral epistaxis with nasal obstruction and visible posterior mass must not be treated as benign anterior bleeding. Would be correct only in true anterior Little area bleeding (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Attempt bedside biopsy of the visible posterior mass with cup forceps under topical lidocaine to confirm histology before imaging or specialist referral
options.rationale: JNA is exceptionally vascular and clinic biopsy can cause life-threatening haemorrhage; imaging precedes biopsy and biopsy done under GA at theatre. Would never be correct (Source: ENT Society Australia).

options.text: Refer urgently to ENT and arrange contrast-enhanced MRI or CT of the nasopharynx without biopsy in clinic
options.rationale: Recurrent severe unilateral epistaxis with progressive nasal obstruction and a posterior nasal mass in an adolescent male is the classic JNA triad. Urgent ENT referral with contrast cross-sectional imaging is required; biopsy is performed in theatre after imaging and angiographic assessment if needed, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis and BMJ Best Practice.

options.text: Apply silver nitrate cautery to both sides of the nasal septum at Little area today plus topical antibiotic ointment and GP review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Bilateral simultaneous septal cautery risks perforation and does not address posterior nasopharyngeal mass. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Commence oral tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily for 6 weeks as definitive antifibrinolytic therapy
options.rationale: TXA is an adjunct only; does not substitute for ENT assessment and imaging of suspected vascular tumour. Would never be correct (Source: ENT Society Australia).

explanation.summary: Most paediatric epistaxis is anterior and benign, but red flags require ENT referral. The classic triad of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is recurrent severe unilateral epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction and a posterior nasal mass in an adolescent male; clinic biopsy is contraindicated and management requires contrast imaging and specialist surgical (often pre-embolised) resection, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis.
key_points: JNA almost exclusively occurs in adolescent males
Other red flags: bleeding from multiple sites, family history of bleeding disorder, easy bruising, bleeding after dental work
Posterior epistaxis is more common in adults / hypertensive bleeders
Investigations: FBC, coagulation, group and hold; contrast imaging for suspected mass
explanation.pearls: Adolescent boy with severe unilateral nose bleeds plus blocked nose equals JNA until proven otherwise (Source: BMJ Best Practice - JNA).

subtopic_detail: Adolescent epistaxis - red flags for juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

stem:
A term male infant born at 39+4 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth is reviewed on the postnatal ward at 72 hours of age. Birthweight was 3460 g and current weight is 3260 g (5.8 percent loss). He is exclusively breastfed and feeding 3 hourly with audible swallowing, has had 4 wet nappies in the last 24 hours and passed meconium and changing stools.

Mother is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; the cord direct antiglobulin test was negative and cord bilirubin was 38 micromol/L. Maternal serology was unremarkable and there is no family history of haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency or significant neonatal jaundice. The midwife notes that the baby looks visibly yellow to the mid-thigh and orders a serum bilirubin which returns at 340 micromol/L total, with a conjugated fraction of 8 micromol/L. The baby is alert, has a normal Moro and suck, no hepatosplenomegaly, and is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 138 bpm, RR 44 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Visibly jaundiced to mid-thigh, alert, normal tone and Moro, no hepatosplenomegaly, anterior fontanelle soft, no petechiae or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 340 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L, Hb 175 g/L, reticulocytes 3 percent, blood group A positive, DAT negative
data_table.Maternal history: Group O positive, antibody screen negative, no maternal infection, no medication exposure

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure, continue breastfeeding on demand and repeat serum bilirubin within 24 hours
options.rationale: SBR 340 micromol/L at 72 h in a term baby crosses the AU phototherapy threshold on the postnatal nomogram; conservative monitoring risks rising levels. Would never be correct above threshold (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice).

options.text: Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and substitute formula to exclude breast milk jaundice before treating
options.rationale: Routine cessation of breastfeeding is not recommended; continuing feeds with phototherapy is preferred. Would never be correct as routine (Source: RCH CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy and repeat SBR in 6 hours, exchange if rising towards 450 micromol/L
options.rationale: At 72 hours of age in a term infant with no risk factors, 340 micromol/L exceeds the Australian phototherapy line on the consensus nomogram and intensive phototherapy is started, with exchange transfusion considered if SBR approaches roughly 450 micromol/L despite intensive phototherapy, per RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice.

options.text: Arrange immediate double-volume neonatal exchange transfusion in the neonatal unit today
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is for SBR approaching 450 micromol/L despite intensive phototherapy or for acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Would be correct at SBR approaching 450 or with neuro signs (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Order abdominal ultrasound and split bilirubin trend to investigate biliary atresia first
options.rationale: Conjugated fraction 8 is normal (under 20 percent of total or under 25 micromol/L) and does not indicate cholestatic workup. Would be correct only with elevated conjugated fraction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Phototherapy thresholds in Australia are read off a postnatal age vs SBR nomogram with separate lines for risk factors (prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis). A term low-risk infant with 340 micromol/L at 72 hours sits above the phototherapy line; exchange transfusion is reserved for levels nearing approximately 450 micromol/L despite intensive phototherapy or for clinical encephalopathy.
key_points: Threshold depends on postnatal age in hours and risk factors, not just absolute level
Conjugated bilirubin > 25 micromol/L or > 20 percent of total prompts cholestatic workup
Intensive phototherapy means high-irradiance light over maximal skin area
Re-check SBR 4 to 6 hours after starting phototherapy
explanation.pearls: Visible jaundice past the umbilicus in a term newborn always warrants a measured bilirubin; clinical estimation alone is unreliable.

stem:
A male infant born at 36+2 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a mother with gestational diabetes on diet control is reviewed on the postnatal ward in a level 4 maternity unit. Birthweight is 2640 g (25th centile). He had skin-to-skin contact from delivery and a first breastfeed at 40 minutes of life. The local hypoglycaemia protocol mandates 3 hourly prefeed BSLs for the first 12 hours in at-risk infants.

At 2 hours of age the prefeed heelprick capillary blood glucose, confirmed on a calibrated point-of-care device, is 1.8 mmol/L. He latches briefly but tires quickly and falls asleep at the breast within 2 minutes. He is pink, has a strong cry on handling, normal tone, and a normal newborn examination with no dysmorphic features, no hepatomegaly, and no respiratory distress.

He has had no jitteriness, no apnoea, and no seizures. He has not yet received expressed colostrum or formula top-up. The mother's last HbA1c was 5.6 percent and she had no insulin during labour. Maternal observations are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C axillary, HR 142 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 98 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink, normal tone, no jitteriness, no respiratory distress, no hepatomegaly, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 1.8 mmol/L at 2 hours of age, prefeed
data_table.Risk factors: Late preterm 36+2, infant of diet-controlled GDM mother, birthweight 25th centile, breastfeeding established but ineffective

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding on demand and recheck BSL in 3 to 4 hours before the next feed
options.rationale: BSL 1.8 is below operational threshold 2.6 for at-risk infants and requires active intervention. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus, 10% dextrose infusion at 80 mL/kg/day, continue feeds, recheck BSL 30 min
options.rationale: A BSL below 2.0 mmol/L in an at-risk infant warrants immediate IV 10 percent dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus and maintenance infusion at around 80 mL/kg/day (delivering approximately 5.5 mg/kg/min of glucose), with rapid recheck, per RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia.

options.text: Offer 5 mL/kg of expressed breast milk or formula by cup and recheck BSL in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Enteral feeding is for BSL 2.0-2.6 in asymptomatic at-risk infants; below 2.0 requires IV dextrose. Would be correct at BSL 2.0-2.6 (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Administer IM glucagon 30 microg/kg as a single bolus dose and continue exclusive breastfeeding without recheck
options.rationale: Glucagon is for refractory hypoglycaemia where IV access delayed/impossible and requires hepatic glycogen stores; not first-line in late-preterm IDM with IV access. Would be correct only with delayed IV access (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Apply 40 percent buccal dextrose gel 0.5 mL/kg and continue exclusive breastfeeding without recheck
options.rationale: Buccal dextrose gel plus feeding is for BSL 2.0-2.6 in asymptomatic infants, not below 2.0; recheck always required. Would be correct at BSL 2.0-2.6 (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Operational thresholds in Australian neonatal units are 2.6 mmol/L for at-risk asymptomatic infants and 2.0 mmol/L as the level requiring IV dextrose. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia or BSL under 2.0 mmol/L gets a 10 percent dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus plus infusion at 60 to 90 mL/kg/day, titrated to keep BSL above 2.6 mmol/L.
key_points: At-risk groups: late preterm, IDM, SGA, LGA, perinatal stress
BSL 2.0 to 2.6 mmol/L asymptomatic: feed plus or minus buccal dextrose gel and recheck
BSL under 2.0 mmol/L or any symptomatic infant: IV 10 percent dextrose 2 mL/kg then infusion
Always recheck within 30 minutes of any intervention
explanation.pearls: Glucose delivery in mg/kg/min equals (percent dextrose x mL/kg/day) divided by 144; an 80 mL/kg/day infusion of 10 percent dextrose delivers about 5.5 mg/kg/min.

stem:
A 38-year-old G3P2 woman at 41+3 weeks is in second-stage labour when the obstetric team note thick meconium-stained liquor after artificial rupture of membranes. She had two previous uncomplicated vaginal births at term and her current antenatal course was unremarkable with normal serial growth scans and normal screening serology. CTG is reassuring with normal baseline variability and no late or variable decelerations.

The baby is born vaginally 12 minutes later with a single nuchal cord that was easily reduced. At delivery the baby cries vigorously within the first 15 seconds, has good tone with flexed limbs, is pink centrally with peripheral cyanosis, and has a heart rate above 100 bpm by auscultation. There is visible thick meconium on the perineum, on the baby's skin and around the mouth. The neonatal team is present at delivery with a prepared resuscitaire, the radiant warmer is on, and suction is checked. No previous obstetric complications.

data_table.Birth details: Term plus, 41+3 weeks, vaginal birth, thick meconium-stained liquor
data_table.Examination at 30 seconds: Vigorous cry, good tone, HR > 100 bpm, peripheral cyanosis only, visible meconium on skin

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Routine newborn care: drying, warmth, ongoing observation, keep mother and baby together
options.rationale: A vigorous newborn with meconium-stained liquor does not require tracheal suctioning; routine care with drying, warming and observation is recommended, per ANZCOR Guideline 13.4 and the Australian NRP.

options.text: Direct laryngoscopy with tracheal suction before drying or stimulation today
options.rationale: Routine tracheal suction of vigorous meconium-stained newborns is no longer recommended and may delay resuscitation. Would be correct only in non-vigorous newborn with airway obstruction (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).

options.text: Bag-mask ventilation with 21 percent oxygen for 60 seconds and reassess heart rate
options.rationale: PPV is indicated only with apnoea, gasping, or HR under 100, none of which apply. Would be correct in those situations (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).

options.text: Intubate, suction the trachea and transfer to NICU for prophylactic CPAP
options.rationale: Intubation is for ineffective bag-mask or specific indications; prophylactic CPAP/intubation not indicated in vigorous term newborn. Would be correct only with failed PPV (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).

options.text: Bulb suction the oropharynx and nasopharynx on the perineum before delivery of the shoulders
options.rationale: Intrapartum oro/nasopharyngeal suctioning on the perineum is no longer recommended and does not reduce MAS. Would never be correct (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).

explanation.summary: Since the 2015 ILCOR update, ANZCOR has recommended that vigorous newborns with meconium-stained liquor receive routine care without tracheal suctioning. Non-vigorous infants (poor tone, apnoea, HR less than 100 bpm) go to the resuscitaire and follow the standard algorithm; tracheal suction is only considered if ventilation is ineffective and meconium is suspected to obstruct the airway.
key_points: Vigorous = good tone, good cry or breathing, HR > 100 bpm
Routine intrapartum oro/nasopharyngeal suction on the perineum is not recommended
Non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn: dry, stimulate, then standard NRP
Tracheal suction only if PPV is ineffective and meconium obstruction is suspected
explanation.pearls: The change reduces delay to effective ventilation, which is the single most important resuscitation step.

stem:
A male infant born at 28+1 weeks by emergency caesarean for severe pre-eclampsia and absent end-diastolic flow on Doppler is now day 7 of life in the level 3 NICU of a tertiary perinatal centre. Mother received a full course of antenatal betamethasone and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection. Birthweight was 1040 g (25th centile for gestation). He has been receiving minimal enteral feeds of expressed breast milk at 20 mL/kg/day for 4 days, advanced cautiously, and parenteral nutrition via a peripherally inserted central catheter; umbilical lines were removed on day 4.

He is on nasal CPAP with FiO2 0.21 after extubation from surfactant therapy on day 2. Over the last 6 hours the nurses note new abdominal distension, two episodes of bilious aspirate, a single small bloody stool and a temperature instability with a low of 36.1 deg C. On examination he is mottled with a capillary refill of 4 seconds, the abdomen is tense and tender with visible bowel loops, and there is mild erythema of the abdominal wall.

The treating team obtains a supine abdominal radiograph and a left lateral decubitus film, plus blood cultures, a venous gas and a full blood count.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.1 deg C, HR 178 bpm, RR 70 /min on CPAP FiO2 0.21, SpO2 91 percent
data_table.Examination: Mottled, tense distended tender abdomen, visible bowel loops, abdominal wall erythema, lethargic
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.2 x10^9/L, platelets 78 x10^9/L, CRP 65 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: Supine AXR shows dilated bowel loops with intramural curvilinear lucencies; left lateral decubitus film shows no free intraperitoneal gas; no portal venous gas seen

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue current feeds, add oral probiotic, and repeat AXR in 24 hours
options.rationale: Continuing feeds in confirmed NEC (Bell IIA with pneumatosis) is contraindicated and risks progression to perforation. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: NEC).

options.text: Increase enteral feed volume to advance gut maturation and start oral gentamicin for bowel decontamination
options.rationale: Advancing feeds is contraindicated; oral aminoglycosides not indicated for established NEC; bowel rest with parenteral broad-spectrum is standard. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Urgent laparotomy with bowel resection for suspected NEC-related intestinal perforation today
options.rationale: Surgery is for pneumoperitoneum, fixed bowel loop, palpable mass or deterioration despite medical therapy; Bell IIA without perforation is medical with surgical review on standby. Would be correct only with perforation or deterioration (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Cease feeds, large-bore OG free drainage, IV benzylpenicillin/gentamicin/metronidazole, fluid resuscitation, surgical review
options.rationale: Bell stage IIA NEC (definite, with pneumatosis intestinalis) is managed medically with bowel rest, orogastric decompression, parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms (benzylpenicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole) and supportive care, per RCH CPG: Necrotising enterocolitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

options.text: Cease feeds, give a single dose of IV cefotaxime and continue monitoring without surgical review
options.rationale: Cefotaxime monotherapy does not adequately cover anaerobes; surgical review is mandatory at diagnosis. Would never be correct as sole therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: NEC peaks in preterm infants in the second week of life. Bell staging: I suspected; IIA definite with pneumatosis intestinalis; IIB with portal venous gas or ascites; IIIA severe medical disease; IIIB perforation. IIA management is bowel rest, OG decompression, triple antibiotics (benzylpenicillin or ampicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole) for 7 to 10 days, parenteral nutrition, and serial AXR every 6 to 12 hours.
key_points: Pneumatosis intestinalis is pathognomonic for NEC
Portal venous gas suggests advanced disease (Bell IIB)
Free intraperitoneal air on lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral indicates perforation and surgery
Triple antibiotic cover for Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms
explanation.pearls: Falling platelet count and rising lactate are markers of deterioration and prompt surgical review even without radiographic perforation.

stem:
A male infant born at 39+0 weeks by elective caesarean section without labour is admitted to the special care nursery at 1 hour of life for ongoing respiratory distress. Birthweight 3520 g, APGARs 8 and 9. He developed tachypnoea, mild grunting and intercostal recession from 15 minutes of age. He is now 4 hours old on nasal high-flow at 6 L/min with FiO2 0.30, maintaining SpO2 96 percent preductal and 96 percent postductal.

Mother had a negative group B Strep screen, no fever, no prolonged rupture of membranesplications; no meconium-stained liquor. T 36.9 deg C, HR 152, RR 78, BP 62/40 with capillary refill 2 seconds and warm peripheries. Chest is clear with no asymmetry. Chest radiograph at 30 minutes showed hyperinflation, prominent perihilar streaking, fluid in the right horizontal fissure, and no air bronchograms or focal consolidation.

He has not yet fed. Blood gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 48 mmHg, BE -2. Sepsis bloods are pending. You are confident this is transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN).

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 152 bpm, RR 78 /min, SpO2 97 percent on high-flow FiO2 0.25
data_table.Examination: Mild grunting, intercostal recession, equal air entry bilaterally, no asymmetry, no scaphoid abdomen, normal peripheral pulses
data_table.Imaging: CXR: hyperinflation, prominent perihilar vascular streaking, fluid in the right horizontal fissure, no air bronchograms, no focal consolidation, no pneumothorax

lead_in: Which next management step is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue nasal high-flow titrated to SpO2 91-95 percent, nil by mouth on IV maintenance, reassess at 72 hours
