options.rationale: TTN is managed supportively with non-invasive respiratory support (nasal high-flow or CPAP) titrated to keep SpO2 91 to 95 percent, gut rest until work of breathing settles, and IV maintenance fluids while waiting for fetal lung fluid to clear (usually within 24 to 72 hours). Persisting tachypnoea beyond 72 hours mandates reconsideration of the diagnosis (sepsis, cardiac, surfactant deficiency), per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress and Safer Care Victoria neonatal eHandbook.

options.text: Administer endotracheal surfactant via the INSURE technique now, given the persisting FiO2 requirement at 4 hours of postnatal life
options.rationale: Surfactant therapy is for respiratory distress syndrome (preterm, ground-glass with air bronchograms, surfactant deficiency); the CXR pattern and term gestation here are inconsistent with RDS, and surfactant is not indicated for TTN, per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress.

options.text: Commence empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending blood culture results and continue the current respiratory support level
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics in a term infant with negative maternal GBS, no fever, no prolonged ROM and a CXR pattern characteristic of TTN are not routinely required; antibiotics are reserved for clinical concern for sepsis or persisting illness beyond 72 hours, per RCH CPG: Early onset sepsis.

options.text: Wean nasal high-flow off now and commence demand breastfeeding to encourage fetal lung-fluid clearance and feeding tolerance
options.rationale: Weaning support and commencing feeds while the infant remains in significant respiratory distress (RR 78, grunting, FiO2 0.30) risks aspiration and worsens work of breathing; nil by mouth and continued support are appropriate until respiratory effort settles, per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress.

options.text: Urgently transfer to a tertiary neonatal intensive care unit for elective intubation and mechanical ventilation now
options.rationale: The infant is stable on non-invasive support with adequate saturations and a normal blood gas; intubation and tertiary transfer are reserved for failing non-invasive support, persistent hypoxaemia, or alternative diagnoses, per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress.

explanation.summary: TTN results from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, classically after elective caesarean without labour. It resolves within 24 to 72 hours with supportive oxygen and CPAP if needed. Key CXR differentiators: RDS = ground-glass with air bronchograms (preterm); MAS = patchy coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation (term with meconium); pneumonia = focal consolidation; pneumothorax = hyperlucent hemithorax.
key_points: TTN: term, caesarean without labour, perihilar streaks and fissural fluid
RDS: preterm, diffuse ground-glass, surfactant deficiency
MAS: term post-dates, meconium liquor, patchy infiltrates
Pneumothorax: asymmetric breath sounds, hyperlucent on transillumination and CXR
explanation.pearls: If tachypnoea persists beyond 72 hours, reconsider the diagnosis.

stem:
A term female infant born at 39+5 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth is reviewed at 12 hours of age on the postnatal ward. Mother is a 28-year-old G2P1 who had a positive GBS rectovaginal swab at 36 weeks of gestation and was penicillin allergic with a remote history of a non-anaphylactic rash documented in her records; she received two doses of IV cefazolin intrapartum, the second dose 6 hours before delivery.

Membranes were ruptured for 20 hours. Maternal temperature peaked at 38.2 deg C during labour and white cell count was 16 x10^9/L. The baby is now lethargic with poor feeding for the last 3 hours, has had one episode of grunting respiration with transient desaturation, and looks pale and mottled. She was previously well from birth, with APGARs 9 and 9, no resuscitation required, and birthweight 3300 g.

The receiving registrar reviews her promptly and recognises the combination of maternal fever, prolonged ROM and clinical deterioration as warranting urgent septic workup and empirical antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.2 deg C axillary, HR 178 bpm, RR 70 /min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, BP 58/32 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, pale, mild grunting, mottled peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: FBC, blood culture and CRP taken; lumbar puncture deferred pending stabilisation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV cefotaxime twelve-hourly as initial empirical monotherapy
options.rationale: Cefotaxime monotherapy is not standard empirical cover for EOS in AU; synergistic penicillin plus aminoglycoside is preferred. Would be correct only with cefotaxime added to a penicillin-aminoglycoside backbone with meningitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 12-hourly plus gentamicin every 24 hours
options.rationale: Early-onset neonatal sepsis (< 72 hours) is most commonly caused by group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli; the recommended empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and RCH CPG: Early onset sepsis.

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 6-hourly plus gentamicin every 24 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin targets Staph aureus and is for late-onset sepsis with line infection, not first-line cover for EOGBS and E. coli. Would be correct for late-onset with line sepsis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: IV vancomycin 12-hourly plus cefotaxime 12-hourly
options.rationale: Vanc plus cefotaxime is for late-onset hospital-acquired sepsis with meningitis suspicion or MRSA risk; not standard for early-onset community-presenting. Would be correct in late-onset (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and observe 4-hourly for 12 hours given intrapartum cefazolin
options.rationale: Intrapartum cefazolin does not exclude sepsis with clinical deterioration; empirical antibiotics must be started. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Early-onset neonatal sepsis (less than 72 hours) is dominated by GBS and Gram-negatives, especially E. coli. Australian empirical therapy is benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) plus gentamicin. Late-onset sepsis (greater than 72 hours, particularly in the NICU) adds coagulase-negative Staphylococci, S. aureus and Gram-negatives, and typically uses flucloxacillin plus gentamicin or vancomycin in MRSA-prevalent units.
key_points: EOGBS empirical: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin
Late-onset: flucloxacillin plus gentamicin (community) or vancomycin plus gentamicin (NICU)
Add cefotaxime if meningitis is suspected or proven
Lumbar puncture should be done once the infant is stable enough
explanation.pearls: Cefazolin intrapartum prophylaxis is acceptable in non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy; clindamycin is reserved for anaphylactic allergy with proven susceptibility.

stem:
A term female infant is born at 38+4 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth with a birthweight of 2360 g (below the 3rd centile), a head circumference of 31.5 cm (below the 3rd centile), and scattered petechiae on the trunk and limbs noted on first examination. APGARs were 8 and 9 and no resuscitation was required. The mother is a 24-year-old preschool teacher who had a flu-like illness with malaise, sore throat and mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy at around 14 weeks gestation; the GP attributed it to a viral URTI and routine maternal serology was not repeated and TORCH screening was not done.

On day 2 of life, the baby has a moderately enlarged liver palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, a spleen tip palpable, mild conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and thrombocytopenia on FBC. A cranial ultrasound performed by the neonatologist shows scattered periventricular calcifications and mild ventricular dilatation, prompting paediatric infectious diseases review. Initial automated otoacoustic emission screen on day 2 is REFER bilaterally and is repeated next day with the same result.

Audiology brainstem testing is pending. The treating team obtains urine and saliva PCR samples within the first week of life to confirm the suspected diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 150 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: SGA, microcephaly, petechiae on trunk, hepatomegaly 3 cm, mild jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 62 x10^9/L, total bilirubin 110 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 35 micromol/L, ALT 90 U/L, AST 120 U/L
data_table.Imaging: Cranial ultrasound: periventricular calcifications, mild ventricular dilatation
data_table.Microbiology: Saliva and urine CMV PCR collected on day 3 of life

lead_in: Once congenital CMV is confirmed by PCR within 21 days of life, what is the single most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Oral valganciclovir twice daily for 6 months with weekly FBC/LFT and audiology
options.rationale: Symptomatic congenital CMV with end-organ involvement (microcephaly, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, intracranial calcifications, or sensorineural hearing loss) treated with oral valganciclovir 16 mg/kg BD for 6 months improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes; haematology and LFT monitoring is required because of neutropenia and hepatotoxicity, per RCH CPG: Congenital CMV and AAP Red Book.

options.text: Observe with serial audiology, no antiviral, treat only confirmed progressive hearing loss after 12 months
options.rationale: Symptomatic congenital CMV warrants prompt antiviral; delaying to 12 months misses the window when valganciclovir improves outcomes. Would never be correct in symptomatic disease (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital CMV).

options.text: Commence IV ganciclovir twice daily for 6 weeks followed by no further therapy
options.rationale: Six weeks IV ganciclovir was older regimen, superseded by 6 months oral valganciclovir (non-inferior, better neurodevelopmental/audiological). Would be correct only if oral not tolerated (Source: AAP Red Book).

options.text: CMV hyperimmune globulin infusion and arrange paediatric infectious diseases service review today
options.rationale: CMV hyperimmune globulin is not standard postnatal therapy for symptomatic congenital CMV; oral valganciclovir is recommended. Would never be correct postnatally (Source: AAP Red Book).

options.text: Treat only audiological component with hearing aid fitting after ABR; provide no antiviral therapy
options.rationale: Hearing rehab is part of care but does not replace antiviral, which improves hearing trajectories. Would never be correct alone (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Congenital CMV is the leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children. Diagnosis requires viral detection (urine or saliva PCR) within the first 21 days of life to distinguish from postnatal acquisition. Symptomatic infants (CNS, hepatic, haematological or SNHL) benefit from 6 months of oral valganciclovir, with regular FBC for neutropenia and LFTs. All affected children need longitudinal audiology because hearing loss can be late-onset or progressive.
key_points: Saliva PCR is the first-line screening test; urine PCR confirms
Diagnostic window is the first 21 days of life
Treat symptomatic disease with valganciclovir 16 mg/kg BD for 6 months
Monitor for neutropenia, anaemia and transaminitis on treatment
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic congenital CMV with isolated SNHL is an area of active research; many AU centres treat with valganciclovir, but practice varies.

stem:
A male infant is born at 38+1 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a 21-year-old G1P0 woman from a remote community who had limited antenatal care, with her first antenatal visit at 34 weeks of gestation. Routine antenatal screening at that visit returned a reactive treponemal EIA, a non-treponemal RPR titre of 1 in 64, and confirmatory TPPA positive. The mother received a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g (2.4 million units) at 35 weeks of gestation and a planned second dose was missed because she returned to her community without follow-up.

There is no documented prior syphilis treatment and contact tracing of her partner is incomplete. Repeat RPR at 38 weeks remained 1 in 64 with no fourfold drop. HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C serology were negative. At birth the baby weighs 2680 g (10th centile), has a maculopapular rash on the palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly with the liver palpable 3 cm and spleen 2 cm below the costal margins, and clear persistent rhinorrhoea (snuffles). He is alert with normal vital signs and no respiratory distress. APGARs were 8 and 9.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 144 bpm, RR 46 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: SGA, maculopapular rash palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, clear nasal discharge (snuffles), no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Infant RPR titre 1 in 128 (fourfold higher than maternal), FBC platelets 120 x10^9/L, ALT 70 U/L, long bone radiographs show metaphyseal lucencies; LP CSF VDRL pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate treatment regimen for this infant?

options.text: Single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin with outpatient RPR follow-up at 3, 6, 12 months
options.rationale: Single-dose IM benzathine is for infants with normal examination/investigations and adequately treated mothers; this infant has proven congenital syphilis. Would be correct only with normal exam/labs and treated mother (Source: Australian STI Guidelines).

options.text: Oral azithromycin daily for 14 days as macrolide cover for spirochaete infection
options.rationale: Azithromycin is not recommended for congenital syphilis (resistance, CNS penetration); parenteral penicillin is only acceptable treatment. Would never be correct (Source: Australian STI Guidelines).

options.text: Defer treatment until FTA-ABS IgM positive and CSF VDRL reported, then treat only if both confirm
options.rationale: Treatment should not be delayed pending all confirmatory tests when clinical/serological/radiological findings establish probable congenital syphilis. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin q12h first 7 days then q8h, total 10 days, monitor reaction
options.rationale: Proven or highly probable congenital syphilis (fourfold higher RPR than maternal, clinical signs, abnormal radiographs or bloods) requires 10 days of IV benzylpenicillin 30 mg/kg per dose, dosed 12-hourly in the first week and 8-hourly thereafter, per RCH CPG: Congenital syphilis and Australian STI Management Guidelines.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone once daily for 10 days as a penicillin-sparing regimen today
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone has limited data in neonatal congenital syphilis and is not first-line; penicillin desensitisation should be performed if true allergy. Would be correct only with documented severe penicillin allergy after desensitisation failure (Source: Australian STI Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Congenital syphilis is increasing in Australia, particularly in remote and Indigenous communities. Treatment of proven or highly probable disease (fourfold RPR titre difference, clinical features, abnormal CSF/long-bone films/LFTs) is IV benzylpenicillin for 10 days. Asymptomatic infants of inadequately treated mothers can sometimes receive a single IM benzathine dose if the full workup is normal.
key_points: Maternal treatment is inadequate if not benzathine penicillin, less than 4 weeks before delivery, or no fourfold drop in RPR
Long bone films show metaphysitis or periostitis; CSF VDRL confirms neurosyphilis
IV benzylpenicillin 30 mg/kg per dose for 10 days
Follow up RPR titres at 3, 6 and 12 months; expect fourfold decline
explanation.pearls: Antenatal screening in Australia now includes third-trimester syphilis serology in high-prevalence regions; a positive maternal test at 34 weeks should never be missed.

stem:
A male infant is born at 38+5 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a 32-year-old G3P2 woman on methadone 80 mg daily through pregnancy as part of an established opioid treatment program at a metropolitan tertiary centre. She has been engaged with antenatal care and the perinatal addictions team throughout pregnancy, attending all scheduled appointments and counselling sessions. There is no other substance use on serial urine drug screens, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology are negative, and she has tested negative for syphilis.

She smokes 5 cigarettes daily and uses no alcohol. Birthweight is 3120 g (50th centile) and APGARs were 8 and 9 with no resuscitation required. He is breastfeeding well with audible swallows. From 36 hours of age the midwives note increasing irritability, a high-pitched cry, frequent yawning, mild tremor with handling, loose stools that have caused excoriation around the buttocks, and a sleep period of less than one hour after a feed.

Modified Finnegan Neonatal Abstinence Scoring System scores done 4-hourly have been 9, 11 and 10 over the last 12 hours despite optimised non-pharmacological care including swaddling, low stimulation environment, demand breastfeeding, and skin-to-skin contact.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.1 deg C, HR 168 bpm, RR 60 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Tremulous with handling, mottled, hyperreflexic, no seizures, loose yellow stools, excoriation over the chin, breastfeeding established
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 3.4 mmol/L, FBC and CRP normal, maternal toxicology positive for methadone only

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch to formula feeding and continue non-pharmacological care alone without any pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is encouraged in stable methadone-maintained mothers and reduces NAS severity; switching to formula is not indicated. Would never be correct as routine (Source: RCH CPG: NAS).

options.text: Commence oral phenobarbital as monotherapy for opioid withdrawal syndrome
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is adjunctive for polysubstance exposure or refractory NAS, not first-line monotherapy for opioid NAS where opioids are the agent of choice. Would be correct as adjunct in polysubstance NAS (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Administer naloxone IM to reverse residual maternal opioid effects in the neonate
options.rationale: Naloxone is contraindicated in babies of opioid-dependent mothers (precipitates severe acute withdrawal/seizures). Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Discharge home now with community midwife follow-up and a parent-completed NAS scoring sheet
options.rationale: Persistent Finnegan 8+ requires inpatient monitoring and consideration of pharmacotherapy, not community follow-up. Would be correct only with Finnegan under 8 (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Optimise non-pharmacological care and commence oral morphine q4h titrated to Finnegan below 8
options.rationale: Three consecutive Finnegan scores at or above 8 (or two at or above 12) after maximal non-pharmacological care indicates pharmacological treatment; oral morphine is first-line for opioid-related NAS in Australia, typically starting at 0.04 to 0.05 mg/kg per dose 4-hourly, titrated to scores, per RCH CPG: Neonatal abstinence syndrome and Therapeutic Guidelines: Neonatal.

explanation.summary: NAS from in-utero opioid exposure typically presents at 24 to 72 hours for methadone (later for buprenorphine). Non-pharmacological care (rooming-in, breastfeeding if not contraindicated, swaddling, low stimulation) is first. Pharmacological treatment with oral morphine begins when modified Finnegan scores remain at or above 8 for three consecutive measurements or two at or above 12 despite optimisation.
key_points: Methadone NAS peaks at 48 to 72 hours; buprenorphine later
Breastfeeding is encouraged unless co-use of cocaine, methamphetamine or untreated HIV
Morphine titration to Finnegan less than 8; wean by 10 percent every 24 to 48 hours
Phenobarbital is adjunctive for polysubstance or refractory cases
explanation.pearls: Naloxone in a baby of an opioid-dependent mother can precipitate seizures and is contraindicated even in apparent respiratory depression.

stem:
A male infant is born at 40+1 weeks by emergency caesarean for placental abruption after a sentinel maternal collapse 25 minutes before delivery; the mother presented to a regional birthing unit with sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding and was transferred urgently to theatre when the CTG showed prolonged bradycardia at 60 bpm. Estimated time of insult to delivery is 22 minutes.

APGARs were 1 at 1 minute, 3 at 5 minutes and 5 at 10 minutes. Cord arterial gas shows pH 6.92, base deficit 18 mmol/L, and lactate 11 mmol/L. He required positive pressure ventilation from birth, intubation at 4 minutes for ongoing bradycardia, and three doses of intratracheal then intravenous adrenaline 10 microg/kg via emergency umbilical venous catheter before return of spontaneous circulation at 8 minutes.

He is now 45 minutes old, intubated on conventional ventilation in the NICU at a tertiary centre with active servo-controlled cooling preparations underway, including a cooling mattress and oesophageal probe. He has reduced spontaneous activity with intermittent generalised tonic posturing of the limbs lasting around 20 seconds, sluggish pupils that are 3 mm and equally reactive, a weak suck and absent gag, and an exaggerated Moro reflex with prolonged opening.

His axillary temperature on arrival was 36.4 deg C and the team has held active warming, allowing passive cooling, while preparing servo-controlled cooling. There is no congenital anomaly, no major birth trauma, and no clinical evidence of bleeding. The treating consultant must decide on definitive neuroprotective therapy in the next 15 minutes, well within the 6 hour therapeutic window from birth.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4 deg C axillary on arrival, HR 130 bpm post-resuscitation, mean BP 38 mmHg on dobutamine 5 microg/kg/min, SpO2 95 percent on FiO2 0.4
data_table.Examination: Reduced activity, intermittent tonic posturing, weak suck, absent gag, exaggerated Moro, hypotonia in limbs, sluggish pupils, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Cord gas: Arterial pH 6.92, base deficit 18 mmol/L, lactate 11 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Permit passive cooling to 35.5 deg C until 24 hours of age then rewarm over 12 hours
options.rationale: Passive cooling to 35.5 degC does not provide target therapeutic range; servo-controlled cooling to 33-34 is required. Would never be correct as definitive (Source: ANZNN Cooling Protocol).

options.text: Maintain strict normothermia 36.5-37.5 deg C and commence prophylactic phenobarbital loading dose
options.rationale: Normothermia is not the goal in confirmed moderate/severe HIE within 6 h; therapeutic hypothermia is evidence-based neuroprotection. Would never be correct (Source: ANZNN).

options.text: Whole-body therapeutic hypothermia 33-34 deg C for 72 hours with aEEG, rewarm 12 hours, phenobarbital for seizures
options.rationale: Term or near-term infants (at least 35 weeks gestation) within 6 hours of birth with evidence of perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia and moderate to severe encephalopathy (Sarnat 2 or 3) meet criteria for whole-body cooling to 33 to 34 deg C for 72 hours, with rewarming at 0.5 deg C per hour, per ANZNN Cooling Protocol and Cochrane: Cooling for HIE. Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is first-line for clinical seizures, per RCH CPG: Neonatal seizures.

options.text: Initiate selective head cooling with cap to scalp temperature 28 deg C for 48 hours and rapid rewarming
options.rationale: Selective head cooling is alternative but duration is 72 h not 48, and AU/NZ units predominantly use whole-body cooling. Would be correct only with selective head cooling protocol at correct duration (Source: ANZNN).

options.text: Delay cooling for 12 hours pending MRI brain, commence hypothermia only if injury confirmed
options.rationale: Cooling must start within 6 h to be neuroprotective; waiting for MRI misses the window. Would never be correct (Source: Cochrane HIE).

explanation.summary: Therapeutic hypothermia (whole-body or selective head cooling) reduces death and major neurodevelopmental disability in moderate to severe neonatal encephalopathy. Eligibility: at least 35 weeks gestation, age less than 6 hours, evidence of perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia (cord pH 7.0 or below, base deficit 16 or higher, or APGAR 5 or less at 10 minutes, or ongoing resuscitation), and clinical or aEEG evidence of moderate or severe encephalopathy (Sarnat 2 or 3). Target temperature 33 to 34 deg C for 72 hours, rewarm at 0.5 deg C per hour.
key_points: Window: less than 6 hours of birth
Sarnat 1 (mild) does not require cooling; Sarnat 2 to 3 do
Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is first-line for neonatal seizures
Side effects of cooling: sinus bradycardia, thrombocytopenia, subcutaneous fat necrosis
explanation.pearls: Apparent shivering and decreased seizure threshold during rewarming are recognised; rewarm slowly and monitor aEEG closely.

stem:
A male infant is born at 40+3 weeks after a labour complicated by thick meconium-stained liquor and a non-reassuring CTG with late decelerations in the second stage. Birthweight is 3680 g. APGARs were 4 at 1 minute and 7 at 5 minutes. He required brief positive pressure ventilation in the delivery room and is now 6 hours old in the level 3 NICU at a tertiary perinatal centre, on conventional ventilation with FiO2 0.85, peak inspiratory pressure 24 cm H2O, PEEP 6 cm H2O, mean airway pressure 14 cm H2O, and an oxygenation index of 22 calculated from an arterial blood gas with PaO2 50 mmHg.

Preductal SpO2 measured on the right hand is 92 percent and postductal SpO2 on the right foot is 78 percent, a sustained difference of 14 percent. Chest radiograph shows patchy coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation consistent with meconium aspiration. Urgent echocardiography by the neonatal cardiologist shows right-to-left shunting across the patent ductus arteriosus, tricuspid regurgitation with an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 70 mmHg, septal flattening at end-systole, and structurally normal cardiac anatomy with normal pulmonary venous return on detailed views.

Surfactant 100 mg/kg has already been given via the endotracheal tube. He has a normal capillary refill of 2 seconds on milrinone 0.5 microg/kg/min and dobutamine 5 microg/kg/min, with a mean arterial pressure of 42 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, mean BP 42 mmHg on inotropes, preductal SpO2 92 percent, postductal SpO2 78 percent, T 36.9 deg C
data_table.Ventilation: Conventional ventilation, FiO2 0.85, mean airway pressure 14 cm H2O, oxygenation index 22
data_table.Echocardiography: Right-to-left ductal shunt, RVSP 70 mmHg, septal flattening, structurally normal heart, normal pulmonary veins

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
options.rationale: PGE1 is for duct-dependent CHD; structurally normal heart with PPHN does not benefit and PGE1 can worsen pulmonary congestion. Would be correct in duct-dependent CHD (Source: RCH CPG: PPHN).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.text: Inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm via ventilator and reassess oxygenation index after 30-60 min
options.rationale: PPHN with an oxygenation index above 20 in a term infant after optimisation of ventilation and surfactant warrants inhaled nitric oxide at a starting dose of 20 ppm; if response is inadequate or OI rises despite iNO, ECMO referral should be considered, per RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn and BMJ Best Practice: PPHN.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.text: Switch to high-frequency oscillatory ventilation immediately and avoid pulmonary vasodilators today
options.rationale: HFOV is useful adjunct to recruit atelectatic lung in MAS and may combine with iNO, but does not replace pulmonary vasodilator therapy in established PPHN. Would be correct as adjunct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.text: Refer immediately for emergency ECMO without commencing iNO or HFOV trial
options.rationale: ECMO is for refractory PPHN with OI persistently over 25-40 despite iNO and HFOV; bypassing iNO at OI 22 is premature. Would be correct at OI over 25-40 despite optimised therapy (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.text: Commence oral sildenafil every 6 hours as primary pulmonary vasodilator therapy
options.rationale: Oral sildenafil is adjunctive or weaning therapy after iNO; not first-line in acute severe PPHN. Would be correct as weaning therapy (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is failure of the normal postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance, producing right-to-left shunting through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, severe hypoxaemia and preductal-postductal SpO2 difference of 10% or more. Common antecedents include meconium aspiration, severe perinatal asphyxia, pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and pulmonary hypoplasia. Diagnosis is by echocardiogram showing right-to-left shunting, elevated pulmonary pressures, and a structurally normal heart - it is critical to exclude obstructed infradiaphragmatic total anomalous pulmonary venous return before treatment, because pulmonary vasodilators worsen pulmonary oedema in TAPVR. Management ladder: optimise ventilation (lung recruitment, PEEP, mild hyperventilation), correct acidosis, maintain adequate systemic BP (vasopressor support to drive shunt left-to-right), inhaled nitric oxide 20 ppm. HFOV combines well with iNO. Sildenafil, milrinone and prostacyclin are adjuncts. ECMO is reserved for refractory disease with OI persistently above 25-40.
key_points: Differential cyanosis (preductal greater than postductal SpO2) suggests PPHN or coarctation
Echo must confirm shunt physiology and exclude structural heart disease before iNO
iNO 20 ppm is the standard starting dose
ECMO criteria: OI greater than 25 to 40 despite iNO and HFOV, plus reversible cause
explanation.pearls: In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm is first-line pulmonary vasodilator after optimising ventilation; rule out obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return on echo first - using iNO in obstructed TAPVR worsens pulmonary oedema dramatically (RCH CPG; RANZCN).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

stem:
A female infant born at 39+3 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth in a rural hospital is now 18 hours old. She had APGARs of 9 and 9 and was initially well, but the midwives have noted increasing central cyanosis over the last 2 hours, particularly with feeds. She remains alert with mild tachypnoea but no respiratory distress and no grunting.

Preductal SpO2 is 78 percent and postductal SpO2 is 76 percent, both on room air. She does not improve on 8 L/min of facemask oxygen, with preductal SpO2 rising only to 84 percent after 10 minutes. Examination reveals a soft 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge, palpable femoral pulses, no hepatomegaly, and a normal newborn examination otherwise.

A chest radiograph shows clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette. ECG shows sinus rhythm. The on-call neonatal retrieval consultant accepts the case for transfer.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 150 bpm, RR 60 /min, BP 64/40 mmHg, preductal SpO2 78 percent room air, 84 percent on 8 L/min O2
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed, alert, mild tachypnoea, 2/6 ESM at LUSE, femoral pulses palpable equally, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hyperoxia test: preductal SpO2 84 percent and PaO2 78 mmHg after 10 minutes of 100 percent oxygen; CXR clear; ECG sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management while awaiting retrieval and echocardiography?

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion and prepare for intubation given the risk of apnoea
options.rationale: A cyanotic newborn who fails the hyperoxia test (PaO2 staying below 150 mmHg or 20 kPa) is presumed to have a duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart lesion until echo proves otherwise; PGE1 0.05 microg/kg/min maintains ductal patency, with awareness of apnoea, hypotension and fever, per RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Continue facemask oxygen at 100 percent and observe for a further 4 hours before any intervention
options.rationale: Failed hyperoxia test indicates fixed right-to-left shunt; continued oxygen alone is inadequate and risks collapse if duct closes. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic CHD).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Commence inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm for presumed persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
options.rationale: iNO is for PPHN with right-to-left ductal shunting on echo and structurally normal heart; presumptive PPHN before echo may worsen ductal-dependent CHD. Would be correct after echo confirms PPHN (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus and arrange transthoracic echo in working hours next morning
options.rationale: Fluid bolus does not address the underlying shunt physiology; delaying echo risks ductal closure. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Administer indometacin IV to close any patent ductus and reduce shunting
options.rationale: Closing duct in duct-dependent lesion is catastrophic; indometacin is for haemodynamically significant PDA in preterms without duct-dependent CHD. Would be correct only in haemodynamically significant PDA without ductal-dependency (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease (transposition, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, severe Fallot, severe Ebstein) presents in the first hours to days with persistent cyanosis poorly responsive to oxygen. The hyperoxia test (PaO2 less than 150 mmHg / 20 kPa after 100 percent oxygen) supports cardiac cause. PGE1 0.05 microg/kg/min maintains the duct; lower doses (0.005 to 0.01 microg/kg/min) maintain an already open duct.
key_points: Hyperoxia test: PaO2 less than 150 mmHg suggests cardiac shunt
PGE1 side effects: apnoea (40 percent), fever, hypotension, jitteriness
Have intubation kit at bedside; transport by retrieval team
Always confirm with urgent echo before complex decisions
explanation.pearls: Differential cyanosis (preductal greater than postductal) suggests coarctation or interrupted arch; reverse differential cyanosis suggests TGA with coarctation.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease
RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

stem:
A term male infant born at 39+6 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth to a 27-year-old G1P0 woman is now 36 hours old on the postnatal ward of a tertiary maternity hospital. APGARs were 9 and 9 and the perinatal course was uncomplicated with no maternal infection, no chorioamnionitis gas (arterial pH 7.32, base deficit 4 mmol/L). Birthweight was 3380 g.

He has been breastfeeding well with audible swallows, with normal heelprick BSLs of 3.0 to 4.5 mmol/L throughout, and has had three wet nappies and meconium passed at 8 hours. At 36 hours he develops sudden onset rhythmic jerking of the right arm and right leg lasting around 90 seconds, with lip smacking and a brief apnoea with desaturation to 88 percent, followed by a similar focal motor seizure 20 minutes later.

He is now post-ictal with reduced tone in the right limbs but rouseable to handling. He has not been cooled and has no risk factors for HIE. Sodium is 138 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.25 mmol/L, magnesium 0.8 mmol/L, BSL 4.2 mmol/L, ammonia 60 micromol/L, blood gas pH 7.36 with normal lactate, and a sepsis screen including blood culture, FBC, CRP and lumbar puncture is in progress. EEG and cranial ultrasound are being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 158 bpm, RR 50 /min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, BP 70/42 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal, reduced tone right side, rouseable, no dysmorphism, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Na 138 mmol/L, ionised Ca 1.25 mmol/L, Mg 0.8 mmol/L, BSL 4.2 mmol/L, ammonia 60 micromol/L, pH 7.36, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, FBC and CRP normal pending culture

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer rectal diazepam and observe for cessation of seizure activity
options.rationale: Diazepam is not first-line in neonatal seizures and rectal route is unreliable; phenobarbital IV gives sustained levels and proven efficacy. Would never be correct in neonates (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures).

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate 10% empirically for presumed hypocalcaemic seizure
options.rationale: Ionised calcium 1.25 is within normal range; empirical calcium is not indicated and can cause arrhythmia if extravasated. Would be correct only with documented hypocalcaemia (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Commence pyridoxine 100 mg IV and withhold antiepileptic therapy until response is assessed
options.rationale: Pyridoxine is for refractory neonatal seizures unresponsive to standard antiepileptics; should not delay phenobarbital. Would be correct as second-line after phenobarbital failure (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: IV phenobarbital load, blood/urine for metabolic and infection screen, LP, urgent MRI
options.rationale: Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is first-line for confirmed neonatal seizures in Australian protocols; concurrently the cause must be sought (sepsis, metabolic, intracranial bleed or infarct, structural). MRI is preferred for parenchymal injury and stroke detection, per RCH CPG: Neonatal seizures and Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology.

options.text: Initiate therapeutic hypothermia at 33.5 deg C for 72 hours as initial seizure therapy
options.rationale: This baby does not meet cooling criteria (no perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia, normal cord gas, normal APGARs). Would be correct only with HIE features (Source: ANZNN).

explanation.summary: Causes of neonatal seizures, in rough order of frequency: HIE, ischaemic stroke and intracranial haemorrhage, infection (meningitis, encephalitis, sepsis), metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyponatraemia, inborn errors), structural, and pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. A term infant without perinatal hypoxia and with normal initial bloods should prompt urgent MRI and LP. Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is the first-line antiepileptic in Australia.
key_points: Subtle seizures (eye deviation, cycling, lip smacking, apnoea) are common in neonates
First-line: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV load, repeat 10 mg/kg up to total 40 mg/kg
Second-line: levetiracetam or phenytoin; pyridoxine for refractory
Always seek the cause: imaging, LP, metabolic screen, glucose, electrolytes, ammonia
explanation.pearls: Perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke commonly presents as focal seizures in the first 72 hours of life in a previously well term baby; MRI with DWI is diagnostic.

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 woman is reviewed in the antenatal clinic at 36 weeks gestation by the midwifery and obstetric team. She and her partner have a written birth plan declining intramuscular vitamin K for their baby because of concerns about historical claims linking IM vitamin K with childhood leukaemia. They are willing to consider oral vitamin K as a compromise but want to know the specific regimen and the residual risk.

The pregnancy has been uncomplicated with reassuring serial growth and screening, the mother is on no medications (no anticonvulsants, antibiotics, rifampicin, or anticoagulants), and there are no risk factors for fetal coagulopathy or maternal liver disease. Their first child received IM vitamin K and had no problems. They intend to exclusively breastfeed and the booking is for a planned vaginal birth at 39 weeks. They specifically ask you to compare the oral and IM regimens by Australian guidance and have read that the leukaemia link has been refuted.

data_table.Maternal history: G2P1, no anticoagulants, no antiepileptics, no rifampicin, no significant medical history
data_table.Plan: Booked for vaginal birth at 39 weeks if uncomplicated

lead_in: Which counselling and recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: IM vitamin K 1 mg single dose at birth first-line; if declined, oral 1 mg at birth, day 3-5, and 4 weeks with residual-risk counselling
options.rationale: NHMRC and RCH guidance recommends single-dose IM vitamin K 1 mg at birth as the most reliable prophylaxis against classical and late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB). When IM is declined, the recommended oral alternative is THREE 1 mg oral doses (birth, day 3 to 5, and 4 weeks) - not a single oral dose - with documented informed consent including the higher residual late VKDB risk, particularly with exclusive breastfeeding and undetected cholestasis, per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis and NHMRC Statement on Vitamin K.

options.text: Recommend a single oral 1 mg vitamin K dose given at birth as an equivalent alternative to IM with comparable late-VKDB protection
options.rationale: A single oral dose does not provide adequate protection against late VKDB; the recommended oral regimen requires three 1 mg doses (birth, day 3 to 5, 4 weeks), per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis.

options.text: Recommend no vitamin K prophylaxis at all, since the historical leukaemia link is refuted and modern Australian background bleeding risk is negligible
options.rationale: Vitamin K is required to prevent classical and late VKDB; the refutation of the leukaemia link does not eliminate the need for prophylaxis, and declining is not equivalent to safe practice, per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis and NHMRC Statement on Vitamin K.

options.text: Recommend maternal oral vitamin K 20 mg daily from 36 weeks until delivery as a substitute for any neonatal prophylaxis given at birth
options.rationale: Maternal supplementation does not provide adequate neonatal vitamin K stores or protect against late VKDB and is not a recommended substitute, per NHMRC Statement on Vitamin K.

options.text: Defer the decision until after delivery so the family can meet the baby and decide with the postnatal midwife in the hours after birth
options.rationale: Antenatal informed consent allows the family to consider evidence and ask questions in a low-pressure setting; deferring this discussion to the immediate postnatal period is not best practice and risks unprepared decision-making, per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis.

explanation.summary: Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (now vitamin K deficiency bleeding, VKDB) is preventable with prophylaxis. Classical VKDB occurs in days 1 to 7; late VKDB occurs from 2 weeks to 6 months and presents with intracranial haemorrhage in exclusively breastfed infants. IM vitamin K 1 mg as a single dose at birth is the gold standard; the oral alternative is 1 mg at birth, day 3 to 5, and 4 weeks. The historical leukaemia link from the 1990s has been refuted by multiple subsequent studies.
key_points: IM 1 mg single dose at birth is first-line
Oral regimen: 1 mg at birth, day 3 to 5, and 4 weeks; higher residual late VKDB risk
Late VKDB risk particularly in cholestasis (biliary atresia) and exclusive breastfeeding
Document consent process when families decline
explanation.pearls: If a baby on oral vitamin K develops cholestatic jaundice, switch to IM immediately.

stem:
A male infant is born at 32+0 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a 28-year-old G1P0 woman with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 5 days before delivery. She was admitted for monitoring, received prophylactic erythromycin and a course of antenatal corticosteroids; specifically, two doses of antenatal betamethasone with the second dose 48 hours before delivery, and a single dose of magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection commenced 4 hours before delivery.

There was no maternal fever, the CRP remained normal, and the white cell count was 11 x10^9/L pre-delivery. APGARs were 7 and 8 with brief CPAP via T-piece in the delivery room. Birthweight is 1640 g (50th centile for gestation). He is transferred to the level 3 NICU at 10 minutes of age. From birth he has had moderate work of breathing with intercostal recession, mild grunting, and SpO2 of 89 percent in room air.

He is now on nasal CPAP 7 cm H2O with FiO2 0.35 delivered via short binasal prongs, has mild grunting that is gradually improving, and is haemodynamically stable with a mean BP of 38 mmHg. The team prepares to administer surfactant in the next 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 160 bpm, RR 65 /min on CPAP, SpO2 92 percent on FiO2 0.35, BP mean 38 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild grunting and intercostal recession, equal air entry, capillary refill 2 seconds, no peripheral cyanosis
data_table.Antenatal: Single course antenatal betamethasone 48 hours pre-delivery, MgSO4 for neuroprotection, no maternal fever, no chorioamnionitis

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate surfactant administration strategy in this infant?

options.text: Continue CPAP without surfactant unless FiO2 rises above 0.6 or work of breathing worsens
options.rationale: AU threshold for surfactant in preterm RDS is sustained FiO2 over 0.3 (under 28 weeks) or 0.3-0.4 (28-32 weeks); ignoring 0.35 in 32-weeker risks worsening RDS. Would be correct only with FiO2 under threshold (Source: RCH CPG: Surfactant).

options.text: Intubate, give surfactant, and continue mechanical ventilation for at least the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Prolonged ventilation after surfactant increases BPD risk in spontaneously breathing preterm; less invasive strategy preferred. Would be correct only in apnoea or failed CPAP (Source: ANZNN).

options.text: Repeat a second course of antenatal corticosteroid postnatally as IM betamethasone to the infant to enhance lung maturation
options.rationale: Postnatal corticosteroids in this context are inappropriate; antenatal steroids must be given to mother pre-delivery, and postnatal dexamethasone is for ventilator-dependent infants at risk of BPD. Would never be correct here (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Give nebulised surfactant via the CPAP circuit over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Nebulised surfactant remains investigational and not recommended outside trials in AU; tracheal delivery is required for proven efficacy. Would never be correct (Source: RCH CPG).

options.text: Continue CPAP and give surfactant via thin catheter using LISA technique with spontaneous breathing
options.rationale: In a preterm infant breathing spontaneously on CPAP, LISA (also called MIST in some AU centres) allows surfactant administration via a thin tracheal catheter while CPAP and spontaneous breathing continue, and reduces the rate of mechanical ventilation and BPD compared with INSURE, per RCH CPG: Surfactant administration and Cochrane: LISA versus INSURE.

explanation.summary: Preterm RDS is managed primarily with antenatal corticosteroids, early CPAP from delivery room, and surfactant delivered to those needing it. LISA delivers surfactant via a thin catheter while the infant continues spontaneous breathing on CPAP, reducing mechanical ventilation and bronchopulmonary dysplasia compared with INSURE (intubate, surfactant, extubate). Threshold for surfactant is typically FiO2 sustained above 0.3 (less than 28 weeks) or 0.3 to 0.4 (28 to 32 weeks).
key_points: Antenatal betamethasone halves RDS, IVH and neonatal mortality
Early CPAP at 6 to 8 cm H2O is first-line respiratory support
LISA / MIST reduces BPD versus INSURE in spontaneously breathing infants
Surfactant dose: poractant alfa 200 mg/kg initial; beractant 100 mg/kg
explanation.pearls: A second course of antenatal corticosteroids is considered if more than 7 to 14 days have elapsed and delivery remains likely within 7 days at gestation under 32 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Roseola - recognition of post-defervescence rash pattern
stem:
A 14-month-old fully immunised boy is reviewed in suburban general practice after three days of high fever to 39.7 deg C that resolved overnight. He is now afebrile and playful with a blanching, maculopapular, trunk-predominant rash that appeared this morning, sparing face, palms and soles. He has had no cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, oral lesions, or diarrhoea. There is no lymphadenopathy and no meningism, capillary refill is under two seconds, and mucous membranes are moist.

He attends family daycare, where a 4-year-old sibling of another child has confirmed measles diagnosed yesterday by the public health unit and other children with similar fever-then-rash presentations have been seen at this practice in the past fortnight. The MMR vaccine is due at 18 months and has not yet been given. There is no household member who is immunocompromised or pregnant. The mother asks about diagnosis, time off daycare, and whether her son needs anything more.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C (previously 39.7), HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Blanching pink maculopapular rash on trunk/neck, sparing face/palms/soles; no Koplik spots, no conjunctivitis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Immunisations: Up to date for age (MMR not yet due)

lead_in: Which combination of diagnosis and exclusion advice is most appropriate?

options.text: Roseola infantum; he may return to family daycare once afebrile and well, with no formal childcare exclusion period required under Australian guidance
options.rationale: Fever-then-rash in a well 6 to 24-month-old (trunk-predominant blanching rash after defervescence) is classical roseola (HHV-6). Under NHMRC Staying Healthy and RCH guidance, roseola does not require formal childcare exclusion; exclusion ends once the child is afebrile and well, per NHMRC Staying Healthy and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

options.text: Measles given the daycare contact; exclude from family daycare for 4 days from rash onset and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Measles requires fever PLUS cough, coryza or conjunctivitis with a cephalocaudal rash, none of which are present here; the well, post-defervescence trunk-predominant rash is roseola. Notification is required for measles but is not appropriate here, per NCIRS: Measles fact sheet and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

options.text: Rubella; exclude from family daycare for 7 days from rash onset and arrange confirmatory serology before any return
options.rationale: Rubella shows tender suboccipital and post-auricular lymphadenopathy with a face-first cephalocaudal rash, not the trunk-predominant post-defervescence pattern seen here, per RCH CPG: Rubella.

options.text: Scarlet fever; commence oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days and exclude from daycare for 24 hours after starting antibiotics
options.rationale: Scarlet fever has a sandpaper-textured rash with strawberry tongue, exudative pharyngitis and circumoral pallor; none are present and antibiotics are not indicated, per eTG: Group A streptococcal infection.

options.text: Roseola infantum; commence oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days and exclude from daycare for the duration of treatment
options.rationale: Roseola is self-limiting; antivirals are not indicated in immunocompetent infants, and there is no daycare-exclusion requirement beyond being afebrile and well, per RCH CPG: Viral exanthems and NHMRC Staying Healthy.

explanation.summary: Roseola (HHV-6) classically causes 3 to 5 days of high fever in a well-appearing 6 to 24-month-old, with a blanching trunk-predominant rash erupting AS the fever resolves (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
key_points: Fever-then-rash pattern is the defining clinical clue (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
Self-limiting; no specific treatment beyond antipyresis and reassurance (StatPearls: Roseola).
Febrile convulsions occur in around 10 to 15% of cases during the fever phase (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
explanation.pearls: If a well child has a rash AS the fever breaks, think roseola; if the rash appears DURING fever with cough/coryza/conjunctivitis, think measles.

subtopic_detail: Measles - prodrome and Koplik spots before rash onset
stem:
A 3-year-old unimmunised boy is brought to a regional Victorian emergency department with four days of fever to 39.8 deg C, barking moist cough, profuse coryza, and red watery photophobic eyes. He returned 10 days ago from a 3-week family trip to a rural province in Vietnam. He has no skin rash yet. On examination he is miserable with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, clear nasal discharge, and several 1 to 2 mm bluish-white papules on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa opposite the second molars.

Temperature 39.6 deg C, HR 138, RR 32, SpO2 97 percent room air. He has no rash, no lymphadenopathy, chest is clear, and he is haemodynamically stable. He is currently in an open paediatric ED bay alongside other waiting children, including a 6-month-old infant and a pregnant accompanying parent. You strongly suspect measles based on Koplik spots and the three Cs.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 deg C, HR 138, RR 32, SpO2 97% RA, BP 95/55
data_table.Examination: Bilateral conjunctivitis, coryza, productive cough, Koplik spots on buccal mucosa; no skin rash yet
data_table.History: Unimmunised; recent travel from Vietnam 10 days ago
data_table.Investigations: Pending

lead_in: Which next step is most appropriate before laboratory confirmation?

options.text: Move him to a negative-pressure single room with airborne and contact precautions, and phone the public health unit to begin notification now
options.rationale: Measles is a notifiable disease in all Australian jurisdictions and clinical suspicion (especially with Koplik spots and an epidemiological link) triggers immediate isolation in a negative-pressure room with airborne and contact precautions and same-day phone notification to the public health unit BEFORE laboratory confirmation, to enable rapid contact tracing and PEP within the windows (MMR within 72 h, NHIG within 7 days), per CDNA: Measles SoNG and NCIRS: Measles fact sheet.

options.text: Send measles IgM and PCR (throat swab and urine) and await laboratory confirmation before notifying public health or isolating
options.rationale: Waiting for laboratory confirmation before isolation and notification breaches Australian public health practice and delays contact tracing and post-exposure prophylaxis for susceptible contacts (the infant and pregnant parent in the bay), per CDNA: Measles SoNG.

options.text: Place him in a standard single room with droplet precautions only and await senior review before any notification action
options.rationale: Measles is airborne; droplet precautions alone are inadequate and a negative-pressure room with N95 respirator entry is required, per CDNA: Measles SoNG.

options.text: Administer stat MMR vaccine and oral vitamin A 200 000 IU now, then discharge with isolation advice and review tomorrow
options.rationale: MMR is contraindicated in active suspected measles infection; vitamin A is recommended in confirmed cases of severe measles but does not replace isolation, notification, and inpatient assessment, and discharge before notification is unsafe, per WHO Measles guidelines and CDNA: Measles SoNG.

options.text: Commence empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and admit for full sepsis workup including lumbar puncture before any isolation measures
options.rationale: The clinical picture is classical measles, not bacterial sepsis or meningitis; antibiotics and LP are not indicated and isolation plus notification take priority, per RCH CPG: Febrile child and CDNA: Measles SoNG.

explanation.summary: Koplik spots, found on the buccal mucosa 1 to 2 days before rash onset, are pathognomonic for measles and allow earlier diagnosis and public health action before the typical caudal-spreading exanthem appears (NCIRS: Measles fact sheet).
key_points: Measles prodrome: fever + cough + coryza + conjunctivitis (the three Cs) (NCIRS: Measles).
Koplik spots appear 1 to 2 days BEFORE the rash (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
Rash starts at the hairline/face and spreads caudally over 3 days (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
Notifiable disease - urgent public health notification required at clinical suspicion (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
explanation.pearls: Suspect-then-isolate-then-test: place the child in a negative pressure single room with airborne and contact precautions and phone the public health unit before laboratory confirmation.

subtopic_detail: Measles - public health management and contact prophylaxis
stem:
A 4-year-old unimmunised child has measles confirmed on PCR after a maculopapular rash spread from the face caudally over 24 hours. He had three days of fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis before the rash, and Koplik spots were identified at the GP visit the day before rash onset. He attended a community playgroup on the day before his rash appeared and the morning of rash onset, while infectious.

The public health unit has been notified and is contacting the playgroup register. Among the playgroup contacts identified within the 4 hours before to 4 days after his rash, several need urgent post-exposure management decisions. They include: a 5-month-old infant whose mother is rubella-immune but has no documented measles history or serology; a 13-month-old child who received a single dose of MMR five days ago; a 35-year-old pregnant playgroup helper at 22 weeks gestation with no documented measles immunity and a negative measles IgG on urgent serology done this morning; a 7-year-old child with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in week 2 of induction chemotherapy and currently neutropenic; and a 30-year-old playgroup leader born in 1992 with two documented MMR doses on her workplace immunisation record.

data_table.Exposure window: 4 hours before prodrome to 4 days after rash onset (still infectious)
data_table.Contacts requiring decision: 5-month infant; 13-month with one MMR five days ago; pregnant 22-week non-immune helper; 7-year-old on induction chemo for ALL; 30-year-old with 2x MMR documented
data_table.Time since exposure: Within 72 hours for all listed contacts

lead_in: Which post-exposure action for one of the listed playgroup contacts is the single most appropriate?

options.text: Give the 5-month-old infant intramuscular MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure
options.rationale: MMR is not used under 6 months because maternal antibody blunts the immune response and the vaccine is unreliable in this window; this infant should instead receive NHIG within 6 days. The action stated here would expose the infant to a live vaccine without conferring protection (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

options.text: Give the 13-month-old who had one MMR five days ago an additional MMR dose now as post-exposure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Seroconversion takes around two weeks after a dose, so the MMR given five days ago is unlikely to be protective at this exposure - but a second early dose is not the standard PEP either; the child is over 12 months with a documented dose and is observed for prodrome with the routine 18-month MMR retained on schedule (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

options.text: Give the pregnant 22-week non-immune playgroup helper NHIG intramuscularly within 6 days of exposure
options.rationale: MMR is a live vaccine and contraindicated in pregnancy. A non-immune pregnant contact within 6 days of exposure receives NHIG to attenuate or prevent maternal measles and its severe pregnancy complications (pneumonitis, prematurity, miscarriage). Her negative IgG on urgent serology confirms susceptibility (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles; CDNA: Measles SoNG).

options.text: Give the 7-year-old with ALL on induction chemotherapy intramuscular MMR within 72 hours of exposure
options.rationale: MMR is a live vaccine and contraindicated in severe immunocompromise including induction chemotherapy; the action stated would carry vaccine-strain dissemination risk in a profoundly neutropenic child. The correct PEP for this contact is NHIG within 6 days (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

options.text: Give the 30-year-old playgroup leader with two documented MMR doses a third MMR dose as a precautionary booster
options.rationale: Two documented MMR doses meet the Australian definition of presumptive immunity; no further dose or NHIG is indicated. The action stated would be over-treatment of an already immune contact (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

explanation.summary: For susceptible measles contacts, MMR within 72 hours is preferred in those eligible for live vaccine, but NHIG within 6 days is indicated in those for whom live vaccine is contraindicated: infants under 6 months, pregnant non-immune contacts, and severely immunocompromised patients (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).
key_points: MMR within 72h of exposure for eligible non-immune contacts (AIH: Measles).
NHIG within 6 days for pregnant non-immune, infants <6 months, severely immunocompromised (AIH: Measles).
Two documented MMR doses count as presumptive immunity in Australia (AIH: Measles).
Measles is notifiable - phone the public health unit on clinical suspicion (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
explanation.pearls: Pregnant non-immune contacts get NHIG, never MMR - live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is in week 3 of induction chemotherapy for high-risk B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia at a tertiary paediatric oncology centre. He shared a 1-hour indoor classroom session in the day hospital school room with another child who has since been confirmed by PCR to have early varicella, with a vesicular rash that had been present for less than 24 hours during the session.

The exposure was 36 hours ago. The boy has had no past episode of clinical varicella, no varicella vaccination on his record (his older sibling refused MMRV at 18 months for the family on philosophical grounds and the patient was diagnosed before catch-up), and his pre-treatment baseline varicella IgG was negative on serology drawn before induction. He is currently profoundly neutropenic with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.4 x 10^9/L, has no rash, no fever, and feels well.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 96, RR 20, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Well; no rash, no vesicles, no oral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.4 x 10^9/L, pre-chemo varicella IgG negative
data_table.History: ALL induction week 3; significant face-to-face exposure 36 hours ago to a child with early varicella

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine within 72 hours of exposure as post-exposure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Varicella vaccine is live attenuated and CONTRAINDICATED in severely immunocompromised including those on induction chemo. Would be correct only in immunocompetent contacts (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Administer zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG/VZIG) intramuscularly within 96 hours of exposure as post-exposure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Severely immunocompromised susceptible contacts (varicella IgG negative, no prior infection or vaccination) with a significant exposure should receive ZIG within 96 hours (preferably as soon as possible, but the AIH allows extension up to 10 days in some circumstances) to attenuate or prevent disseminated varicella (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella).

options.text: Commence prophylactic oral valaciclovir from day 7 to day 21 post-exposure
options.rationale: Antiviral prophylaxis (days 7-14) is adjunct or alternative when ZIG unavailable; ZIG is preferred first-line. Would be correct when ZIG unavailable (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Reassurance and observation, treating with intravenous aciclovir only if a rash develops
options.rationale: Waiting for the rash forgoes the proven benefit of ZIG given before viraemia; disseminated varicella in immunocompromised carries significant mortality. Would never be correct (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Send urgent varicella IgG and IgM and decide on prophylaxis based on the result
options.rationale: Pre-treatment varicella IgG was negative documenting susceptibility; waiting for repeat serology delays ZIG and reduces effectiveness. Would never be correct (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Severely immunocompromised susceptible children with significant varicella exposure should receive ZIG (zoster immunoglobulin) as soon as possible, ideally within 96 hours; live varicella vaccine is contraindicated in this group (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella).
key_points: Significant exposure = household OR >=1 hour indoor face-to-face OR shared room OR substantial hospital contact (AIH: Varicella).
Susceptible = no past disease, no vaccination, and seronegative if tested (AIH: Varicella).
ZIG first-line in immunocompromised, neonates, and non-immune pregnant women (AIH: Varicella).
Antiviral prophylaxis day 7 to 14 is an adjunct/alternative when ZIG unavailable (AIH: Varicella).
explanation.pearls: Neonates born to mothers who develop varicella from 7 days before to 2 days after delivery also need ZIG - very high mortality without it.

subtopic_detail: Meningococcal disease - non-blanching rash recognition vs HSP
stem:
A 2-year-old fully immunised girl is brought to a regional emergency department by ambulance after her parents noticed a rapidly spreading rash. Six hours ago she became unwell with fever and irritability; she has now had two episodes of non-bilious vomiting and is increasingly drowsy and floppy. On examination she is grey, mottled, and lethargic with poor central tone. Temperature 38.9 deg C, heart rate 168, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 96% on room air, blood pressure 78/40, capillary refill 5 seconds peripherally and 4 seconds centrally.

There are scattered non-blanching petechiae and several larger irregular purpuric lesions on the trunk, abdomen and proximal limbs that have spread visibly while in the resuscitation cubicle over the last 10 minutes. Her neck is supple but she cries when picked up and her anterior fontanelle is no longer palpable. No focal neurology. She has had no recent URTI, no arthritisay. Her routine immunisations including MenB and MenACWY are up to date as confirmed on the Australian Immunisation Register printout her parents have brought.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 deg C, HR 168, RR 44, SpO2 96% RA, BP 78/40, CRT 5 sec
data_table.Examination: Grey, mottled, drowsy; spreading non-blanching purpuric rash on trunk and proximal limbs
data_table.History: 6h illness; fully immunised including MenB and MenACWY
data_table.Investigations: Pending

lead_in: Which is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Obtain IV or IO access and give IV ceftriaxone without delay
options.rationale: This is meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise - rapidly spreading non-blanching rash with shock. Empirical IV (or IO if access difficult) ceftriaxone should be given as soon as access is obtained, ideally after cultures but NEVER delayed for them; fluid resuscitation, ABC support, and ICU/retrieval activation run in parallel (RCH CPG: Meningococcal infection; ANZCOR/APLS).

options.text: Arrange urgent CT head and then lumbar puncture given the drowsiness and rash
options.rationale: LP is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, coagulopathy, or rapidly evolving purpura; CT-then-LP delays the only intervention that changes outcome. Would be correct only in stable patient with normal coags (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Defer antibiotics until blood cultures are processed to maximise diagnostic yield from cultures
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcal sepsis worsens mortality; cultures drawn only if access rapid, antibiotics must NOT wait. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence IV hydrocortisone before antibiotics to pre-treat Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal failure
options.rationale: Routine steroids are not the immediate priority and do not replace urgent antibiotics; stress-dose steroids may be considered later for refractory shock. Would be correct only later as adjunct in refractory shock (Source: ANZICS).

options.text: Reassess in 30 minutes after antipyretics as her current immunisations make invasive bacterial illness unlikely
options.rationale: Even fully immunised children can develop IMD from non-vaccine strains or vaccine failure; the picture mandates immediate empirical therapy. Would never be correct (Source: CDNA IMD SoNG).

explanation.summary: Suspected meningococcal septicaemia mandates immediate IV/IO ceftriaxone alongside fluid resuscitation - antibiotics must not be delayed by imaging or laboratory workup. Cultures are taken if access is fast; otherwise antibiotics go first (RCH CPG: Meningococcal infection).
key_points: Spreading non-blanching rash + shock = meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise (RCH: Meningococcal infection).
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV/IO without delay (eTG: Meningococcal disease).
Activate paediatric retrieval (NETS or state equivalent) early (RCH: Meningococcal infection).
Antibiotic prophylaxis for household and intimate contacts via public health unit (CDNA: Meningococcal SoNG).
explanation.pearls: If the petechiae are spreading WHILE you watch, you have minutes - antibiotics now, lines + fluids in parallel, retrieval call goes in before the third bolus.

subtopic_detail: Scarlet fever - recognition and antibiotic selection
stem:
A 7-year-old previously well Aboriginal girl from a remote community in the Northern Territory is reviewed during a paediatric outreach clinic in her community with a 2-day history of fever, sore throat and a rash that began today on the neck and chest before spreading to the trunk. She has no cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis. Temperature 38.6 deg C, HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent room air, capillary refill under two seconds.

On examination she has a fine, blanching, erythematous papular eruption with a sandpaper texture accentuated in the antecubital and inguinal flexures, prominent fungiform papillae against a coated tongue, exudative tonsillitis, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and circumoral pallor. She has no known drug allergies, is fully immunised, has no history of acute rheumatic fever, and the family confirms she will be staying in community for at least the next two weeks. Throat swab for group A streptococcus has been collected. There is no current penicillin shortage in the community pharmacy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 deg C, HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Sandpaper rash with flexural accentuation, strawberry tongue, exudative tonsillitis, tender cervical nodes, circumoral pallor
data_table.History: No allergies; non-remote setting; fully immunised

lead_in: Which first-line antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg (up to 500 mg) twice daily for 10 days, with community follow-up at completion
options.rationale: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days is first-line in non-high-ARF-risk Australian settings, but in high-ARF-risk settings (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in remote/regional areas, Maori and Pacific children) the preferred regimen is a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin to ensure compliance and prevent acute rheumatic fever, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline and eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

options.text: Single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin (900 mg if 20 kg or more, 450 mg if under 20 kg) administered now
options.rationale: In an Aboriginal child from a high-ARF-risk remote setting with clinical scarlet fever (group A streptococcal pharyngitis with toxin-mediated exanthem), a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is the recommended Australian regimen to guarantee adherence and reduce ARF and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis risk, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline and eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg once daily for 10 days as a more palatable equivalent to first-line oral penicillin
options.rationale: Amoxicillin is acceptable where penicillin V is unpalatable, but in high-ARF-risk settings an IM regimen is preferred to remove adherence as a failure mode, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline.

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg (up to 1 g) twice daily for 10 days as initial therapy
options.rationale: Cefalexin is broader-spectrum than necessary and reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy; it is not first-line in either standard or high-ARF-risk Australian settings, per eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

options.text: Symptomatic care with paracetamol and reassurance, with antibiotics only if the throat swab returns positive in 48 hours
options.rationale: Clinical scarlet fever with high ARF risk warrants immediate empirical antibiotics; awaiting culture results delays prevention of ARF and is not consistent with Australian guidance, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline.

explanation.summary: Scarlet fever is group A streptococcal pharyngitis plus a toxin-mediated sandpaper-textured rash with strawberry tongue. First-line in Australia is phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg (max 500 mg) BD for 10 days (eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis).
key_points: Sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue + flexural accentuation + circumoral pallor = scarlet fever (RCH: GAS).
First-line: penicillin V 10 days (eTG).
Severe penicillin allergy: macrolide (eTG).
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in high-ARF-risk settings have a different regimen and stricter follow-up (RHDAustralia).
explanation.pearls: Desquamation of fingertips and palms 1 to 2 weeks after the rash is a late clue if you missed the initial illness.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Group A streptococcal disease

subtopic_detail: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease - recognition and discrimination from HSV
stem:
A 22-month-old fully immunised girl is reviewed in general practice with three days of low-grade fever to 38.4 deg C, drooling, and reduced oral intake. Her mother noticed today that she has spots on her hands, feet, and inside her mouth. On examination she is alert and well-perfused. Temperature 37.6 deg C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent room air.

There are shallow ulcers on the tongue, buccal mucosa, and posterior pharynx, and several small grey-roofed oval vesicles on an erythematous base on the palms, soles, and dorsa of the hands and feet. There is no lip clustering, no gingival inflammation, and no lymphadenopathy. The nappy area shows a few similar vesicles. Mucous membranes are slightly dry but she has just taken 50 mL of cold water in clinic.

There is a known outbreak of vesicular illness at her childcare centre that includes one recent admission to the local children's hospital. You diagnose hand-foot-and-mouth disease. Her mother asks what to do about childcare attendance and what warning signs would warrant urgent return.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 deg C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Oval grey-roofed vesicles on palms/soles/dorsa of hands and feet, shallow oral ulcers including posterior pharynx, sparse nappy-area lesions
data_table.History: Childcare outbreak; fully immunised; no prior cold sores

lead_in: Which combination of childcare exclusion advice and red-flag escalation criteria is most appropriate?

options.text: Exclude from childcare until all blisters have dried; return urgently for vomiting, ataxia, myoclonus, or reduced wet nappies
options.rationale: Australian guidance (NHMRC Staying Healthy, RCH) recommends childcare exclusion until all blisters have dried (not just until afebrile). Red flags for severe enterovirus disease (especially EV71) include neurological signs (ataxia, myoclonus, irritability), persistent high fever beyond 3 days, persistent vomiting, and inability to maintain hydration, all of which warrant urgent reassessment, per NHMRC Staying Healthy and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

options.text: Exclude from childcare only until afebrile for 24 hours, then return regardless of any remaining skin lesions
options.rationale: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease requires exclusion until blisters have dried under NHMRC Staying Healthy, not merely until afebrile; the lesions remain shedding virus, per NHMRC Staying Healthy.

options.text: No childcare exclusion required as HFMD is self-limiting; return whenever the child is willing and able
options.rationale: Australian public health guidance does specify formal exclusion until blisters dry for hand-foot-and-mouth disease; no-exclusion advice is incorrect, per NHMRC Staying Healthy.

options.text: Commence oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days and exclude from childcare for the duration of treatment
options.rationale: Aciclovir has no role in enteroviral HFMD; the diagnosis is not herpes simplex and antivirals are not indicated, per eTG: Herpes simplex and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

options.text: Admit now for IV fluids and serial neurological observations, given the childcare outbreak link to EV71
options.rationale: She is clinically well, alert, perfused, and tolerating oral fluids in clinic; routine admission is not required and supportive outpatient care with explicit red-flag advice is appropriate, per RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

explanation.summary: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is an enteroviral infection (often coxsackie A16, less commonly EV71) causing low-grade fever, posterior-predominant oral ulcers and oval vesicles on palms, soles, and dorsa of hands/feet, often with nappy-area involvement in toddlers (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
key_points: Self-limiting; supportive care with hydration and analgesia (RCH: Viral exanthems).
Childcare exclusion: until all blisters have dried (NHMRC Staying Healthy).
EV71 strain can cause severe complications including aseptic meningitis, brainstem encephalitis, and acute flaccid paralysis (StatPearls: HFMD).
Differentiate from HSV gingivostomatitis: HSV = anterior/gingival, ill child, no acral lesions; HFMD = posterior oropharynx, acral lesions (RCH: Viral exanthems).
explanation.pearls: If a toddler refuses to drink because of mouth pain, accept dehydration is the real risk and admit for IV fluids - it is the only common reason HFMD comes back to ED.

subtopic_detail: Pregnant contact of parvovirus B19 - obstetric implications
stem:
A 32-year-old early childhood teacher at 18 weeks of her second pregnancy attends her GP after multiple confirmed cases of erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek) in the kindergarten class she teaches over the past fortnight.
